full_text:
Pro Football Hall of Famer Darrelle Revis attends a game between the New York Jets and the Los Angeles Chargers in 2023 at MetLife Stadium. Revis, 41, has expressed a desire to get into coaching. Jim McIsaac / Getty Images
Darrelle Revis was a first-ballot Pro Football Hall of Fame cornerback. Yet when he and undrafted safety Jim Leonhard played together with the New York Jets, he never viewed Leonhard as a sidekick.
Revis, in fact, still considers the Buffalo Bills’ new defensive coordinator a lead dog. So much so that Revis would love to join Leonhard’s staff right now.
“I’m not joking at all,” Revis said by phone from Canton, Ohio. “I’ve always loved the game, and I’ve always loved playing with Jim.”
Revis dropped what he was doing during Hall of Fame induction weekend to talk about his deep admiration. While voicing his praise, an unexpected job pitch materialized.
But that’s just part of the serendipity.
Revis, 41, explained that football is pulling at him again. He said retirement has been eventful, with commercial real estate and venture capital investments, but no man is an island — not even Revis Island. He’s an empty nester now that his daughter is a junior nursing student at the University of Kentucky and his son is a freshman business major and defensive back at Mercyhurst University.
That’s Mercyhurst. In Erie, Pa. About 85 miles from Highmark Stadium.
“I think Jim will be a future head coach,” Revis said. “Tell him if he needs a secondary coach to give me a call. Maybe this is my interview where I tell Jim that if he ever needs help, to keep me at the top of the list.”
Informed Saturday night about Revis’ offer, Leonhard grinned, unfolded a practice call sheet from his pocket and jotted down Revis’ phone number.
Bills coach Joe Brady’s staff features three coordinators and 21 assistants. It includes secondary coach Joe Danna, who worked with Revis as the Jets’ defensive backs coach in 2015 and 2016, and cornerbacks coach Jay Valai.
NFL staffs have no size limit.
Leonhard and Revis first hooked up in 2009, when the Jets named Rex Ryan head coach. Leonhard spent the previous season with the Baltimore Ravens, turning a long-shot tryout into a critical role on Ryan’s heralded defense.
Baltimore was so vicious that Revis knew Leonhard possessed the proper bona fides. Leonhard started 16 games, including all three in the postseason, lined up with safety Ed Reed and behind alpha linebacker Ray Lewis, members of the NFL’s 100th anniversary team.
“You have a guy like Ray Lewis at linebacker, and the way that he demands the same type of approach to the game from everybody,” Revis said. “That’s what Jim did for us.
“When you replay your career and remember those flashbacks in the huddle and just going to war with your teammates, you always knew Jim had your back.”
Their first season together was the best of Leonhard’s career and arguably Revis’ best, too. That’s when the Revis Island nickname emerged. The Jets gave up the fewest points, fewest yards per play, fewest yards per pass attempt and fourth-fewest rushing yards per carry. Opposing quarterbacks posted a 58.8 passer rating with eight touchdown passes, 17 interceptions and 32 sacks.
Leonhard started every game, recording one interception, five breakups, 2 1/2 sacks, nine tackles for losses and a forced fumble. Revis earned his first All-Pro selection and was Defensive Player of the Year runner-up with a career-high six interceptions and an NFL-record 31 breakups.
That postseason, New York made the first of its back-to-back AFC Championship Games. In three road games, Leonhard intercepted a pass, forced two fumbles and recovered another, while Revis intercepted a pair.
“I really loved playing with him,” Revis said. “His intellect, his football IQ, the way he communicated, he was just very tuned in and detailed.”
Revis is convinced those traits will translate into Leonhard being a successful NFL coordinator and future head coach — and maybe Revis’ boss.
“I understand the coaching life and how guys have to relocate and move certain places,” Revis said, “but the kids are out of the house. I have time and opportunity to do other things.”
Revis splits time between South Florida and New York. Would he be willing to grind out an assistant coach’s lifestyle in suburban Buffalo?
“I wouldn’t mind,” Revis said with a laugh. “They have a new stadium, and it’s football, man. Wherever I need to be, I’ll go.”
Jayden Revis will play defensive back at Mercyhurst. He also was a receiver and kick returner at Moon Area High in the Pittsburgh area. Darrelle is from nearby Aliquippa, Pa., and was an All-American at Pitt.
Granted, Darrelle Revis doesn’t have coaching experience aside from working with his son. But as colleges will waive doctorate requirements for professors with enough real-world expertise, his playing background is tough to beat. He is a four-time All-Pro and member of the 2010 All-Decade Team. He owns a Super Bowl ring.
When the trade-off was pointed out, Revis delivered a deadpan reply.
“The resume is pretty solid,” he said, eventually breaking into laughter again.

full_text:
Xavier Legette makes a catch in front of Corey Thornton to end practice Wednesday. The Panthers are looking for more from their third-year receiver. Jim Dedmon / Imagn Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — The Carolina Panthers’ practice ended on a good note for the offense Wednesday when Xavier Legette went up to snatch a Bryce Young pass in the end zone.
But it was a less dramatic play earlier in practice the Panthers hope is the product of a renewed focus from Legette and a sign of things to come in his third season. Facing cornerback Corey Thornton in one-on-one drills, Legette ran an out route, caught Young’s throw around waist level and tapped both his toes inbounds for a clean reception.
Too often early in Legette’s career, the first-rounder seemed to be unaware of the situation or where he was on the field, resulting in botched plays or incompletions like one in the 2025 season opener at Jacksonville when he failed to get a second foot down despite having plenty of room to do so.
“I had a couple mishaps where I would step on the line and I was out of bounds last year,” he said.
Legette, the former South Carolina wideout who was the 32nd pick in the 2024 draft, heard the criticism of what looked like lackadaisical play his first two seasons. And he took steps over the offseason to be more “honed in,” a phrase he used twice Wednesday while speaking with reporters.
As part of that process, Legette ended each of his offseason workouts with a series of boundary catches, much like his sideline snag Wednesday against Thornton. Panthers coach Dave Canales has noticed a difference.
“What I’ve seen him do is just make great plays on the boundary, back of the end zone, just some of those spatial plays where he can go attack the ball, find a way to get his feet down,” Canales said. “He’s really attacked that part of his game. That’s something I’ve seen him really improve on.”
Some of the spatial — and self — awareness might have stemmed from seeing two other young receivers lap him on the depth chart and the drafting of another wideout. While Tetairoa McMillan was the NFL’s Offensive Rookie of the Year in 2025, former undrafted free-agent Jalen Coker took over the WR2 spot from Legette with a strong finish.
With his sculpted 6-foot-3 frame and good straightaway speed, Legette has always looked the part of an NFL receiver. But his route-running and ball skills don’t appear to come as naturally as they do for McMillan, for example.
Former Panthers’ Pro Bowl wideout Steve Smith, who attended Sunday’s practice with an NFL Network crew, at one point stretched his arms out as a reminder for Legette to catch balls away from his body. A few days later, after Legette’s hands catch wrapped up Wednesday’s work, a reporter asked him if the play would help boost his confidence.
“I ain’t never lost my confidence in any way,” Legette said. “Just trying to continue to make plays like that throughout the season and have a good year.”
That said, Legette realized he had to do things differently. He worked out as many as four times a day, dropped some weight and revised his offseason regimen to try to “bulletproof” his hamstrings after dealing with soft-tissue issues in the past.
He flew out west three times to attend throwing workouts with Young, McMillan and other receivers, including a summer session in Los Angeles after OTAs. Besides improving their timing, Legette said hanging out with Young has helped him be more communicative with his quarterback.
“I’m talking to him a little more, going up to him and asking him things like how he feels about this and (does) he like this? Am I in the right spot?” Legette said. “So we’re getting it right.”
All of this feels like progress for a player who saw his targets decrease from 84 as a rookie to 64 last year, when his receptions (from 49 to 35) and receiving yards (497 to 363) also dipped.
“I feel like X is more dialed in on everything, from his body to his craft. I feel like as we go through life, you go through trials and tribulations and it’s up to you to grow through it,” second-year receiver Jimmy Horn said.
“And I feel like X was going through a phase where God took him through some things during the season. And I feel like he’s taking advantage of the opportunity he’s getting now and taking things more serious.”
Legette faced scrutiny early last season. In a Week 2 loss at Arizona, Legette finished with minus-2 yards on eight targets, only the second time in NFL history a player managed negative receiving yards on at least eight targets.
Compounding matters, Legette walked back toward the line of scrimmage with the Panthers in hurry-up mode at the end of the first half. Legette’s lack of urgency gave officials time to review a catch by Ja’Tavion Sanders, which was overruled and forced the Panthers to punt. The Cardinals then tacked on a touchdown before halftime.
“Stuff like that can get you benched,” Legette said. “I just can’t do stuff like that.”
After losing third-round pick Chris Brazzell to a season-ending knee surgery during training camp, the Panthers could use a bounce-back year from Legette. Canales said Legette looks explosive and comfortable in the scheme.
Legette, Young and the rest of the first-team offense will make their preseason debuts Saturday at Buffalo. There will be bigger tests to come, but the exhibition gives Legette another chance to show Young, Canales and the organization he can be counted on.
“I just had to take a step back. I felt like I was probably a little too loose,” Legette said. “I just had to take a step back and focus on the main thing, for real.”

title: Why the Bears love backup QB Tyson Bagent: 'Magic when he's out there' Because of his work ethic and what he's learning under coach Ben Johnson, Bagent believes his grandest NFL dreams will come true. Dan Wiederer

full_text:
Most Bears fans probably don't remember the preseason finale in Kansas City last summer, but Tyson Bagent does. “I could f------ cry right now just talking about it,” he says. “I get so fired up.” Jamie Squire / Getty Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — OK, this is downright wild — the zone Tyson Bagent has entered. The sudden energy in his eyes, the bobs of his head, the juice pumping into the room.
The Chicago Bears quarterback has been given only a month and a place — August 2025, Arrowhead Stadium — and he’s back inside a core memory.
Bagent has no video to reference, no official game book as a cheat sheet. Yet with elite recall, he details how the Bears rallied to defeat the Kansas City Chiefs 29-22 in their preseason finale last summer. Exactly how .
At the dining room table of his suburban townhome, and from memory alone, Bagent rattles off vivid descriptions of all 10 plays from that game-winning drive. All 87 yards. From his first completion — 15 yards to wide receiver Jahdae Walker along the right sideline — to his final throw. Walker again. Six yards. Touchdown.
Those bookends are easy to recall. The first Walker grab, ruled incomplete on the field, was overturned after replay review showed the rookie dragging his right cleat inside the sideline. “Best catch I’ve ever seen in person,” Bagent says.
The touchdown pass, obviously, won the game. But how, with nothing but his memory, is Bagent also dead on in describing every snap in between?
Play 3? “They overloaded us to the right,” he says. “I drifted (back), hit Joel.”
Indeed, Bagent’s drift away from pressure helped create a 10-yard completion to tight end Joel Wilson.
Play 7: “T. Scott! Right across the field,” Bagent says, beaming. “That was nice. We get the first down, and he gets out of bounds.”
Checks out — an ultra-calm 13-yard connection to wide receiver Tyler Scott on a crosser.
Play 8: “We hit Boykin. But that wasn’t pretty. It wasn’t the smartest play, because that went only 8 yards. Luckily, we got (a defensive penalty). Take the gain. Clock stops.”
At this point, the cross-check is unnecessary but offers confirmation. Bagent hit wide receiver Miles Boykin for 8. The Bears are now down to the Chiefs’ 14. Eleven seconds left.
Says Bears veteran quarterback Case Keenum: “Tyson’s got a little bit of that photographic memory. And I don’t know if ‘a little bit’ is doing it justice.”
Indeed, nearly a year after that Friday night in Kansas City, Bagent absolutely rolls through this energizing slideshow, grateful for how that final drive unfolded, still amped by the celebration it uncorked and hyper-aware that it was the last stretch of meaningful game action he had.
That’s partly why, this summer, Bagent’s fourth training camp has him so jacked up, his enthusiasm akin to a busload of kids unloading at a waterpark. Camp has become Bagent’s paradise. Preseason games are now his showcase.
The heat and humidity, Bagent says, ignite him. The smell of the practice field grass pushes him toward his flow state. Habits solidify, confidence builds.
The fatigue, physically and mentally, intoxicates Bagent.
“I could f—— cry right now just talking about it,” he says. “I get so fired up.”
To outsiders, August football may feel like just a tasting, cocktail hour before the big reception. For Bagent, this is his feast, his all-you-can-accomplish opportunity to showcase competence, growth, value, potential. For his teammates. To his coaches. As a resume for the rest of the NFL.
Thus, no matter how many snaps Bagent takes Saturday in the preseason opener against the Cleveland Browns or the following two weekends in road exhibitions versus the Cincinnati Bengals and Tennessee Titans, Bagent will lock in with his own brand of focus.
Admittedly, this has become an odd existence: this role of QB2 behind an established and ascending starter in Caleb Williams — particularly with Bagent’s self-assurance that he deserves a starting job somewhere.
Yet in the Bears’ ideal world, the only snaps he’ll ever take during the regular season or playoffs will be garbage-time reps in blowout wins.
Grueling days. Long weeks. Endless months in which Bagent’s engine is “Just in case.”
Chew on this nugget. Bagent completed more passes on that preseason drive in Kansas City last summer (eight) than he did across the past two regular seasons combined (five).
After throwing 2,400 passes across four seasons at Division II Shepherd University, Bagent has now gone almost three years since he last attempted 10 passes in a game that counts. Not even he, so enthusiastic and optimistic, can evade the frustration of that, the occasional bitterness and impatience that bubble up as he awaits a bigger opportunity.
“I do feel all those things,” Bagent acknowledges. “As I get older, I know there’s a time limit on this whole thing. And I am itching, even maybe a little more, to get in the game.”
Just as quickly, though, Bagent knows his gratitude is the tool to obliterate such feelings, reminding him of the journey he’s taken to this career peak. He is thankful, he says, for his brain, for his work ethic, for his love of the game and for the fact that he has never once felt burnt out.
He credits his mom, Casey, for being so nurturing and his dad, Travis, for “constantly spewing life into whatever dream I was chasing.”
Bagent is beyond proud that he’s just a kid from Martinsburg, W.Va., a product of Shepherd but now an established NFL quarterback and beloved member of one of the league’s charter franchises. And playing for one of the sport’s smartest offensive minds.
“It’s silly,” he says. “You’re playing for the Chicago Bears . … Wonderful f—— gig.”
Still, Bagent isn’t at all afraid to stay greedy, to chase so much more. He badly wants to win a Super Bowl. He believes he can one day become All-Pro.
“I want everything the league can offer me while I’m here,” he says. “I’ll never be closer than I am right now.
“I’m not gonna sit here and tell you I want to be a second- and third-string quarterback for the rest of my career.”
Bagent isn’t just hopeful that a bigger opportunity will come. In his mind, it is inevitable. On that front, there is almost no dissent inside Halas Hall, where the 26-year-old quarterback’s approach has become model behavior and where an odd feeling percolates. No one wants to see Bagent ever leave. Everyone will be thrilled when he’s gone.
“I just want what he wants,” Johnson says.
Adds Keenum: “I don’t know if I’ve seen anybody work at the craft as hard as he does. It’s just in him.”
Johnson has frequently told Bagent that he’s more than capable of being an NFL starter and, this offseason, when a sprinkling of calls came into Halas Hall checking into Bagent’s potential trade availability, it became obvious others around the league had taken note of the quarterback’s confidence; his high-end operational skills; the acclaim from so many coaches and teammates, past and present.
“It’s hard here with our situation,” Johnson acknowledges. “Yet I admire the fact that he still competes every single day. He walks into this building (with the attitude of), ‘These guys are crazy. I’m better than Caleb.’ Like that is how he’s wired. And that’s how he needs to be wired.”
A year ago, even with an emerging franchise quarterback in Williams inside the building, general manager Ryan Poles slid a two-year, $10 million contract extension Bagent’s way and stamped it as “a reward for everything he stands for.” Effort plus attitude. Drive mixed with confidence. The kinds of things that offset ordinary arm strength and, as importantly, energize a locker room.
Says Johnson: “He cares so deeply about doing it exactly the way you want it done.”
Walker can’t get over how frequently Bagent dominates the Bears’ “Kahoot!” competitions, the digital quiz sessions used to test players’ knowledge of the offense.
“A lot of times,” Walker says, “it’s not even close. I’m like, this dude knows everything about the offense. Formations. Plays. What’s this split?…

full_text:
Dohnte Meyers was an unknown when he joined the Bengals, but his underdog story keeps growing. Albert Cesare / USA Today Network via Reuters Connect
CINCINNATI — When Dohnte Meyers takes the field for his NFL debut in the Cincinnati Bengals’ preseason opener, years of rejection letters, practice squads, overnight shifts, workouts with no target and tryouts with no promises won’t matter anymore.
All Meyers ever wanted was an opportunity. He put his life on hold fighting fairy-tale odds to land one.
“For me,” the 26-year-old rookie wide receiver said, “I was just chasing a dream.”
The dream becomes a reality Thursday night. Since signing from the CFL on Jan. 8, Meyers has been the talk of camp for everyone, including head coach Zac Taylor, offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher and star receiver Ja’Marr Chase.
He’s repeatedly made plays, earned respect and forged an improbable path to making the roster.
“He’s got real juice,” Pitcher said.
And an unparalleled underdog story.
In a league of NIL millionaires, national champions and genetic wonders, the 5-foot-11, 186-pound Meyers does not fit the template.
A zero-star recruit out of Norcross High near Atlanta who earned only a few Division III offers, Meyers landed at FCS school Presbyterian College in South Carolina, playing on an academic scholarship.
“I got to Presbyterian because I was smart and I returned kicks,” he said.
After one season canceled by the pandemic and two productive years as a receiver at Division II Delta State in Mississippi, Meyers went undrafted, was unsigned as a free agent and only managed one unsuccessful rookie camp tryout with his hometown Atlanta Falcons.
He found himself at a crossroads, and the phone wasn’t ringing.
Not only did he refuse to find a normal job and give up on football, he doubled down.
“After the Falcons minicamp, I told myself, I’m going to do every tryout, every opportunity, and let the chips fall where they may,” Meyers said.
Except, for nearly all of 2023, his only opportunities involved working out and driving for DoorDash.
Meyers’ days involved a morning workout with trainer Manny Rodriguez, an afternoon session with receiving coach Stephon Brown and hours of specialized recovery. Then, the real work began.
“All night I would delivery drive, until like 2 or 3 in the morning,” Meyers said. “Then go wake up and train again at 8 or 9. I structured my whole life around pursuing a dream.”
Meyers admits his parents, Dwayne and Tracey, provided the motivation and means to go through with the plan, no matter how long the odds felt.
“They kind of just allowed me to be in a position to where I could chase my dream. I didn’t have other extenuating circumstances that forced me to pivot on a crossroad,” he said. “They were like, ‘You chase your dream. You’re young. Do it.’ My parents are big believers in chasing dreams. This is what you want to do? Act on it.”
Division II football is better than many people realize, and in two seasons Meyers racked up 120 receptions, 1,542 yards and 13 touchdowns. But a resume that included one year as an All-Gulf South Conference performer didn’t exactly offer a track record commensurate with pro football success.
Meyers felt differently, though.
“I always knew I could play football,” he said. “I feel like I needed an opportunity. I felt like I was a late bloomer.”
Then an opportunity came, sort of.
Rodriguez reached out to Trevor Harris, a veteran Saskatchewan Roughriders quarterback, and put Meyers’ name on his radar. The CFL team was holding an open tryout. It cost $100 to participate.
Meyers hopped a flight across the border, put the money down and took his shot.
He landed a futures contract. It provided no guarantees, minimal money and the No. 74.
“Seventies are eligible numbers in the CFL,” Harris said. “When he first came in, Dohnte was wearing 74. He was like, ‘Trev, I can’t be wearing this ugly number, man.’ I said, ‘You got to go make some plays and they will get you a new number.’ Next day, they put him in 88.”
Harris, an Ohio product out of Marion Pleasant High, dabbled in the NFL himself, with cups of coffee and tryouts. He spent two years in the UFL before starting a 14-year career in Canada playing for five teams.
He knew immediately that the Roughriders mined a gem in Meyers, gawking at his acceleration and separation. His intelligence, dedication to asking questions and mentality forged through his journey won Harris over, though.
“Guys from Division II that grind through the muck, they are tougher than a $2 steak, mentally and physically,” Harris said. “He ended up catching a touchdown and broke his wrist in his first preseason game and played through the game.”
When Meyers was finally healthy in that 2024 season, he was placed on the practice squad until finally being promoted to the roster in Week 10. Once the 2025 season arrived, the late bloomer bloomed.
Meyers racked up 1,056 yards on 65 receptions with eight touchdowns and four 100-yard games as Saskatchewan won the Grey Cup.
“Not only did he have that explosiveness in his route running, he was just a tremendous guy, he was learning every day, staying after practice,” said Harris, the Grey Cup MVP that season. “He is constantly in my ear asking how can I do this route, shave this route better. He’s really good about finding voids in zones and (slowing) his body down. He’s kind of the full package.”
Dohnte Meyers goes 66 yards to the HOUSE! #CFLGameDay 🗓️: @sskroughriders vs. REDBLACKS LIVE NOW 🇨🇦: TSN, RDS 🌎: CFL+ pic.twitter.com/AFbfunjACY
— CFL (@CFL) October 4, 2025
Bengals scouting executive Andrew Johnson is in charge of monitoring the CFL. He brought Meyers to the attention of the personnel department, and the Bengals signed him to a futures deal in January.
To nobody’s surprise, Meyers arrived at the earliest moment possible and immediately started drawing whispers. He impressed during OTAs and minicamp, but a lot of players impress during OTAs and minicamp.
The last 10 practices, though, have been a Meyers highlight reel. He caught a back-shoulder throw from Joe Burrow, a toe-tap along the sidelines and a smooth route over the middle. He broke free for a deep touchdown catch from Joe Flacco during Friday’s practice in the stadium.
“We noticed him in the spring, certainly,” Taylor said. “So then you get a chance to really go back and pay attention to his past in Canada and college. He’s had a lot of production in his lifetime. It’s just finding ways for him to try to make a play, and he’s shown up. We’re not going out of our way to showcase him. He’s just finding ways to show up and make some plays.”
Those plays might make an impression, but they won’t make the 53. In order for Meyers to make the team, he will likely have to capture the returner role. Charlie Jones currently holds it, and Ke’Shawn Williams is challenging. Meyers is also in that mix, and special teams coordinator Darrin Simmons made clear that the job is open.
There’s a blueprint Meyers can follow in that regard. In 2011, Andrew Hawkins made the Bengals as a resilient, unknown former CFL player, helped by a 32-yard preseason punt return and a dynamic camp at receiver. In 2016, undrafted rookie Alex Erickson lit up the preseason with two receiving touchdowns and an 80-yard punt return for another Bengals touchdown.
The two combined to play 15 years and 184 regular-season NFL games.
Returning punts and kicks helped Meyers get his start, all the way back to Presbyterian. He’ll need it to help him reach the NFL finish line.
Unsurprisingly, Meyers doesn’t view the game that way. He merely sees an opportunity. It’s all he ever wanted.
“Honestly, I just cherish every opportunity,” he said. “Regardless if it’s at the returner, in the offense, every opportunity is scarce. I believe if you’re on a professional football team, they call your number, whatever that role is, you’re trying to maximize it just so that you know you can be trusted. I feel like that’s kind of what my role is now. Just…

full_text:
Second-year running back Dylan Sampson has been heavily involved in the passing game during camp. Andrew Dolph / USA Today via Reuters Connect
BEREA, Ohio — With two full weeks of Cleveland Browns training camp now complete, the unsettled quarterback competition between Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders continues to drive the most conversation. It even produces an occasional touchdown.
First-year Browns head coach Todd Monken did announce to the team following Wednesday’s practice that Watson will start the preseason opener against the Chicago Bears on Saturday. Sanders will then get his chance to start the second preseason game on Aug. 22 against the Buffalo Bills.
But while Monken continues to evaluate — at least on some level — when it comes to the game’s most important position, the rest of the offensive depth chart has taken shape.
Unsurprisingly, rookie first-round pick Spencer Fano has taken over as the starting left tackle. Convincingly and quickly, rookie wide receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston have played their way into first-team roles . And the remade offensive line is pretty much down to one decision, with holdover Teven Jenkins the current leader at right guard over KT Leveston, who started seven games at tackle last season.
There’s much to be settled in the second wave of the wide receiver rotation. Same at tight end, where Harold Fannin Jr. is a rising star and no one behind him has emerged. Elgton Jenkins is slated to be the starting center assuming he’s healthy. And though he’s missed a number of practices, the belief is the team is being cautious given that Elgton Jenkins’ 2025 season ended due to a broken leg.
Leveston’s transition to guard seems to be going well, but Teven Jenkins is taking the majority of the starter’s reps now that he’s back from an injury-related absence of more than a week. And now that Fano has semi-officially beaten out Dawand Jones for the left tackle job, Jones has played right tackle with the No. 2 offense over the last two practices. That’s left third-round rookie Austin Barber at left tackle, Barber’s college position.
Rookie center Parker Brailsford remains out due to a hand injury. So when veteran Elgton Jenkins is being rested — as was the case Wednesday — Luke Wypler and Kingsley Eguakun split the starter’s reps at center.
Right now, signs point to both Jones and Barber making the team, and players like Wypler and holdover guard Zak Zinter — who’s also missed several days due to injury — potentially being on the wrong side of things. The Browns initially tinkered with the idea of giving Barber some right guard reps this summer, but he’s been needed at tackle to this point. Expect Monken to play Barber at both left and right tackle over the team’s first two preseason games.
Boston has been arguably the most impressive offensive player of both spring practices and the first three segments of training camp. But the quarterback battle has provided lots of opportunity for pass catchers to make plays, and several have delivered.
Running back Dylan Sampson was heavily involved in the pass game in the just-completed week of camp. Quinshon Judkins is the clear lead back, but Sampson seems set for a pass-game role. The Browns probably won’t play Judkins or Sampson much past the first quarter of Saturday’s preseason opener, leaving the bulk of the run-game work to Rocket Sanders and Ahmani Marshall.
Wide receiver Cedric Tillman seems to be on the wrong side of the roster bubble at this still-early stage, but he also was busy collecting targets and receptions earlier this week. On Wednesday, Tillman was not practicing due to an undisclosed injury. If he doesn’t play Saturday, look for Gage Larvadain, Luke Floriea and Malachi Corley to all potentially move up a spot in the current wide receiver rotation.
Right now, Larvadain is behind veteran Tylan Wallace in the rotation, and both are behind second-year speedster Isaiah Bond, who’s made several big plays in recent days after having a quiet start to camp.
The highlight of Wednesday’s practice — and arguably the best combination of throw and catch all summer — came on a Shedeur Sanders bomb that Bond extended to grab along the sideline in a late-practice one-minute drill. Bond is currently fourth behind the rookies and Jerry Jeudy, but if Cleveland develops any kind of consistent vertical passing game once the quarterback situation is settled, it certainly seems like Bond will be a part of that.
Floriea probably won’t be one of the 53 players the Browns keep on their initial roster, but he’s been a productive training camp player for the second straight summer and likely will be on the practice squad in case he’s needed at some point. Floriea has gotten a handful of reps with the No. 1 offense the last two weeks, and on Tuesday he caught a deep touchdown pass from Dillon Gabriel in a full-speed, full-team session.
The team believes Concepcion will be the primary punt returner in the regular season, but Larvadain and Floriea will each get preseason opportunities in the punt return game.
After an injury emergency at defensive tackle developed early in camp, the Browns have been hit hard by cornerback injuries. A day after July acquisition Damarri Mathis suffered a season-ending injury, Tyron Herring left the practice field early Wednesday. Herring had an interception Tuesday while playing with the starters.
Veterans D’Angelo Ross and Myles Bryant, both of whom are competing for roster spots as backup cornerbacks and special teams players, have missed multiple days due to injury. Three undrafted rookie cornerbacks — Nate Evans, Jeadyn Lukus and Michael Coats Jr. — are expected to see extended action in the preseason opener.
The situation at defensive tackle has only slightly improved as Mike Hall Jr. and Kalia Davis have both missed multiple weeks of practice, and starter Maliek Collins remains on the physically unable to perform list. Collins is working out each day as he rehabs the quad injury that ended his outstanding 2025 season early and aims to return for the start of the regular season.
The Browns continue to look for help at defensive end, too, as they worked out some edge rushers Wednesday, including former Baltimore Raven Tyus Bowser and Genard Avery, a Browns draft pick in 2018. Cleveland is set with starting defensive ends Jared Verse and Alex Wright, with Isaiah McGuire as the third defensive end in his contract year, but the search for more depth continues.
The Browns tried to sign A.J. Epenesa in March before an agreed-upon deal fell apart, then the team publicly pursued Jadeveon Clowney during the first week of training camp before he chose to sign a one-year deal with Houston . The player to watch in the pass-rush group in Saturday’s preseason opener is probably undrafted rookie Khordae Sydnor.
Over the first week of camp, the obvious standout players were all front-line regulars: Verse, Pro Bowl cornerback Denzel Ward, defensive tackle Mason Graham, Judkins and Boston were in that group. Over the last several sessions, Bond, McGuire and rookie safety Emmanuel McNeil-Warren have all made notable plays on multiple days.
Though the first preseason game is generally for younger players and provides a stage for them to continue to make an impression, that might be different for this year’s Browns with so much new on the offensive side.
Monken said his plan for Saturday’s preseason opener is for all healthy players to participate, though it’s hard to believe players like Ward and Verse will play much at all.

Preseason football has finally arrived for Dan Campbell’s Detroit Lions. For him and his staff, it’s their first chance to see whether their message is being received.

full_text:
Ahmed Hassanein speaks with Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard. Hassanein will get an opportunity to show his progress Thursday. Junfu Han / Imagn Images
Preseason football has finally arrived for Dan Campbell’s Detroit Lions. For him and his staff, it’s their first chance to see whether their message is being received.
“How do they compete? Do they use what they’ve been taught? You want to see the development, you’re excited for some of these young guys,” Campbell said when asked what he’s looking forward to. “Some of these rookies, young players, to have a chance to see where they’ve grown. Do they take what you’re teaching them to the field? And then some of these veteran guys that are playing for a spot, to watch them go out and compete. That’s what’s fun about all this.”
There’s quite a bit of competition unfolding — some expected, some out of necessity — so the preseason opener couldn’t come at a better time. The Lions aren’t expected to play key starters, but their opponent, the Cincinnati Bengals, will trot out Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins and others when these teams face off Thursday night at 7 ET.
It should be a good test for the roster hopefuls, looking to prove they can be counted on during the regular season. Here are five players I’m keeping an eye on Thursday.
Two weeks into training camp, the Lions lost starting center Cade Mays to a wrist injury. He’s expected to miss eight to 10 weeks, per a league source who was not authorized to speak publicly, which means the Lions could be without him through mid-to-late October. This is a brutal loss, considering the Lions were counting on Mays to be an answer in the interior of their offensive line. Without him, they’re back to square one, trying to adjust on the fly, but are they better positioned to handle the loss of a starting center this year versus last year? Players such as McLaughlin can answer that.
McLaughlin, a 2025 UDFA out of Ohio State, enters his second NFL season, but it’s really more like his first. McLaughlin ruptured his Achilles in November 2024, his final year of college. Before that, he was playing the best football of his life — a consensus All-American and the winner of the 2024 Rimington Trophy, awarded to the nation’s best center. However, the Achilles injury was enough for McLaughlin to go undrafted. He spent the 2025 season on the Bengals’ practice squad, essentially redshirting as he recovered from injury. After signing a futures contract with the Lions in January, McLaughlin has been around to learn the playbook and earned most — if not all — of the first-team reps since Mays’ injury.
McLaughlin is an intriguing option, and Thursday night, he’ll get a chance to face Dexter Lawrence in perhaps a welcome-to-the-NFL moment. If he holds his own this preseason, he could push for a starting gig over Juice Scruggs.
Few players have made more noise than Hassanein this training camp. Feel free to take that literally. If you hear someone yelling along the second-team defensive line, there’s a good chance it’s Hassanein. His energy is infectious, and his motor never runs cold. He’s one of the best stories on the team, given his background moving to the U.S. in high school and taking up football a few years later, but it’s time for Hassanein to prove he belongs in the defensive line rotation.
The Lions have been experimenting with Hassanein this offseason, moving him to the big end role in their defense, rather than playing the rush end behind Aidan Hutchinson. You can view it as a way to get him on the field more and see what he can do. Hassanein is a smaller defensive end, but he’s strong as a bull and feels he’s better equipped to handle what’s asked of him in the structure of the defense. If that can lead to a rotational edge who can hold his own against the run and clean things up as a pass rusher, Hassanein can provide value to this team.
“Listen, he’s had a really good camp,” Campbell said. “He is all out, all the time. The guy never takes a play off, literally never takes a play off. He doesn’t take a water break off, I mean, the guy is all out. Some of his things, honestly, is we’ve got to rein him back in a little bit. Sometimes he gets out of his mind and goes a little rogue on some stuff. But you’d rather it be that way and pull back on him than the other, where you’re constantly having to prod him. So, he’s really grown, kind of moving him to the big end. That was a move that was made. So, he’s a little bit of an undersized big end, but it doesn’t affect him. He plays so dang hard, plays with leverage. And he has — he’s grown, man.”
The secondary is an obvious question mark. Its two safeties are recovering from serious injuries and won’t be ready for the start of the season, and its 2024 first-round pick was arrested and released this summer .
We probably won’t see much of D.J. Reed (soft tissue) and Rock Ya-Sin (veteran) this preseason. If the season started today, they’d be the projected starting corners, and the Lions can’t afford to lose one of them at this stage. That said, expect a heavy dose of Rakestraw and Whiteside on Thursday. The Lions need to see what they have in Rakestraw, a 2024 second-round pick who hasn’t been able to stay healthy in his career. Training camp has been a mixed bag for Rakestraw, as the Lions have consistently paired him with Jameson Williams and Amon-Ra St. Brown to test him. How will he fare against the likes of Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins?
Then there’s Whiteside — a cornerback who isn’t supposed to be here but keeps showing up. A 2023 UDFA out of Saginaw Valley State, Whiteside is an Auburn Hills, Mich., native who continues to impress this staff. He spent the 2025 season with the Lions and was even called to play major snaps when cornerback depth was thin. He’s back with the team for training camp this year, and there aren’t many players who’ve helped their stock more. He’s won reps against Isaac TeSlaa, St. Brown and Williams in camp, and the coaching staff gave him first-team reps in practice leading up to the preseason game. They’re eager to see what he can do.
“You can’t ignore him,” Campbell said. “And a guy like him, he is rising. What I love about Ironsides is it is not too big for him. He doesn’t care who’s across from him, he will compete, and he’s going to try to use his craft. And he doesn’t go in a shell, and he’s defeated before the play is even snapped. I mean, really, I know this sounds crazy, but some guys, man, all of a sudden, man, Jamo’s across from me or Saint and I’m already done, and the fear is already there. He is not that way. This guy, it doesn’t matter who’s there. He’s going to try to use his craft and compete, and you love that. Special teams, he makes plays every day. And so I like where he’s at right now. We’ll see where this goes.”
If the Lions are resting starters, we probably won’t see much of Alim McNeill or Tyleik Williams. Those two are entrenched in the defensive interior; however, the depth behind them is an open competition. Yes, the Lions have Levi Onwuzurike back, but he’s off to a slow start in camp, and the Lions might not want to push a player coming back from a torn ACL. Mekhi Wingo has missed time with a groin injury, so his status for Thursday is TBD. This means we should get a long look at Gill-Howard, the Lions’ sixth-round pick.
The Lions need more interior juice. With McNeill and Onwuzurike missing time with torn ACLs last year, it was severely lacking. In search of defensive tackles who could provide a spark, the Lions selected Gill-Howard out of Texas Tech and believe his best days are ahead of him. A former linebacker who worked his way from Division II Upper Iowa to Northwestern to Texas Tech, Gill-Howard just keeps getting better and better, and though his 2025 season was cut short because of an ankle injury, he put enough on tape for the Lions to target him on Day 3. He’s mostly been repping with the second-team defense but has received some…

full_text:
Chiefs personnel have raved about Kenneth Walker III's personality and down-to-earth attitude — qualities that stand out even more given what Walker has already accomplished. Denny Medley / Getty Images
ST. JOSEPH, Mo. — Patrick Mahomes shook his head side to side, looking into the distance while taking an extra moment to think.
The Kansas City Chiefs’ 10th-year quarterback was asked what intrigued him most about the 2026 version of the team’s offense — one that, based on this year’s training camp, has the potential to feature more under-center dropbacks, versatility and speed compared with a season ago.
In the end, though, Mahomes couldn’t get one thought out of his mind.
“ No. 9,” Mahomes said. “ That’s all I can say.”
Mahomes, in other words, is most excited for a part of the Chiefs offense the outside world hasn’t seen just yet.
That would be free-agent signing Kenneth Walker III — “K9” is the running back’s nickname, thanks to his uniform number — and how he could potentially revamp Kansas City’s offense with his ability to run, catch and pass protect.
“M ake a play out of nothing to a 20-yard gain,” Mahomes said. “T hat’s going to be the biggest impact I think we’ll have.”
Another future Hall of Famer is seeing things a similar way.
Tight end Travis Kelce, when asked about his first impression of Walker this week, first answered with a sound instead of words:
“Ken Walker is going to be a hell of a ball player for us, i f you didn’t know that already,” Kelce said. “H e’s got every trait you can possibly want at the running back position.”
Both Mahomes and Kelce, however, are quick to point out that this seemingly strong marriage of team and player has been about more than just football skills — and goes deeper than the potential for more explosive plays.
Walker, who joined the team in March after signing a three-year contract worth $43 million (with $28.7 million guaranteed), has immediately become a culture fit thanks to his football-first mindset. And that was especially important for a Chiefs organization that feels small details were some of their biggest issues during last season’s disappointing 6-11 campaign.
“He’s a hard worker, does not take anything for granted. He’s what you want,” offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy said of Walker in June. “You love his approach in the building. He’s very professional in the classroom, and he hates being wrong. ”
Chiefs personnel have raved about Walker’s personality and down-to-earth attitude — qualities that stand out even more given what Walker has already accomplished.
The fifth-year pro is coming off a Super Bowl victory with the Seattle Seahawks. Not only that, he was his team’s best player in Seattle’s 29-13 win, breaking nine tackles, per NFL NextGenStats, on his way to 135 rushing yards and Super Bowl MVP honors.
Mahomes said you wouldn’t know all that from how Walker works — or treats others. In May, Mahomes said his first impression of Walker was simply that he was “a great dude.”
“You can tell he truly cares about football; he cares about his teammates,” Mahomes said. “If he’s not in the play, he’s helping the guys on the sideline, and he’s trying to learn and ask me questions.”
Others have benefited from those team-first thoughts as well.
That includes rookie running back Emmett Johnson, a fifth-round pick getting his first experience as a professional. He said Walker’s approach to his work stood out immediately, but then something else right after:
Walker was somebody who cared about the entire group.
“He’s very unselfish, and that’s what I love about him,” Johnson said. “We push each other on the football field, but he’s an unselfish player, and he obviously has a lot of experience. So I’m gonna do my job of picking his brain, too.”
Walker, for his part, says he believes in the power of “bringing guys with me.”
Though he’s only 25, Walker says he feels like a veteran. And he also knows he made mistakes early in his career that kept him from becoming more productive.
One example? Walker says he didn’t take his diet seriously during his first few years. That’s why he’s talked with Johnson and the other backs about the benefits of eating cleaner and the impact it’s made on his game.
“ I want them to learn quicker than I learned,” Walker said, “ and I don’t want it to be a drop-off at all.”
There remains more for Walker to prove himself. Seattle mostly used him as an early-down back while in a timeshare with Zach Charbonnet, meaning he surrendered carries on third downs and in the red zone.
That won’t be the case in Kansas City. The Chiefs will have to be smart while trying to keep Walker fresh and healthy, but he’s primed to be the clear workhorse on a team that typically rotated its backs by series last season.
He’s already showcased dynamic ability on practice fields in both Kansas City and St. Joseph.
“He’s going to be tough to tackle,” pass game coordinator Joe Bleymaier said.
“Explosive for sure,” running back Emari Demercado said.
“Sometimes you’ll be like, ‘I don’t know how he did that,'” right tackle Jaylon Moore said, “but it’s awesome to see.”
Walker’s potential as a Chiefs player shouldn’t be a secret much longer.
If training camp is any indication, Walker figures to be heavily involved in what was a dormant screen game last season. Walker showed off his skills with a one-handed catch in organized team activities, and Reid has previously complimented the way he “catches the ball easy.”
During training camp practices, Mahomes also has become the most fired up during well-executed screens to Walker. A few times, Mahomes could be heard a field away cheering Walker on as he sprinted into the open field for big gains.
“Now,” Mahomes said, “it’s just finding ways to get him the football.”
Handoffs will be part of that, too, as the Chiefs try to break an unwanted streak.
Kansas City hasn’t had a 1,000-yard rusher since Kareem Hunt in 2017; that’s tied for the longest drought in the NFL, along with the New Orleans Saints and Los Angeles Rams.
But just as the Chiefs haven’t had a running back like Walker in previous years … he also likely hasn’t run behind an offensive line as good as the Chiefs’. General manager Brett Veach shared in April that he believed adding Walker would pair well with the team’s mauling offensive linemen like Kingsley Suamataia, Creed Humphrey and Trey Smith.
“When you combine a back like that, and you have as talented an inside three as you do,” Veach said, “I think it would make sense to want to go out there and impose your will on other teams’ defensive lines.”
The Chiefs certainly seem committed to giving Walker a bigger role than he had in Seattle. And the running back, to his credit, has taken well to his new team while arriving with a no-nonsense mentality.
Coaches, veterans and rookies have all seemed to appreciate that approach.
Along with one of his new biggest fans in Kansas City.
“ I can’t say enough about him as a teammate,” Kelce said. “ We got an absolute superstar on and off the field .”

full_text:
Kindle Vildor (in blue) is pushing for one of the final cornerback spots on the Patriots' 53-man roster. Eric Canha / Imagn Images
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Drake Maye and several other New England Patriots stars aren’t expected to play in the team’s preseason opener Thursday night against the Indianapolis Colts.
Instead, coach Mike Vrabel kept Maye and other veterans on the field for a long joint practice against the Colts on Tuesday that went well for the Pats.
Still, Thursday night’s game is an important one for plenty of players. Here’s a look at who has the most at stake Thursday night.
Coaches continue to speak highly of Williams, who was an offseason award winner. They say they’ll find a role for Williams, and the way Vrabel talks about him, it seems like he’s a roster lock.
However, it’s also fair to note that Williams has not made a significant impact in training camp and has spent a lot of time with the backup offense. Maybe that’s to make Williams the primary option on a certain play, but it’s curious given the praise he has received. So it’ll be interesting to see if Williams makes any plays on Thursday night.
The other thing to watch is how he fares as a kick returner. He was there on Tuesday and projects as the Week 1 starter in that role.
With Carlton Davis out for most of the last two weeks, Vildor has gotten plenty of run with the first-string defense as he vies for one of the last cornerback jobs on the roster.
However, it’s going to be tough competition. Karon Prunty has had some nice moments, as has undrafted rookie Channing Canada. Kobee Minor is still in the mix, as well.
This is going to be a big game for those corners, especially since Tuesday didn’t go great for them against the Colts. But the guess is Vildor is the leader in the clubhouse at this point for one of the final cornerback jobs.
It’s hard to pick just one, especially since it’s difficult to evaluate running backs in training camp practices when tackling isn’t allowed.
So this is the first real opportunity for one of the backups to take a lead in the race for the job behind Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson.
Terrell Jennings is probably the early front-runner, but rookie Jam Miller should get plenty of touches on Thursday night and could be a factor on special teams, too, given his speed.
If Miller replaces Williams as the kick returner, that would go a long way toward solidifying Miller’s spot. Lan Larison is the other player vying for this job.
The tight end got off to a slow start in training camp thanks to an injury that landed him on the PUP list. However, Dippre has been back at practice for a week now and has had a chance to shake off the rust.
He has seemingly fallen behind in the race for the No. 3 tight end job thanks to the blocking prowess of undrafted rookie Tanner Arkin. But Dippre has more pass-catching upside than Arkin, and this preseason game should offer him a chance to make a positive impression.

It wasn’t the smoothest transition to the NFL, as a degenerative left knee issue delayed Jacas’ contract signing until after training camp had started.
However, Jacas seems to play quickly and is often in the backfield in practice. Still, the 22-year-old missed meaningful time away from the team during his contract dispute, so it wouldn’t be a surprise if Jacas hasn’t fully mastered the playbook yet.
I’d expect Jacas to play with a high motor on Thursday night. As Vrabel has noted, it’s a lot easier to dial back a rookie who plays fast while perhaps not understanding every aspect of their role, rather than asking a rookie to pick up the pace.

full_text:
Coach John Harbaugh and the Giants need Cam Skattebo and his fellow running backs to lead a more explosive running game in 2026. Chris Carlson / Associated Press
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — For the New York Giants offense to get to where it wants to go and be the high-scoring unit it wants to be — safe to say that’s putting up more than the 21.6 points per game it averaged in 2025 — they’ll need to run the ball better. Every team wants to dominate on the ground, of course, but for a Giants offense trying to develop a young quarterback, it is vitally important they become more efficient and more explosive running the ball in 2026.
“I played quarterback my entire life, and having a run game is the friendliest thing in the world,” new offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said this week. “You want to be able to run the football. Everybody says it, but you’ve got to be able to do it.”
Last year, the Giants finished 18th in yards per carry (4.3), 25th in rushing success rate and 16th in explosive run rate. However, some of the heavy lifting in those numbers was done by quarterback Jaxson Dart, who rushed for 487 yards and nine scores last season. When you remove QB runs, the Giants fell to 25th in yards per carry (4.0), 27th in rushing success rate and 20th in explosive run rate.
Those numbers beg the question: Do the Giants have the necessary components to be as effective on the ground as they want to be?
They worked to strengthen their offensive line, drafting guard Francis Mauigoa with the 10th overall pick in April’s NFL Draft and adding physical players like fullback Patrick Ricard in free agency. While they seemed interested in adding another playmaker to their running back room, the Giants ended up returning to the primary threesome they had last year: Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Devin Singletary.
Perhaps that trio can lead them where they want to go — Nagy and coach John Harbaugh have expressed optimism about the running back room, even sharing compliments about annual training camp favorite Dante “Turbo” Miller, as well.
Still, it’s interesting to recall the Giants’ offseason, as they were linked — though never seriously entered the bidding, per my beat partner Dan Duggan — to Kenneth Walker III, the 2026 Super Bowl MVP who ended up signing a three-year free agent deal with the Kansas City Chiefs, and Notre Dame product Jeremiyah Love , who wound up being drafted at No. 3 by the Arizona Cardinals, two spots before the Giants were on the clock.
Again, it’s worth repeating that the Giants have seemed pleased with what they’ve seen from their backs so far in training camp. The Giants like where the fan-favorite Skattebo, who tallied 487 yards and five touchdowns on 86 carries in eight games before a gruesome ankle injury, is at.
“He looks really good,” Nagy said. “I think he’s slowly, every day, improving, which is great.”
Skattebo has been splitting first-team reps with Tracy so far during camp, with Skattebo up first quite a bit and Tracy coming in for many of the two-minute drives. The two were both listed as starters on the team’s first unofficial depth chart released Wednesday.
“He’s a super smooth guy that just does everything the right way,” Nagy said of Tracy.
Singletary has been the only other back to get more reps with the starters.
“Obviously (Singletary) is a really good football player,” Harbaugh said. “He always has been. He’s had a great camp. You know exactly what he’s going to give you.”
So, perhaps it’s fair to suggest the Giants were only interested in supplementing their running back room if the player they were adding gave them an element their room was missing.
Walker and Love each possess explosiveness, a trait one could argue the Giants are missing. Walker’s 10 percent explosive run rate (runs of 12-plus yards) ranked second among all running backs with at least 200 carries. Meanwhile, Love tallied 49 plays of 10-plus yards, third most in the FBS last year, according to Dane Brugler .
Explosiveness was an element the Giants lacked last season. Giants’ running backs ranked in the bottom half of the league in explosive run rate, finishing 18th at just 8.3 percent (24 total explosive runs for the season). By comparison, Harbaugh’s former team, the Baltimore Ravens, finished first at 12.4 percent with 39 explosive runs. Even with Skattebo leading the running back room from Weeks 2-7, Giants backs totaled just seven explosive runs (six from Skattebo, one from Tracy), a rate of 6.9 percent, which ranked 21st in the league in that span.
Another way to gauge how well running backs find extra yards and turn in explosive runs is to look at their yards after contact. Again, New York lacked in that area in 2025. Giants running backs finished 30th in the league last season in yards after contact per rush, tallying just 2.68, per TruMedia. Again, even with Skattebo healthy and in control of the backfield (Weeks 2-7), the Giants’ running backs ranked 24th (2.74). Skattebo himself was slightly better than that at 3.09, but that still only ranked 19th among qualified RBs in that span.
Of course, there’s reason to expect Skattebo will improve with another year of experience; the same can be said for Tracy, who didn’t even play running back for most of his career in college. Factor in the new coaches — not just Harbaugh and Nagy but also run-game guru Greg Roman as the team’s senior offensive assistant — bringing a new scheme and an improved offensive line, and it’s realistic to believe the Giants already have everything they need to take a step forward in the running game.
“I like what we’re doing,” Nagy said when asked about the team’s run game and the position room’s depth. “Again, we’re halfway through camp right now. We still have two and a half weeks. … We still have a lot left, and we’re trying to just figure out, ‘OK, what do we want to do as we go through it?’ And we think we have a good idea.”

full_text:
Pro Football Hall of Famer Darrelle Revis attends a game between the New York Jets and the Los Angeles Chargers in 2023 at MetLife Stadium. Revis, 41, has expressed a desire to get into coaching. Jim McIsaac / Getty Images
Darrelle Revis was a first-ballot Pro Football Hall of Fame cornerback. Yet when he and undrafted safety Jim Leonhard played together with the New York Jets, he never viewed Leonhard as a sidekick.
Revis, in fact, still considers the Buffalo Bills’ new defensive coordinator a lead dog. So much so that Revis would love to join Leonhard’s staff right now.
“I’m not joking at all,” Revis said by phone from Canton, Ohio. “I’ve always loved the game, and I’ve always loved playing with Jim.”
Revis dropped what he was doing during Hall of Fame induction weekend to talk about his deep admiration. While voicing his praise, an unexpected job pitch materialized.
But that’s just part of the serendipity.
Revis, 41, explained that football is pulling at him again. He said retirement has been eventful, with commercial real estate and venture capital investments, but no man is an island — not even Revis Island. He’s an empty nester now that his daughter is a junior nursing student at the University of Kentucky and his son is a freshman business major and defensive back at Mercyhurst University.
That’s Mercyhurst. In Erie, Pa. About 85 miles from Highmark Stadium.
“I think Jim will be a future head coach,” Revis said. “Tell him if he needs a secondary coach to give me a call. Maybe this is my interview where I tell Jim that if he ever needs help, to keep me at the top of the list.”
Informed Saturday night about Revis’ offer, Leonhard grinned, unfolded a practice call sheet from his pocket and jotted down Revis’ phone number.
Bills coach Joe Brady’s staff features three coordinators and 21 assistants. It includes secondary coach Joe Danna, who worked with Revis as the Jets’ defensive backs coach in 2015 and 2016, and cornerbacks coach Jay Valai.
NFL staffs have no size limit.
Leonhard and Revis first hooked up in 2009, when the Jets named Rex Ryan head coach. Leonhard spent the previous season with the Baltimore Ravens, turning a long-shot tryout into a critical role on Ryan’s heralded defense.
Baltimore was so vicious that Revis knew Leonhard possessed the proper bona fides. Leonhard started 16 games, including all three in the postseason, lined up with safety Ed Reed and behind alpha linebacker Ray Lewis, members of the NFL’s 100th anniversary team.
“You have a guy like Ray Lewis at linebacker, and the way that he demands the same type of approach to the game from everybody,” Revis said. “That’s what Jim did for us.
“When you replay your career and remember those flashbacks in the huddle and just going to war with your teammates, you always knew Jim had your back.”
Their first season together was the best of Leonhard’s career and arguably Revis’ best, too. That’s when the Revis Island nickname emerged. The Jets gave up the fewest points, fewest yards per play, fewest yards per pass attempt and fourth-fewest rushing yards per carry. Opposing quarterbacks posted a 58.8 passer rating with eight touchdown passes, 17 interceptions and 32 sacks.
Leonhard started every game, recording one interception, five breakups, 2 1/2 sacks, nine tackles for losses and a forced fumble. Revis earned his first All-Pro selection and was Defensive Player of the Year runner-up with a career-high six interceptions and an NFL-record 31 breakups.
That postseason, New York made the first of its back-to-back AFC Championship Games. In three road games, Leonhard intercepted a pass, forced two fumbles and recovered another, while Revis intercepted a pair.
“I really loved playing with him,” Revis said. “His intellect, his football IQ, the way he communicated, he was just very tuned in and detailed.”
Revis is convinced those traits will translate into Leonhard being a successful NFL coordinator and future head coach — and maybe Revis’ boss.
“I understand the coaching life and how guys have to relocate and move certain places,” Revis said, “but the kids are out of the house. I have time and opportunity to do other things.”
Revis splits time between South Florida and New York. Would he be willing to grind out an assistant coach’s lifestyle in suburban Buffalo?
“I wouldn’t mind,” Revis said with a laugh. “They have a new stadium, and it’s football, man. Wherever I need to be, I’ll go.”
Jayden Revis will play defensive back at Mercyhurst. He also was a receiver and kick returner at Moon Area High in the Pittsburgh area. Darrelle is from nearby Aliquippa, Pa., and was an All-American at Pitt.
Granted, Darrelle Revis doesn’t have coaching experience aside from working with his son. But as colleges will waive doctorate requirements for professors with enough real-world expertise, his playing background is tough to beat. He is a four-time All-Pro and member of the 2010 All-Decade Team. He owns a Super Bowl ring.
When the trade-off was pointed out, Revis delivered a deadpan reply.
“The resume is pretty solid,” he said, eventually breaking into laughter again.

full_text:
Charles McQuillan / Getty Images
LATROBE, Pa. — Last summer, shortly after Will Howard lugged his suitcase into the dorm at Saint Vincent College to begin his first Steelers training camp, Aaron Rodgers invited the sixth-round pick into his room. The rookie and the old gunslinger were talking through hand signals when Rodgers paused for a minute.
“Look man, I’m here for you,” Howard remembers Rodgers saying. “I don’t want to overstep …”
“I’m like, ‘Dude, you’re not overstepping,’” Howard told him. “‘You’re one of the greatest to play. I’m just trying to soak in as much as I can.’”
The relationship between a veteran quarterback and his young backups can sometimes be challenging, even contentious. No one knows this better than Rodgers. When the Green Bay Packers drafted him in 2005, the thrill of sharing a QB room with one of his idols quickly turned into something else.
“My contract doesn’t say I have to get Aaron Rodgers ready to play,” Brett Favre famously said.
Even before Rodgers put on a helmet for Pittsburgh, he displayed a willingness to pass his knowledge to the next generation. On Day 1 of mandatory minicamp in 2025, former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin wanted Rodgers to be a spectator as he got up to speed on a new offense. Instead, Rodgers was on a knee, giving detailed feedback to Howard about his footwork.
This offseason, the Steelers doubled down on development by drafting Drew Allar in the third round, making Rodgers’ presence even more crucial. When Howard and Allar make their preseason debuts Thursday night against the Packers, they’ll have Rodgers on the headset — and in their corners. He has proven to be the mentor he never had.
“To coin a phrase after a guy that I’ve followed, it’s not in my job description,” Rodgers said. “But I think it’s a great opportunity, for sure, to be able to mentor those guys.”
Last season, Rodgers stood in front of the room every Thursday for a player-led meeting. Howard, whose season was derailed by a broken pinky during training camp, said he became the QB’s “assistant,” dialing up clips on the computer.
“He gave me little jobs here and there just to make me feel included, and that went a long way,” Howard said. “It definitely helped my confidence just being on the team, even though I wasn’t doing anything physically.”
During weeks of preparation, Rodgers asked the rookie to study the defense’s hand signals or put together two-minute cut-ups. Sitting next to the four-time MVP in meetings, Howard got a window into the way Rodgers views the game and dissects defenses, starting with the defensive front.
“The front’s going to tell you what’s going to happen,” Howard said. “Is it a field under front? Maybe they’re going to bring a nickel pressure. There’s different things like that that he kind of tied me into and got me looking at more than I ever had before.”
When the Steelers are analyzing their QB School film, Rodgers often provides his own coaching points. Or when they’re breaking down clips from practice, QB coach Tom Arth allows Rodgers to stop the film and provide his own feedback.
“There’s a willingness from him to share his knowledge — tips and tricks and almost cheats on certain progressions,” Allar said.
Rodgers, like first-year head coach Mike McCarthy, is a firm believer in footwork. On the practice field, it’s common to see the backup quarterbacks mimicking Rodgers’ footwork on play-action, especially his signature “guitar” fake, on which he hides the ball behind his hip and fakes the exchange with an empty hand to freeze the back-side defenders.
“The way that he looks at his footwork, everything’s tied through your feet,” Howard said. “Your feet are going to tell you where you’re going to throw the ball and how you’re going to throw the ball.
“In the red zone, chop your feet down, never more than a three-step drop, because everything happens faster. On third-and-long plays, where you’re maybe taking a quick five-(step drop) from the gun, cheat up a yard so that you’re not getting out of the tackles’ fan box.”
Some of the most valuable feedback comes when Rodgers is using his two-plus decades of NFL experience to tell the young quarterbacks things they won’t find in the playbook. One example came about a week ago during a seven-on-seven drill.
“We had talked about controlling the defense with our eyes,” Allar said. “Kind of hitching and still having our eyes down the middle of the field. You want to control that hook defender, so you can open up that space for that hook route.”
Even as McCarthy takes a methodical approach to building the quarterbacks up, slowly and surely, Rodgers encourages the young passers to incorporate new elements into their games.
“I’m the old bastard that says ‘Hey don’t do too much,’” McCarthy joked. “But it’s good to see him pushing and giving these guys an education of a lifetime.”
Almost every practice, there’s some new coaching moment. Last week, for example, Allar threw on the run during a scramble drill and missed the target. Rodgers explained to the QB how his arm angle and the flick of his wrist have to change based on the direction he’s rolling out of the pocket.
“Aaron’s been great with that, helping me with different arm angles and really more tailoring it to specific throws,” Allar said. “He’s been more than willing to pull me aside, whether it be in meetings or out on the field during drill work to talk me through things. Then, he has me repeat a rep and try it, just to feel what he’s talking about and him also seeing me do it.”
At the end of the Steelers’ 2025 season, Rodgers’ future in football appeared uncertain — even the QB thought he might call it a career. This time, Howard was the one who initiated the conversation.
“He was in Green Bay and was in a kind of a similar situation with one of his heroes, Brett Favre, who wasn’t always the best to him,” Howard said. “I just said, ‘Thank you for giving me what you didn’t have.’
“He wanted to break the cycle and wanted to give back. God willing, I can play for a long time and be able to give back like he did because that went a long way.”

title: One Under-the-Radar Player Who Stood Out to Cardinals HC Mike LaFleur in Training Camp
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals, in terms of talent, have notable names on both sides of the ball.
Safety Budda Baker has earned Pro Bowl nods in all but one season of his career. Tight end Trey McBride is one of the best players at his position. Outside linebacker Josh Sweat looks to build off his 12-sack performance from last season while rookie running back Jeremiyah Love headlines an exciting crop of young Cardinals talent.
Those guys will dominate headlines throughout the 2026 season, and rightfully so.
However, if the Cardinals will truly get to where they're wanting to go this year, they'll need a plethora of players to make the next step. Maybe not quite relying on some overlooked guys at the bottom of the roster, but rather players who can step up when their name's called.
Head coach Mike LaFleur, speaking with reporters for the final time at training camp , couldn't talk highly enough about second-year safety Kitan Crawford.
"He is the epitome of play style. He loves ball. You know how you just have some of those guys that you can look in their eyes, and you're like, 'man, he's got bad intentions in a good way.'" said LaFleur .
"Because you got to have bad intentions when you head out on the football field. It's violent, and if you don't, someone probably that you're going against does. So he is made of all the right stuff. He just wants to do whatever is best for the football team, whether that's on special teams or obviously on defense. I think he's carving himself out even more of a role on defense as he's gotten more and more comfortable in this [defense]."
Crawford didn't play much in 2025 — just about 14% of defensive snaps, though he did fill-in well when needed. That, on top of his 80% of special teams snaps played last season, made him a solid floor-raiser for a Cardinals safety room that saw Jalen Thompson depart in free agency.
Crawford won't start, at least not with Budda Baker, Andrew Wingard and Dadrion Taylor-Demerson ahead of him.
Yet when it comes to Arizona's heavy usage of dime packages and the grueling reality of an NFL season, Crawford's sure to get more opportunity in 2026 — which is also thanks in part to the unfortunate departure of fellow safety Joey Blount to injured reserve.
"What an awesome deal for a young safety to be in a room with Budda Baker every single day, right? And just learn from someone like him. So couldn't be more pleased with him. Really think the player is ascending. Really think the player can be special. I think the person is even better," LaFleur added on Crawford.
Crawford, affectionately called "Bug" by his teammates and coaches, is impressing coaches both young and seasoned. Even senior defensive coach Teryl Austin offered promising remarks on Crawford:
"I think there's some young guys [who have stood out]. I think Bug has stood out. You watch his play temperament, like it's fun," said Austin.
Crawford was one of Arizona's top-graded players from their Hall of Fame Game last week, according to Pro Football Focus. Thus far, his mix of rookie tape, training camp improvement in year two and preseason debut makes for an exciting young presence in the Cardinals' safety room.

title: 6 Overlooked Cardinals Who Look Like Final 53-Man Roster Locks
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals are officially done with training camp. Now, head coach Mike LaFleur and the rest of his staff move forward into the depths of preseason play with three goals.
First, Arizona simply wants to stay healthy and avoid any major injuries. Second, the Cardinals want to continue installing LaFleur's offense ahead of their regular season opener. The third and final piece of the puzzle is figuring out who will land on their final 53-man roster.
Perhaps you've heard some of these names, perhaps you haven't. Regardless, these players were overlooked entering training camp, and as the Cardinals push the pedal to the floor, they only boosted their stock leaving Glendale:
Why he can make the roster: This will be a tough decision, as the Cardinals will have to weigh keeping four running backs over other bodies in highly competitive position groups. Arizona does plan to run the ball, often, and that could pave the way for Knight.
If you've followed our work, you're no stranger to Knight. He was one of training camp's biggest winners after usurping Trey Benson in the pecking order and has special teams acumen to justify his place on the roster. That, combined with a strong mode of running, can see him in a nice supporting role behind Arizona's trio of Jeremiyah Love, Tyler Allgeier and Trey Benson.
Why he can make the roster: The Cardinals, as stated above, are going to run the ball early and often. They'll likely rank near the top of the league in tight end usage in 12/13 personnel to accomplish this, which perfectly paves the way for Quitoriano's presence.
Trey McBride is an All-Pro. Elijah Higgins is a pass specialist while Tip Reiman is their primary in-line blocker — who has yet to be activated off the PUP list. Even when that does happen, Quitoriano's specialization in run blocking could give him a leg-up over his other counterparts hoping to squeeze onto the roster.
Why he can make the roster : It feels like we're the conductor of the Smith-Marsette hype train, so hop aboard. ISM has performed well all training camp, gaining traction with the first and second team offense while also serving as a backup kick return man and gunner for special teams duties.
Equally as important — he's made plays on offense. His speed is noticeable when between the white lines and he's been a big play waiting to happen at the intermediate/deep level during camp. If the Cardinals keep a sixth receiver, he's heavily in the conversation.
Why he can make the roster : Brooks is also in that conversation, especially after his Hall of Fame Game performance where he tallied 99 receiving yards with two big catches down the field.
Brooks has also turned up his performances during camp, putting him close to Smith-Marsette in conversations to make the final roster. It feels like every time Brooks is thrown the ball, he's making a play before or after the catch.
Why he can make the roster: Williams might not be quite under the radar now, but as a late seventh-round pick in the draft, his status to even compete for a roster spot was up in the air.
Fast forward to training camp, where the Cardinals are seeing their rookie tackle alternate between the left and right sides as a backup swing tackle. While he may not leapfrog Josh Fryar for those duties as an immediate fill-in, Williams undoubtedly has secured his spot on the final 53 thanks to strong play we saw on his tape from Ole Miss.
Why he can make the roster: Leota has been a quietly impressive presence in the Cardinals' outside linebackers room this camp, consistently finding himself in the backfield. With so much noise around Josh Sweat and others falling in line, there hasn't quite been any standouts emerging from that room.
Leota would be the closest thing to that, and the coaching staff noticed after giving him some run with the first team defense towards the end of training camp. Leota still needs to perform in preseason, but with BJ Ojulari's stock trending down, this could be one of the biggest surprises on the roster.
