title: 14 Biggest Winners and Losers From Cardinals Training Camp
full_text:
Arizona Cardinals training camp is officially a thing of the past.
The Cardinals put a bow on their time at State Farm Stadium this week after 15 practices as preparation for the second portion of preseason will fully commence at Tempe the rest of the way.
It was a productive outing for head coach Mike LaFleur and his first summer running the Cardinals. Now, we inch closer to crafting a final 53-man roster with the regular season slowly but surely approaching.
Our biggest winners and losers from Glendale:
*Note, this is purely from a training camp practice perspective*
Why: The Cardinals' quarterback was already under contract and clearly won't be part of the team's future plans beyond 2026 — and still managed to get $15 million guaranteed from the organization. Brissett negotiated on his own (without an agent) and knew the Cardinals were in a position to meet him in the middle after already committing to him as their starter.
Brissett's a fine quarterback, better than most give him credit for. His overall cap number this year still doesn't sniff average starting quarterback money — though Brissett still was able to almost triple his money even after a statistically solid but overall poor 2025 season. That's a massive win.
Why: Benson needed to have a strong training camp to make the Cardinals think twice about moving on from him, especially after adding Jeremiyah Love and Tyler Allgeier this offseason. The results? Benson barely practiced during team drills thanks to his ongoing recovery from meniscus surgery while Bam Knight clearly established himself ahead in the pecking order.
In a league where the best ability is availability, Benson hasn't sniffed that and is considered to be a stretch to play in the preseason. The overwhelming feeling in the desert is Benson will either be traded or cut before the regular season, which is sad considering the former Day 2 pick was being talked about as a 1A/1B starter next to James Conner at this time just a year ago.
Why: Arizona's practically guaranteed to keep three running backs in Love, Allgeier and Conner. Conversations around potentially keeping a fourth rusher are ongoing, especially with the Cardinals pigeonholed in keeping three quarterbacks on the roster. If Arizona does keep a fourth running back, it's clearly Knight.
Knight impressed last preseason and has proven himself in new opportunities while the aforementioned Benson was sidelined. He also began practicing with special teams units later in camp, which improves his overall value and could be the deciding factor if he's one of the final candidates to crack the 53-man roster, especially after the Cardinals lost ace Joey Blount .
Why: Bisontis was a second-round pick, and a high one at that. There were massive expectations of Bisontis starting right away... but that hasn't been the case. Isaiah Adams has had a stranglehold on the position since the first moments of camp and never looked back.
Calling Bisontis a loser here feels harsh. He looked strong in the Hall of Fame Game, but it does feel as if it will take Adams playing poorly and "lose" the job for the rookie to enter the starting lineup in 2026. Given how high Bisontis was drafted, expectations of contributing immediately now have to be dampened.
Why: Adams was hit-and-miss through his first two seasons in the NFL, and if the Cardinals were supremely confident in his abilities, they wouldn't have taken Bisontis so high. Adams was shaky entering this summer, though it's been so far, so good for the third-year guard.
Adams has impressed the entire coaching staff and essentially has the starting job in his hands. Considering the overall outlook on Adams' trajectory and the Cardinals taking a potential replacement high in the draft, Adams emerging from camp as the starting right guard is a big win for him.
Why: Slovis had the chips stacked against him entering this training camp with two fresh additions to the quarterback room. Slovis, effectively Arizona's fourth quarterback, was relegated to not participating in team drills after Brissett returned.
Slovis' bags are all but packed at this point, as it's only a formality that he'll be cut barring an injury to any of the three quarterbacks ahead. Even if that were to happen, the Cardinals would likely cut Slovis and attempt to bring him back on the practice squad. Slovis, unfortunately, was doomed for this fate from the start.
Why: Seventh-round picks are often coin-flips to make a roster, let alone carving out roles with their play in training camp. Williams, a rookie tackle, went from being a massive question mark to an undeniable second-teamer that is getting reps on both the left and right side of the line of scrimmage.
Williams played some strong college ball but struggled with injuries, which hurt his draft stock. Now, the Cardinals could be on the verge of having a developmental gem on the roster. His rise up the depth chart has been nothing short of impressive.
Why: Christian Jones was a fifth-round pick in 2024 who made one start in his rookie season but didn't register an offensive snap last year. Jones landed on injured reserve during both of his first two seasons, and this offseason that led to the Cardinals signing a handful of cheap veteran placeholders to fill the depth.
The camp opportunities for Jones have dwindled, as he's often rotated with the third team when other times he's been off the field completely. Now, Jones is on the outside looking in of the roster with Williams and Fryar ahead of him as backup tackle options.
Why: This is a laundry list of players, but a blend of talent and play-design from LaFleur has seen Cardinals receivers open — often. Marvin Harrison Jr. bounced back nicely after early camp drops while Michael Wilson continues to steadily make plays. Kendrick Bourne, a free agent arrival, has quietly been a playmaker during camp, too.
Yet the list doesn't stop there. Rookie Reggie Virgil came on strong during the late stages of camp while Ihmir Smith-Marsette and Jalen Brooks are going to force a difficult decision on what the final receiver spot looks. Other depth guys such as Simi Fehoko, Xavier Weaver, Bryson Green and Harrison Wallace have made respective plays, too.
Quite frankly, all of have made plays.
Why: This was supposed to be a strong training camp outing for Ojulari after successfully recovering from his severe knee injury. In a weak Cardinals OLB room outside of Josh Sweat , Ojulari had every opportunity to kick that door down.
That's yet to happen. Ojulari has rotated up and down the depth chart with no noticeable impact as a pass rusher, and quite honestly he just might be one of the biggest cut candidates entering the next few weeks despite being a second-round pick.
Why: This seems like a same old song and dance with Robinson, who has previously had strong training camp performances before failing to make a regular season impact. While that can be true, Robinson has looked particularly strong this camp.
He's always looked the part in terms of size and speed, though this camp he was specifically winning one-on-one battles to reach the quarterback in pass rush opportunities, which was one of his biggest deficiencies as a player. This isn't a promise that he'll be better in 2026, but he's undoubtedly been a winner from camp.
Why: After the departure of Jalen Thompson this offseason, many (including yours truly) believed Taylor-Demerson was clearly in line to start next to Budda Baker. Even after Andrew Wingard signed, Taylor-Demerson was a favorite to finally step into starting duties after two seasons of impressive play as a backup.
When Wingard began taking snaps next to Baker in camp, not much was thought of it. Defensive coordinator Nick Rallis loves to rotate safeties and utilize a dime defense (which deploys three safeties), so it's not as if Taylor-Demerson wouldn't see the field.
However, it's become extremely apparent Wingard will be starting for the Cardinals this season,…

title: Kyler Murray Gives Classy Response When Asked About Cardinals Remarks
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals and Kyler Murray are handling their divorce amicably.
It's been months since the Cardinals released Murray, ending a seven-year relationship after making the former Heisman winner the No. 1 overall pick back in 2019.
Arizona quickly made the decision to move off Murray once new head coach Mike LaFleur entered the picture — that's from the head coach himself.
"I'd say pretty quickly. Once we made the decision that we were going to do that, the show goes on," LaFleur said after the Hall of Fame Game. "And that's quarterback all the way down to the punter to any coach. Like I've put on record, I think best for both parties, and so here we are."
This week, when asked about those words from LaFleur and if he was motivated by the Cardinals releasing him at the prime of his career, Murray responded with:
"I'm honestly not too worried about what's going on over there. Focused on what I got going on here in Minnesota. I'm glad to be here. Loved every part of being here and I'm focused on the future," he said.
#Vikings QB Kyler Murray’s thoughts on #Cardinals HC Mike LaFleur’s comments about Arizona moving on from K1 “quickly” “I’m not too worried about what’s going on over there. Focused on what I got going on here in Minnesota. Im glad to be here.” pic.twitter.com/sLHhqEk4ab
Murray just won the Minnesota Vikings' starting quarterback job ahead of the 2026 season. He inked a one-year deal to sign with Minnesota after Arizona released him.
As for the Cardinals, they signed veteran backup Gardner Minshew in free agency and drafted third-round pick Carson Beck to be behind the recently restructured Jacoby Brissett.
It was a move that was unfortunately needed from both parties, as Murray clearly wasn't working out in the desert while the Cardinals couldn't piece together a strong roster or coaching staff around him.
Once Murray departed Week 5 due to injury last season and Brissett took over, it was clear Murray's tenure in Arizona was running out.
"7 years…damn. I never wanted things to end like this," said Murray in a goodbye post once the transaction was made official.
"I want to acknowledge how grateful I am for the overwhelming love and optimism I’ve received since the news broke. I am so appreciative to all the genuine supporters I’ve made throughout my career. There’s not enough words to express how much the positivity has helped throughout this transition, I love you all."
Neither the Cardinals or Murray have bad-mouthed each other through the entire process, which has been refreshing to see — and quite honestly is welcomed after we've seen so many similar situations unfold differently.

title: Cardinals Had a Great Training Camp — Mike LaFleur Knows There's Still Work to Do
full_text:
GLENDALE — Mike LaFleur knows what a good training camp looks like.
After spending ample time under two of the NFL's best coaches in Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay, LaFleur's has a solid idea of what to expect walking into camp, how to navigate the dog days of summer and how to feel departing.
Yet LaFleur also knows what unsuccessful camps look like, too. His two-year stint as the New York Jets' offensive coordinator yielded forgettable results before being fired and eventually landing in Los Angeles under McVay.
The dust is now settling on LaFleur's first training camp with the Arizona Cardinals, one that was inspired by his time with the Rams. LaFleur says his four-day "block" setup of practice days was taken from McVay while other wrinkles such as utilizing instant replay during camp were also borrowed from prior stints.
What's one common denominator of a successful training camp — and did the Cardinals have one?
"They compete, and they compete the right way. It's like you got to be able to toe the line even with your brothers, and it's got to be physical," said LaFleur. "But it can't be reckless, and you got to take care of each other. So that's an ongoing process with every group I've ever been on. Even you know some of the best ones.
"That's the biggest thing. Just go out there, compete. Compete against your brothers, toe the line, play with that play style and go for it."
Whether the Cardinals had a successful training camp remains up to personal opinion. The offense and defense largely had respective ups-and-downs, though such is life during camp. Arizona emerged somewhat unscathed when it came to injuries, save for injured reserve additions such as Kaleb Proctor and Joey Blount.
It's especially difficult when LaFleur's balancing roster evaluation with installation of his first-year offense, one that admittedly has produced more promising days than negative ones. The run game has transformed and receivers are often open thanks to scheme and play-design.
"He's got a plan, and it's good to see. Not only just the offensive side of things, which obviously he's putting a lot of focus in there, but really the big picture and the whole team," said Cardinals GM Monti Ossenfort on LaFleur.
LaFleur, who admitted he was still figuring out minor details like where to stand on the sidelines while juggling attention to both sides of the ball now as a head coach, liked where his team was at overall, though there's still several strides to be made.
"They are where their feet are. They come to work every single day. They want to improve," he said when asked about what he's most pleased with.
"Again, I thought our operation was good — got a long way to go. I thought our play style was good — got a long way to go. And then they also know that we have a long way to go once that ball snapped in terms of details, fundamentals, all those kind of things within our scheme. So again, I was pleased with the work that we put in within that time, but a long way to go."
The Cardinals do have a long way to go, both physically and metaphorically. We're over a month removed from their regular season debut against the Los Angeles Chargers — which is just under 400 miles one-way.
Preparation for Week 1 is already well underway, and quite honestly it has been for awhile. The Cardinals admitted so back in June. Arizona will be far from a complete team at that point in time, though it will be a good starting point where wins and losses begin to matter.
There's plenty to be excited about regarding the Cardinals as they depart from camp with preseason battle No. 2 ensuing on Thursday. After returning from Las Vegas, they'll return to their home base in Tempe to get settled in before the regular season begins.
The offense looks promising in a multitude of ways while Arizona's defense will be tested. There's hope coordinator Nick Rallis — with a fresh but short leash after Jonathan Gannon was fired — will be able to right the ship with player health hopefully on his side.
As cliché as it sounds, only time will truly be able to tell how LaFleur's first training camp went. Arizona has a grueling regular season schedule, but excuses are like podcasts — everybody has one. The Cardinals have to be ready at SoFi Stadium on Sept. 13 and build off each performance that follows.
The heat in the desert is unique. It's not quite humid like parts in the Southeast while it reaches temperatures some along the West Coast wouldn't dream of.
While LaFleur says the team successfully kept his guys out of the scorching sun, soon he'll face a different kind of heat when records begin to matter.
"Absolutely. I think first and foremost, like we talked about, the weather and just keep these guys out of the heat," said LaFleur when asked if he accomplished what he wanted to in camp.
"We got to go battle it when we get back to Tempe, we'll be smart about that, obviously, but we are going to have to be out there at some point for obvious reasons. That was first and foremost, and like I said, we took it one day at a time, one block at a time, and I thought there was improvement, but still a long way to go."

title: How Marvin Harrison Jr. Flipped the Script After Viral Cardinals Camp Drop
full_text:
GLENDALE — The beginning of Arizona Cardinals training camp got off to a rocky start for star wideout Marvin Harrison Jr., as a string of early drops went viral for the third-year wideout.
Clips infested the internet, and it felt like everywhere you turned, you found videos or memes on Harrison.
Harrison, who had a roller-coaster start to his NFL career, is hoping to see a resurgence under new head coach and offensive play-caller Mike LaFleur .
Training camp is all about progression and improvement, and after Harrison's shaky start, LaFleur says the former No. 4 overall pick has bounced back quite nicely.
"Steady improvement," LaFleur said of Harrison's overall camp before diving into the prior drops.
"You could go very elementary, and it's like 'catch the football, never drop a ball.' Well, if you drop enough balls in this league, I don't care who you are, you're just not going to be in the league. So it's like, 'no kidding, put that away. Okay, why'd you drop it? Was it focus? What exactly was it?' All right, then you put that away, and then you really look at the process of everything. Are we creating separation? Are we coming off the ball? Like, are we in our right split? Are we are we loaded? Getting every inch of grass off the ball.
"That's one of the big things that Marv and I talk about every day. I just kind of give him one of these [leans], and what does that mean? Body lean, come off the rock, because once he gets going, he's a big dude, right? And if I'm a DB standing there, knowing I got a big dude that could run by me or can stop on a dime, that's tough.
"... Yes, he had a drop back in whatever it was, practice five, where he was wide open. Hasn't had one of those since. Great. Is he going to have probably another one at some point over his career? Yes, he is. Just like all these guys are. Then I'll flip it to the other side. What does it look like when he doesn't have the ball? What does it look like when he's getting connected? And [when] I say he, I mean all these guys. If you don't block, if you don't get sticky on DB's in this offense, you're just not going to be out there. Like, point blank period. I've been pleased with his progression and the receivers' progression in that facet of what we're trying to get done in the run game."
Harrison was open nearly as much as anybody after that point. That was never the problem, though from that moment forward, Harrison flipped a switch and made plays when called upon.
The Cardinals will need every bit of strong play possible from Harrison if they'll get things back on track. Harrison possesses all the tools needed out of a primary NFL receiving option — he's just got to go and do it.
Perhaps another year with quarterback Jacoby Brissett tossing him the ball will help.
"I think he's taken tremendous steps as far as understanding this is a long process," Brissett told reporters.
"The end result is not going to be tomorrow, and that's a battle. That's a battle for him, me, everybody on the team. The hard part is you want the results now. You want to go out there and do everything the right way, but that's why we're in the room that we're in, and and we have the opportunity to go out there and play in the National Football League because we know we can. It's just a matter of, now you got to sustain that competitive edge on a day in and day out process."
The good news? Harrison is in an advanced offense that won't solely rely on him to make plays. We've seen LaFleur consistently scheme receivers open and between the likes of Michael Wilson, Trey McBride and Jeremiyah Love among others, there's plenty of help around him.
This doesn't have to be a one-man band with Harrison — nor will it. It was encouraging to see Harrison bounce back after such a rocky start to camp.
Perhaps this is a springboard to something bigger.

title: Mike LaFleur Delivers Preseason News Cardinals Fans Have Been Waiting For
full_text:
GLENDALE — Last week, the Arizona Cardinals sat roughly 35 players who were considered starters or borderline guys.
This week, it's a different story.
The Cardinals will play their starters in Las Vegas, according to LaFleur.
"They're going to play. So we'll have our guys out there. How much? It's not going to be much. Could be one drive, max of two [drives] for those main guys. But yeah, they'll be playing, and they know that," LaFleur said ahead of the Raiders game.
Arizona's biggest veteran names that featured last week were all of Dadrion Taylor-Demerson, BJ Ojulari and Andrew Billings.
This week, the Cardinals are set to see most of their starting lineup on the field for at least a drive or two — which will see players such as Jacoby Brissett, Marvin Harrison Jr., Trey McBride, Jeremiyah Love and Budda Baker among others who weren't dressed for the Hall of Fame Game.
The Raiders are expected to play their starters this preseason, though we'll also get our first look of No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza in a Las Vegas uniform on Thursday night.
"From just an actual game plan standpoint, we're not doing any of that. Like I haven't watched the snap of Vegas from last year," LaFleur said. "It's a new defensive coordinator. He was on the staff. Don't know if he's going to do the exact same or complete opposite. Have no idea."
After a big game last week, the Cardinals again will be in the national spotlight.
Today's practice puts a bow on training camp for the Cardinals, and LaFleur says the team had a successful outing in 2026:
"Absolutely. I think first and foremost, like we talked about, the weather and just keep these guys out of the heat," said LaFleur.
"We got to go battle it when we get back to Tempe, we'll be smart about that, obviously, but we are going to have to be out there at some point for obvious reasons. That was first and foremost, and like I said, I mean, we took it one day at a time, one block at a time, and I thought we there was improvement, but still a long way to go."
The Cardinals face the Raiders at Allegiant Stadium at 5:00 PM on Thursday night.
Arizona will have practiced 15 times before gathering their belongings and heading back to Tempe to finish out the preseason. The Cardinals, after this week, have preseason battles against the Dallas Cowboys and Green Bay Packers before the start of the regular season.

title: 2 Big-Name Cardinals On The Verge of Being Cut
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are one practice away from completely finishing training camp.
The team has spent weeks at State Farm Stadium in an attempt to perfect its craft, define roles and identify the best 53 players to carry into the regular season.
We've seen numerous players grow into their respective roles — while others have simply fallen out of favor.
In particular, two notable names find themselves on the verge of potentially being cut with three preseason games remaining:
Benson, a former third-round pick, clearly has potential to be a big-play running back. He's flashed that on multiple occasions through his first two seasons in Arizona.
Yet a mix of injuries and inconsistent play has put his Cardinals tenure in jeopardy as we enter the depths of the preseason. Arizona brought in Tyler Allgeier and Jeremiyah Love this offseason to take over the backfield, and with James Conner on the roster, Benson is at best battling with Bam Knight for RB4 duties.
That's a battle Knight is winning, as Benson hasn't practiced lately due to his knee injury while Knight is getting reps ahead of him. Another point to Knight's favor is his recent participation in special teams, which can make or break a player's chances of making the roster.
The conversation has now shifted from "Benson vs Knight" to "will Arizona keep Knight as a fourth running back?" ahead of cut-down day.
"Versatility comes into play there. Whether it's versatility on what they can do positionally, whether it's first and second down or third down. When it comes to special teams, that starts weighing into it," Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort said.
As for Benson, the possibility of either trade or release looms in the coming weeks barring an eye-opening turnaround.
Benson feels closer to actually being cut than Ojulari, though the former second-round pick very much finds himself on the ropes this preseason similar to Benson.
Injuries decimated a once exciting young career for Ojulari, who was shaping up to be a strong presence at outside linebacker before a severe knee injury knocked him out for 1.5 seasons. Ojulari's been on the bounce-back since the second half of last season, though he hasn't quite looked like the player he did coming out of LSU.
The good news for Ojulari? The Cardinals added no substantial help at outside linebacker this offseason, opting to run it back with virtually the same crew of names as before in Josh Sweat, Baron Browning, Jordan Burch, Zaven Collins and Ojulari.
However, Ojulari has struggled to separate himself during training camp, and last week's preseason outing was quite telling. In a game where the Cardinals didn't play any of their starters, Ojulari played deep into the second half against Carolina — and failed to make an impact.
"He's a fast rusher off that edge right there, and I just think it's just for him just continue to get time on task, value received. Continuing to practice," head coach Mike LaFleur said on Ojulari.
"Obviously, there's history in terms of just some of the injuries with him obviously, and just getting back out there, getting his feet underneath him, getting comfortable, using his fastball — which he has a fastball."
That fastball hasn't crossed the plate in 2026, and while Eku Leota continues to climb the Cardinals' depth chart, Ojulari is in serious danger of being off the roster.

title: Cardinals GM Monti Ossenfort Said 6 Big Things Today: Carson Beck, Josh Sweat & More
full_text:
GLENDALE — The Arizona Cardinals are nearly done with training camp.
The Cardinals wrapped up a jog-through today and are set for one last practice tomorrow before officially wrapping things up here at State Farm Stadium.
Arizona made general manager Monti Ossenfort available for reporters today — here's our biggest takeaways from what he said:
The Cardinals have all of Paris Johnson Jr., Michael Wilson and Garrett Williams eligible for massive contract extensions, though Arizona hasn't inked any of the aforementioned players just yet.
"I think the track record here the last three years is we've done extensions before the season, during the season, after the season. I think as with any negotiation/extension, those things take time, and there's a lot of conversations that go on," Ossenfort said.
"Sometimes the timelines are different, and when those match up, and when those discussions can come to agreement. I don't think there's any hard or fast rule, and I think really they come by a case-by-case basis."
Names such as Hjalte Froholdt and Dante Stills are also possible names to watch.
LaFleur, entering his first season as a head coach, has arrived prepared according to Ossenfort.
"He's got a plan, and it's good to see. Not only just the offensive side of things, which obviously he's putting a lot of focus in there, but really the big picture and the whole team," said Ossenfort.
"When you sit in that chair, a lots on your plate in terms of organization, not just the football product, but it's everything that we do. Meeting schedule, practice schedule, how we travel, everything that goes into it, and he's been he's been ready for it. He's had a plan, and it's been exciting to watch him put it in place here over the last few weeks."
Beck has been the talk of the town really since he arrived in the desert, though last week's preseason performance has plenty of buzz around the third-round pick.
So far, so good from Ossenfort's standpoint.
"I thought he got off to a good start. I think the most optimistic thing was just the clean operation," said Ossenfort.
"The way they got in and out of the huddle, the way that he handled the checks that came his way, he got the ball out of his hand, put it in the right spot. He was accurate, so [a] very positive start. A good start. It kind of builds off of what he's been doing since he got here in the spring and the early part of training camp. Obviously still got a long way to go, but thought that was a good next step in his development."
The current starter, Jacoby Brissett, is still catching up to the team's playbook after recently ending his holdout. Brissett saw a restructured deal pay him at least $15 million guaranteed for 2026.
Why did the Cardinals negotiate with a player who was already under contract through this season and clearly was not part of their plans moving forward?
"I think when we signed him, it was in a different role, and so we signed Jacoby to be a backup quarterback, and his role changed. His job changed, and the expectation changed, and so really that is what it came down to," said Ossenfort, who also added:
"With what Jacoby did last year, what he meant to the locker room — I think you guys saw just the the reaction of his teammates and how excited they were — we were excited to get the deal done with him and move forward."
Sweat's been mentioned in consistent trade buzz after the Cardinals fired Jonathan Gannon, though the team is adamant Sweat will not only be healthy for the regular season opener as he manages a knee issue — Ossenfort says the team flat-out is not interested in trading him.
"I'd say [trade] discussions that come by that, there's always a lot of talk that goes around that. We have no interest in trading Josh. We're excited to have him," he said. "Some of those discussions [we're] going to keep private. But excited to have Josh here, [he] had a great year last year. Excited for more good things out of him this year."
Love, since arriving to the desert, has been a showstopper in nearly every opportunity. He looks the part, has proved he can get open as a receiver and obviously has hit some home runs when toting the rock.
Ossenfort had a laundry list of things he liked about the No. 3 overall pick:
"Mature, professional, eager to learn, very coachable, versatile, able to do a lot of different things with him. I think coachability is a big thing. Jeremiyah was obviously a very talented player coming out [as] a high draft pick, but his improvement over the last couple weeks, just with his running style and his reads, and putting his foot in the ground and getting upfield, I think we've seen growth in that in a very short time once the pads came on," said Ossenfort.
"That's great to see out of a young player that wants to learn, wants to contribute, wants to find a role for the team, and he's been great in that respect. So excited to keep using him in multiple ways, and he's a guy that's going to help us put pressure on the defense."

title: Cardinals GM Slams Door Shut on Josh Sweat Trade Rumors
full_text:
GLENDALE — Josh Sweat has made headlines throughout the 2026 offseason, and as the team ramps up for their second preseason game, the Arizona Cardinals' top sack artist still has yet to practice.
Sweat, placed on the Physically Unable to Perform list at the beginning of camp, hasn't been spotted on the sidelines during Cardinals training camp practices as he is working through a knee injury according to head coach Mike LaFleur.
While he can't technically practice due to his placement on PUP, Sweat was also not a participant during mandatory minicamp while he wasn't present during offseason team activities, either.
Trade buzz has followed Sweat since the Cardinals fired head coach Jonathan Gannon, someone Sweat was close to. Today, when speaking with reporters, general manager Monti Ossenfort shut those talks down.
"Josh is making good progress. Josh is getting closer every day. I think Josh is going to be out there in due time to get ready for the season opener, and we're excited to get him out there and get him going," said Ossenfort.
"I'd say [trade] discussions that come by that, there's always a lot of talk that goes around that. We have no interest in trading Josh. We're excited to have him. Some of those discussions [we're] going to keep private. But excited to have Josh here, [he] had a great year last year. Excited for more good things out of him this year."
Sweat, who just turned 29, reportedly had multiple NFL teams calling the Cardinals about his availability this offseason. Yet with a thin Cardinals pass rush room, it didn't make sense for the organization to part ways with their only productive outside linebacker.
Sweat's managing a knee issue, which has mostly led to his absence throughout the bulk of the offseason and camp. The Cardinals are confident he'll be ready for the start of the regular season.
"He's in all the meetings. He's around. I know I've said it, so broken record there, but he looks really good in terms of [being] healthy, in shape, all those kind of things," LaFleur said earlier in camp.
"He's putting a lot of work in behind the scenes to make sure when he gets the green light and everyone feels good. Ultimately [we're] making sure Josh feels good both mentally and physically to go out there and perform the way [he can] because he takes a lot of pride in what his product looks like. That tape matters a lot to him as I've gotten to know him. So he's earned the right to communicate with us to say, 'hey, I feel good, I'm ready to go.'"
It will be interesting to monitor how things go for the Cardinals this season and if their trade deadline plans change at all.
It's clear there's a market for Sweat.

title: Falcons Name QB Plan vs. Broncos: 5 Key Observations from Final Practice
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - The Atlanta Falcons have gone through free agency, the NFL Draft, rookie minicamp, OTAs, mandatory minicamp, and training camp, and they finally get to open the 2026 season against the Denver Broncos on Friday for preseason game one.
The quarterback battle between Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr. was settled by default for the matchup against the Broncos. Penix hasn't been fully cleared for contact, and head coach Kevin Stefanski named Tagovailoa the starter for Friday night's game.
Stefanski also said he plans to play the starters at least one series , and maybe more depending on the player, a drastic change over recent years when Arthur Smith treated the preseason with disdain and Raheem Morris tried to avoid them altogether.
The Falcons were in a short session on Wednesday, in their last full practice before Friday (Thursday is a walk-through). Here are some of the key things we saw and learned, other than the starting quarterback.
Cooper Rush will be the next man up after Tagovailoa's game is finished. Undrafted free agent rookie Jack Strand will finish the game. Rush joined the team on the first day of training camp, and Strand had gotten a lot of action with Penix and Tagovailoa limited, but has seen that scaled back in recent days with Rush taking more snaps with the No. 2 offense.
Second-year edge rusher is the only serious injury of the preseason, but there have been several players missing from action this week. Safety Jessie Bates, edge rusher Bralen Trice, linebacker Divine Deablo, defensive tackle Da'Shawn Hand, and cornerback Avieon Terrell have all been held out of action. It would be a surprise to see any of them on Friday.
Offensive tackle Jawaan Taylor was on the field Wednesday, and Zach Harrison has been a full participant this week. Taylor likely won't play on Friday, but we may see some snaps from Harrison.
With Deablo out, rookie linebackers Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins Jr. have seen extensive time working with what we would call the first-team defense. Safety Sydney Brown was acquired in a trade before the draft and should see plenty of time along with veteran DeMarcco Hellams.
Jake Matthews had a veteran rest day on Wednesday, and Michael Jerrell saw all of his reps at left tackle. Jerrell had been part of a rotation at right tackle that has also included rookie Ethan Onianwa and Brandon Walton. All three players should see extensive action against the Broncos.
Nickel has been the other position that's seen a lot of rotation, including Terrell. With Terrell out and Brown seeing more time at safety, it's a chance for A.J. Woods and Darnay Holmes to hoover up the bulk of the reps.
They were helped by a stiff wind at their backs, but punters Jake Bailey and Matthew Hayball were routinely hitting 60+ yard punts inside the 10-yard line. Bailey will be the team's punter this year, and when they moved to midfield, Bailey still showed good placement on his short punts.
Rookie Zachariah Branch should get his first chance to return punts and kicks against a live defense this week. He's looked electric as a wide receiver, but the team has been going through the motions in kick returns and coverage.
No, not that one, and probably not the other one you're thinking of either. Safety Jammie Robinson was back on the field for the first time. He had a nice interception on a tipped pass from Tua Tagovailoa. The quarterback extended the play, then extended it some more in what likely would have been a tackle-or-throw-away situation in a real game, before throwing into traffic that included Kyle Pitts and Drake London.
Robinson came down with the ball and will hope to push for a spot on the 53-man roster.
The Falcons will have a walk-through at Flowery Branch on Thursday before taking on the Broncos on Friday night at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. Long-time Falcons tormentor Sean Payton brings a strong Broncos squad to Atlanta, and he has typically played a lot of starters in the preseason as well.
The Falcons had 44 of 90 players on one-year, or the last year, of their contracts, and competition should be fierce despite the generally blase nature of preseason games.

title: Kevin Stefanski Explains Why Falcons Starters Will Play in Preseason vs. Broncos
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – Kevin Stefanski officially announced that Tua Tagovailoa and several starters will be active for the Atlanta Falcons ’ Friday night preseason game with the Denver Broncos. The plan is written “in pencil,” but it will be the first time that the starters have seen action in several years.
Under Stefanski, the Falcons are taking a very different approach, and the preseason playing time of starters is just the most recent of these changes. The head coach has also instituted live tackling periods to build calluses for the players ahead of a rough regular season.
“It’s callus, but don’t blister,” he explained about his methodology during the summer. “The mindset being, we’re not just going to work for the sake of doing work, or beat guys up for the sake of beating guys up. It’s all with a plan in mind to get the guys ready for a 17-game season, and then more if you earn it. In order to do that, you need to be physically ready for that challenge, and you need to be mentally ready for that challenge.”
Atlanta enters the season with several unresolved position battles and a quarterback competition still underway, so this evaluation period is at a premium. They have several prominent players, namely Bijan Robinson, Drake London, and others who may still not play, but also plenty of other question marks.
“Preseason football will resemble the closest [thing we have] to regular season football,” Stefanski said. “Schematically, it’s not exactly the same thing, but the fundamentals and techniques don’t change. I think there’s value in getting game reps with your fundamentals and techniques in mind.”
Aside from the quarterback, they need answers at right tackle, linebacker, wide receiver, and nickel corner. Stefanski did not specify who would play at these spots, but several players are competing for playing time and will see sufficient action.
“We will vary playing time by players,” he said. “So, there are some guys who may get more. Some guys who may get less, but we are just trying to get our guys ready for the season based on what we think they need in these games.”
The Falcons will prepare for this matchup, but it will not be a “full game plan.” Stefanski said they will look back at previous preseason games the Broncos have played, just to get a feel for coverages and fronts.
“I don't believe in showing a lot in the preseason and doing all sorts of exotic things and whatnot,” Stefanski said. Later explaining “It’s really about us, and for it to be about us, we have to keep it simple and let those guys just play.”
As of Wednesday, the expectation is that Tagovailoa and the starters will get a series, or about 10 plays, whichever comes first. Stefanski later clarified that this does not mean that Tagovailoa will be the starter come Week 1, saying the team “will cross that bridge when we get to it.”
After that drive, backup quarterback Cooper Rush will rotate in under center, followed by rookie undrafted free agent Jack Strand. Incumbent starter Michael Penix Jr., who has yet to be cleared for team drills, will not be available on Friday. Stefanski said he remains encouraged by Penix's progress, though the quarterback has yet to receive medical clearance for team drills.
Penix will travel with the team ahead of their second preseason game with the Indianapolis Colts, but he will again be limited to individual drills and 7-on-7 action.

title: Kevin Stefanski Names Starting QB for Falcons' Preseason Clash with Broncos
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - With two days remaining before the Atlanta Falcons open up their preseason against the Denver Broncos on Friday evening at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, the only thing we really knew going in was that Michael Penix Jr. would not be playing .
Penix has yet to be cleared for 11v11 at training camp, while Tua Tagovailoa, Cooper Rush, and Jack Strand took turns running team sessions. Penix has competed in everything else at training camp, dating back to OTAs in June, but the Falcons and his medical team are taking extra precautions with his surgically repaired knee.
Tagovailoa missed the first week of training camp as well with back tightness. He was cleared as a full participant this week and has looked sharp running the offense. Head coach Kevin Stefanski confirmed Tagovailoa will start against the Denver Broncos.
"The plan for play time it's in pencil, and we need to get through this practice to then get it into pen, but feel good about it," Stefanski said on Wednesday afternoon. "We'll play our starters a series, maybe 10 plays to see how that feels, and then we'll roll our guys through. We'll also vary playing time by player. Some guys may get more; some guys may get less.
"Tua will start in this game. I won't go up and down the roster player by player, but just understand that we'll vary."
Stefanski was quick to point out that Tagovailoa being named the starter doesn't mean he's named a starter for Week 1 against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
"I know the semantics (of what he said). I'm not there yet," Stefanski said. "We're not there to name a starter for Week 1. We'll cross that bridge."
Strand was signed as an undrafted free agent by the Falcons out of Minnesota State-Moorhead. With both potential starting quarterbacks limited or out in the first week of training camp, he took advantage of his opportunity . He's a big quarterback at 6'5 and 240+ pounds and has a quick, 3/4 release and a strong arm.
He stands to get a lot of action during the Falcons' three preseason games as he attempts to make the initial 53-man roster as a third quarterback. The Falcons took just two quarterbacks last year, Penix and Kirk Cousins.
Cooper Rush joined the Falcons on the first day of training camp. Trevor Siemian was signed as a free agent in the spring, but he was waived before ever suiting up for Atlanta. Rush got the call the day before camp, signed, and was on the field the next morning. He has looked like a steady presence the Falcons needed at camp to help run the 90-man practices and get everyone reps.
Rush has 16 starts in his career, including eight in 2024 with the Dallas Cowboys. He has a 9-7 record as a starter in an eight-year NFL career.
Stefanski confirmed Rush would be the second quarterback in behind Tagovailoa, followed by Rush to finish the game against the Broncos.
Stefanski noted last week that he believed in starters playing in the preseason and pegged game one against the Broncos and game three against the Dolphins as the games starters will see action. The Falcons travel to Indianapolis next week for joint practices with the Colts before they face each other in game two. Stefanski said the presumed starters will get the bulk of the reps in joint practices, giving reserves a much bigger chance to shine in the second game.

title: Falcons Rookie Linebacker Getting Surprise Reps with 1st Team
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - Harold Perkins Jr. is making an early impression on the Atlanta Falcons defense.
The rookie linebacker out of LSU has already earned significant reps with the starting defense throughout training camp.
But the sixth-round NFL Draft pick isn’t surprised. It’s what he expected.
“I feel regular. I do this every day,” Perkins told reporters after practice on Monday, Aug 10. “This ain’t nothing new.”
Perkins is primarily playing the inside linebacker spot in Atlanta’s starting rotation. It’s one of many positions he played for the LSU Tigers, where he starred as an edge rusher, inside linebacker, and safety.
His versatility made him a potential draft steal for the Falcons.
“I think anytime that you have an opportunity as a young player to get reps with the ones or move up from the threes or the twos, it’s a great test for our guys,” Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski said.
“I think ‘Perk’ has continued to get better every day,” the head coach added. “Certainly, I’ve shared that with ‘Perk,’ just making sure he stacks these days. He’s being very diligent about what he has to do on our defense and on special teams.”
Perkins has ascended as an echoing voice and a helping hand for the Falcons’ defense.
He’s part of a youth movement that also features former Oklahoma Sooner and fellow rookie Kendal Daniels earning valuable time in the first defense as a mike linebacker. Daniels wears the green dot for the second-team defense, meaning he handles defensive play-call communications.
Perkins and Daniels are training camp roommates, and also lived together during rookie minicamp earlier this summer.
“Great person,” Daniels said of Perkins. “Keeps me going. Tells me the plays when I mess up. He helps me out a lot. Great player.”
Though taking linebacker responsibilities, Perkins could also get increased playing time as an edge rusher during the 2026 season. The Falcons will be without their rising star Jalon Walker, after the second-year edge tore his left ACL at training camp .
“It’s just football,” Perkins said, “My mindset is just to go out there and kill.”
Perkins will make his NFL preseason debut on Friday, Aug. 14, against the Denver Broncos.
That will be the first in-game evaluation of his impact in defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich’s system.
“The mentality of our defense, we want to be the alphas,” Perkins said. “We want to come out and stamp things from the go.”
Falcons-Broncos will kick off at 7 p.m. at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. It will be televised locally on Fox 5 Atlanta, the ESPN app with an unlimited plan, or NFL+.

title: Falcons' Zachariah Branch Is Turning Heads at Training Camp
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons believe they have something in Zachariah Branch, and the early returns from training camp have done nothing to dampen those expectations for the rookie.
The Falcons saw a player too talented to pass up, with the Georgia product dropping to them in the third round (12th wide receiver taken) despite finishing with 811 receiving yards and an SEC-leading 81 receptions during his lone season in Athens. Despite his output and outstanding measurables (4.35-second 40-yard dash and 20 reps of 225 pounds on the bench press), there were concerns about his diminutive frame and lack of a route tree coming out of college.
Ian Cunningham was happy to take the chance on him, and whether it has come on the practice field or in front of the media, the rookie has done nothing but impress since. After many initially thought he would be relegated to a kick return/gadget role as a rookie, Branch has quickly raised the bar for what could come from his first professional season.
“Zachariah, we continue to give a little bit more to each day,” Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski said. “It goes back to really all these guys just trying to find roles for them as they earn them and trying to find different things that they can do that can help our offense or our defense. In this case with Zachariah, it's what routes do we feel like he can run really well, and then what personnel groupings do we want to get him in there.
“He's earning that because he practices very hard, [and] is showing up in these drills. When you go to team drills and it's 11-on-11, he continues to show up.”
Branch is finding a role, ironically being utilized in one of the things that helped him drop to the Falcons back in April. The offense has spent much of the early weeks of camp working on its screen game, heavily utilizing both Branch and All-Pro running back Bijan Robinson.
This usage plays nicely into what the rookie does best, and that role will help him adjust to life in the NFL this season, even if he sees more for himself. Branch’s new teammates are learning firsthand how he can change a play once the ball touches his hands.
“He's very explosive – down the field, in the short game, catching the ball and transitioning into a runner,” Michael Penix Jr. explained about what makes Branch such a dangerous player. “With the ball in his hands, he’s definitely special. That's somebody we want to get the ball to a lot this year, so he's definitely been looking good.”
“That dude can be anywhere,” Tua Tagovailoa added during the first week of training camp. “You find him, he’s open. That dude, he’s fast. He can get away from guys. Great separation, great hands and great elusiveness when the ball’s in his hands.”
Branch has made an impression, but the early success comes as no surprise to Cash Jones. The other Georgia rookie on the Falcons’ roster this summer spent only one year with Branch, and his early impact was expected.
Jones knew from “day one” that Branch was different, both on and off the field. The two met briefly, but he quickly learned that the former five-star wideout was much more than just a speedster.
“He’s a freak athlete, and he can be running at full speed and stop on a dot. He has great hands. He’s a super smart kid,” Jones said. “I’m super excited to see what happens this year for him.”
Finding small improvements and carving out a role is paramount in the do-or-die NFL, whether that comes on offense or special teams. To this point, Branch has accomplished that and then some.
The next test comes Friday night, when Branch will make his preseason debut at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. For a rookie who has spent the first week of camp expanding expectations, it will be his first chance to show that the hype can translate to game action.

title: Falcons Add More OL Depth, Sign Former Eagles, Alabama OL
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - The Atlanta Falcons got some good injury news on Monday morning when they cleared offensive tackle Jawaan Taylor for practice and removed him from the PUP List. Taylor wasn't seen at practice yet on Tuesday morning, and the Falcons are still looking far and wide to address their offensive line depth.
On Tuesday afternoon, they put a claim on former Alabama Crimson Tide offensive lineman Jaeden Roberts, who was previously with the Philadelphia Eagles as an undrafted free agent. Roberts was placed on waivers by the Eagles, and he didn't last long before the Falcons claimed him.
Roberts was a combine invite in February. He didn't participate in any of the agility drills, but he measured a massive 6'5 1/4" and 333 pounds and did 25 reps on the bench press with 33 3/8" arms.
He was a three-year starter at Alabama and was a preseason All-American heading into 2025. He played in 10 games last season after starting 12 in 2024. He was on the Outland Trophy watch list in both 2024 and 2025, but regressed some last season with Alabama.
Roberts will compete with Kyle Hinton, Kam Dewberry, and Layden Robinson for a reserve guard spot. The Falcons took nine offensive linemen on their 53-man roster last season, and if they take nine again this year, it's likely to be Jake Matthews, Matthew Bergeron, Ryan Neuzil, Chris Lindstrom, Jawaan Taylor, Wanya Morris, Michael Jerrell, Hinton, and either Corey Levin or James Brockermeyer as the backup center.
Roberts has an uphill battle to climb to make the 53-man roster, but he could be a practice squad candidate after cuts on August 30th, when the roster must move from 90 players to 53.
The Falcons take on the Denver Broncos on Friday night in their first preseason action of 2026 under new head coach Kevin Stefanski. Roberts isn't likely to see much, if any, action with just a maximum of two days of preparation before Friday night's contest.
However, Stefanski has said he prefers starters to play in preseason games to get ready for the season. He has pegged Friday night's game against the Broncos and the preseason game three against the Miami Dolphins on August 28th as starter games. Game two next week against the Indianapolis Colts will not include many, if any, starters, as the team uses its joint practices to get first-team reps.
Roberts is just the latest player to join the Falcons this week. They've also added edge rusher Cameron Sample , running back Trey Sermon , and tight end Nick Muse as they work their way through the dog days of August to get ready for their Week 1 clash with the Pittsburgh Steelers on September 13th.

title: Will Tua Tagovailoa Play In Preseason Opener? Potential Falcons QB1 Weighs In
full_text:
Tua Tagovailoa is days away from his first opportunity to showcase himself with the keys to the Atlanta Falcons offense.
However, it remains unclear if the quarterback will play in Friday, Aug. 14’s preseason opener against the Buffalo Bills at Atlanta’s Mercedes-Benz Stadium.
“Whatever is asked of me, whatever’s asked of the guys,” Tagovailoa told reporters after practice on Tuesday, Aug. 11. “I think that’s what we’re going to go with, whatever Stefanski has.”
Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski has said in training camp that he plans to play starters in the first preseason game against the Bills and the finale against the Miami Dolphins on Aug. 28. Starters will likely rest during game two at the Indianapolis Colts on Aug. 22, with most of their reps coming in the joint practices.
Stefanski may have an answer on Wednesday, Aug. 12, on whether Tagovailoa plays in Friday’s preseason game.
“I’ll let you guys know I think, Wednesday when we talk what the plan is for the preseason games,” the head coach said. “I want to obviously sit down with the coaches and Ian and Matt, and talk through the plan, and finalize that, share it with the players, and then I’ll share it with you guys.”
Preseason could be key for Tagovailoa getting ahead in his ongoing quarterback battle with Michael Penix Jr. The former Miami Dolphin and seventh-year NFL veteran has picked up the majority of the 11-on-11 reps. Conversely, Penix takes most of the 7-on-7 plays due to not being cleared for 11-on-11 while he recovers from a left ACL tear.
There’s currently no timetable for Atlanta to name a starting quarterback.
“Preseason plays a big role for your team collectively,” Tagovailoa said. “You don’t have the coaches out there. You’ve got to go out there, make the calls, whether it’s right or wrong, you’ve got to live with them. And from there, you come in the next day, watch film, talk about it, and go from there.”
Tagovailoa has been impressive in the days leading up to the NFL preseason, following a back tightness flare-up that forced him to miss the first day of training camp .
His field vision and ability to exploit defensive breakdowns have turned heads.
“He’s getting better every day,” said Falcons quarterbacks coach Alex Van Pelt. “I think he’s getting more comfortable with the system, the play calls, and the protection adjustments. It’s tough always coming into a new system. So, picking that up, missing the first part of camp, set him back just a little bit. But the last three or four days, he’s really come on.”
The Falcons-Broncos preseason opener kicks off in Atlanta at 7 p.m. It will be televised locally on Fox 5 Atlanta, the ESPN app with an unlimited plan, or NFL+.

title: Atlanta Falcons Diving Into the Void (Years) with Latest Contracts
full_text:
With all of the changes in the Atlanta Falcons front office this past season, there was a move that went mostly unnoticed but is already having an impact. That move was the hiring of Bryce Johnston as the Senior Vice President of Football Administration/Senior Personnel Executive.
This is a big title that pretty much just means Johnston is in charge of all contract negotiations and the team's cap management strategy. Johnston has had plenty of work to do early in his tenure with the team, extending the contracts of wide receiver Drake London, running back Bijan Robinson, guard Matthew Bergeron, and tight end Kyle Pitts.
Those contract extensions included a bunch of void years, which many football fans have become used to hearing recently. But what is a void year and what does it do?
A void year is essentially “fake” years added to the end of a contract to help spread out the cap hit over more years. The signing bonus cap hit will be spread out across these void years as long as the player stays with the team he signed the contract with. Teams can add up to five void years in a contract.
This allows teams to be more flexible with their cap space now at the risk of it coming back to bite them in the future if the player decides to leave. A new contract or extension can include some of the money that was pushed into void years to avoid the balance coming due all at once.
This void year strategy has gained popularity recently and was heavily used by Johnston's former employer, the Philadelphia Eagles, where he served as a cap space strategist.
The strategy works well at creating some extra cap space and doesn’t really have any drawbacks as long as the players re-sign with the team and your owner has a lot of cash on hand to give out large signing bonuses.
So how did Johnston apply this void year strategy to the Falcons' recent contract extensions?
To start, there are four void years applied to Pitts' extension, and five applied to London, Robinson, and Bergeron’s deals. In total, that is 19 void years for signing bonuses to be extended over.
The result is over $10 million in cap savings for this year, despite handing out massive extensions. The team has the flexibility to use on plugging holes that are bound to pop up as the season progresses, including a possible edge replacement following the Jalon Walker injury. The Falcons can also carry the savings into next season.
The collateral is a possible $115 million dead cap hit if none of them resign with the team when their extensions run out. That is why these extensions and void years in particular point to an obvious point the front office is making: invest in young talent. Bergeron is the oldest of the quartet at just 26 years old.
Matt Ryan, Ian Cunningham, and Johnston believe that the Falcons have a strong young core on the offensive side of the ball and want to keep these players around for years to come despite the risk that comes with it.
Void years, contract extensions, and cap space are all very confusing and are handled by people much smarter than me, but hopefully this story gave some insight into the Falcons' extensions and cap space strategy.

title: Falcons Making Moves, Sign former Minnesota Vikings Tight End
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - The Atlanta Falcons have been busy this week making roster moves as they fine-tune their 90-man training camp roster ahead of their clash on Friday night with the Denver Broncos.
On Monday, they announced they had activated offensive lineman Jawaan Taylor and signed edge rusher Cameron Sample and running back Trey Sermon.
They announced another move on Tuesday morning with the signing of former Minnesota Vikings tight end Nick Muse. In a pair of corresponding moves, they waived undrafted free agent wide receiver Le'Meke Brockington and linebacker Malik Verdon.
Muse was originally a seventh-round selection by the Vikings in the 2022 NFL Draft from the South Carolina Gamecocks. Muse spent three years in Columbia and had his best season in 2020 with 30 catches for 425 yards and a touchdown.
He played 16 games with the Vikings in three years, mostly on special teams. He had one catch for 22 yards in 2023.
He's spent the last year playing the roster shuffle on several teams' practice squads, including the New York Jets, Detroit Lions, and LA Rams.
New head coach Kevin Stefanski has expressed interest in playing some three-tight-end sets on offense, and Atlanta has three tight ends that appear to be locks to make the roster in Kyle Pitts Sr., Austin Hooper, and Charlie Woerner. Joshua Simon and Jack Velling are the only other tight ends at training camp, and neither of them appears to definitively warrant a spot on the 53.
More likely, the Falcons could keep two tight ends on the practice squad and take turns using game-day elevations if they want to add a fourth tight end for games.
Brockington was signed by the Falcons as an undrafted free agent, but he wasn't able to separate himself from the crowd to try and make the Falcons' roster as a fifth or sixth receiver, if they decide to keep six.
Drake London, Jahan Dotson, Olamide Zaccheaus, and Zachariah Branch are all but locks to make the team. Chris Blair has been the best receiver outside of that quartet, and his special teams contributions may help determine if he can beat out Dylan Drummond and/or Cash Jones for a 5th spot. Jones looks like he could be the guy if the Falcons keep six. He has versatility to play slot receiver, running back, and help special teams.
The new-look Falcons play on Friday night in their first preseason action against the Denver Broncos. Roster cutdowns happen on August 30th, and players like Muse, Simon, and Velling are all on the bubble to make the initial 53.

title: Falcons Fans Get Brutal Suspension Rumor on James Pearce Jr.
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons are bracing for a decision from the league office on the immediate future of James Pearce Jr., and Josh Kendall of The Athletic believes that it could be far more significant than some fans think.
The team has not heard anything from the NFL, but there is a reasonable expectation that word could come down before rosters trim down at the end of the month. Guesses from most around the organization have hovered around six games, but Kendall thinks that number could grow as high as eight, or half the regular season.
ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler seems to agree with Kendall’s sentiment, saying there is still “uncertainty” regarding the 2026 position and that how the team deals with the edge position is “worth watching” this summer. One such update came earlier Monday, with the Falcons signing Cameron Sample and moving DeAngelo Malone to the reserve/PUP list.
With Pearce’s unknown situation and the training camp injury to Jalon Walker that will cost him the season, the position remains in a worrying state. Both players saw late-season surges in 2025 that put them atop the rookie sack leaderboard, and both were expected to build on that success in 2026.
Now, the Falcons are left scrambling for answers.
The early returns from the summer appear to indicate that the Falcons do not expect to have Pearce in the early portions of the year. He rotated in with the starters on Saturday but has largely worked with the reserve units.
That could also have something to do with his absence for most of the team’s offseason program, but time will tell.
“He's doing a nice job, and I appreciate the work that he's putting into it,” Stefanski said Monday about continuing to work Pearce into the rotation. “We'll continue to roll guys in at all positions. We've had a lot of injuries now at the edge in particular. We're going to ask everybody to do a little bit more, but he's continuing to do everything we're asking him to do.”
As it has since Pearce was first arrested in February, this story will continue to evolve . In the meantime, the Falcons will continue preparing for Friday night’s preseason game with the Denver Broncos. Kickoff for that game is set for 7:00.

title: The More Declan Doyle Talks About His Influences The More We Learn About Ravens New Offense
full_text:
The more Declan Doyle talks about the offense he is concocting for the first time and his goals and objectives and influences, the clearer it becomes how much it will change from years past in Baltimore.
It’s confirmation of trends and alterations we reported at length on through the spring, and there have been no surprises if you’ve been reading along. And when we discussed what Doyle is trying to accomplish with his primary mentor, Broncos coach Sean Payton, and the architect of the most ripped-off offense in the modern NFL, Rams coach Sean McVay, on “The Daily Flock Show” they helped us determine how the final few pieces fit. and what it means for Lamar Jackson.
Doyle will try to hold back a lot of what he wants to accomplish from the preseason games – which begin Saturday against the Eagles – wanting to save as many surprises as possible for the games that count. And now he will have to operate without veteran third-string quarterback Skylar Thompson, a significant wrinkle that will impact evaluations of critical young players . And it will undoubtedly result in an even more watered down and rote version of what was previously in store.
But now weeks into training camp, we’ve heard Doyle himself talk about the importance of altering tempo and cadence, taking early-down, play-action deep shots and attacking defenses downfield in short yardage . The overwhelming reality that this offense will be under center like never before in Jackson’s tenure isn’t a secret at this point. And Doyle has strongly alluded to the use of Jokers  - hybrid players fulfilling multiple positions at once – without using the word Payton engrained into his football psyche .
For all the talk of throwing the ball, Doyle’s work under Payton (New Orleans and Denver ) and Ben Johnson (Chicago) means he is going to run the ball a ton and do it old school with I formations and blocking tight ends and hybrid fullbacks (Jokers) and Doyle isn’t even shying away from another 300-carry season from 32-year-old back Derrick Henry .
“Sean McVay, [Kyle] Shanahan, Sean Payton, Ben [Johnson] — these are guys that I have watched for a long time,” Doyle said after Wednesday’s practice. “You watch the sequencing, and this is my eighth year in the NFL. Really, since the beginning, you start to watch those guys and how they craft a game plan, how they attack a defense.
“Those are things you're trying to emulate when you're building a plan as an assistant, and certainly something that we're trying to do as an offensive staff as well."
He isn’t hiding who he is stealing from, and that’s the case for everyone. McVay broke down for us what he took from Bill Walsh on the show, and Payton told us he isn’t too big to steal from McVay. It’s not about what he is picking and choosing at this point, it’s about how quickly the players adapt to it, and whether they can avoid pre-snap foibles and procedural mishaps.
Doyle is going to have to learn to adapt in-game and determine when it’s time to chuck a game plan and whether an opponent is too prepared for what he had cooked up. It came as no surprise Wednesday, and was a nod to the reality of his novice status, when Doyle said he will lean heavily into his pre-game script of playcalls.
“I would say that in general, we try to script as much as we can so that our guys have a really good feeling of what we're going to do,” Doyle said. “I read a book by Bill Walsh a long time ago, and he basically talked about how the more decisions you make in the air conditioning, [the better,] because guys have a good feel for what you're going to call.
“You've made the decision based on data and facts, rather than being out there and it kind of feels a certain way and you may lead yourself astray from where you should go.”
What’s most important in the second half of camp is that the offensive line can fall into place, and Doyle builds a deep enough reservoir of potential playmakers he can thrust into as many different situations as possible. The fact that so few players and coaches have strong ties to the coaching family tree he is closest aligned with remains surprising, and the personnel on his side of the ball simply have far more warts and questions than on head coach Jesse Minter’s side of the ball.
For all of the excitement and hype and talk of Doyle being a genius, anyone who thinks this offense is coming out of the gates looking like a juggernaut is probably fooling themselves. He can borrow quite a bit from his mentors, but there is no substitute for doing it yourself.

title: Ravens Rookie Coordinator Declan Doyle Putting No Limits On Derrick Henry's Role
full_text:
Derrick Henry, unicorn that he is, has never carried the ball 300 times or more three straight years in his career as he heads into his age 32 season. Rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, 30, who has never called a play before in his life, is not shying away from dialing it up roughly that much for him in 2026.
Doyle isn’t offering any direct projections, and as a total novice he isn’t sure exactly how any of this is going to play out. Heck, he doesn’t even know yet if he’s going to station himself on the sidelines or in the pressbox on game day. But he made it abundantly clear after Wednesday’s practice that he has no intentions to back off of Henry or nurse him through anything. Let’s face it, if you are doing a job as an offensive coordinator for the first time and you can hand the ball off to a guy who has averaged 5.5 yards per carry in his Ravens career, that’s a pretty tempting default.
Given an opportunity to strike a cautionary tone about Henry – surely aware of 55 years of age 32 running back data that would speak to this being when careers collapse – Doyle did anything but that. Sounds like he is fully vested in finding out if Henry can remain the ferocious bell cow he’s always been, and he in no way intimated that his normal Baltimore workload is out of the question.
“He is a special talent,” Doyle said on Henry. “There are not many guys in the league who can do what he does. The vision for him in the offense is an immense role. Obviously, I don't want to put a number on the amount of [carries], because obviously, as you look at every single week, every week is different. You want to be able to deploy things in different ways, and at the same point in time, he's going to have a pretty large workload.”
Alright then! Strap it up!
Well, if it is to be another 300 carry season, Henry would become just the third age 32 back to hit that total, joining Walter Payton (321 in 1985) and Otis Anderson (325 in 1989). To call that a different era in NFL timelines is a massive understatement. Only four backs in history have surpassed 250 carries in their age 32 season (Frank Gore and Emmitt Smith as the others).
In the only previous instance when Henry has carried 300 times or more in consecutive seasons, he suffered a Jones fracture in his foot midway through the following season (2021), missing nine games but returning for the playoffs. Henry remains in tremendous shape, beyond chiseled and beyond driven, still chasing a Lombardi Trophy. He made it clear when he met the media early in training camp that retirement is nowhere near his mind, but we all know Father Time’s record by now.
Eventually, he gets everyone.
“I don’t try to enter another season thinking about retirement or having that on my mind,” Henry explained. “That’s not even in my mindset.”
As to how much he can handle at this stage of his career , Henry offered: “I ain’t really trying to get into the expectation thing,” Alrighty then. Henry has his game face on. Our buddy Ross Tucker, former offensive lineman and CBS game analyst, FWIW, said on "The Daily Flock Show" that Henry might be impervious to Father Time. "I wouldn't put anything past that guy."
Rookie head coach Jesse Minter didn’t put any blinders on precisely how much Henry could see the ball either, but at least seemed to acknowledge the 32-year elephant in the room when probed about a pitch count or some plan for how to help Henry best get through the season.
“I do think - like all the players – we’re going to have to be really smart to get him through the long season,” Minter said. “I don’t look at that as he’s slowing down, from that standpoint. But that’s our job.”
The numbers paint a fairly bleak portrait of what happens to these older legs as the collective weight of 3000 carries mounts . It’s where even the greatest of the greats truly hit the wall. Few maintain their workloads and the ones who have, become plowhorses with far diminished explosiveness.
It’s quite tell that the best age 32 back in NFL history – Ricky Williams – had roughly 1000 fewer carries than Henry at this stage of his career (including playoffs) given his multiple suspensions and time spent away from the game and on the larger fields of the Canadian Football League.
Age 32 RB Seasons Since 1970
RBs to Amass 250 carries: 5
Avg Y/C With 200+ Rushes: 3.8
RBs With 200+ Rushes To Average 4.5/Carry: 2 (Ricky Williams 4.7, DeAngelo Williams 4.5)
Age 31 RB Seasons Since 1970
Avg Y/C With 200+ Rushes: 4.3
RBs With 200+ Carries To Avg 4.5/Carry: 8
Age 30 RB Seasons Since 1970
RBs To Amass 250+ Carries: 18
Avg. Y/C With 200+ Rushes: 4.2
RBs With 200+ Carries To Avg 4.5/carry: 11
Doyle seems undaunted by any of this. He knows a good thing when he sees it, and, for once, his nativity and inexperience may have come to fore a bit on Wednesday when he opined about this topic. This offensive line still might not be particularly good, Henry’s yards before contact dropped from 2.41 in 2024 to 1.60 last season. His yards per carry facing an 8-man box dropped from 6.3 to 3.8, but Lamar Jackson barely running the football and fewer option looks might have had plenty to do with that.
Doyle clearly also knows that Henry was good for 1600 yards again last season and averaged a robust 6.0 yards per attempt on first down. And this team will be running under center more than the Ravens ever have during the Lamar Jackson era , and Henry did more of that than any RB in the NFL during his time in Tennessee. Doyle's time spent on the staffs of Sean Payton and Ben Johnson ensure as much.
“I was telling the offensive staff how cool it is when you call a run play, first-time play caller, and Derrick Henry is the running back,” Doyle noted. “And you're like, 'The odds of this working are a lot higher.'”
So maybe it will be 300 carries for three years in a row. If Henry can hold up yet again.

title: 3 Ravens Veterans Trending Toward the Roster Bubble (And Who is Replacing Them)
full_text:
At multiple positions on both sides of the ball, the Baltimore Ravens are showing a commitment to developing their young talent that has either been drafted or signed as undrafted free agents in recent years during this year's training camp.
This will result in several of the more experienced players at those positions on the fringe of the roster not making the final cut, barring injury.
Here are three of those veteran players on the bubble, and who, at their respective positions, are likely going to prevent them from earning a spot on the team come September, when the regular season rolls around.
Even with no current timeline for the top cornerback Nate Wiggins after he avoided a major injury in Tuesday's practice that saw him get carted off the field, the eighth-year veteran still faces an uphill battle to make the team. According to several accounts from practice, he's been having a solid-to-strong training camp thus far, but he's in a tight battle with a host of youngsters who were recently drafted or made the team as undrafted free agents for one of the final spots on the roster at the position.
Oruwariye plays on the outside, where his main competition for a role as a quality or possibly even a rotational depth piece is third-year pro T.J. Tampa, who has been one of the stars of training camp, and second-year pros Bihlal Kone and Robert Longerbeam, both of whom missed their entire rookie seasons with lower-leg injuries and have been looking better and better as camp as gone on.
The Ravens brought in the 12th-year veteran as experienced tackle depth to fill out the roster and compete for the swing-tackle spot after Hakeem Adeniji was placed on the reserve/retired list a week after being signed by the team.
While there's a chance he could be a prime candidate to be brought back on the practice squad as emergency depth at the premium position, all signs are pointing to second-year pro Carson Vinson being the frontrunner to win the job, if he hasn't secured it already.
The 2025 fifth-rounder has been the first man up to protect Lamar Jackson's blindside whenever two-time Pro Bowl veteran starter Ronnie Stanley has been absent from the practice field dating back to Organized Team Activities.
The Ravens reunited with their former fourth-round pick from the 2016 NFL Draft at the onset of training camp to provide depth at both receiver and on special teams, essentially to serve in the Tylan Wallace role.
Unlike his predecessor, who was pretty much penciled into a roster spot each of the last two years under former head coach John Harbaugh, who placed a high value on core special teams players, Moore faces long odds of making the final cut on this team because their depth chart at his position is all but set in stone with second-year pro LaJohntay Wester primed to secure the sixth and likely final spot, given their needs at other positions to carry a fourth running back and tight end.
He could very well extend his second stint in Baltimore on the practice squad, but it'd take an injury or two at a couple of different positions, including his, for him to be on the initial or final 53.
