title: Ravens No. 3 QB Skylar Thompson Going On IR Is A Bigger Problem Than You Think
full_text:
The Ravens placed veteran third-string quarterback Skylar Thompson on Injured Reserve Wednesday, likely ending his season and delivering a significant blow to their summer plans. Thompson has an NFL resume, he has performed gamely in a postseason start and offered the team a high level of competency to execute their offense in the preseason.
They signed journeyman Austin Reed to take his roster spot, and they had better get on the phone immediately to try to upgrade that position on the depth chart. If nothing else, the Ravens will be very active scooping up a veteran QB when final roster cuts are made. Two-time MVP Lamar Jackson is not expected to play at all in the preseason and we’ll see how much they want to put No. 2 Snoop Huntley behind a second-string offensive line that has looked compromised in camp.
The Ravens are short on proven playmakers on offense by any standard, their tight end room looks particularly suspect , with Mark Andrews nearing the end no matter what the Ravens opt to pay him. Zay Flowers, nursing a minor injury, is the only consistent playmaker in his prime in the entire passing game. They are counting on four rookies offering them something this season – receivers Ja’Kobi Lane and Elijan Sarratt and tight ends Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas – and the preseason games are vital to establishing baselines on their ability.
You risk putting those young players, who don’t really understand the game yet, in harms way if forced to rely on highly inaccurate and skittish quarterbacks with virtually no pro experience themselves playing significant stretches of these preseason games. The Ravens spent considerable time e valuating quarterbacks in the last two drafts only to use those picks on other positions – we implored them to draft Georgia Tech UDFA Haynes King in the late round, who starred in the Hall of Fame Game FWIW) – and the lack of a true No 3 or developmental prospect with real potential is a double whammy of sorts.
Thompson is highly functional and could put youngsters in positions to succeed and showcase what they can do in the exhibition games. He also, in my opinion, was in a similar tier to Huntley in terms of ability (I espoused a true competition between them), and provided real depth at the most important position in pro sports. The team did not disclose the nature of Thompson’s injury and earlier this week head coach Jesse Minter expressed hope he could come back and play in Saturday's preseason opener.
The Ravens enter practice Wednesday with undrafted rookie free agent Joe Fagnano (UCONN) as their third quarterback – sorry, that’s a problem folks – and they will try to get Reed up to speed ASAP when he arrives. Reed recently completed a season in the UFL and played at tiny Southern Illinois and Western Kentucky in college and is not close to in the same caliber of standing as Thompson.
Reed spent the 2024 preseason in Chicago – prior to Ravens coordinator Declan Doyle’s arrival there – so there aren’t really any obvious ties in that regard. Longtime back up QB/hybrid Wildcat Joker Taysom Hill remains an unsigned free agent; he is at the end of his career but worked with Doyle on Sean Payton’s staff in New Orleans.
Payton probably isn’t in a hurry to part with No 3 QB Sam Ehlinger,  who also has regular season starting experience, with starter Bo Nix coming off season-ending surgery. But Payton also might not carry three QBs and Ehlinger understands Doyle’s verbiage and concepts from his time in Denver.
The Bears signed Case Keenum to add depth to their QB room and, according to league sources, rebuffed overtures about young back-up Tyson Bagent in the past – who has legit NFL starting experience and impressed the Bears coaching staff last season as i hear it. Especially if anything happens to Huntley, even minor, in these preseason games, the Ravens might need to start probing Chicago for help.
Landing a QB who has been in this coaching family tree should have been an offseason priority, given how new all of this is, a nd had better be on their minds now with the season fast approaching.

title: One Major Starter Won’t Play for Ravens in Preseason Opener Saturday
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens are beginning the preseason against the Philadelphia Eagles at home on Saturday.
Fans that are expecting to see their favorite players suit up may be highly disappointed. Ravens head coach Jesse Minter spoke to the media on Tuesday and discussed the team’s potential absences come gameday.
"I would say some established players [will] not [be] playing in this first game,” Minter said on Tuesday, per the team’s transcript . “[It's a] good opportunity for a lot of the guys. It's an individual basis, I would say, based on maybe some of the experience and how many snaps they've played and things like that. I do think there's value [playing during the preseason]. We will have three joint practices, which I view in high regard for the work that we'll be able to get there in a more controlled environment for specific positions especially. So, it's a little bit of an individual basis, for sure."
Quarterback Lamar Jackson hasn’t suited up for a preseason game since 2021. Jackson played one game, completing 3-of-4 passes for 29 yards and was sacked twice for a passer rating of 94.8. He’s only played eight preseason games in his career between the 2018-2019 seasons and 2021. Jackson was beginning to grasp a new offensive system under Greg Roman in 2019 and hasn’t had a change in offensive coordinators until this season.
"Yes, Lamar [Jackson] is not going to play,” Minter said with a laugh.
Baltimore’s two-time MVP-winning quarterback wasn’t the only starter to not participate in preseason games last year. Derrick Henry, Mark Andrews , Zay Flowers, Ronnie Stanley and Roger Rosengarten didn’t play in the 2025 preseason.
Returning defensive starters Marlon Humphrey, Kyle Hamilton, Chidobe Awuzie, Travis Jones, Roquan Smith, Nnamdi Madubuike and Nate Wiggins each did not play in the 2025 preseason. Madubuike, who suffered a season-ending neck injury last season and Wiggins, who suffered a knee injury in Tuesday’s practice , will most likely be long shots to play.
There have been major contributors that played in last year’s preseason. Malaki Starks, Mike Green, Trenton Simpson and Teddye Buchanan (knee) played last year. However, Buchanan’s knee injury suffered an ACL tear and LCL sprain against the Cincinnati Bengals in punt coverage on Dec. 14 last season. Buchanan is currently on the physically unable to perform list and is making good progress, according to Minter.
"I would say that [Teddye Buchanan] falls into that — the next week or two, I think he'll be making some real progress,” Minter said. “We'll start to look out there at times and have all the guys that may be available on September 13. This dude has been incredible in how he's attacked coming off the injury that he's come off of. And again, it's our job to make sure that when we put him into the football environment that he's ready and he doesn't have any setbacks off of that."
With a new coaching staff and new systems in place, players could play who haven’t gotten live repetitions in their respective coaches’ schemes.

title: Durham Smythe Is The Only Raven Who Has Worked With Their Rookie Offensive Coordinator. He's A Big Fan
full_text:
One of the more fascinating aspects of the Ravens hiring a then-29-year-old who had never called a play to run their new offense is the fact he also isn’t seeing many familiar faces on the roster or coaching staff.
There is nary an assistant coach or a player on the roster with serious ties to Declan Doyle or his primary mentor, Broncos coach Sean Payton. In a situation like this, with so much new and so much new for Doyle, you’d think there might be more coaches on the staff with deep ties to Payton (Joe Lomardi is one of them). And if not key veterans who were with Doyle in Chicago last season, then several who at least were stalwarts at some point for Payton (who Doyle was with in New Orleans and Denver).
Just blocking tight end Durham Smythe, who will likely prove to be a sage signing and real factor in a multiple and diverse run game that will be under center more than we’ve ever seen during quarterback Lamar Jackson’s tenure here . We believe Smythe has plenty to offer in that regard and is a great value (think of a mauler in the vein of Nick Boyle).
But we’re not talking someone who is going to be on the field all the time and not exactly playing a position where his mastery of Doyle’s nascent scheme if going to be readily amplified Heck, most of the tight end room is compromised of guys who even the Ravens aren’t sure can play in the league yet .
This isn’t like a center or a No. 1 wide receiver. Regardless, based on one year with the Bears in which Doyle wasn’t even really the offensive coordinator (he didn’t call plays), Smythe is the resident Doyle expert for now.
“He’s built for this,” Smythe said of Doyle after Tuesday’s practice. “Obviously, he's risen pretty quickly in this field, but it's deserving. You could see that last year — obviously [Chicago Bears head coach] Ben [Johnson] is calling the plays, but Declan is right there knowing what to do.
“He could have called plays if he needed to. He's built for this. He's been around some great offensive minds in the last decade, and now he's kind of making all of those his own thing. It's pretty exciting, and I'm excited to work with him."
Doyle is bringing quite a bit of what Payton believes in most , as the Broncos coach explained to us in depth on “The Daily Flock Show” last month. He will take early-down deep shots out of play action, believes deeply in selling play action under center and operating the quarterback in those traditional five-and-seven-step drops, with “Joker” body types toggling between positions.
Smythe is an old-school impact player at the line of scrimmage and won’t be targeted much. But with Doyle asking so many players to try to operate from multiple positions during this install, his depth of understanding about those concepts is invaluable; again, it’s surprising there aren’t a few more like him sprinkled across various position groups.
"I think the way this offense is taught,” Smythe said, “whether it be last year in Chicago or this year here — you kind of want to stress the players as much as possible, as fast as possible. So, at the beginning of teaching things, it can be a little rough because there's so much information thrown at you at once.
“But, I think over the longevity of the season — which you kind of saw with us last year in Chicago — we started a little slow and then everything caught on at once. Obviously, we're in a race to master it faster than that … There's a lot to work on in that regard, but we're definitely in a race over the next three weeks."
Smythe could be a resource for the offensive linemen, too, with pre-snap penalties and out-of-sync linemen a major issue with the Bears last season into about the midpoint of the season. That’s something Doyle wants to avoid if possible. Easier said than done and especially with the backups playing so much in the upcoming preseason games, the flags are going to fly.
Perhaps during the flurry of roster transactions that come around final roster cuts to 53 more players with past ties to the system will show up on the roster. For now, Smythe pretty much stands alone

title: Early Reports Indicate Ravens May Have Avoided Major Injury With Top CB Nate Wiggins
full_text:
There is no definitive timetable yet for Ravens cornerback Nate Wiggins after he went down in practice Tuesday and had to be carted off the field. Head coach Jesse Minter said after practice that he is “optimistic” about the outcome and reports from The Athletic and NFL Network are indicating that will be the case.
While there are still no details on the extent of the injury, an MRI was conducted and Wiggins avoided any real structural damage , according to those reports. Of course, a scenario such as that still doesn’t necessarily mean that Wiggins won’t miss several weeks or more. Minter, also the defensive playcaller, was very nebulous about injury inquiries in general in the offseason, and in his first instance as a head coach, it remains to be seen how directly he will assess these situations.
Wiggins suffered the still-undisclosed injury after tangling with rookie receiver Ja’Kobi Lane. The fact he was carted off, the import of this player and the fact we are still in early August would all point to at least some time on the shelf for Wiggins, who carries a slight frame. Wiggins was already not going to play in Saturday’s pre-season game as one of the team’s key players.
“One of those plays, really not much between those guys,” Minter said of the collision that ended Wiggins’s practice.  “I think there is optimism, but, again, we’ll look at it and see where it’s at.”
Wiggins’s departure came at a time when the Ravens defense was getting quite healthy. Defensive linemen John Jenkins and Travis Jones recently returned from the PUP list and Minter said on Tuesday that he believes young linebacker Teddye Buchanan, returning from surgery, could perhaps do the same in the coming weeks.
With Marlon Humphrey coming off a poor 2025 season and off to a rough start in camp – the $19M corner noted Minter rightfully referred to his play as “trash’ this summer –the Ravens need Wiggins to make plays on the ball and continue his ascent. Staying healthy is a big part of that.
Minter lives in nickel and dime coverages loaded with defensive backs and plays as much quarters coverage as anyone in the NFL, something that should help Wiggins flourish. Humphrey is best suited for the slot, and the boundary corner situation gets very murky all of a sudden without Wiggins.

title: Jesse Minter Confident in Ravens’ Cornerback Depth After Nate Wiggins Injury
full_text:
Just when it seemed like the Baltimore Ravens dodged their first significant injury scare to a prominent starting player, with two-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Zay Flowers missing just one practice after suffering a quad contusion on Saturday, they got hit with another on Tuesday when starting cornerback Nate Wiggins was carted off the field about an hour into practice.
According to multiple reports from reporters in attendance, the third-year pro went down with what looked like a left knee/leg injury while covering rookie wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane and was in noticeable pain. He couldn't put any weight on his injured leg and was helped off the field by trainers.
" He got his feet tangled with Lane while covering a go route and fell hard to the ground," ESPN's Jamison Hensley accounted . "Trainers looked at the left leg and knee of Wiggins, who was in visible pain. He is the first player to be carted off in this year’s training camp."
Head coach Jesse Minter addressed the unfortunate development in his opening statement when speaking with the media during his post-practice press conference. While he didn't have any updates to give or declarative statements about Wiggins' injury, as the former first-rounder will need to undergo further testing to determine the severity of it, he did express hope that it might not be anything long-term.
“I don’t have a ton of information on that yet. We'll kind of get it looked at, see where it's at," Minter said. “I think there’s optimism.”
Wiggins has been on an ascent since he finished strong in the second half of his rookie season in 2024. The former first-round pick established himself as the Ravens' top cornerback last year, leading the team with a career-high 14 pass breakups and finishing second in interceptions with three. Heading into the 2026 season, he is slated to be a central figure in Minter's coverage plan for the overall secondary and is projected to break out in a good way.
Without him, they might have to rely more on a zone-heavy approach instead of using as much man-coverage that someone of Wiggins' ability would've allowed them to deploy more regularly.
"Obviously, Nate is an elite player," Minter said. "I think Nate has [the] potential to be one of the top corners in the whole league."
While losing Wiggins for any amount of time would be a tough blow for a Baltimore defense looking to rebound from what was a widely inconsistent and overall abysmal 2025 campaign, the team's cupboard at the position is far from bare.
They still have a pair of 10th-year veterans in four-time Pro Bowler Marlon Humphrey and Chido Awuzie, who were slated to play prominent roles even before Wiggins went down and have been performing well in training camp as of late, further inspiring more belief in the coaching staff that they are still well-equipped at cornerback.
"I got a lot of confidence in the corner room," Minter said. "I look at Marlon, [and] he's probably had his best couple days that last couple times out here. Chido, this guy has played a ton of football and played at a really high level. I think he's had a great camp up to this point.
The Ravens also have a handful of young talent that they're really excited about and have also been putting together strong showings in camp thus far in third-year pro T.J. Tampa, second-year pro Keyon Martin and fifth-round rookie Chandler Rivers.
"T.J. Tampa has done a lot of great things; Keyon Martin has done a lot of good stuff, Chandler [Rivers] has done a lot of good stuff and we got some young guys battling for trust and spots so I feel really good about the secondary overall."
The aforementioned other "young guys" include second-year pros Bilhal Kone and Robert Longerbeam, who were 2025 sixth-round picks, and Marquise Robinson, who was an undrafted free agent last year. Wiggins' injury won't impact the approach that the coaches already take with the other players at the position because they are always preparing them for bigger roles if and when their numbers are called.
"I don't think you're ever not rushing guys to go play; we're doing everything we can to get T.J. Tampa ready to play, to get the young guys ready to play," Minter said. "I don't think [Wiggins' injury] changes that. It might change the amount of reps they get against a certain group and the opportunities they get in practice but again, I like where that room is at."

title: The Ravens TE Room Is Underwhelming. Even The Coaches Can't Really Spin It Otherwise
full_text:
The Ravens are short on tight ends.
Perhaps, woefully short on tight ends.
They are at least a Darren Waller short at tight end , and probably more than just a Darren Waller short. July and August are the time in the NFL calendar centered around hype and false hope. It’s when all the key veterans are undoubtedly in “the best shape of their lives” and youngsters are “about to make the leap” and in a Ravens camp with no shortage of all of the above narratives in abundant supply across their roster, not a peep about the promise or progress of any of their tight ends. Veteran or newbie.
Now, it’s still early of course. Okay, not for Mark Andrews, who looked cooked last year and whose contract extension – the timing of which was more to rub it in the face of ongoing tight end Isaiah Likely that an actual reward for anything trending in the right direction with Andrews – will be a massive mistake . And he isn’t explosive and he has no twitch and he can’t even run like he used to or jump like he used to at a position where those are carrying traits now more than ever.
And no one has been overtly impressed with the two project tight ends they drafted because they are project tight end and late-round picks with huge holes in their game as it pertains to the NFL. We had general managers and scouts we fully trust break them down for us in the spring, and we aren’t expecting much from either this season . Plenty of time for them prove everyone wrong, but even Ravens tight ends coach Zack Grossi made it clear where rookies Matthew Hibner (133rd overall) and Josh Cuevas (173rd overall) stand after Tuesday’s practice.
“Pleased with the way those guys have approached things so far, but we’ve got a long way to go,” Grossi said, in what could go down as quite the understatement.
I believe this is the worst position group on the roster, and it’s not particularly close. Long-term, maybe they have a diamond in the rough or two for down the road, but short term they need impact options at this position if Andrews is what I think he is. And they simply doesn’t exist. And general manager Eric DeCosta better to ready to step in and fix it, because the wide receiver room aint brimming with proven NFL difference-makers, either.
Good on the Ravens for landing a legit blocking tight end in Durham Smythe in free agency, who knows the system from being under Ravens coordinator Declan Doyle in Chicago – HYPER. But that ain’t gonna do much for two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson in trying to unlock deep options in a brand new offense being installed by a 30-year-old coordinator calling plays for the first time.
As for how far this group needs to go, they haven’t been shining even in drills that are designed by their very nature to showcase them. They aren’t flashing. As Grossi explained it, a lot of what Hibner and Cuevas are being asked to do in the full panorama of NFL tight end duties is “very foreign to them” and vastly different from anything they were asked to do in college.
That’s the reality. This is projection and guesswork in spades with this group. The Ravens passed on grabbing more polished top college tight ends to grab developmental edge Zion Young in the second round, and that gamble could have major ramifications on how this season plays out.
“We’re throwing a lot at them,” Grossi noted, “and they’re doing a good job of just working, just keeping their head down and not getting too worried with the results right now.”
Cuevas said: “They’re giving us a lot of stuff really quicky. And going from that college offense to an NFL offense, it can get pretty overwhelming.”
Gulp. An understandable gulp. But gulp.
Holding up in the trenches in the NFL – even if just engaging a block for an instant before releasing – is a whole new world for these two. Grossi said he is “pleased with how they are attacking it,” but just basic footwork and hand placement – as rudimentary as it gets – is part of their learning curve.
“Look, you have to be able to block in this league as a tight end,” Grossi said. “You have to be able to win the C Gap - all the different places we put tight ends. We put them on the ball and off the ball. We do two-back runs.
“We line them up at receiver. We do perimeter schemes … zone schemes and gap schemes. So, you have to be versatile, and you have to be able to handle different blocks.”
Color me concerned about every individual in this room, save for Smythe, as well as the total construct of it. There isn't one metric with Andrews that isn't in steep decline and he's never scored a postseason touchdown and comes up most small when it matters most . Losing Likely and Charlie Kolar in free agency is a big deal.
“The room is built around Mark, and everybody compliments him,” as Grossi explained it.
That’s precisely the problem.

title: Ravens Holding Their Breath As Top Corner Nate Wiggins Carted Off From Practice
full_text:
Of all the young players on the Ravens roster, few are carrying higher immediate expectations than top corner Nate Wiggins. And he provided the first major injury scare of Jesse Minter’s first training camp as a head coach on Tuesday.
Wiggins tangled with rookie receiver Ja’Kobi Lane in a one-on-one drill and had to be carted off the field with what for now is an undisclosed injury. Anytime a player of this stature is unable to finish a camp practice it’s a big deal, and leaving on a cart is never a great sign, either.
Minter, who took over for John Harbaugh after a nearly 20 year run as head coach in Baltimore, offered few details after practice as the Ravens medical team gathers more information about the extent of the injury. Wiggins was already not going to play in Saturday’s preseason game as one of the team’s key players.
Minter agreed there “was not a whole lot there” in the interaction with Lane, though Wiggins did fall to the ground. “One of those plays,  really not much between those guys,” as the coach explained it.
“I think there is optimism,” Minter said, “but, again, we’ll look at it and see where it’s at.”
The setback, if significant, comes at a time when the Ravens just activated defensive tackle Travis Jones from the Physically Unable to Perform list, getting the defense back to full health save for a few young players still coming back from surgery (most notable linebacker Teddye Buchanan).
Wiggins, a first round pick two years ago, has a rough second half to the season, but nearly as rough as veteran Marlon Humphrey, who was one of the most successfully picked on starting corners in the NFL. Humphrey has had a rough go of it so far this summer, saying the staff rightfully called his play “trash” at times, and we suspect he was likely headed to the slot more fulltime.
Veteran Chidobe Awuzie was brought back on a less free agent deal after a great 2025 season – one of few standouts on one of the worst defenses in the NFL – but injuries have been an issue for his as well and keeping him on a pitch count makes sense. The Ravens have some young corners dealing with injuries as well.
The expectation is Wiggins will get his hands on the football more in this zone-based scheme, with Minter’s defenses with the Chargers top three in interception rate the last two seasons . Wiggins is sticky in coverage but all the defensive backs were exposed last season with no pass rush and an over-reliance on Cover-1 and Cover-0.
The secondary has long been an area where general manager Eric DeCosta invests most heavily, and Minter expressed confidence in the overall group Tuesday.
“I feel really good about where were at overall,” he said.

title: Jim Leonhard Exposes Two Sean McDermott Shortcomings That Cost Bills' Defense Dearly
full_text:
Although he didn't know not at the time, Buffalo Bills' first-year defensive coordinator  Jim Leonhard was a firsthand witness to Sean McDermott's final playoff stinker .
Heading into the 2025 AFC Divisional Round road contest against the Denver Broncos, the Bills' defense had allowed 33.2 points per game over its last five playoff losses (2020-24).
Rather predictably, even with inexperienced quarterback Bo Nix leading the way, the Broncos put up 33 points on the McDermott-influenced unit this past January. The Bills' defense did not record a sack and registered only one takeaway in the overtime loss.
Meanwhile, the Broncos' defense, with Leonhard as the pass game coordinator, sacked Josh Allen three times and came away with five turnovers.
Only months later, Leonhard, a former 10-year NFL safety, leads the Bills' defensive overhaul in the wake of McDermott's dismissal. Ahead of the August 15 preseason opener, Leonhard highlighted the two major areas where Buffalo must begin to improve.
With the preseason opener being the first chance for Leonhard to evaluate his personnel during live game action, the former 10-year NFL safety is placing a heavy focus on tackling.
"It's the first opportunity to finish. Tackling, right? Tackling, tackling, getting guys on the ground in live situations, making plays on the ball. You go through an entire training camp, the quarterback doesn't get hit," said Leonhard.
The Bills struggled mightily against the run under McDermott in 2025 due in large part to poor tackling. With an inability to consistently get the ball carrier to the ground, Buffalo allowed 5.14 yards per run play, ranking 30th on the circuit.
"Who can finish, get guys on the ground? That's was an Achilles heel here last year, so that's the number one thing we have to to correct, and the number one way to do it is getting population to the football," said Leonhard.
The Bills seemingly struggled to pressure the passer in key spots throughout McDermott's tenure. They totaled one sack combined over two playoffs games last season.
Buffalo's former head coach was insistent on generating a pass rush by using only the front four, rarely dropping any fewer than seven men in coverage. Even when blitzing, the Bills were unable to get home the majority of the time.
"You can't pressure just to pressure. You can't do it recklessly. I've mentioned that multiple times," said Leonhard. "If you don't get home, the coverage is stressed. It's just what it is, so there's always a balance."
With Leonhard on board, the Broncos found that balance in 2025, leading the NFL by making 68 sacks.
"You have to understand the DNA of your team. Some guys can be aggressive and overaggressive because that fits who they've got in the building and others are a little bit different. That's what I have to find out. I'm getting a better sense of it as these practices go on of what we can and can't do," said Leonhard.

title: Bills Add Former Division III All-American to Preseason Roster for Opener vs. Panthers
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills made a roster move on Wednesday, likely in response to having two cornerbacks banged up with the August 15 preseason opener looming.
Cornerbacks Maxwell Hairston and Kani Walker were not seen participating by media in attendance at the August 11 practice. Later that afternoon, the Bills hosted tryouts for five different players , including three defensive backs.
Apparently seeing enough from tryout cornerback Anthony Kendall, Buffalo signed the former small-school product three days prior to its home exhibition against the Carolina Panthers.
In a corresponding roster move, the Bills waived undrafted rookie defensive lineman Kody Huisman, who had been with the team since May .
With first-year defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard bringing a new scheme to the Bills' defense, some players may see more preseason game reps than the norm during past summers.
"I think the plan is for guys to play and get a taste of the scheme, live, let's go finish. So, as far as I'm concerned, guys are gonna go play. To be determined a little bit on how much, but it's gonna be exciting for guys to get out there," said Leonhard.
One would think, however, that Hairston won't be out there on Saturday despite head coach Joe Brady suggesting the injury isn't serious .
If the Bills have been unwilling to push Hairston, who has been sidelined since last Friday, in practice, all signs point to holding the 2025 first-round pick out against the Panthers even if he's physically ready for action. We wrote about the Bills' need for injury insurance when Hairston missed the Friday practice. On Tuesday, he was seen working on the side with trainers.
As for Walker, the undrafted rookie was absent Tuesday. Although he wore a sleeve on his left leg during Monday's practice, there was no indication he was injured when addressing reporters afterwards.
While no one presumably wants to risk further injury, Walker needs as many live reps as possible considering he's trying to make the team after going undrafted. He was listed as a second-team cornerback on the Bills' first unofficial depth chart.
Playing his entire collegiate career for NCAA Division III member Baldwin-Wallace, Kendall went undrafted in 2023 before landing a free agent rookie deal with the Tennessee Titans.
Kendall, a 2022 D3 All-American at the Ohio-based institution, wound up playing in 16 games for the Titans as a rookie. Although he saw only three defensive snaps the whole season, he was a fixture on special teams, logging 323 live game reps.
After Tennessee cut ties, Kendall proceeded to spend the bulk on the 2024 season as a member of the Baltimore Ravens' practice squad. The Cleveland Browns signed the local cornerback in 2025, but a summertime injury forced him onto Injured Reserve for the season.

title: Bills' K Tyler Bass' Bloated Contract Makes Preseason Debut More Critical
full_text:
Buffalo Bills veteran kicker Tyler Bass has had a rough stretch—both on the field and off it—since signing a four-year extension with the Bills in April 2023 that was worth up to $21 million and included $12.3 million in guarantees.
At the time, it appeared as if Buffalo had just locked down one of the premier young kickers in the National Football League at a reasonable rate.
Bass—a former 2020 sixth-round pick of the Bills out of Georgia Southern University—had just registered back-to-back years of making above 87% of his field goals in 2022 and 2023. StatMuse ’s database says that the NFL average for kickers was around 85% for field goals made during those seasons.
So, the decision to secure Bass' services seemed to be a good idea by team president of football operations/ general manager Brandon Beane .
From that moment on, however, the contract’s shine has worn off.
Once revered by fans, Bass' previously deemed “golden leg” is no longer adored by Bills Mafia like the leg lamp sitting in the window of the famous holiday movie “ A Christmas Story”.
Well, immediately following his extension , Bass' field goal percentage dropped to 82.8%, below the league average.  His percentage on extra-points made dropped, as well, as he went from making 98% in 2023 to a measly 92.2% of his extra points in 2024.
In the postseason, he made just 8-of-11 of his kicks, and he also missed a potential game-tying 44-yard field goal against the Kansas City Chiefs with 1:47 remaining in the fourth quarter of the AFC divisional round on January 21, 2024.
Simply put, Bass hasn’t been good enough.
And, last year’s hip/groin/pelvic ailment that required sports-hernia surgery—which landed him on injured reserve for the 2025 season—was just the cherry on top of his most recent mishaps.
"I wouldn't say it was a relief, but it was just . . . I finally had an answer to the problem," Bills’ kicker Tyler Bass said when speaking to reporters at training camp.
"I knew it was (going to) be hard—the recovery—and it was hard to get out of bed for a couple of weeks, but—once I got through that—I showed myself, and my body, that I can kind of do anything."
Now that the seventh-year veteran is back to being fully healthy again, the team appears dead set on Bass being their kicker for the upcoming 2026 campaign.
Heck, there’s not even any competition in training camp so far, which hasn’t always been the case in past seasons even when Bass wasn’t coming off a terrible stretch of play or a questionable injury situation.
The injury recovery process to get here has been long.
"It was tough. (It was) a situation I've never been in: being injured. But, (I’m) really grateful for how (everyone) kind of handled it, and I'm grateful for Prater coming in (last season),” Bass said regarding his 2025 replacement, veteran Matt Prater.
“He did a great job, and I learned a lot from just being around him. It was tough. But, you just want to get back out there . . . we're just grateful to be here.”
Buffalo’s current top—and only—option at the position mysteriously didn’t start kicking much to begin training camp at St. John Fisher University earlier this summer, at least not within visibility of fans or reporters . It seems it was all a part of the plan to ease the placekicker back into a groove and a comfortable routine.
Bass did kick at the Bills’ most recent “ Return of the Blue and Red ” scrimmage at the team’s new home venue on August 8—and he did fairly well by most accounts—but there’s something different about kicking in a game versus a practice or scrimmage: preseason or not.
"It probably took a few months before I started kicking, but we started with baby steps— 20-yarders, 10-yarders—(and) kind of worked from there. And, then it wasn't really until, like, midway through OTAs where I started really feeling kind of like myself again,” Bass said.
“The body is feeling good. We’re excited to get back, and the process has been really just recovering, strengthening what we had worked on, and just taking it one day at a time. We’re ready to go. We’ve worked really hard (together), and—like I said—we’re excited to be here, and I can’t wait.”
As for his jersey number? You’ll see Bass donning the No. 16 now that veteran wide receiver D.J. Moore has taken over No. 2 in Western New York.
But, the veteran placekicker doesn’t mind. Hopefully, the change—which actually really isn’t much of a change at all—is a good omen for the upcoming NFL season.
“(It was my) college number,” Bass added. “I’m excited: a lot of good memories with it.”

title: Josh Allen Shares Special Vision for What His Daughter Will See from 2026 Bills
full_text:
The 2026 season has been filled with change for the Buffalo Bills, Josh Allen included.
That was always going to be the case with this being the first year in the new Highmark Stadium after saying goodbye to the stadium they have called home since 1973. The change has gone well beyond this, however, thanks to some major adjustments to the coaching staff.
Sean McDermott was fired after nine seasons and replaced by offensive coordinator Joe Brady. The first-year head coach also employs a new staff, led by offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael, defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard , and special teams coordinator Jeff Rodgers.
The roster itself has undergone some change as well. Key players such as Josh Allen, James Cook, Khalil Shakir, Ed Oliver, and Greg Rousseau remain in place but Buffalo added several new faces. Players such as DJ Moore, Bradley Chubb, and C.J. Gardner-Johnson are bringing new hope to a franchise trying to break through the playoff wall.
Off the field, their biggest star is also going through massive changes in his life.
Josh Allen and his wife, Hailee Steinfeld, welcomed their first child this year .  We wrote about how the new dad chose to forego his annual American Century Championship golf tradition back in July.
Entering his first season as a father , Allen hopes he can make some special memories for his daughter, Harper. While speaking with Kyle Brandt, Allen was asked what he hopes to tell his daughter happened during this season. Allen said he hopes he can tell her how strong the team was and how their bond led to a title.
“Well, hopefully she's sitting there saying, this picture of you holding me on the field under the confetti is pretty cool. So that's, that's the vision that I have,”Allen said.
“And what I'll tell her is we worked really hard and this is a team that loved each other and accomplished something so great, and that's, that's sometimes what it takes. It takes a lot of sacrifice from those around you, everybody in the building here, outside, all of our wives and girlfriends making sacrifices for us to come out here and do what we do.”
Allen and the Bills have been to the playoffs in seven consecutive seasons but have yet to make it to the Super Bowl. Twice they were in the AFC Championship Game but fell short.
They had a golden opportunity this past season with teams such as the Kansas City Chiefs, Cincinnati Bengals, and Baltimore Ravens out of the playoffs. Unfortunately, they still fell short, which was a huge reason for the many changes. Now, Allen and the rest of the Bills franchise. Hope those changes lead to the type of success they can still be excited about decades from now.

title: One Undrafted Rookie Pushing for Bills' Roster Spot Following Jim Leonhard's Path
full_text:
Buffalo Bills ’ undrafted rookie defensive back Kani Walker was a rather unknown commodity heading into this summer’s training camp.
But, the 6-foot-2, 203-pound defensive back has quickly flipped the script in terms of the familiarity the one-time University of Arkansas defender has amongst the fans—as well as his current perceived roster chances from outside observers—in a mere matter of weeks .
“Every day is a new restart. So, as long as you’re coming in every single day and attacking it—shoot—it really doesn’t, I guess, matter how your role has been (before this) . . . like, based on my own reflecting,” Bills’ rookie defensive back Kani Walker said following Monday’s practice at One Bills Drive.
“I’ve had a pretty good camp, and—shoot—the job’s not finished, but (I’m) just staying determined.”
With that said, it has been an impressive start for Walker : no doubt.
Instead of fans mundanely asking, “ Who’s No. 41? ”, like they were probably doing to begin camp practices at St. John Fisher University in Pittsford, New York, back on the morning of July 29, they’re now likely emphatically asking themselves internally, “ Did Kani Walker make another play in camp today? ”
Either way, regardless of where some fans might still stand with their knowledge of the rookie, the lanky cornerback is certainly making some noise within his own team—from both his new teammates and his new coaches—this summer.
There’s been no shortage of praise to go around.
And, new Bills’ defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard appears to have a bit of a soft spot for the former Razorback and the current position that he finds himself in.
After all, Leonhard was a former undrafted free agent just like Walker when he first entered the league out of the University of Wisconsin as a player 21 years ago, and he managed to make the 53-man roster with the Buffalo Bills as a rookie.
Leonhard appeared in 10 games that first season and wound up parlaying it into a 10-year professional career that spanned between Buffalo, the Baltimore Ravens, New York Jets, and three other NFL teams.
He was one of the ultimate underdog stories during his time in the league.
And, seemingly the only difference between Leonhard and Walker is that one was an undersized safety playing in a different era of professional football, while the other is a physically-gifted cornerback being thrown into a league that is now like a passing gauntlet on a weekly basis.
However, needless to say, Buffalo’s current young rookie has caught his coordinator’s eye more than once so far this July and August.
Walker just needs to keep it up and continue stacking days .
“Obviously, (I’ve) got a little history with the undrafted thing, but you always like guys who are the underdog a little bit, (and) that know they have something to prove,” new Bills’ defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard said about Walker when talking during his media availability before Day 6 of training camp at the end of last week.
“To me, there’s an understanding of—certain guys just get (it)—like, they know that they have to shut their mouth, do their job, and just find a way to be noticed, and (Kani’s) one of those guys. Obviously, from a skill set, he’s got size; he’s got speed; he’s got length. And, that excites you as a corner. He’s playing really well. . . . He’s a big, athletic kid who competes, and he’s got a chance, you know? He flashes.
“He does something every day that gets you a little bit excited.”
Entering the beginning of July, it was thought by some that the Bills might bring in another veteran defensive back—like Buffalo’s former longtime corner Tre’Davious White , for instance—in order to help better supply more veteran depth at outside cornerback behind the likes of Christian Benford, Maxwell Hairston , and 2026 second-round pick Davison “IGB” Igbinosun.
But, aside from team president of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane bringing in former UFL defensive back D.J. Miller at the very end of July due to an injury suffered by another player, that previously mentioned presumed transaction of bringing in an established veteran at the outside corner spot never took place in Pittsford, New York. And, since the move was made for Miller on just the third day of training camp on July 31, there’s been no further roster gymnastics in the secondary.
Walker appears to be the chief reason why.
Despite missing his first practice of training camp with an undisclosed injury on Tuesday, the former Razorback—who, according to Sports Reference , finished his college career with 104 total tackles, six-and-a-half tackles for loss, and three interceptions while playing for Louisville and Oklahoma at the collegiate level in addition to his time with Arkansas—has been a consistent presence as one of the top depth options at the fourth boundary spot behind Benford, Hairston, and Igbinosun.
He’s more than held his own while going up against players like fellow rookie Skyler Bell in practice, as well, and Walker attributes a lot of his unexpected early success to one of Leonhard’s assistants: cornerbacks coach Jay Valai .
Valai, a former co-defensive coordinator with the Oklahoma Sooners before joining the Bills’ staff this offseason, coached Buffalo’s current shining undrafted rookie cornerback during their time together on the campus in Norman, Oklahoma, from 2022 to 2024.
Walker finished his three seasons with the Sooners with 48 total tackles, 10 pass breakups, two tackles for loss, one forced fumble, and one fumble recovery in 27 games.
“Coach Valai, like, huge shoutout to him. He takes those things that he (did with) me in 2022 and applied it to me (here) . . . and, shoot, (he’s) built a whole even more elite catalog towards (this defense) because, of course, everybody still has to choose to improve,” Walker added on Monday.
“So, I feel like (this defense) works well with me. Like, I’m very physical. I’m very smart, athletic, and then—once it’s time to play ball—like, I compete. . . . I know I’m elite, and I’m a closer. So, shoot, that’s really all (the coaches) care about. And, I know that fits right into my game . . . right in my alley.”
On that note, assuming Walker is healthy enough to play in Buffalo’s preseason opener against the Carolina Panthers at the new Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, New York, at 1:00 p.m. ET on Saturday, it sure seems like he’ll be ready.
It’s an opportunity he’s been preparing for all offseason.
He's focused and determined.
But, Walker would also be lying if he said that he wasn’t just at least a little bit giddy about his NFL debut.
It’s been seven months since the defensive back’s final collegiate game at Arkansas: it’s time to get back on the grass for some action outside of practice.
“I love (the new stadium). Like, the grass—I ain’t going to lie—the grass is ‘OC’ on there. I’m like, ‘Yo, I can really put my feet in the ground.’ Like, it’s been so long since I’ve been (on) grass (in college). . . . It’s felt like a decade since I’ve been in Arkansas,” Walker continued in his most recent interview with reporters.
“I feel like it’ll just be the same thing that I come out here (in practice and do). Like, don’t give nobody (any) reason to say no, and give everybody a reason to say yes. And, demand everything from yourself, so everybody can demand it from you and have that expectation of you. But, it starts with you.
“So, just coming out there, being ready to attack whoever’s in front of me, of course, but making sure I’m proving myself right.”
Saturday likely can’t soon enough for the young—surprising—budding star in Buffalo’s secondary this summer.
Make sure to keep an eye out for No. 41 on Saturday afternoon, Bills Mafia .

title: Who Are Buffalo Bills' Five Tryout Players Auditioning as Injury Reinforcements?
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills have been hit with a handful of injuries in recent days , and they are apparently exploring the idea of adding reinforcements to the roster.
Although none of the injuries appear to be overly serious, Bills' cornerback Maxwell Hairston along with safeties Cole Bishop and Chauncey Gardner-Johnson have all missed practice reps since the team returned to Orchard Park for the remainder of the summer. Fifth-round rookie defensive lineman Zane Durant was absent for multiple sessions before reportedly returning on Tuesday.
Following Tuesday's practice, the Bills held player tryouts for three defensive backs and two defensive linemen.
Here's a quick rundown of the five players that Buffalo hosted.
The San Francisco 49ers waived the defensive tackle at the beginning of training camp following two seasons of service that included 12 regular season appearances followed by a full year on the practice squad.
Anderson initially joined the 49ers as an undrafted rookie from Florida Atlantic in 2024. He saw 267 defensive snaps for San Francisco, totaling 24 tackles and two quarterback hits over 12 games.
The Baldwin-Wallace product landed an UDFA rookie contract with the Tennessee Titans in 2023. He made the 53-man roster that season, appearing in 16 games almost exclusively on special teams.
Kendall spent most of the 2024 season on the Baltimore Ravens' practice squad. Last summer, the Cleveland Browns placed him on Injured Reserve for the year.
The well-traveled cornerback went from Incarnate Word to UAB to Texas A&M, where he finished his collegiate career in 2024. Mayes signed with the Indianapolis Colts last August, but failed to survive cutdown day.
The 23-year-old Mayes resurfaced in the UFL this past spring, playing for the Houston Gamblers.
Pride is the lone draft pick of the five tryout players who auditioned in Orchard Park. The Carolina Panthers' 2020 fourth-round selection made 14 appearances, including eight starts as a rookie when he overlapped with Joe Brady, who was the team's offensive coordinator at the time .
Becoming somewhat of a journeyman, Pride has spent time with five different teams, but played only three games, since being released by the Panthers. Most recently, the Notre Dame product logged 58 defensive snaps over two games for the 2024 Dallas Cowboys.
The rookie defensive tackle has been unable to latch on with a team since going undrafted in April.
After playing two seasons for Division II West Liberty, Rice made one-year stops at Ohio and Maryland. In 2025, he started all 12 games for the Terps.

title: Spencer Brown Reveals Must-Have Breakfast Items for Bills' Starting Tackle
full_text:
Despite what modern medicine and science might tell athletes —and non-athletes —these days, for generations it’s been said that breakfast is the most important meal of the day.
Wheaties made an empire off that idea: “the breakfast of champions.”
And, much to the annoyance of children across the country, mothers have consistently been heard saying, “ You can’t skip breakfast! ”, for many years.
In addition to that, nutritionists have also always insisted that people must pump the protein, which means that they should start each morning with items such as eggs, yogurt, and a choice of bacon or sausage, while also supplementing with whole-grain products like oatmeal and toast.
It was always the golden rule.
And, to some extent, those are all still fairly decent options to choose from, as long as everything is in moderation, of course.
Don’t forget the coffee, too, while you’re at it.
But, what about two Cool Mint Zyns to top it off?
Well, for current Buffalo Bills ’ starting right tackle Spencer Brown, that’s the perfect way to start his day: whether it be at home or at the facilities at One Bills Drive in Orchard Park, New York.
“Dale makes me a burrito every single day,” Bills ’ veteran offensive lineman Spencer Brown said when recently talking to the media following Tuesday’s practice ahead of the team’s preseason opener against the Carolina Panthers in Western New York this weekend.
“Two yogurt parfaits . . . with a bunch of blueberries, an orange juice, a milk, two slices of sourdough toast with grape jelly, and top it off with a coffee. And, then two Cool Mint Zyns.”
At the end, Brown jokingly emphasized the importance of having the two specifically flavored tobacco-free oral nicotine pouches, but maybe he’s on to something.
Like in the famous movie “ Space Jam” with former NBA legend Michael Jordan—if you can follow this reference—maybe Buffalo’s 6-foot-8, 311-pound former third-round pick has found his “secret stuff.”
What Spencer Brown eats for breakfast EVERY DAY: -Burrito -2 yogurt parfaits -A bunch of blueberries -Orange juice -Milk -2 slices of sourdough toast with grape jelly -Coffee -2 Cool Mint Zyns #BillsMafia @BuffaloPlus pic.twitter.com/w46sZeDsxa
Instead of it coming in a sports drink like it did for Jordan in the movie, though, Brown’s special elixir just so happens to come inside of a conveniently discreet tiny white pouch that he can slide behind his lip after—hopefully, of course—finishing his coffee first.
All joking aside, though, the one-time Northern Iowa standout has clearly found his stride since entering the league as a somewhat unknown commodity in 2021.
The 28-year-old Lenox, Iowa, native has since started 69 of 73 regular-season games and 11 postseason contests according to Pro Football Reference .
And, heading into his sixth NFL season, the behemoth lineman appears more motivated than ever to have his best professional year yet.
Apparently, Zyns after a giant breakfast are just all a part of the plan of attack this offseason for him.
Fans will soon see if Brown’s current morning routine pays dividends moving forward.
Kickoff for Saturday afternoon’s preseason opener for the Bills is slated to take place at the new $2.1 billion Highmark Stadium in Buffalo’s southeastern suburb on Saturday afternoon at 1:00 p.m. ET.

title: Nine Surprises Spotted on Buffalo Bills' First Preseason Depth Chart
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills released their unofficial depth chart heading into their August 15 preseason opener against the Carolina Panthers in Orchard Park, and there are more than a few surprises.
Of course, to no one's surprise five-time NFL MVP finalist Josh Allen sits in the QB1 slot, but there's real interest in the battle to be his understudy.
The backup quarterback competition is one of multiple spots that will be determined over the next few weeks.
With two weeks of training camp practices in the books, here are the nine positions that caught our attention when examining the first depth chart.
Bills' First Released Depth Chart (Preseason Week 1) 👀 [ @BuffaloBillsPR ] pic.twitter.com/Z1B0Jlbh0e
Mitch Trubisky is gone, and two familiar faces are vying to replace him. Kyle Allen, who was QB2 for the Bills in 2023, returns to compete against Shane Buechele, who has spent three seasons with Buffalo, primarily in a practice squad role.
Allen holds second-team status on the depth chart, but neither has been overly impressive during open camp practices. The preseason games will go a long way in determining the winner.
Despite Josh Palmer's strong start to training camp, the Bills have listed embattled 2024 second-round pick Keon Coleman as the third wide receiver when starting the game in trips formation.
Palmer is listed on the second team, directly behind WR1 DJ Moore. Fourth-round rookie Skyler Bell currently stands as Coleman's backup.
The Bills deployed fullback Reggie Gilliam for 21 percent of offensive snaps in 2025. Despite Gilliam's departure, it's presumed Buffalo desires to keep a fullback in its bag of tricks.
The decision will be between undrafted rookie Jackson Acker and former Philadelphia Eagles' converted linebacker Ben Van Sumeren, who is currently first on the depth chart. The real test will be how each competitor responds in the run game during live preseason action. It's worth noting that Acker was contributor for Wisconsin under interim head coach Jim Leonhard , who is now the Bills' defensive coordinator.
With Davis Edwards landing a mega contract with the New Orleans Saints, the Bills need to settle on a new starting left guard. Utilityman Alec Anderson, who has spent the past two seasons as Buffalo's sixth lineman, entered as a slight favorite and holds first-team status ahead of the preseason opener.
Veteran free agent addition Austin Corbett, the starting right guard for the Super Bowl LVI champion Los Angeles Rams, is the primary challenger to Anderson . He's second on the depth chart with undrafted rookie Bruno Fina on the third team.
The three first-team down linemen include two second-year players. While Deone Walker is the presumed nose tackle, fellow 2025 pick TJ Sanders is listed at defensive end opposite veteran Ed Oliver .
The second-team trio consists of a bulked-up Landon Jackson and fifth-round round Zane Durant on the ends with former Washington Commanders' second-rounder Phidarian Mathis in the middle. In a troubling sign for Dewayne Carter , who is coming off an Achilles tear, the 2024 third-round pick is on the third team behind nose tackles Walker and Mathis.
It doesn't appear as if the unsigned Matt Milano will return, meaning the Bills need a starter to pair with two-time returning captain Terrel Bernard. Despite what's been an impressive showing thus far from fourth-round rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr, returnee Dorian Williams is listed next to Bernard on the first team.
Elarms-Orr is the current second-teamer behind Williams while Joe Andreessen is backing up Bernard. Keonta Jenkins and Jimmy Ciarlo are the third-teamers.
With Cole Bishop, who is coming off a breakout season, entering camp as an incumbent starter, there is a loaded competition for the spot alongside him. Three veterans, all with prior NFL starting experience, are in the mix along with a rookie.
Chauncey Gardner-Johnson, a Super Bowl LIX champion, is the current leader . Meanwhile, familiar veteran Damar Hamlin and free-agent addition Geno Stone are listed on the second team. Hamlin is behind Gardner-Johnson with Stone backing up Bishop. Notably, Fifth-round rookie Jalon Kilgore, who generated some buzz before the pads came on, currently holds third-team status.
The burning question here is who will earn the spot playing opposite CB1 Christian Benford? Right now, the odds are trending in Max Hairston's favor with the 2025 first-round draft pick listed on the first team. After beginning his rookie season on Injured Reserve, Hairston eventually earned three starts before a different injury sidelined him for the playoffs.
Second-round rookie Davison Igbinosun, who is viewed as Hairston's main competitor , holds second-team status behind Benford. Meanwhile, undrafted rookie Kani Walker, who has been one of the top surprises of camp thus far, is listed behind Hairston.
While returnee Mitch Wishnowsky was seemingly put on notice when the Bills used a seventh-round draft pick on rookie Tommy Doman, the 34-year-old veteran currently holds an incumbency advantage.
Wishnowsky enters the preseason lid-lifter as the Bills' primary punter and holder.

title: Bills’ Rookie Skyler Bell Being Held Back in Buffalo’s WR Battle
full_text:
Despite being the second player selected by the Buffalo Bills in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft in April—and the fourth player in the overall pecking order of the team’s 10-player draft class this spring—there may have been no player that received greater hype entering their first NFL offseason over the past few months leading up to training camp in Pittsford, New York, than rookie wide receiver Skyler Bell, who was quickly snatched up by the Bills at pick No. 125 out of the University of Connecticut on Day 3 of the league-wide event four months ago.
Bell was instantly beloved by many in Bills Mafia . . . and he felt it.
“It’s just motivation. I want to show people (around the league that)—y’all [expletive] up—I’m really that (guy),” Bills’ rookie receiver Skyler Bell said in an interview with The Buffalo News earlier this offseason.
“I’m just trying to get better every day. So, when the season comes, I’m ready to put it all together."
The wide receiver position has seemingly always been a hot-button topic of discussion in Western New York in recent years, especially since the departure of former veteran All-Pro wide receiver Stefon Diggs in 2024.
And, the outside noise has only grown louder with the recent struggles of third-year wideout Keon Coleman and last year’s top free-agent signing Joshua Palmer, who’s a former 2021 third-round draft pick of the Los Angeles Chargers out of the University of Tennessee.
Combine that with the fact that Bell finished second in the entire FBS in 2025 with 1,278 receiving yards and 13 receiving touchdowns on 101 receptions for the Huskies, and it’s not hard to see why the anticipation to finally witness him on the field this offseason had been mounting from fans.
The Bronx, New York, native, who originally attended the University of Wisconsin from 2021 to 2023 before transferring to Connecticut in 2024, was simply sensational as a senior while playing for UConn this past fall. And, with that in mind, many outside observers thought that the transition of going from catching passes from former Huskies quarterback Joe Fagnano in college to being the recipient of balls supplied by Bills’ franchise quarterback Josh Allen in the pros would be seamless.
So far, however, that has not been the case for the 5-foot-11, 192-pound wideout this summer through the first slate of practices at training camp .
It hasn’t been due to too much fault of his own, though.
Bell, who—at the age of 24—is actually older than Coleman despite being a rookie, and is just two years younger than the previously aforementioned 26-year-old Palmer, hasn’t been receiving much time catching passes from Allen thus far in August at all.
Instead, it’s been backup quarterbacks Kyle Allen and Shane Buechele throwing the rookie receiver the “rock” as both players are currently in a battle for the right to be Buffalo’s former 2024 league MVP’s backup this season.
And, with that being the case, it has seemingly hindered Bell’s development as he no longer looks like the odds-on favorite to win a top rotational spot on the wide receiver depth chart this fall in his first professional season.
While he got off to a nice start at St. John Fisher University two weeks ago, things have since cooled off quite significantly for the once highly-favored rookie.
In fact, he’s missed the last couple of practices to start this week due to an undisclosed injury, as well, which included Tuesday’s morning session in Orchard Park, New York.
Clearly, it hasn’t been ideal.
But, his offensive coaches aren’t giving up on him: not in the slightest. They’ve seen incremental improvements when Bell’s been between the white lines.
“Yeah, I think that we have thrown a ton at him. We’ve put him at a ton of different positions, (and had him run) a ton of different routes. I mean—we have asked him to do a lot—and he has gone out there, and he’s done everything we’ve asked. He’s smart. He can play those multiple positions. He can run a lot of routes,” new Bills’ offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael Jr. said in an interview at One Bills Drive on Monday.
“I think that, again, maybe the last couple days there just hasn’t been (a connection). He’s been open, and maybe there are (misreads) . . . (or) I should say that maybe (the coach) called the play to get him the ball, and a specific coverage took it to somebody else. . . .
“We’re excited with where he’s at.”
On that note, the fact that Bell is being relegated to practicing mostly with the second- and third- string offenses so far in camp appears to be due to a combination of things.
First, the adjustment period from making the jump from playing at a somewhat smaller—at least in terms of football—school at the collegiate level to playing in the NFL might be taking a little longer than initially expected.
And, that’s OK: it’s normal.
However, what’s more concerning is his inability to earn more increased reps with the starting unit through his play in practice.
Is it due to Kyle Allen and Shane Buechele’s incompetency, which Carmichael somewhat tried to avoid mentioning in his interview, or is it due to a lack of current comfortability?
Whatever the case may be, Bell hasn’t blown anyone away in Buffalo so far.
He’ll need a string of strong preseason performances to end the summer if he’s going to earn the right to see the field for any significant amount of time in his rookie campaign, at least early on.
Right now, Coleman and Palmer appear to be firmly entrenched on the depth chart ahead of the “youngster” heading into Saturday’s exhibition opener against the Carolina Panthers on Saturday at 1:00 p.m. ET at the new $2.1 billion Highmark Stadium , and it’ll be up to Bell to change that.
If not, his rookie year might go off the rails before it even gets started. But, it’s not time to panic just yet, either.
First, he must get back on the field quickly. And, if can get back in time—once Saturday rolls around—the former Taft School standout must show up and show out in his NFL preseason debut.
And, Carmichael Jr. —despite there being many outside opinions to the contrary—believes that his backup quarterbacks can give Bell the chance that he needs to shine.
“I think that they both bring a ton of value—not only on the field—but what they bring to the meeting room, their relationship with Josh, their ability to communicate with him, and kind of from their vision, too: what they see,” Carmichael Jr. added on Monday.
“But, I think that—as we get into the preseason and play some games—it’ll be a great opportunity to see them both.”
Hopefully, it’ll be a great opportunity for the once highly-anticipated rookie receiver, as well.
Fans will soon find out. The preseason opener is just days away from taking place in Western New York.
It’s almost time to celebrate some more, Bills Mafia .

title: Buffalo Bills Respond After Widespread Complaints About New Highmark Stadium
full_text:
What was supposed to be a celebration quickly turned into a list of concerns. The Buffalo Bills hosted fans for the first time at their new Highmark Stadium this past Saturday as they held their annual Return of the Blue & Red practice .
There was an attendance record set as more than 50,000 fans packed the new stadium and watched the Bills' scrimmage. While there were plenty of positive aspects to take in , social media was buzzing with complaints.
Some of the biggest concerns involved seats that had obstructed views , which does happen at times at stadiums, but many fans felt they were misinformed before purchasing their season tickets. Another major complaint was the size of the video boards , which were on the smaller side for a stadium that exceeded $2 billion.
The Bills have heard the complaints and decided there were sufficient concerns that they should respond. For that reason, they released a statement, saying that they will utilize the next six weeks to address and refine any details possible.
"Thank you to Bills Mafia for setting a new attendance record with more than 50,000 fans at the Return of the Blue & Red. Saturday's practice was a great opportunity to test the new stadium. We are currently addressing internal and external feedback regarding the facility's operation following the first event. We'll utilize the next six weeks to refine any details as we prepare for the home opener on Thursday, September 17,” the Bills said in a statement via ESPN’s Alaina Getzenberg .
Initially, that statement makes it sound as though the front office is going to see what changes can be made. That said, later comments relayed by Getzenberg suggest otherwise.
In her piece, Getzenberg quotes a source saying that the team heard from "less than 1% of PSL holders" about issues with the view. They also said some of the pictures being shared were from seats that are not designed for football events.
This isn't to say that no changes will be made, but it sounds as though the powers that be might not believe the concerns are valid enough to make sweeping alterations. That said, it's also highly illogical to believe that any significant changes can be made to such a massive product in a mere six weeks. Instead, some fans will have to deal with some inconveniences and small video boards.

title: Major Losing Streak in Middle of Season Wrongly Predicted for Panthers
full_text:
It’s a traditional exercise that really cranks up once the National Football League releases its weekly schedule. Some get an even earlier start once a team’s opponents for the upcoming season are revealed after the final results of the previous season.
But let’s be serious. How on Earth can you look at an NFL team’s slate of games and predict wins and losses weeks of even months in advance? A club’s strength of schedule is based on the combined winning percentage of it 17 opponents from the previous season. Of course, a team that is bad one year can be much-improved while a playoff participant the previous season can suddenly fall apart.
Just a reminder. There were seven new division winners in 2025, with the NFC East champion Philadelphia Eagles the lone team to repeat. The New England Patriots went from 4-13 in ’24 to 14–3 a year ago, capturing the AFC East on the way to an appearance in Super Bowl LX. Meanwhile, the Chicago Bears won the NFC North and the San Francisco 49ers were a wild card team in 2025—both finishing dead last in their respective division the previous season.
This week, Moe Moton of Bleacher Report came out with his predictions for the upcoming season. He has the improving New Orleans Saints capturing the NFC South with an 8-9 record. As for the reigning NFC South champion Carolina Panthers, the forecast for Dave Canales’s squad, the pick is a third-place finish with a 7-10 record. That would mean a ninth consecutive losing campaign for the franchise.
It’s safe to say that Moton isn’t overly high on the Panthers chances in 2026. He mentions the team’s 1-3 finish a year ago (after a 7-6 start), and doesn’t appear to have a lot of faith in quarterback Bryce Young. He summed up his forecast mentioning a four-game stretch in the middle of the season. “ Between Weeks 8 and 11 against the Green Bay Packers (on short rest),” said Moton, “Denver Broncos, Saints and Baltimore Ravens, this team will fall apart on a losing streak.”
If there was one thing that stood out about the Panthers this past season, Canales’s team was marked by inconsistency. The club dropped its first two games and got off to a 1-3 start before stringing together three straight wins to get above the .500 mark.
Ryan Fitzgerald with a 49-yard game winner against the Packers! pic.twitter.com/B94AenuXeo
A Week 7 road victory over the Jets was the start of a 10-game stretch that saw the team alternate wins and losses. One of those victories was a last-second 16-13 triumph over the Packers at Lambeau Field in Week 9 . Another win over that stretch was a 31-28 surprise of the Los Angeles Rams at Charlotte in Week 13. Then again, two of their five setbacks over that span were to Kellen Moore’s last-place Saints.
Admittedly, it’s been a rough summer to date for Canales’s club with edge rusher Nic Scourton and rookie wideout Chris Brazzell II out for the season, and veteran right tackle Taylor Moton (blood clots) on the shelf for now.
However, this was a team that showed a resiliency this past season, and it’s hard to fathom that the team—with four of its final five games at home and three of its final seven contests vs. divisional rivals—will go away quietly.

title: Panthers Linked to Former Pro Bowl CB in Wake of Hall of Fame Game Struggles
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers learned a lot about themselves in the Hall of Fame Game last week. The team didn't play any starters, as well as some of the backups, but they learned plenty about where their depth is, isn't, and could come from.
Their depth is at wide receiver, and their depth isn't in the secondary. The secondary, including players like Will Lee, got absolutely run through by the Arizona Cardinals. Carson Beck diced them up, and the wide receivers got open frequently.
If the Panthers lose someone like Jaycee Horn or Mike Jackson, they are in deep trouble. They can, according to one NFL insider , and perhaps should sign Kenny Moore II to help offset that risk.
The Panthers have the outside cornerback depth set up with Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson, and Will Lee. The slot is in worse shape, but Carolina has also experimented with Horn in the slot so they can get creative with everyone.
Still, they're just one injury away from things going awry, especially in the slot. Enter Kenny Moore, who was released by the Indianapolis Colts earlier this offseason. Bleacher Report's Moe Moton believes he is the perfect fit for Carolina.
"The Carolina Panthers should look for an upgrade at slot cornerback. Chau Smith-Wade has manned the position for two seasons, and undrafted second-year pro Corey Thornton is his only competition for that role," Moton began, citing Smith-Wade's 105.8 passer rating allowed and Thornton's injury.
While Moore won't solve the missed tackle rate, which is 9.7% for Smith-Wade, his coverage is much better. His passer rating allowed has been below 88 for the last two years, and since 2023, he's recorded 19 pass breakups and seven interceptions.
Moton fully admits that Moore would be a "Band-Aid solution" for one of Carolina's weakspots, but they don't need much more than that right now. It's too late in the game to find a real replacement/upgrade, and Moore is one of the best options left.
The Panthers would have a ton of depth, versatility, and creativity in the secondary, as Horn could move inside and Moore could take some reps on the outside. This could mitigate any injuries and keep everyone fresh.
Moore would also be a great veteran mentor for Smith-Wade and Thornton, both of whom are still developing. They would learn more from a true slot cornerback like Moore than Horn or Mike Jackson.

title: Panthers Finally Make Needed TE Splash with Risky Darren Waller Signing
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers have languished without a tight end of note for a long time. They've tried and failed to replace Greg Olsen. Yes, it's been that long. They have drafted and signed players to no avail.
Now, they're finally taking a bit of a bolder swing, although it's worth noting that signing a soon-to-be-34-year-old Darren Waller this late in training camp is not a safe move. There is a chance he doesn't even make the roster.
Former Pro-Bowl tight end Darren Waller and the Carolina Panthers reached agreement today on a one-year deal, per source. pic.twitter.com/RYGXfLeXY8
However, the tight end struggles prompted the Panthers to finally make a move, and we're glad they see that the trio just isn't cutting it right now. Tommy Tremble is a great blocker, but that's it.
Ja'Tavion Sanders has upside, but he has no chemistry with Bryce Young, can't block, and struggles to make plays when called upon. Mitchell Evans is a good combination of blocking and receiving, but he isn't that great at either.
Darren Waller may or may not be the solution, but thankfully, the Panthers are giving it a shot. It's just a one-year deal that, at this point, mostly functions as a tryout. He will have three preseason games to learn the playbook and outdo his counterparts.
Make no mistake, this is a really uphill battle. Waller has to come in and start from scratch. His teammates may not be all that good, but they all have multiple years in Dave Canales' system.
Tremble has been around for all three seasons of Canales' tenure. Sanders has been there for two, and Evans has a year under his belt. Waller may have more talent than them, but he's facing an uphill battle while out of his prime.
Carolina's offense doesn't necessitate the use of a tight end. Dave Canales has historically not used the position much. However, he also hasn't had a good one to work with.
In Tampa Bay, he had Cade Otton before Otton became the solid if unspectacular tight end he is today. Then, in Carolina, the struggles to find a good tight end have been well documented.
It remains to be seen if Canales just doesn't need a tight end or if roster constraints have forced him and Brad Idzik to change their ways. The Waller signing may reveal that, because he has been a better receiving threat than the Panthers have had.
Unfortunately, the clock is running low for Waller and the Panthers, but it was well worth the shot.

title: The Good and Not So Good From Wednesday's Panthers Camp: Bryce Young's Down Day
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers wrapped another day of training camp practice on Wednesday after a day off on Tuesday. It was, like all camp days, a day full of good things and bad things. The team continues to work through everything ahead of their preseason matchup with the Buffalo Bills this weekend.
Evans with another nice catch in tight coverage by Nick Scott. https://t.co/ViItF2rFSs
Ja'Tavion Sanders, currently TE3, said that any of the three could be TE1 at any point. Well, Mitchell Evans seems to be confirming that. He is TE2, but he had a really excellent day with a few outstanding highlight-reel catches. He's making a strong case to get more playing time. He had a solid but quiet rookie year, and he could be pushing for a sophomore leap instead of slump.
Jalen Coker v Jaycee Horn. pic.twitter.com/xisLO7kWfp
Bryce Young has had an outstanding training camp . Full stop. And today, he was far from awful, but it was a down day for him. He went a little viral for an abysmal missed throw in one-on-one drills, where Jalen Coker beat Jaycee Horn, and Young's throw was nowhere close. He was decent in team drills, but nothing that helped make up for an alarming misfire.
Lathan Ransom just laid out Ja’seem Reed in team pass. Reed is on his feet thankfully.
We've covered at times how the training camp fights can be good, as they showcase the intensity needed to win football games. But fights every day are not good, and fortunately, the Panthers managed to keep up the intensity today without it boiling over. Lathan Ransom continues to play really hard, but this time, it didn't lead to a skirmish. That kind of intensity is great, but it can't lead to fights all the time.
