title: 88-Catch Free Agent Could Provide Big Lift to Packers’ Passing Attack
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers are going with the less-is-more approach at receiver. The obvious counterpoint to that is what if less is actually just less?
At receiver, they have three players they trust to start games in Christian Watson, Jayden Reed and Matthew Golden. Savion Williams had a productive day at practice on Sunday but has a long way to go before he can be considered reliable.
At tight end, less is actually just barren.
Tucker Kraft is working his way back from last season’s ACL tear. While he is practicing and his goal is to be ready for a full workload in the season opener, the Packers are unlikely to have him play every snap in a game. As things stand, though, they may not have another choice.
Luke Musgrave is on the shelf with a neck injury. Josh Whyle just returned to practice from an injury. He’s more of a role player, anyway. The back of the depth chart includes a bunch of players with extremely limited experience (or none at all) with Drake Dabney, Messiah Swinson and McCallan Castles.
If only there was someone available on the free-agent market who has familiarity in Matt LaFleur’s offense who could help as a secondary pass-catching option.
As it turns out, the Packers are in luck. Tight end Jonnu Smith is available and, because he’s looking for a team halfway through training camp, isn’t likely to cost much.
Signing with a new team always requires an adjustment period, but if the Packers were to make the move for Smith, his adjustment would likely be accelerated.
Smith and coach Matt LaFleur are not strangers. Smith was in Tennessee when LaFleur was the Titans’ offensive coordinator in 2018. He caught 20 passes on 30 targets in 13 games, scoring three touchdowns.
Since then, Smith has played most prominently in Arthur Smith’s system with the Titans and Falcons. Arthur Smith was LaFleur’s successor when LaFleur took the head job in Green Bay in 2019, leading to Jonnu Smith becoming a more prominent figure in the passing game.
Jonnu Smith’s most productive season came with Mike McDaniel’s Dolphins in 2024, when he caught an eye-popping 88 passes for 884 yards and eight touchdowns. That includes a late-season game at Green Bay in which he caught 10-of-11 targets for 113 yards.
While that season is an outlier, Smith has been productive throughout his career. Since 2020, he’s never caught less than 27 passes. He caught 38 passes last season for the Steelers. Plus, he’s played all 17 games each of the past three seasons.
“I was with Jonnu back in Tennessee. He’s one of the more explosive guys in regards to being able to catch and run,” LaFleur said before last year’s game at Pittsburgh.
With Tucker Kraft assuming full duties as the top tight end on the roster, the Packers might be looking for someone who can fill responsibilities as a secondary tight end. That player is more of a role player in LaFleur’s system, which means he better be able to block.
That’s part of the reason Musgrave has struggled since falling behind Kraft prior to the 2024 season.
Smith isn’t a great blocker, either. At 6-foot-3 and 247 pounds, he’s not a traditional tight end. In desperate times, however, the Packers and LaFleur might need to be willing to make some adjustments on what they’re looking for at the position.
Smith caught 38 passes from Aaron Rodgers last season but for only 222 yards. He gained just 10 first downs. The Packers’ receiver trio of Savion Williams, Bo Melton and Skyy Moore, on the other hand, combined to catch 19 passes. Even if you include Golden, that number only rises to 48. The moral of the story is there is not a lot of experience in Green Bay’s pass-catching corps beyond Watson, Reed and Kraft.
All three of those players have significant injury histories, and Golden missed time last year with shoulder and wrist injuries.
Green Bay already got a glimpse of what its fate could look like if the injury bug bites. Savion Williams had a big day at practice on Sunday, but that was buoyed by the fact that Golden and Reed were on the sideline nursing injuries.
The two players returned to the lineup after a short absence, but the Packers may not be so lucky in the future.
In a different world in which the Packers are not vying for a Super Bowl, they could roll the dice that a young tight end behind Kraft would step up. They could make the bet that they’ll be OK with Williams, Melton or Moore stepping into more of a full-time role.
This is not a normal world. The Packers are looking to compete for a Super Bowl in 2026. Their defense is likely to experience some growing pains with a new defensive coordinator who will have to navigate at least the first month without its best defensive player.
The Packers’ path to a good start to the season, and perhaps a glorifying finish, falls on the right arm of Jordan Love.
If nothing else, Smith, who will turn 31 on Aug. 22, would provide an insurance policy if Kraft is not fully ready to start the season or has to miss time later in the year. He’d also provide a secondary passing threat and give LaFleur options for two-tight-end sets. As an added bonus, he carried the ball nine times for 70 yards last season.
General manager Brian Gutekunst has broken his mold in terms of signing veterans on the wrong side of 30, with Javon Hargrave and Zaire Franklin making their way to Green Bay this offseason.
With desperation looming at tight end, it might be time to do that again.

title: Five Packers With Soaring Stock Who Flipped Depth Charts at Training Camp
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The hot starts to Green Bay Packers training camp for players like Jaylin Simpson mean everything and nothing, all at once.
“Honestly, one day at a time,” Simpson said this week. “I know it’s cliché as hell, but one day at a time, one play at a time. What happened today is already over.”
With the preseason starting on Thursday at the Steelers, here are five players with soaring stock because of their excellent training camps.
Anthony Campbell was 82nd in our pre-training camp ranking of all 91 players on the roster. Maybe even that was too high. As a sixth-year senior at Miami, Campbell made one tackle. He went undrafted in 2025 and spent most of his rookie season out of the league until the Packers signed him to their practice squad toward the end of the regular season.
It’s from those humble roots where one of the daily standouts of training camp was born. He’s shown a surprising ability for getting to the quarterback. When he’s not getting to the quarterback, he’s shown a knack for batting down passes. And with long arms, he’s been a force against the run.
The Packers have an unexpectedly strong group of defensive tackles. Making the 53-man roster is going to be a challenge, but he’s shown he is more than good enough to play in the NFL, even if he apparently wasn’t good enough to play in college.
“It's not over yet,” he said on Tuesday. “It's working but, at the end of the day, I want to look back and I'm saying, ‘Damn, I'm strong.’”
We’ll have more on the native of Jamaica before Thursday’s game.
Warren Brinson was a sixth-round pick last year. He was a healthy scratch to start the season and finished with a half-sack and 13 tackles in 11 games.
Brinson needed to take a big step forward in Year 2. Instead, he’s taken a big leap. He’s been one of the best players on the field this summer, whether it’s as an interior rusher or as a nose tackle. Brinson seemingly has played his way off the bubble and into a key role on defense.
Brinson said he did “two-a-days” all offseason with Tom Bender, who was the performance coach for Justin Houston, the NFL sacks champion in 2014, and MLB home-run king Aaron Judge.
“I got a long way to go,” Brinson said after a huge Family Night. “He always tells me I’m only 70 percent of where he says I could be at. I just got to keep going back, keep working. He was up here like two days ago working with me. I got to keep my body straight and keep believing in the goals he has for me and the goals I have for myself.”
Speaking of players who went from the roster bubble to start training camp to earning a key role entering the preseason, there’s Jacob Monk.
Monk was a fifth-round pick in 2024. He played exactly zero snaps on offense as a rookie and the first 15 games of 2025. He got some garbage-time snaps in the blowout loss to Baltimore in Week 17 and started the Week 18 preseason-style game at Minnesota.
After the Packers drafted Jager Burton in the fifth round and gave hefty contracts to undrafted free agents Dillon Wade and Josh Gesky, Monk’s spot on the roster appeared precarious.
Instead, he is well on his way to being the team’s starting right guard instead of last year’s second-round pick, Anthony Belton.
It means, “Nothing,” he said after Tuesday’s practice. “It's nothing right now. I feel like our end goal is get better each and every day and then, hopefully, host the Lombardi. So, right now is not the end goal. It’s nothing really that we're thinking about.”
He did admit it was rewarding to see a lifetime of hard work paying off.
“Yeah, I know I've worked my tail off,” he said. “You know, I've prayed hard for an opportunity. But, at the end of the day, the person who looks back on yesterday loses today. So, I really can't look back at all.”
This offseason, the Packers signed Benjamin St-Juste in free agency and drafted Brandon Cisse in the second round and Domani Jackson in the sixth round.
It was a clear signal that good wasn’t good enough at a critical position.
To say Simpson, a fifth-round pick by the Colts in 2024 who made his NFL debut in Week 18 of last season, opened training camp on the roster bubble might be generous. With Keisean Nixon, Carrington Valentine, St-Juste, the rookies and Kamal Hadden, Simpson faced a serious uphill climb.
Injuries to Valentine and Jackson and last year’s injury to Hadden opened the door, and Simpson has taken full advantage. After a solid start to training camp, he strung together big-time performances at Family Night on Friday and again on Sunday and Monday.
With experience at cornerback, safety and the slot, which is where he lined up on Tuesday, he could provide multipositional depth.
“I had a good friend of mine and we would call it ‘magazine mode.’ We ended up being on the cover of a magazine one time. And so it would be midgame in high school and we would just look at each other and say ‘magazine mode.’ And that’s just like a reset – like lock in, being on the front of a magazine, you that guy. Just chill and go magazine mode.
“It was an inside joke. I still say that to myself to this day. It’s a sense of comfort. Just calm down, be cool, you been doing this.”
Simpson has spent most of training camp with the No. 2 defense. He figures to get a lot of playing time in the preseason.
“I think he’s really making an impact,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “I think he’s made a lot of plays. Certainly, you could see it on the last play of practice yesterday [a 99-yard pick-six on Monday], where he picked that ball off. But I think I see a guy that’s growing, that’s playing with more confidence. He’s like a lot of these guys – you’re just excited to see him play in preseason.”
Brandon Cisse, of course, did not start training camp on the roster bubble.
His rise, though, has been just as noteworthy. Remember, Jaire Alexander was a first-round draft pick in 2018. He was not a starter to open his rookie season. Eric Stokes was a first-round draft pick in 2021. He also was not a starter to open his rookie season.
Cisse was a second-round draft pick this year. He is well on his way to being a Week 1 starter.
Following a promising offseason, Cisse figured to get his shot with the starters at some point in training camp. When Carrington Valentine suffered a hamstring injury early in the fourth practice, Cisse got his opportunity. Even when Valentine is fully back at practice – he took part in individual drills on Tuesday – Cisse has earned the right to stay in the lineup.
He is talented and athletic with a professional mindset.
“I set a really high standard, so it’s going,” he said of his camp. “Obviously, I’ve got really high expectations for myself. I’m just looking at the plays I can get better from, and I’m excited for those. Obviously, there’s going to be moments where you see flashes and things like that, but there’s a lot of growing pains I’m also going through. I need to get better at those things. I’m just excited to clean it up and continue to get better every day.”

title: Sleep? New Packers Receiver Chris Hilton Doesn’t Have Time for That
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – What a rollercoaster it’s been for new Green Bay Packers receiver Chris Hilton, both mentally and physically, as he quickly shifted gears from being released by the Commanders on Sunday to getting ready to play in game for his new team on Thursday.
“I ended up getting released, found out they claimed me (off waivers),” Hilton said after his first practice with team on Tuesday. “So, I was on the way to Dulles Airport, got there, flight was delayed, then there was a misconnect at the next airport. So, I had to Uber to D.C., get on the plane there, got to Chicago. That got delayed till like midnight. I didn’t get on the plane until like 1, landed at 2, went to bed at 3, and was here at 6:45. …
“So, it’s been a long 48 hours for me, but we’re making it.”
Hilton doesn’t have time to catch up on sleep. With one practice under his belt and a crash course into the offense, he will be on the field for Thursday night’s preseason game at the Steelers.
Fortunately for Hilton, he’s got a history with learning playbooks in short order. After a disappointing senior season at LSU, he played in an unprecedented four all-star games
“Really, the whole thing was to give myself the best opportunity,” he said. “I wanted to go through that thing and leave no stone unturned. I didn’t have the college season that I wanted to, so I tried to put myself in the best position possible. And if doing all four was what I had to do, that was what I was going to do.”
That meant a lot of learning and unlearning, which should come in handy as he forgets the Commanders’ playbook and learns the Packers’ playbook.
“Getting to the first one [the American Bowl], I think I came like a day late, so everybody was already ahead. So, I played catch-up there. It was kind of the same thing (with) different terminology, but that’s how I was able to pick it up quick.”
With the Packers, there will be early mornings and late nights to pick up an offense that was installed during the offseason and installed again during the opening week of training camp.
How will he do it so he can play at a high level on Thursday?
“You got to do what you got to do, you know what I’m saying?” he said. “If there’s a will, there’s a way, and I got a will, so I’m going to figure it out.”
The Packers claimed Hilton after starters Matthew Golden and Jayden Reed suffered minor injuries on Family Night. They returned to practice on Tuesday, though. That means Hilton’s spot with the Packers might not last for long unless he gives them a reason to give him an extended look.
On the other hand, none of the young receivers have been able to string together a bunch of productive days at training camp, so, from that perspective, there’s a real chance for Hilton.
“Yeah, most definitely,” he said. “I’m just here to do my job, you know what I’m saying? Catch the ball. That’s the name of the game for me, so that’s what I’m here to do.”
In five seasons at LSU, Hilton finished with only 41 passes for 780 yards and six touchdowns. He ended the 2024 season in explosive fashion with touchdowns of 40 and 45 yards against Oklahoma and a 41-yard touchdown highlighting his four catches for 113 yards in the bowl game against Baylor.
However, he caught just 10 passes for 122 yards in 2025. He went undrafted and signed with the Commanders, who released him upon signing Stefon Diggs.
“I would say my IQ, football intelligence” is the strength to his game. “Obviously, everybody would say my speed. But I think the underrated part of my game would be how smart I am.”
Yeah, about that speed. He ran his 40 in 4.41 seconds before the draft. So, he’s fast. But can he play fast and allow his talent to show following a whirlwind week?
“Like I said, if there’s a will, there’s a way,” he said. “I’m going to figure something out.”

title: New Packers DBs Face Challenge of Lifetime for Life-Changing Opportunity
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – At one point during Tuesday’s practice at Green Bay Packers training camp, Trey Dean III and Tra Fluellen lined up together as the safeties.
Who are Trey Dean III and Tra Fluellen?
That’s probably the same thing they were asking each other.
“Don’t really know him,” Dean said.
The Packers waived/injured safety Johnathan Baldwin with a knee injury on Sunday, which left the team with only six safeties. One of them, Javon Bullard, is out with a foot injury and plays in the slot, anyway.
So, the Packers worked out Dean, Fluellen and Josh Minkins, with Dean and Fluellen signing contracts.
To clear roster spaces, they released tight end Drew Biber and offensive lineman Karsen Barnhart.
“It’s been really a blessing,” Dean said. “It was a great opportunity, joining a winning culture here. You know, we got a great staff, got great players, so it’s been like a blessing to be a part of a great organization.”
Dean (6-foot-2, 201 pounds), who had four interceptions and 20 passes defensed in five seasons at Florida, signed with the Jets as an undrafted free agent in 2023. He spent most of his rookie season on the Jets’ practice squad before joining the Chiefs’ practice squad just in time for their run to the Super Bowl.
Dean was released by the Browns before the start of their offseason practices in 2025. He spent the 2025 and 2026 seasons in the UFL.
“Just my big faith in God,” he said of his perseverance after being out of the league for more than 15 months. “I knew I always could play. I was with the Browns last year, just fighting through injury. Had a chance to win the Super Bowl with the Chiefs, so everything has really been a blessing.
“So, I just keep going and put God first. God’s going to prevail. I knew I always could play every time I got on a professional field. I had great film. I had great film in college. So, with God, I’m in a great organization with great coaches and everything’s going to fall together for the good common goal.”
Dean was fortunate to join a roster with some familiar faces. He said he was roommates with Brenton Cox and Ty’Ron Hopper while they were together at Florida. Moreover, he is longtime workout partners with Xavier McKinney.
“Yeah, we’re still in contact,” Dean said. “I kind of surprised him [in the locker room] and he was so happy. ‘Now I get to play with you,’ because I was committed to Bama all the way to Signing Day and then I flipped. So, he was kind of mad. But we’re real tight.”
McKinney isn’t holding Dean’s college choice against him. After all, they might need him.
“I think he could provide depth for us,” McKinney said. “Obviously, he’s a talented player. I’ve been with him, I’ve seen him play for a long time. I think the biggest thing is going to be depth. We’re down a couple guys so as far as making sure that we’ve got backups to go out there and fill a role if somebody goes down and not having it be a complete dropoff, I think he’ll help us.”
After intercepting five passes and adding 168 tackles during his final two seasons at Middle Tennessee State, Fluellen (6-foot, 212 pounds) went undrafted in 2024 and spent his rookie season on the Saints’ practice squad. He has not-so-fond memories of Green Bay.
“I came here two years ago with the Saints. I was on the practice squad, had to sit and watch through negative-9 degrees,” he said. “But getting to see the Pack kind of show out and come out, it was, obviously, just a realization of how together this town and this state is. And can’t describe a better place for myself right now coming in with some greats.”
Fluellen, who has been out of the NFL since being released by the Saints in June 2025, spent the spring playing with the Dallas Renegades of the UFL.
“I’m still considering myself as a rookie just because I haven’t been out there active on the field but, man, it’s been great,” he said of his early impressions of the team. “Everybody’s so welcoming and pushing me to be my best already, so I just love how we carry each other out here. Looking forward to opportunities and coming here and doing my job.”
That first opportunity will come against the Steelers on what likely will be a crash course in the defense.
Yeah, it’s a challenge, and it’s one he’s eager to tackle.
“At the end of the day, we’re all pros, so we’re all running the same things; just different terminology,” he said. “So, part of being a pro is coming in, doing your job and making those adjustments and realizing what you have to do.
“So, I got to do my part as a professional and learn the plays. You’re never going to be perfect – nobody’s ever perfect – but, to the best of my ability, I’m going to learn the plays as fast I can. Obviously, there’s no limit, but it’s going to be a quick turnaround, you know what I’m saying?”
With just one practice to get ready, Dean and Fluellen will be asked to be the last line of defense on Thursday at the Steelers.
It almost sounds like Mission Impossible, but the reward is impossibly big.
“I’m going to learn the playbook, play to my fullest potential,” Dean said. “They know I can play, you know? So, put all the work together, put God first and I think I got a good shot to make this team.”
There is a real opportunity for Dean and Fluellen. Yes, it’s true that they are with the team to provide a couple sets of fresh legs and to prevent the starters from having to take too many reps.
However, it’s not as if there isn’t a roster spot there for taking. McKinney, Bullard and Evan Williams are locked into three places and Kitan Oladapo almost certainly will be the fourth. If the Packers keep five, which they typically do, the other options are Mark Perry, who went undrafted in 2024 and hasn’t played in a regular-season game, and Murvin Kenion III, an undrafted rookie.
So, it’s not as if they are fighting for roster spots against in-their-prime versions of Nick Collins and LeRoy Butler.
Dean said he worked out for the Titans a few days earlier and they were interested in signing him, but “everything” about the Packers “really fit for me” as a place to restart his NFL career.
“Shoot, it’s just thanking God, you know?” he said. “I trained my whole life to get this opportunity to showcase my skills. I knew it was going to come, no matter if it was here or somebody else, but I was praying it was going to be here because it’s a great organization.”
He added, “Any way I can help this team win the championship, I’m going to do it.”

title: Domination: Everything I Saw From Practice 11 of Packers Training Camp
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers’ cornerback competition took an interesting turn at Monday’s practice . It took an interesting U-turn on Tuesday.
After veteran starter Keisean Nixon lost snaps with the No. 1 defense to Benjamin St-Juste on Sunday and especially on Monday, Nixon and rookie Brandon Cisse played every snap with the starters on Tuesday. St-Juste and Jaylin Simpson were locked in with the No. 2s.
“Everything's a competition right now, so we’re going to put different guys in different situations in different spots and see how they respond,” LaFleur said before Tuesday’s practice.
We’ll see if Nixon vs. St-Juste continues when the team returns to practice next week. We’ll also see if Carrington Valentine – who returned to practice on Tuesday after missing more than a week with a hamstring injury – will challenge Cisse. Valentine’s injury opened the door for the team’s first draft pick this year to play with the starters, and Cisse has taken full advantage.
“I set a really high standard, so it’s going,” Cisse said when asked about his training camp. “Obviously, I’ve got really high expectations for myself.
“I’m just looking at the plays I can get better from, and I’m excited for those. Obviously, there’s going to be moments where you see flashes and things like that, but there’s a lot of growing pains I’m also going through. I need to get better at those things. I’m just excited to clean it up and continue to get better every day.”
From top to bottom, cornerback has been the wildest position battle of Packers training camp. There were more twists and turns on Monday. ⬇️ https://t.co/8wrYjor0Bk
Here’s everything that happened at the 11th practice of Packers training camp, leading off with the headline of domination.
There haven’t been many days like this over the past three decades of Packers quarterbacking brilliance.
It was complete domination by Green Bay’s defense. On the first play of the day, Jordan Love and Sean Rhyan botched the snap. On the second play, MarShawn Lloyd tried to cut but slipped.
So, maybe that was more offensive failure than defensive playmaking. After that, though?
On the third play, Love’s bootleg pass to tight end Josh Whyle gained about a yard. After a completion from Love to Christian Watson against Brandon Cisse gained about 10 yards, Love’s quick pass to Matthew Golden was stopped near the line by Keisean Nixon.
And on and on it went. First unit. Second unit. Whatever unit.
The pinnacle was a red-zone period featuring nothing but third downs. The No. 1 offense ran six plays on third-and-goal but scored one touchdown.
First, Love was forced to scramble. Next, Love had nowhere to go and threw it away. The third play, a third-and-goal from the 3, Love hit Golden at the pylon against Cisse for what was probably a touchdown.
After the No. 2 offense got its crack and failed on three consecutive plays, the starters were back on the field. On third-and-goal from the 12, Love extended the play and spotted Skyy Moore in the back of the end zone. Moore made a leaping catch but was pushed out of the end zone by Evan Williams. On third-and-goal from the 6, Love’s pass to Whyle in the flat was off the mark. Finally, on third-and-goal at the 2, Edgerrin Cooper broke up Love’s pass to tight end Drake Dabney.
“I thought we had a great day in the red zone,” safety Xavier McKinney said. “I thought we were technically sound. Scheme was good, we executed well and we got off the field. I think we might have won every rep.”
Reminded of the pass to Golden at the pylon, McKinney said. “Oh, yeah. I’m not going to count those, but we probably get those tackles and get off the field. But I think we had a good day in the red zone. I thought it was clean. I thought everybody communicated well, and that’s what we’re going to need in the season.”
By our estimation, the defense is 10-1 in 11 training camp practices. The only loss came when Zaire Franklin and Edgerrin Cooper didn’t practice on Sunday.
“Obviously, there’s days where we couldn’t stop them,” Franklin said, though his recollection doesn’t fit reality. “There’s days where Jordan’s throwing bombs to Bo (Melton), to Christian, to Jayden (Reed). It’s like everybody’s catching a bomb, (including) Golden. So, you’re going to put as much energy into that as you put into days like today.
“Obviously, they’re talented, we’re talented. So, I feel like when we are able to execute and run the scheme the right way, we can play with anybody. So, obviously, iron sharpens iron. We’re sharpening them boys. They won’t play against people as good as us and they’re going to run them out the building. So, that’s how that works.”
New injury: Edge Dani Dennis-Sutton (illness).
PUP: Edge Micah Parsons (knee), LS Matt Orzech (calf), TE Luke Musgrave (neck), DT Jordon Riley (Achilles).
Old injuries: RB Josh Jacobs (groin), CB Domani Jackson (unknown).
Returned to practice: WR Matthew Golden (toe), WR Jayden Reed (ankle), CB Carrington Valentine (hamstring), TE Josh Whyle (neck).
Valentine participated in individual drills while the others got some 11-on-11 work.
With the Packers running short on safeties, they signed Trey Dean and Tra Fluellen. To create space on the roster, they released guard/tackle Karsen Barnhart and tight end Drew Biber.
We’ll have more on Dean and Fluellen from our after-practice conversations.
During the backups’ third-and-goal series, Tyrod Taylor was forced to check it down to running back Jaden Nixon. Linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper was there in an instant to either force a fumble (which was recovered by Arron Mosby) or break up the pass.
Safety Evan Williams shined the brightest during the defense’s big day. First, there was the aforementioned play in which he shoved receiver Skyy Moore out of the back of the end zone to prevent a touchdown. Later, Tyrod Taylor threw a bomb to Kisean Johnson but Williams ranged over for the interception.
“It’s been great,” safety Xavier McKinney said of his growth alongside third-year safeties Williams and Javon Bulard. “Just being right by these guys every day, building even off the field with our relationship. Everything has been great.
“Seeing them come out here and ball and do the things that they’re doing and progressing the way that they’re progressing, I love to see it. It makes me happy because it lets me know also that I’m doing something right. Trying to keep doing as much as I can for these guys. Making sure that they’re able to keep progressing and become those All-Pros and Pro Bowlers that I know that they are.”
– The No. 1 offensive line, as has been the case all week, consisted of left tackle Jordan Morgan, left guard Jager Burton, center Sean Rhyan, right guard Jacob Monk and right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele. With Bako-Bewele being eased back into team drills following last year’s knee surgery, Anthony Belton got plenty of action.
– The No. 1 defense included Lukas Van Ness, Barryn Sorrell, Nazir Stackhouse and Jonathan Ford up front. With Javon Bullard out with a foot injury, Kitan Oladapo was back in the slot.
– With the No. 2 defense, Benjamin St-Juste and Jaylin Simpson were the corners. In passing situations, Simpson moved into the slot and MJ Devonshire came in at corner. With Dani Dennis-Sutton out, Collin Oliver joined Brenton Cox on the edges.
– The punt-return rotation consisted of Skyy Moore, Jayden Reed, Matthew Golden, Will Sheppard, Jayden Nixon and Kisean Johnson.
– The day ended with a half-speed 2-minute drill. The defensive unit: Brenton Cox, Barryn Sorrell, Warren Brinson and Anthony Campbell up front, and the usual group of linebackers and defensive backs. Campbell, obviously, is the interesting name from that unit.
It was a shorter-than-normal practice. With the starters’ troubles documented above, this will be a short list of highlight plays that will feature the backups.
– The No. 2 offense’s first play was a toss to Pierre Strong that was stopped by Brenton Cox and Jonathan Ford.

title: One Packers Position Battle Just Took Another Interesting Turn
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – As expected, rookie Brandon Cisse is in the competition to start at cornerback for the Green Bay Packers. Also as expected, Benjamin St-Juste is in the competition to start at corner, as well.
What wasn’t expected? The defense that the Packers will roll onto the field for Week 1 at the Vikings could feature Cisse and St-Juste at cornerback instead of Cisse or St-Juste.
Cisse has been playing with the starters since the fourth practice of training camp, when returning starter Carrington Valentine dropped out with a hamstring injury. At this point, Valentine might be Wally Pipp to Cisse’s Lou Gehrig. Between production and potential, it’s going to be hard to take Cisse out of the lineup.
“We want to see him out there and see what he can do,” new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon said last week of Cisse. “Obviously, we took him where we took him. He’s got the skill-set that we’re looking for, and he’s doing a good job of when he makes a mistake – mistakes are going to happen, especially for young guys in a new scheme – mistakes are OK (but) just don’t make the same mistake again. I think all our rookies are doing a good job of that.”
The next big development started at Sunday’s closed-to-the-public practice, when St-Juste replaced Keisean Nixon with the starters for one period. It was an interesting development, to say the least, but not especially meaningful in the big picture. Nixon was back with the starters for the next period and the rest of the day.
Coach Matt LaFleur did his best Daniel Whelan impersonation as he punted a question about it before Monday’s practice.
“Well, I think there’s always competition,” he said. “All these guys got to be prepared for that. As far as the substitution, that’s not something that I’m always micromanaging. A lot of that’s on the position coach.”
On Monday, it wasn’t just one period. The position coach, Bobby Babich, gave Nixon the first period, St-Juste the second period and they rotated the rest of the day. At this point, it looks like a full-fledged competition between Nixon, who would like a new contract commensurate with his status as “CB1,” and St-Juste.
“Everything's a competition right now, so we’re going to put different guys in different situations in different spots and see how they respond,” LaFleur said, more forthcoming on the topic when asked before Tuesday’s practice.
As noted in our latest Winners and Losers story , here’s the interesting dynamic. Nixon is part of the old regime. He followed Rich Bisaccia from the Raiders to Green Bay, but he’s no longer with the team. He became an every-down cornerback under Jeff Hafley, who’s also no longer with the team.
Gannon and Babich have no such allegiance to Nixon. He’s not one of Gannon’s guys. It doesn’t mean he can’t be – doesn’t mean he won’t be – but St-Juste and Cisse are the cornerbacks added since his arrival.
Nixon was chewed up and spit out during one-on-ones last week, including Matthew Golden torching him on all three reps on Family Night. The one-on-ones are a small part of the equation – and this is nothing but speculation – but it’s possible Gannon saw the effort and performance put out by Nixon, Cisse and St-Juste and decided to open the competition.
At this point, the cornerback competition could swing in several directions. Here are two. One, the starting secondary for the season-opening showdown against the rival Vikings and their high-flying set of receivers will be Nixon and Cisse, with St-Juste the next man up. Or, two, Cisse and St-Juste will start and Nixon will be on another roster.
The developments run beyond who will start. The backup battles have taken a twist, too.
Yesterday was the 10th practice of Packers training camp. Focusing on camp as a whole, here are a total of 1⃣5⃣ winners and losers. ⬇️ https://t.co/lb4FoicQp8
With the returns of Keisean Nixon and Carrington Valentine and the additions of Benjamin St-Juste in the second round, Brandon Cisse in the second round and Domani Jackson in the sixth round, every other cornerback seemed to be chasing the impossible dream of earning a spot on the 53.
Jaylin Simpson has changed that thinking. He had a strong Family Night, including an interception during one-on-ones. In the closed practice on Sunday inside the Hutson Center, he broke up two passes. On Monday, he had a 99-yard pick-six but also another breakup and an impact blitz to blow up a running play.
Valentine has missed more than a week with a hamstring injury. Jackson, who had core-muscle surgery, which kept him out of the offseason practices, missed the last couple days of practice and hasn’t taken part in team drills. That’s allowed Simpson to move in with the No. 2 defense, where he has thrived.
“Those plays yesterday, those were hard plays to make,” Simpson said after Monday’s big day. “I had to really work for those. That’s all just technique, play recognition, splits, everything just coming together with those. You really got to be on top of your stuff.
“Hopefully, it means something, but like I was just saying , man, it’s in the past. The plays are made and the thing with the plays yesterday, is they’re good plays, but nobody remembers PBUs, for real. I want the ball in my hands. Those are cool and all, but I want interceptions.”
Javon Bullard is the team’s standout in the slot. He will start, period, end of conversation.
Who will be the backup for times like now, when he’s out with a foot injury?
That appeared to be Johnathan Baldwin, who took all the No. 2 reps from the start of OTAs through the start of training camp. However, he suffered a knee injury and was replaced in the lineup by safety Kitan Oladapo.
On Sunday, the Packers released Baldwin. On Monday, Kamal Hadden took his first 11-on-11 reps since last year’s horrible ankle injury against Baltimore.
“It went well. I enjoyed it. Built my confidence up and, sh**, I wanted more,” he said after practice.
At the time of the injury, Hadden had just replaced Carrington Valentine at corner with the No. 1 defense. On Monday, he was in the slot. It’s a position he said he hasn’t “played … much” in his career.
“I feel like it definitely allowed me to show my flexibility and what I can do inside and outside,” he said. “You know, the more you can do, the more valuable you are. So, I just think it’s a great opportunity ahead, but it could give me a few pushing points with the guys that are trying to make it.”
What is the challenge compared to playing corner?
“I feel like the challenge is you’re more so in the run fit,” he said. “You’re more in the core of the offense and the defense, and you got to read a lot of things, you got to know a lot of things. You got to be a general out there, as well. I’m already a vocal guy, so that’s really not an issue, but just reading the run fits and knowing where to fit and knowing what to do and things like that is probably the biggest challenge, but I’ve been picking it up well.”
For Hadden, returning to 11-on-11 reps was the next big step in his comeback.
“It meant a lot just to build my confidence up, helping me get my mind right and helping everybody else actually see that I’m back and I’m well and things like that,” he said. “I didn’t really like what I put out there but it was all good, man. It built my confidence up.”
Sure, Hadden wanted to do better, but they were his first reps in about seven-and-a-half months.
“Yeah, that’s the main thing is knocking off the rest and just reassuring myself that you’re all right, you’re good,” he agreed. “When you’re out there, man, it’s a feeling that you can’t describe every time. So, it was good.”

title: 15 Winners and Losers From First 10 Practices of Packers Training Camp
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The 10th practice of Green Bay Packers training camp on Monday looked a lot like the first nine. The defense, even without Micah Parsons, scored a decisive win over the offense.
Here are the winners and losers from the totality of the first 10 practices.
The “loser” designation doesn’t have anything to do with Jordan Love’s performance. Instead, it has everything to do with the first pass of the day on Monday. Love dropped back to pass but nobody blocked blitzing safety Evan Williams. Defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt got through the line, as well.
So, Love scrambled to his right and chucked the ball to the sideline to avoid being sacked.
It’s been that kind of summer for Love, and that was before receivers Matthew Golden and Jayden Reed popped up on the injury report after Family Night. He just hasn’t had time to get into much of a rhythm. And now, two of his top three receivers are injured.
It’s been a perfect-10 summer for running back MarShawn Lloyd. He’s been a full participant at all 10 practices during training camp, a fact that stands in stark contrast to his first two seasons in the league.
At this point, the question isn’t whether Lloyd will be healthy to contribute. It’s what can Lloyd contribute now that he’s healthy? His ability to break tackles, see and pick up blitzes and catch the football remain a bit of a mystery.
“He’s special. He’s a special dude,” fellow running back Chris Brooks said. “He plays at a different speed, and I think the sky’s the limit for MarShawn and his capabilities and what he can do for the offense.”
The only thing holding back Tucker Kraft in his comeback from a torn ACL is the medical staff.
Kraft has been limited to individual drills, but every day at practice provides another hint that the star tight end is going to be ready to roll sooner than later.
Tucker Kraft looking better and better every day. pic.twitter.com/FdFycQw6Q1
At one practice last week, he stood in the end zone to catch passes from scrambling quarterbacks. He made leaping catches and a diving catch. On Monday, he ran an out-and-up, caught the ball in stride, stepped on the gas and sprinted up the right sideline alongside the bleachers. The fans cheered, no doubt sensing that No. 85 is going to be more than ready for Week 1.
“Whether it’s blocking, whether it’s pass catching or getting that YAC, he does it all,” quarterback Jordan Love said. “Obviously, the mentality he brings is another factor that gets guys going on offense, and guys want to be out there with him and give him their all. I think it’s the intangibles, like everything he can do: blocking, catching, getting yards out to catch, and just bringing that mindset.”
In the first 32 games of his NFL career, Jacob Monk played exactly zero snaps on offense.
With the addition of fifth-round pick Jager Burton and a couple high-priced undrafted free agents, it seemed like Monk might be fighting for his spot on the roster. Instead, he’s fighting for a starting job. If the season started today, he would be the starting right guard for Week 1 at the Vikings.
That’s where he made his first NFL start in Week 18 of last season.
“I love football,” Monk said. “I love getting there and going out there to play. I thought I did some things well. I thought there was stuff to work on. I went to the offseason wanting to work on that, but one thing I can give is my play style, because I know as long as you play hard and play fast, you always have a chance on each and every play. Every play’s not going to be perfect, but strain and finish will help you.”
Jacob Monk took the starting job from Anthony Belton, who started seven games after being the 54th overall pick of last year’s draft.
Belton might wind up being the swing tackle this season, which could be a key role. But for a second-round pick to lose his starting job is an organizational loss.
The Packers signed Aaron Banks to a colossal contract in free agency last offseason. It was a head-scratcher of a deal at the time due in part to the fact he started 43 of a possible 51 games during his final three seasons with the Niners. His play on the field last season, due in part to nagging injuries, didn’t exactly reward the team for its faith.
Through 10 practices, Banks has been limited to individual drills by a knee injury.
“No timetable,” on making his debut in team drills, he said on Monday. “We’re kind of just taking it one day at a time. That’s just kind of the nature of it. Kind of hard to set a timeline, but not concerned for Week 1 of the season.”
Entering camp, the defensive tackle group looked like a giant question mark. The best player, Devonte Wyatt, had never been a full-time player. The big addition, Javon Hargrave, was 33 years old. Warren Brinson and Karl Brooks were sixth-round picks, with Brinson coming off a quiet rookie season and Brooks a disappointing third season. Chris McClellan was a third-round rookie at a position in which Kenny Clark started only two games as a rookie. Anthony Campbell and Jaden Crumedy were returning practice-squad players.
Instead, even with Wyatt and Hargrave limited by injuries, this group has been a powerhouse. Brooks has been a force. Brinson and Nazir Stackhouse are in the running for the biggest Year 2 jump. Campbell has been the surprise standout. Every player on the depth chart might wind up on a 53-man roster this season.
“Yeah, I’ll tell you what, those guys have shown up repeatedly,” coach Matt LaFleur said after Family Night. “It’s a tough battle in that room right now, not only for playing time but for roster spots.”
The Packers cranked out their first unofficial depth chart ahead of Thursday's preseason game. @JacobWestendorf examines what's real and what's wrong. ⬇️ https://t.co/JX7Aw8oDEB
Without Micah Parsons (and Rashan Gary and Kingsley Enagbare), the Packers desperately need Lukas Van Ness to step up his game.
With 8.5 sacks in three seasons, his career has been underwhelming, to state the obvious. A broken thumb in 2024 and a foot injury in 2025 were factors, to be sure. Healthy again, there were high hopes for Van Ness entering this season.
So far, those hopes haven’t become reality. Van Ness had a big Family Night but, by and large, he’s sort of faded into the background after getting everyone excited during the shorts-and-helmets practices of May, June and July.
The Packers don’t intentionally decide to get older very often, but that’s what they did when they chose not to re-sign Quay Walker and filled the void by trading for Zaire Franklin.
Franklin, who turned 30 last month, looks like a heart-and-soul type of player. He’s been a dominant player against the run and quickly became the leader of the defense. It’s not a coincidence that the offense’s best day this summer was when Franklin wasn’t on the field on Sunday. It’s also not a coincidence that the defense turned the tables in Franklin’s return on Monday.
“I just feel like every moment that I’ve had in my career has prepared me for this moment,” he said early in camp. “This right here, I truly feel like God placed me here. Like I feel like this is just divine timing. I’m just blessed to be on a team and organization that’s ready, that’s got everything we need. The building’s got everything we need. The organization’s got everything we need.
“I’m just trying to come here and do my part. So, I’m going to be the best version of me. We going to look back a couple years from now and decide whether that was a good decision for them or not, you know? And that’s not for me to decide. That’s for everybody else.”
So far, the decision is easy. He hasn’t been a good addition. He’s been a great addition.
Carrington Valentine started 30 games his first three seasons and opened camp with the No. 1 defense. His hamstring injury opened the door for Brandon Cisse, and that door might never reopen given the play and potential of the rookie.
Brandon Cisse remains with the No. 1 defense. pic.twitter.com/B8yUmS7RfB

title: What's Real, What's Wrong About First Packers Depth Chart
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers released their first unofficial depth chart on Monday night to reveal who has won starting positions for their Week 1 game against the Minnesota Vikings.
Ok, so not all of that is true. Sometimes a depth chart is insight into what the team might be thinking for when the games count. Sometimes it’s not worth the piece of paper it is written on.
That’s why we are here, to help cut through what is real and what is not.
Some things are obvious. Jordan Love is going to start at quarterback. Jordan Morgan is going to start at left tackle. Beyond that? Some things are still pretty murky as the Packers roll toward their first preseason game on Thursday night against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
Perhaps there will be more insight on Thursday if the Packers elect to play their starters, which Matt LaFleur alluded to the possibility of during his media availability on Monday.
“Sometimes you have to push the envelope,” LaFleur said, while citing data that players who play during the preseason are less likely to get injured during the regular season.
Of course, LaFleur said that a year ago and Jordan Love threw five passes in the preseason, and the rest of the starters hardly played as the team relied on joint practices to get themselves ready for the regular season opener.
For now, all we can go on is what the Packers have done in practice, and if it lines up with the depth chart they released on Monday evening. Here is our look at what is real, and what is not real.
The starting lineup has Jordan Morgan, Aaron Banks, Sean Rhyan, Anthony Belton, and Zach Bako-Bewele in the starting lineup.
The backups from left to right are listed as John Williams, Jacob Monk, Jager Burton, Donovan Jennings, and Darian Kinnard.
It’s hard to say at this point as the Packers’ offensive line remains in flux. Anthony Belton is arguably having the most disappointing training camp of any player on the roster as he was supposed to be a stabilizing force on the right side of the offensive line.
Instead, he’s conceding reps to former fifth-round picks Jacob Monk and Jager Burton. Banks has yet to take part in team drills, and it does not sound like that is going to happen anytime soon.
If Belton does not win the job at right guard, he likely converts to the team’s swing tackle, which is another position that has been up for grabs this offseason.
As far as starters, LaFleur and the rest of the team need to get their top five settled before having to face off against Brian Flores and his complex Minnesota Vikings’ defense on opening day.
“Yeah, I think we've, we've talked about that quite a bit in here,” LaFleur said on Monday. “I think right, about the importance of getting all five of those guys out there at the same time. But you know, you got to adjust to the circumstances, and the circumstances are we've had two guys that have started a lot of football games for us that haven't been available.”
In the second group, there’s plenty of intrigue, but perhaps the biggest riser in camp other than Monk is 2025 seventh-round pick John Williams.
The rocket scientist turned offensive lineman did not play at all as a rookie as he was nursing a back injury for the duration of the year. Now, he has the potential to be the team’s backup left tackle and is listed as such on the depth chart.
That lines up with what has happened in practice as camp has progressed. It will be worth noticing where Williams lines up on Thursday night against the Steelers.
Kamal Hadden is listed as the backup nickel corner to Javon Bullard, who missed Monday’s practice with a foot injury.
Bullard’s injury is nothing serious as he joked it was something his mother would tell him to put some dirt on and get back on the field.
Hadden returned to team drills for the first time on Monday as he is shaking off an injury that required much more than dirt to heal from.
Hadden’s story to this point is a remarkable one as he’s not only trying to work his way back onto the field, but trying to learn a position he has not played much of on top of it.
“I did it a little bit in my past before,” Hadden said about playing nickel. “It's fairly, not new, but I haven't played it much. I haven't showed it much outside of practice, but I've been in the slot a little bit.”
Hadden was the backup slot corner at practice on Monday, but if the Packers had to play a game without Javon Bullard, they have options.
Keisean Nixon was their slot corner for the 2023 season before getting bumped outside, where he’s been ever since.
Kitan Oladapo is another potential option in the slot, but he is listed as a backup safety as well. The reality is the Packers love Bullard and hope he does not have to miss any time as he’s one of their core players primed for a breakout season.
“Yeah, yeah, Bull is, he's a dog, man,” LaFleur said on Monday. “You talk about a guy that plays with the right mentality, the right play style, what we want to be about, and so it's been cool just to see his evolution. I think we, you know, one thing that we put him in more situations where there's been some man coverage situations, and I think he's really progressed.”
Carrington Valentine and Keisean Nixon finished the 2025 season as the team’s starting cornerbacks, and they are still listed as the starters for now.
That might be in name only.
Valentine has not practiced in over a week with a leg injury, which has given way to second round pick Brandon Cisse to take starting reps. The other interesting part of the equation started on Sunday when Benjamin St. Juste started rotating into the starting lineup, but he wasn’t rotating with the rookie. He was rotating with Nixon.
Competition is going to be a factor at this spot all season, but it’s worth monitoring what happens throughout the rest of camp.
For now, however, it looks like Cisse is in line to start his first game.
Lukas Van Ness and Barryn Sorrell are listed as starters with their primary backups being Brenton Cox and Collin Oliver.
The edge position is one of intrigue because of the absence of Micah Parsons for the early portion of the season.
Collin Oliver is listed as a primary backup, but rookie fourth round pick Dani Dennis-Sutton has been ahead of Oliver across from Cox. This is a position that should be fluid throughout the year as they try to manufacture pass rush in the absence of Parsons.
Beyond that, the Packers need someone to emerge as rotational players behind Parsons and Van Ness.
The two starting defensive tackles listed on the depth chart are Devonte Wyatt and Karl Brooks. Javon Hargrave was the Packers’ biggest free agent acquisition this offseason, but is listed as the primary backup to Brooks. He has not participated in training camp except for two practices as he works his way back from a knee injury that landed him on the PUP list to start training camp.
It’s hard to say too much at this juncture because Hargrave has not taken any team reps. It’s also hard to envision the Packers would commit the kind of money they gave Hargrave to have him not start next to Wyatt.
One possibility is that they envision Hargrave as their starting nose tackle at this point, and that position is not listed on the depth chart.
If that were the case, their starting defensive front in base makes sense. The Packers will continue to rotate their guys throughout the season as a way to keep them fresh, but expect Hargrave to be a starter once he gets his sea legs underneath him.

title: Everything I Saw From Practice 10 of Packers Training Camp, With Brewing Battle
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Jonathan Gannon’s defense is causing widespread devastation on the Green Bay Packers’ practice field.
Handoffs frequently result in the ball-carrier getting hit at or behind the line of scrimmage. Passes frequently wind up with Jordan Love escaping the pocket and trying to make something happen.
“It’s definitely confusing, just the way he coaches and the way he aligns his safeties, aligns his corners,” receiver Bo Melton said. “You know, sometimes you don’t even know what coverage it looks like. And I’m like, ‘Man,’ so it kind of screws with our rules as a receiver. So, it’s very complex. He’s a smart guy, and he’s definitely calling some great coverages because it’s hard to see.”
Let’s use that as a segue to dive into everything that happened on Monday, the 10th practice of Packers training camp.
From this perspective, the defense won each of the first eight days of training camp. On Sunday, with linebackers Edgerrin Cooper and Zaire Franklin not on the field, we gave the win to this offense.
On Monday, with Cooper and Franklin back in the lineup, the defense – not coincidentally – rolled to another win.
We’ll see what it means for when games are played that count. But the defensive line has done nothing but inflict carnage on the offense. Whether it’s the starters or the backups, it doesn’t matter. Jonathan Gannon has blitzed from here, there and everywhere. And when he doesn’t, it’s the interior defensive line that has wrecked play after play.
On the first snap of the day, Franklin, who got the day off on Sunday after traveling back from the Hall of Fame enshrinement ceremonies to see in the induction of former teammate Adam Vinatieri, clobbered MarShawn Lloyd. That set the tone. On the last snap of the day, cornerback Jaylin Simpson had a 99-yard pick-six.
For the starters’ third-down period, the defense went 3-1. On the first play, Jordan Love hit Christian Watson for a first down. On third-and-6, Love threw incomplete to Skyy Moore while pressured by Karl Brooks and Collin Oliver. On third-and-9, Love had to check it down to tight end Drake Dabney, who gained maybe a couple yards. On third-and-2, Barryn Sorrell had a sack, though the play was allowed to keep going and Love and Isaiah Neyor were on the same page on the scramble drill.
“It’s been good, man,” said Brooks, who seems poised for a bounce-back season. “We been picking it up. We been learning it. Guys are making plays. It's real simplified compared to the last one. Not a lot of thinking required to just allow us to play fast use our play decision.”
New injury: S Javon Bullard (foot).
Bullard was wearing a walking boot at practice but not when he talked to reporters.
He’ll be fine, in other words.
“I need a new foot, huh?” he joked. “Nah, so my rookie year, we ended up taking a bone out of my foot. It was something that was lingering from college. This right foot’s been giving me a little trouble lately. This one is not as excruciating as the last one.
“That’s good news. It’s nothing crazy. I’ll be back in no time. If we had a game tomorrow ,I’d play. It’s nothing crazy. We’re just trying to proceed with caution right now instead of letting it linger and be dealing with it later on.”
If he followed his mom’s advice, he’d “put a little dirt on it” and be “all right.”
PUP: Edge Micah Parsons (knee), LS Matt Orzech (calf), TE Luke Musgrave (neck), DT Jordon Riley (Achilles).
Old injuries: WR Matthew Golden (toe), RB Josh Jacobs (groin), WR Jayden Reed (ankle), CB Domani Jackson (unknown), CB Carrington Valentine (hamstring), TE Josh Whyle (neck).
Returned to practice: LB Edgerrin Cooper (foot), LB Zaire Franklin (personal).
It was impossible to pick only one Play of the Day.
Our daily Play of the Day and Player of the Day features two Plays of the Day, including Bo Melton's highlight-reel catch over Keisean Nixon and what it means for earning the trust of Jordan Love by catching a 50/50 ball. Plus, two bubble stars.⬇️ https://t.co/FqlJuEKMnt
– On Sunday, Benjamin St-Juste replaced Keisean Nixon with the starters for one period and one period only. On Monday, Nixon once again played with the starters for the first period, St-Juste replaced him for the second period and they rotated for most of the day.
At this point, it appears to be a full-fledged battle between St-Juste, who was signed in free agency, and Nixon, who would like a contract extension.
“I think there’s always competition,” coach Matt LaFleur said before practice. “All these guys got to be prepared for that. As far as the substitution, that’s not something that I’m always micromanaging. A lot of that’s on the position coach.”
Meanwhile, rookie Brandon Cisse is going solo at the other corner position with Carrington Valentine sidelined.
Brandon Cisse remains with the No. 1 defense. pic.twitter.com/B8yUmS7RfB
– Once again, the No. 1 offensive line included left tackle Jordan Morgan, left guard Jager Burton (for Aaron Banks), center Sean Rhyan, right guard Jacob Monk and right tackle Zach Tom. Tom played close to half of the team reps. When he was not on the field, Anthony Belton played right tackle. When Belton was shaken up for a moment, Travis Glover entered the fray.
– The No. 2 line had John Williams at left tackle, Dillon Wade at left guard, Donovan Jennings at center, Darian Kinnard at right guard and Glover at right tackle.
– With the injuries at every position group, this was the No. 1 skill group for a 2-minute drill: MarShawn Lloyd at running back, Drake Dabney at tight end and Savion Williams, Bo Melton and Skyy Moore at receiver.
– With Javon Bullard out, undrafted rookie linebacker TJ Quinn joined the No. 1 punt team.
Tucker Kraft looking better and better every day. pic.twitter.com/FdFycQw6Q1
– The best thing the No. 1 offense has done during camp is throw the ball to Christian Watson on the move. So, after the day started with Zaire Franklin stuffing MarShawn Lloyd, Jordan Love having to throw it away while pressured by Evan Williams and Devonte Wyatt and Love throwing inaccurately to Skyy Moore, Love hit Watson on a slant for a big play.
That’s assuming Love would have gotten the ball off in a game, because Karl Brooks was coming in hot.
– After the play, Franklin ruined an end-around to Skyy Moore and Dani Dennis-Sutton’s pressure ruined a bootleg.
– With the No. 2 offense on the field, four running plays might have gained 0 yards. Isaiah McDuffie stuffed Pierre Strong, Damien Martinez tripped at the line of scrimmage, rookie defensive tackle Chris McClellan pushed rookie guard Dillon Wade into the path of running back Jaden Nixon and Nixon went nowhere as cornerback Jaylin Simpson came screaming into the backfield.
– Kyle McCord is taking charge of the No. 3 quarterback battle. On his first pass, he showed deft touch to hit Will Sheppard downfield.
– Back to the starters, Benjamin St-Juste destroyed a running play by MarShawn Lloyd. Keisean Nixon is a good tackler, to be sure, but St-Juste bring a whole other element of physicality.
– A few plays later, a handoff to Strong disappeared into the midsection of McClellan for a tackle for loss.
– Either Watson dropped a pass by Love or Evan Williams got there for a bang-bang breakup.
– We’re not allowed to talk about trick plays, but since the fans were there, we’ll describe a handoff to Lloyd in which he lateralled the ball back to Love, who threw a bomb to Melton for a touchdown.
“I think it was like a fourth-and-1, so I guess the defense wasn’t expecting it,” Melton said. “So, we got the defense and it was a great play.”
– Tyrod Taylor and Sheppard had impressive days. On one play, they teamed up for a big play down the left sideline against an obvious coverage bust.
– On the next play, Taylor ripped a slant to J. Michael Sturdivant between Simpson and safety Murvin Kenion.
Taylor is making due with a banged-up receiver corps that includes some fresh faces.
“That’s part of it, especially in training camp,” Taylor said. “You get new faces.…

title: 3 Biggest Factors to Watch in Texans' Preseason Opener vs. Chargers
full_text:
The Houston Texans kick off their first of three preseason games before the 2026 campaign at home on Thursday night against the Los Angeles Chargers.
It's a long-awaited return to the field for the Texans, as this will be the team's first time back in a live NFL game since their playoff exit against the New England Patriots back in January. And now, they get to start fresh in what could be an even better season from the one they're fresh off.
In their first preseason game against the Chargers, though, there will be a few storylines to keep an eye on as it relates to the Texans; some that can offer hints as to how the depth chart and 53-man roster could look come time for Week 1 after two weeks of training camp are now in the books .
Here are three of the biggest factors to be watchful of for the Texans in their Thursday night game against the Chargers:
The Texans' offensive line will look a little bit different heading into Week 1 of the regular season compared to how they wound up at the tail end of last year. And as preseason begins, we'll be able to land a first look at how we could expect this depth chart to be looking at the start of the 2026 campaign.
How will the Texans determine their first five starters? Will they hold out some of their expected starters to keep them fresh for closer to the season? How will rookies like Keylan Rutledge and Febechi Nwaiwu perform , and how much will Houston decide to play them? If the Texans are primarily running second and third-team offensive lines, who's lining up where and getting the most reps?
There's a ton of questions to be had for the Texans on their offensive line heading into the season, which is why it’s my number one factor to keep watch of as Houston begins preseason.
The first two weeks of the Texans' training camp has seen a couple of frequent highlight playmakers emerge as those who could make a run to the 53-man roster before Week 1 kicks off: wide receiver Lewis Bond and Collin Wright have probably been the two surprise performers hearing their names the most since Houston's been back on the field.
But now is the next step in their process to make noise on the 53-man roster: a live game against another team where both of them will be likely to get a high amount of snaps, given the circumstances.
It's a largely different scenario from what either of them has faced throughout their first steps in the league in practice and camp sessions. But a big performance from either would make their stock look even better heading into the season.
A huge question mark that's been in play throughout the Texans' first two weeks of camp: who will come out as the team's starting punter to start the season? And so far, there still hasn't been an exact verdict.
Kai Kroeger currently stands as the only punter on the roster after UDFA Jack Stonehouse was cut , but that doesn't mean Houston won't go out and sign another name to the 90-man roster for these next two preseason games, in the event that Kroeger struggles here against the Chargers.
That's what makes this game so important for Kroeger to take advantage of. If he can put together a big performance with consistent, positive punts when he's on the field, that can bolster his chances to make the 53-man roster in a big way. If he falls short, the conversation can easily shift in another direction.

title: Texans' Jadeveon Clowney Can Prove He's NFL's Biggest Bargain
full_text:
The Houston Texans are a little over a week removed from bringing in a big upgrade to their defensive line in Jadeveon Clowney .
The Texans had a ton of questions surrounding how they were going to attack their DE3 spot heading into the season. Clowney, a tested veteran who's been in the building once before, made a ton of sense to fill that spot, and now answers a ton of those lingering concerns Houston had off the edge .
And in order to do so, Clowney, who's now entering his 13th year in the NFL, took a pretty significant pay cut from what he'd typically be worth as a free agent––one that might end up making his contract one of the best in the league this season.
According to NFL insider Aaron Wilson of KPRC2 , the Texans will be paying Clowney a one-year, $8 million max value deal, with a base value of $5.5 million. Clowney will also have $4.5 million guaranteed on the contract.
#Texans three-time Pro Bowl edge Jadeveon Clowney one-year, $8 million max value deal: $2 million signing bonus, $2.5 million base salary (fully guaranteed), $58,823 per game active roster bonus, up to $1 million, $4.5 million total guaranteed, base value of $5.5 million, plus…
It's an extremely reasonable, borderline bargain deal for one of the better veteran edge rushers in the NFL. And when looking at what some of the top edge rushers on the market are making on their respective deals, the value looks even better for Houston.
An AAV of $5.5 million for Clowney barely lands within the top 60 of the NFL's highest-paid pass rushers in terms of cash.
According to Spotrac , $5.5 million in total cash is the same as New York Giants' defensive end/linebacker Chauncey Goldston. For reference, he played 10 games during the 2025 season to put together 1.0 sack and one start, playing in primarily special teams snaps.
As for Clowney, he proved he's still capable of playing well in the back-nine of his career in a rotational role with the Dallas Cowboys. And, as long as his production doesn't fall off a cliff in 2026, it will show that his contract is an extremely great deal for the Texans.
In 2025, Clowney played in 13 games with Dallas to put together 41 tackles, 12 TFLs, and 8.5 sacks, which makes for his third time in the past five seasons that he's had eight or more sacks in a year.
Even in what will be his age-33 season, Clowney is able to be respectable, high-end edge rusher who not only sets the edge and is a strong piece defending the run, has developed into a nice pass-rusher as well. His sack numbers have remained high, and could remain around the same in Houston.
But that impact for Clowney might be able to become further heightened on a defensive line like Houston's when he's paired with guys like Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter on the edge with him.
Clowney's individual numbers could see a slight dip, and his snap count could see the same effect, but he allows the Texans to rotate between all three of their high-end edge rushers and create what might just be the best three-man group off the edge in the entire league.
Clowney can play alongside either Anderson and Hunter when the other player is off the field, and really make this defensive line a tough task to stop on every down.
No matter if it’s a pairing of Anderson-Hunter, Hunter-Clowney, or Anderson-Clowney, this edge rush is a problem and offered a fit for Clowney that was hard to replicate with other teams––especially so when factoring in his history being the top draft pick to Houston in 2014.
For many teams, Clowney could be as high up the depth chart as their DE1, and in the process, have a near-double-digit sack season, while playing for a higher contract than what the Texans are paying him.
But Clowney chose to prioritize his role and his place on a winning team to make his fit in Houston come to fruition. And if those efforts from the Texans' former No. 1 pick make it result in a Super Bowl , there's going to be little debate that his $5.5 million contract is one of the best deals in the entire NFL.

title: Texans Sign Rookie Kicker Chris Freeman: Why Houston Added Him
full_text:
The Houston Texans are making a signing at kicker.
According to the Houston Chronicle 's Jonathan M. Alexander, the Texans are bringing in rookie kicker Chris Freeman to their 90-man roster.
The #Texans have signed rookie kicker Chris Freeman, while waiving WR Montrell Washington. This will allow Houston to give K Ka'imi Fairbairn a break.
In a corresponding move, the Texans also released recently-signed wide receiver Montrell Washington, therefore slimming Houston's deep receiver room by one, and allowing them to bring in a second kicker to their 90-man roster .
Freeman will, of course, be joining the Texans' veteran Ka'imi Fairbairn, as the second kicker in Houston, who is the longest-tenured player on the roster, being onboard dating back to 2017.
The Texans aren't signing Freeman as any type of competition for Fairbairn. If he were, Houston wouldn't have signed Fairbairn to a lucrative two-year extension earlier this offseason.
Instead, Freeman is in Houston as a bit of a tryout for himself, but also to give the Texans' veteran kicker a break during the preseason games ahead.
DeMeco Ryans already made it clear earlier this week that a select few players around the roster would be held out of Thursday's preseason game against the Los Angeles Chargers; a strategy many teams implement in the first, or sometimes, all of their preliminary showings to keep them rested for the regular season.
For Fairbairn, it seems as if the Texans are trending towards holding him out of those preseason games. But, as every football team does, Houston will need a kicker for their first game of the year on Thursday––even if they don't intend to sign him to the 53-man roster.
So the Texans went out and brought in Freeman, who comes off of four years playing college ball between the UConn Huskies and the Indiana Hoosiers, and now looks to make the jump to the NFL.
During the last season that Freeman played in UConn, Freeman had 23 field goal makes on 26 attempts. He made all of his 52 field goal attempts throughout the year, and two of his three misses were from 40-49 yards. He was 9-11 from that range.
It was his best season by far at the college level, and a big jump from his previous year with the Huskies, where he made less than 80% of his field goals. Now, he's making 88.5% of them and didn't miss a field goal for a second straight season.
So he's found the opportunity in the NFL after showcasing a ton of his skillset in the past couple of seasons. But the Texans, in all likelihood, won't bring Freeman aboard onto their 53-man roster. They'll have Fairbairn onboard to handle their kicking duties , as he's done for the past several seasons.
At the very least, though, Freeman will be able to get his film in front of NFL personnel, and the hope is that his showing leads to either a practice squad addition in Houston, elsewhere, or even a 53-man roster signing around the league where a team is in need of a kicker.
His first showcase will, most likely, come on Thursday against the Chargers, kicking off at 7 p.m. CT.

title: 5 Surprises Spotted in Texans' First Preseason Depth Chart
full_text:
The Houston Texans released their first unofficial depth chart heading into preseason later this week, giving us a peek into who on the 90-man roster places where , and what their role could be shaping up to look like.
Of course, there were several spots on that depth chart that weren't surprising by any means. Truly, a lot of the Texans' starters, especially on defense, are looking to be the same as they were from when they ended last season.
However, that doesn't mean there weren't a few surprises of note in that depth chart release either. A few players wound up ranking just a little higher (or lower) than many might've expected entering the first week of preseason action.
Let's sort through five of those more surprising listings on Houston's depth chart:
The Texans' preseason star rookie in the receiving room, sixth-rounder Lewis Bond , still might have work to do before he's deemed a true difference-maker, or even a roster lock, based on his standing in the depth chart. He's still listed as a third-stringer, and not within the top-six slots in the room.
There's certainly still time for Bond to make a bigger dent in the wide receiver room. Especially with preseason around the corner, some extended reps, and big plays, his way could slot him in at that WR6 spot––which should be his goal. Until then, the veteran, Justin Watson, may have the edge.
Another rookie who hasn't risen too far up the depth chart: second-round tight end Marlin Klein is fifth in the pecking order at his position, following up each of Foster Moreau, Cade Stover, and Brevin Jordan, in that order.
And it's not exactly too unexpected to not come along as quickly as some other first-year guys, like Keylan Rutledge. And even if he is tight end five, that won't prevent him from making the roster as a day-two rookie. But if his standing is a sign of anything, his rise in the depth chart might be a more gradual process .
Even after the Texans decided to guarantee more of Jarrett Patterson's contract ahead of their first preseason game, that didn't stop them from putting him a bit lower on the totem pole in the offensive line room. He ranked third at right guard behind Ed Ingram and rookie Febechi Nwaiwu.
And that's far from a sign that Patterson isn't in line to make the roster. The numbers on his contract–– which make it appear more likely he'll make the cut ––matter more than a preseason depth chart. If anything, his placement at right guard just showcases Patterson's versatility as someone who can play both guard spots and center.
The Texans solved their third defensive end questions by signing Jadeveon Clowney earlier this month. But with Clowney now locking that spot up , the fourth defensive end spot becomes the latest position battle that's up for grabs on Houston's front seven.
Based on the first depth chart listing, though, those rights are in Dylan Horton's hands, who was right there with Dominique Robinson getting the most looks for that DE3 spot before Clowney came on. Keep watch of Robinson and Solomon Byrd, though, who are the next two in line as a third-string defensive end.
The Texans' linebacker position still feels extremely wide open, with a verdict to be determined in the next couple of weeks, rather than being one that's been sorted out by the first preseason games. However, there is one player who might be falling behind in the race at the position, and that's fourth-year linebacker Jamal Hill, who fell into fourth-string on Houston's depth chart.
This could very well be considered a make-or-break camp and preseason for Hill. He's by no means a roster lock, and is in a linebacker room that's some of the most wide-open it's been since his arrival three years ago. He entered late July as someone who could be one of the biggest risers, or one of the biggest fallers, and seems to be leaning towards the latter side of that right now.
