title: It Might Be Time to Temper Expectations for One Top Jaguars Draft Pick
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Top draft picks have always held a special place in Jacksonville. For years the Jaguars and their base would put their hopes in rookies to not just improve the team, but even to carry it.
Times have changed since then, with only one such Jaguars draft pick (Travis Hunter) under the new regime having those kind of early expectations. And even Hunter's expectations have now shifted after the Jaguars finished 13-4 with Hunter missing 10 games as a result of a knee-ending injury.
The Jaguars' roster has grown and matured, and the days of rookie draft picks needing to play superheroes are gone. As a result, there are some Jaguars draft picks who deserve tempered expectations: including third-round defensive tackle Albert Regis.
Selected at No. 81 overall in April's draft, Regis was the second-highest draft pick the Jaguars made this year, behind only rookie tight end Nate Boerkircher. Any top-100 pick is going to be expected to play early as long as they are available, and Regis has had some good days in camp such as on Tuesday when Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said he showed improvement.
But it is where Regis had to improve from that makes it clear Regis is still very early in his career, and he should not be expected to shoulder the weight of the run defense right off the bat as a rookie. First, he needs reps and consistency, just like any other young defensive lineman.
“I thought today was a better outing. I think maybe the previous few weren't up to his or our standard. Look, it's a work in progress for any of these young guys," Coen said about Regis' performance on Tuesday.
"I think DL, especially IDL, is one of the most difficult positions in the NFL to play young. To play early. I think it's extremely difficult. You're 23 years old playing against a lot of grown men and savvy. O-linemen are typically smart, savvy, tough, strong, those things. And so, you can get exposed a little bit in there, not just because of getting moved, but little details of technique and fundamentals that I think takes time."
In short ... the Jaguars really like Regis, but he still has a ways to go. He will still play as a rookie of course, but it would be fair to say out of the five interior defensive linemen on our latest projected 53-man roster, Regis would be No. 5 in the pecking order and behind Matt Dickerson and Ruke Orhorhoro for total snaps.
But that isn't something that would concern the Jaguars, nor should it concern anyone else. That is the standard developmental track for a Day 2 rookie on a playoff team without many holes. The Jaguars will develop him because they will need him eventually, but they will not need him to be DaVon Hamilton in Week 1, and nobody else should expect it either.
"You look at D-Ham [DT DaVon Hamilton]. How old's D-Ham? 28? 29? Right? And he's what? At this point in his career, he's probably at one of the peaks in terms of the way he played. And so, that does take time, D-Linemen in general, but especially IDL," Coen said.

title: 6 Jaguars With Soaring Stock Who Have Leaped Depth Charts at Training Camp
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have plenty of moving pieces a few weeks into training camp, but things are starting to fall into place.
The Jaguars released their first unofficial depth chart on Tuesday ahead of joint practices and their preseason opener with the New Orleans Saints, and several Jaguars saw their names elevated from where they started in training camp.
So, whose stock is soaring the most ahead of Saints week? We break it down below.
The Jaguars' veteran defensive tackle was a surprise contributor a year ago, going from a spot on the practice squad to eventually becoming a key part of the Jaguars' defensive tackle rotation. Dickerson has been frequently used as an example by the coaching staff of how hard work and effort in practice can lead to a spot on game day, and he made the second-team defensive line on the depth chart ahead of new defensive tackle Ruke Orhorhoro. It is hard to imagine a 53-man roster right now without him on it.
"Matt has done a really good job. I think even in the offseason, in his downtime, he was out working with some guys, getting better," Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said on Wednesday. "He's come in really just physically strong at the point of attack so that shown up, and he's a tough guy. He's really, what you love about our defense in terms of he's always doing his job. It's important to him. He's a great teammate, so I love coaching the guy.”
No player has done more for their overall stock in 2026 so far than Jabbar Muhammad. He flashed as an undrafted rookie a year ago but had to cut his teeth on the practice squad for the season. He then arrived in the spring and seemingly made a big play in every single practice, whether with an interception or a timely pass breakup. This has carried over to training camp, and he was now officially listed as a second-team cornerback. He looks like he will make the roster and even contribute.
“I’d say Jabbar, you go back to the spring, he's probably one of the most improved players on the team. He's doing a heck of a job playing obviously corner and nickel. I’m excited," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said on Tuesday.
"I want to see him get in the game mix. I remember last year in the first preseason game, he showed up on a play just like running it down from the other side of the field and you're just excited to go see what that could look like. And if he's truly taken that next step that we've seen, ultimately, we do need to see it in a game-like scenario.”
This time last year, Travis Hunter was listed as one of the Jaguars' starting receivers alongside Brian Thomas Jr. and Dyami Brown, but he was also listed as a backup cornerback. His snaps in the season then reflected that, with Hunter playing twice as many snaps on offense as he did on defense during his seven-game rookie season. This time around, though, it has been made even more clear than before just how big of a role Hunter is set to play on defense.
Hunter is now listed as a starting cornerback, yet another signal that he is about to see a significantly larger role at cornerback than he did a year ago. While his offensive snaps will be impacted to some degree as a part of that equation, he has still spent every single day of training camp practicing at both positions, unlike last summer.
I would have said Ameer Abdullah was either the No. 5 or No. 6 running back coming into training camp, and I would not have given much thought about it. But all he has done since camp has begun is make plays with the second-team offense, and as a result he was listed as the Jaguars' No. 4 running back and ahead of DeeJay Dallas and undrafted rookie J'Mari Taylor.
This is more or less how things have played out with the backfield in camp, with Abdullah taking the most second-team reps alongside Nick Mullens in training camp as opposed to Dallas or Taylor. It will still be tough for him to make the roster, but he has made a big jump since he signed with the Jaguars in the offseason.
Both sixth-round rookie wide receivers Josh Cameron and CJ Williams are listed as backup receivers and ahead of a group of veteran wideouts in Austin Trammell and Tim Jones, which paints an acurate picture of what the pecking order has been at training camp thus far. This is not to say that the duo was not expected to be in such a spot, but it is evident on the Jaguars' depth chart that most rookies are simply behind veterans because they haven't played yet.
This is not the case with either rookie wide receiver, though, which could help the Jaguars' duo continue to seperate themselves and even make themselves a part of the passing game's short-term plans moving forward.

title: Jaguars 53-Man Roster Projections 3.0: Saints Trip Brings These Questions to Focus
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are getting into the dog days of training camp, which means the 53-man roster is starting to come more and more into focus.
Some jobs are closer to being won now than they were a week ago, though this week's practice and preseason game against the New Orleans Saints could also tip the scale for head coach Liam Coen and general manager James Gladstone.
"Honestly, we had a personnel meeting the other day, yesterday, and it’s still so early. I think we'll have a better idea after this joint, after this game. That's usually when you try to have a little bit of that in terms of you guys have all seen maybe some of the younger guys in their own way stand out here," Coen said on Tuesday.
"We all kind of know who those people are, but, when you actually have to go play tackle football and play in a game… When we do one-on-ones and stuff, that's not football to me. It's a part of football. It's an aspect of it, but we're not grading that as much. So, I want to go see these guys play football.”
We delivered a 53-man roster last week following the first week of camp practices, and we now turn to an updated version after the team's scrimmage and some heavy-hitting practices like Day 10 on Tuesday.
So, what do we think a current version of the 53-man roster would look like? We break it down below.
Trevor Lawrence has had a solid camp overall, though the offense has had some down days. But then there were days like Tuesday where the lack of a running game made it look like the offense was playing catch-up all day, but you look down and see Lawrence still completing most of his passes. Behind him, it feels like Carter Bradley has had a few nice flashes over the last week for the QB3/Practice Squad spot.
Chris Rodriguez Jr. looks like he will have no issues when it comes to Week 1, with the veteran running back getting more and more looks in team drills since starting training camp only doing positional drill work. He has impressed, too, and he has made a mark since the pads have come on. A split with Bhayshul Tuten, plus third-down work from LeQuint Allen, seems like the most likely outcome here.
“I love C-Rod. He’s going to get downhill and he’s going to run somebody over. In those short yardage situations sometimes last year, not saying anything about anybody, but that's just the type of back we need," Jaguars tight end Brenton Strange said on Wednesday. "You need a back like that and you need somebody that's going to get downhill and get those dirty yards. It's all about the hidden yards. Can you get plus-two on contact? And C-Rod does that. So, he's a special guy and I can't wait to see what he does this year for us.”
My guess is that you see a lot of work this Saturday from Josh Cameron and C.J. Williams. The duo has impressed throughout training camp, and they should be able to get plenty of game reps with the starters set to sit vs. the Saints. If the Jaguars did carry six receivers, Austin Trammell and Tim Jones have both had good camps. But with Travis Hunter getting receiver snaps all camp , this feels unlikely.
The tight end room is absolutely going to feature both rookie tight ends by the time the official 53-man roster comes out, which means the only real question is whether Quintin Morris makes the 53. The Jaguars could carry four tight ends because they believe they will need more bodies due to the increase of multiple-tight end sets, or they could attempt to stash him on the practice squad after a quiet start to camp.
How this actually ends up looking come Week 1 depends entirely on Cole Van Lanen and whether he is on the PUP list. But until that actually happens in terms of the Reserve/PUP list, I am factoring him in. The injuries that have ravaged the Jaguars' offensive line could mean Chuma Edoga earns a spot regardless of what Van lanen's status is, too. The Jaguars need several players in this group to get healthy soon.
The Jaguars have had a number of backup pass-rushers stand out during training camp, but these are the top-four. I hada lot of questions about the Jaguars' pass-rush depth entering camp, but so far this unit has done nothing for the Jaguars but produce. We will need to see if that can carry over to Saints week.
Matt Dickerson was ahead of Ruke Orhorhoro on the first official depth chart, which can either be read into or ignored. What can't just be glossed over though is the fact that he has clearly earned favor with the Jaguars' coaching staff and looks like a secure candidate to make the 53-man roster coming out of camp.
Parker Hughes is clearly going to have to fight for his spot in the preseason, but we are going to slot him here until any games may tell us differently. Jalen McLeod is an interesting player to note because he had a strong start to camp and performance in the scrimmage, but he did not practice on Tuesday. He needs to stay healthy to make the team, and this weekend is a big chance for that to happen.
Perhaps the Jaguars carry six cornerbacks and keep veteran cornerback Christian Braswell, but right now it feels like this is their top-five. The fact that they have a number of safeties who can play in the slot might impact how they build out the cornerback group as well, but it feels like Jabbar Muhammad has earned a spot no matter what.
The Jaguars' safety room looks like it has taken shape, with the top three safeties all due to get plenty of playing time. Rayuan Lane will have a spot on the roster due to his special teams ability, while rookie Jalen Huskey has been impressive over the last week or so of practices. He has clear special teams value, but he has stood out when given a chance on defense as well.
“J-Huskey, he's a dog. He's rangy. He's going to come up, he’s going to hit. I see a lot of myself in him. He is going to be a good player. Yeah, he is going to be a good player," Jaguars safety Antonio Johnson said about Huskey this week.
This one isn't going to change for a long time. The Jaguars have one of the NFL's best special teams groups and it is headlined by this top-tier trio of specialists. Outside of a missed PAT in the mock game last week, the special teams unit has made virtually every other kick in team settings this summer. Cam Little says he thinks he wants to try from 70, and I think he will.

title: Everything We've Learned About the Jaguars' Backup QB Battle So Far
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are hitting the midpoint of training camp, and the preseason opener against the New Orleans Saints is right around the corner.
With the Jaguars set to sit starting quarterback Trevor Lawrence in Saturday's preseason opener due to Thursday's joint practice, it is a good time to take a look at the quarterback room behind him. The Jaguars' backup quarterbacks will be running the show on Saturday against the Saints, and it is worth remembering that there is still a battle for the QB3/practice squad spot between two young passers.
So, what is the state of the backup quarterback situation behind Lawrence? We break it down below.
One thing that has been very clear from the jump is that Nick Mullens is, expectedly, unchallenged as QB2. The Jaguars have never seemed interested in finding another option via a trade or free agency, and it is easy to see why. They have a contract committed to Mullens, a veteran passer who has experience in the system and who successful served as a sounding board last year for Lawrence in his first year in the McVay-family style of offense.
Mullens has taken the vast majority of second-team reps in camp, just like he was always set to as QB2. He has had some solid days, including on Sunday when he was able to find Austin Trammell deep for two different touchdowns against what has been an impressive Jaguars secondary. Mullens is the QB2, and that will remain unchanged moving forward.
Perhaps the more interesting question about the No. 2 spot has to do with 2027 since Mullens is set to be a free agent in March. With that said, it feels like a realistic scenario that the Jaguars would sign Mullens to another similar two-year, $4.5 million deal like he signed with them last March.
When it comes to the QB3 battle between Carter Bradley and undrafted rookie quarterback Joey Aguilar, I think Bradley has the edge right now. Nothing is stopping the Jaguars from keeping two quarterbacks on the practice squad, but there are so few reps to go around in practice after training camp that it is unlikely the Jaguars would make such a move. This means that we will get three preseason games of Bradley and Aguilar dueling, and then we get a decision.
Bradley has made plays during training camp and has even impressed in his few reps with the No. 2 offense at times. Aguilar is a bigger passer with a powerful arm, but Bradley has done a good job of making plays with his feet. Both will likely get reps against the Saints on Sunday, and head coach Liam Coen detailed on Tuesday what he expects from Bradley.
"He's going to get a good amount of play, good amount of burn. I really want to see Carter just go execute the offense at a high level. Eliminate any pre-snaps, the delays or pre-snap motion issues. Like, don't overthink it," Coen said.
"Don't overanalyze it, man. Just go play one play at a time, execute the offense, and then let your playmaking skills take over. You guys saw it all season where, on our scout team, he's out there running around, making plays, making throws, running around, doing some good things. And so, you ultimately want to just see him operate, but also, man, do what also makes you good and how you like to play. I don't want to take that away, but we can't have some of the pre-snaps and things. Want it to be clean.”

title: What Should Liam Coen's Concern Level Be With Jaguars' Banged-Up OL?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- If the Jacksonville Jaguars weren't already planning to sit Trevor Lawrence against the New Orleans in Saturday's season-opener, their hand might have already been forced by some recent bumps and bruises along the offensive line.
Nearly a dozen practices into training camp, the injuries along the offensive line have suddenly become the topic of camp. A group that entered camp with two veterans dealing with injuries (Cole Van Lanen & Patrick Mekari) has now seen several names get added to that list over the last few weeks, which has directly impacted practices like Tuesday's.
“Yeah, you just get thin. You get thin. You start putting more reps on other guys that may not be truly prepared for the amount of reps that they then have to take, which, as you could see today, thins out a little bit of the groups," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after practice. "Your twos are more so mixed of threes and fours and it just kind of gets a little bit thinned out, unfortunately.”
So, just how concerned should Coen and the Jaguars be about their offensive line moving forward? We break it down below.
This feels like a big issue for the Jaguars in the short-term, mostly because the Jaguars are set to have joint practices with the New Orleans Saints before they play them in the preseason opener on Saturday. Lawrence and the rest of the starters will not play against the Saints in the preseason game, which puts a big focus on the joint practice on Thursday.
“Hopefully get somebody back before that, one of the guys. I mean, the ones we're planning on getting the majority of the work anyway in the joint, so hopefully we can survive with the ones and twos getting the majority of the joint, and then the younger guys, give them a little bit of a break so that they can play in the game," Coen said.
That focus will primarily be along the offensive line; no, Lawrence will not be a live target for the Saints' pass-rush, but it could impact how the Jaguars are able to run the ball and evaluate their ground game. The Jaguars had a number of backups along their starting offensive line in Tuesday's practice , and it was difficult for the Jaguars to get anything at all going on the ground against the Jaguars' defense.
So as far as one can be concerned about a joint practice setting, that seems like the biggest current hang-up for the Jaguars. That, of course, is much better than the short-term issues arising during the regular-season, but that does bring us to ...
The long-term outlook for the Jaguars' offensive line has to be about Week 1 vs. the Cleveland Browns. And in terms of where the offensive line is right now, it seems like it is far too early for the Jaguars to start hitting any panic buttons or raising any alarms. This would be a different case if the Jaguars played the Browns on Sunday, but we are still 33 days away from the Jaguars' offense lining up against Cleveland.
The biggest concern for Week 1 is likely Cole Van Lanen considering he is still on the Active/PUP list. Patrick Mekari has not taken team reps but is at least present on the field and not actively sidelined, so perhaps he could be back for Week 1 too. Walker Little's injury looks like it could need to be monitored, but it is too early to say the same about the likes of Ezra Cleveland and Emmanuel Pregnon.
It is not a great outlook for today and right now, but the Jaguars do have the gift of time on their side. Coen will likely want to pull his hair out over the next few days, but it is not yet time for the concern level to be peaking.

title: 4 Instant Takeaways on Jaguars' First Depth Chart: Travis Hunter Leads the Way
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars released their first unofficial depth chart ahead of the first week of the preason, and boy do we have takes.
It is important to note that unofficial depth charts are, well, unofficial. But that does not mean there is nothing we can draw from the Jaguars' first listed depth chart of the 2026 season, and we break down a few thoughts on it below following Day 10 of training camp.
The #Jaguars unofficial depth chart ahead of preseason Week 1. Do with this whatever you deem appropriate pic.twitter.com/Fv5ZHB7UVR
Perhaps the most notable aspects of the depth chart have to do with Travis Hunter. That was always going to be the expectation considering Hunter's two-way status on both offense and defense, and the Jaguars did not disappoint when it came to making things interesting.
Hunter was listed as the Jaguars' starting cornerback alongside Jourdan Lewis and Montaric Brown, while he is listed as a backup wide receiver behind Brian Thomas Jr. This is a big shift from where the Jaguars had him on the depth chart last year, which was a starter in the slot ahead of Parker Washington and as a backup at cornerback.
But as far as depth charts go, this one certainly seems to match what we have seen from Hunter over the course of camp. He has played on both sides of the ball each day during training camp, but has ultimately spent more time on defense than offense. When he does play offense, it looks like a different role than the slot-heavy role he played a year ago.
Well, well, well! The Jaguars have had Anton Harrison at left tackle for the longest stretch of his NFL career over the last two weeks of practice, and they put it to print with the depth chart having Harrison listed as the starting left tackle, and with Walker Little listed as the starting right tackle. This would look different in some way if Cole Van Lanen was healthy and not on the Active/PUP list, but this is a potential Week 1 set-up.
If Van Lanen returns by the Week 1 matchup with the Cleveland Browns, then the Jaguars could still have the option having Harrison on the left side since Van Lanen can play right tackle (and any other spot on the line). With each passing day that Harrison spends at left tackle, though, the Jaguars make it seem more and more like it is his new home.
There are only two spots on the roster defined by "or's", which just so happens to comply with the two tightest position battles in camp to this point. The running back spot is split between Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr., while Ventrell Miller shares the linebacker spot with Branson Combs. These were the two biggest battles on the roster entering training camp, and neither spot has yet to disappoint.
At running back, Tuten has spent more time on the field with the first-team offense in camp by default since Rodriguez did not practice in team drills until a few days into training camp since the Jaguars were working him back after his offseason injury. The split between the two has seemed to balance out a bit more in recent practices, but there has not been anyone who has emerged as a clear lead back to this point.
As for linebacker, I have come away from recent practices thinking Miller has gotten a leg-up in the battle with Combs, but not due to anything Combs has done wrong. Both players have flashed a ton over the course of training camp, and it is clear they are the No. 2 and No. 3 linebackers on the roster after Foyesade Oluokun.
Two thoughts on how the Jaguars' stacked there defensive tackles, in which they had veteran defender Matt Dickerson listed as the top backup behind Arik Armstead and in front of new defensive tackle Ruke Orhorhoro.
I do not think this necessarily means that Orhorhoro is the third three-technique in the pecking order once the season comes around. He might be in terms of a run-defending role, but I would still be surprised if he doesn't play a big role in the pass-rush package one way or another.
I had Matt Dickerson making the 53-man roster in my latest projection , and so far training camp and this depth chart have seemingly backed that up. Even if Orhorhoro manages to catch up to Dickerson, it feels safe to say he is going to make this team by the time they cut it down to 53 players.

title: Good and Not So Good From Day 10 of Jaguars Training Camp: Injuries Keep Stacking
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars held their last official practice before they hit the road to New Orleans on Tuesday, and it featured plenty of ups and downs.
Day 10 of Jaguars training camp saw one side of the ball particularly stand out, but what exactly was The Good and The Not So Good from Tuesday's practice at the Miller Electric Center? We break it all down below.
The Jaguars' front seven simply beat up on the Jaguars' offensive line on Tuesday. There is the required context of injuries on the offensive line impacting the first-, second-, and third-team units, but Tuesday was as dominant a day as Anthony Campanile's defensive front has had in training camp to date. Now, it will be up to them to keep it up from here.
"I thought the defense came out with more energy and better mindset and mentality. I thought the offensive skill players, obviously, and some of the pass game stuff was good. But they kind of took the fight to us, to the offense in the run game today," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said following practice.
It is hard to pinpoint any singular dominant performances, though Coen said he was impressed by Albert Regis and Arik Armstead. It instead seemed more like a completely team effort by the defensive line and linebackers to swarm to the ball and totally deny the Jaguars any momentum on the ground. That is the way Campanile had them playing against the run last season, and it has carried over into this year's training camp.
It has been awhile since we had a 53-man roster projection without Jabbar Muhammad on it. The second-year cornerback has been one of the most quickly-ascending players in the building ever since his stellar offseason program in the spring, and he has continued to carry it over into training camp. In fact, Muhammad has been the clear No. 5 cornerback for the Jaguars during camp, which would earn him an active game day jersey during the regular-season.
"I’d say Jabbar, you go back to the spring, he's probably one of the most improved players on the team. He's doing a heck of a job playing obviously corner and nickel. I’m excited," Coen said after practice.
Muhammad will have to prove himself on the practice field in New Orleans and on the game field this Saturday, but he has all of the traits and confidence to do so. He once again made some big plays in coverage on Tuesday, including a near-interception of Nick Mullens. He is carrying a considerable amount of momentum with him into the rest of the week against the Saints, and he has a chance to really solidify a role and roster spot in the weeks ahead as a result of that momentum and what he has put on the practice field.
When it comes to the Jaguars' pass-catchers, it seems like the always-reliable Jakobi Meyers is sometimes forgotten about. Parker Washington is a breakout star who has arguably been the MVP of training camp to this point; Brian Thomas Jr. is a first-round pick who has been a star in his own right; and Travis Hunter is a former No. 2 pick who is one of the most recognizable athletes in sports. That sometimes leads to Meyers not getting as much talk as the rest of the room, but it has no impact on the clear value he brings the Jaguars.
Meyers had a slow-ish start to camp but turned it on around the time the Jaguars got the pads on, and he hasn't turned it off since. He has been the most sure-handed receiver in the room, including a diving third-down catch from Trevor Lawrence on Tuesday that was one of the best plays the Jaguars made on offense all day. We already know just how important Meyers is to the Jaguars after the way he changed their passing game a year ago, but days like Tuesday are a good reminder that even with the noise of the receiver room's talent, his consistency will still show up.
The Jaguars have slowly seen injuries stack up over the last week. After entering camp with minimal injuries, the Jaguars had a number of players either sit out of practice completely (Cole Van Lanen, Walker Little, Zach Durfee) or be limited to only reps in individual drills (Emmanuel Pregnon, Ezra Cleveland). Other players like Jourdan Lewis were undressed and to the side. There is a long way to go before a real game kicks off, but the injury list is getting a bit long.
"I think that you’ve got a couple of guys, I mean, we’ve got an ankle. We’ve got a couple—not a ton of injuries that would maybe pop up from hitting," Coen said. "More so the general soft tissue hammy stuff, right, and groins and things like that that you guys see popping up all over the NFL right now. Thankfully we haven't had a ton of big, big ones, right? Knock on wood. It's just these are the times of the year it happens, it occurs."
We talked about the defense dominating the Jaguars' running game, and it would be hard to not draw the conclusion that injuries were a significant reason. The Jaguars had multiple projected Week 1 starters (Patrick Mekari, Walker Little, Ezra Cleveland) miss practice, which led to the Jaguars having a first-team offensive line of Anton Harrison-Jonah Monheim-Robert Hainsey-Wyatt Milum-Chuma Edoga.
As a result, the Jaguars' first-team offensive line looked a good bit like their second-team line. Then the second-team looked like the third-team, and so on and so forth until the Jaguars simply could not get any positive yardage in team drills. The unit was clearly overpowered on Tuesday, and it is easy to say injuries were the biggest reason why this was the case.
From a dropped snap from Trevor Lawrence in team drills to multiple defensive pass interference calls on the secondary, the Jaguars have had sharper days. Outside of injuries and these self-inflicted mistakes, there weren't many things to truly nitpick, but the Jaguars have to once again prove that they can stay out of their own way when the real games start a month from now.

title: Everything I Saw at Day 10 of Jaguars Training Camp: Defense Gives Liam Coen a Hurdle
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Well, that was certainly a practice.
The Jacksonville Jaguars held Day 10 of training camp at the Miller Electric Center on Tuesday, and the suddenly banged-up Jaguars did not have the most productive day on offense. In fact, head coach Liam Coen was clearly upset with the unit's performance post-practice, and it is easy to see why.
So, what did we see on Day 10? We break it all down below.
It started in the first team period of the day, and it continued for the rest of the practice. The Jaguars' defense simpy bonked the Jaguars' offense over the head with a club repeatedly on Tuesday, and it got to the point that Coen said after practice that he actually cut the day short as a result. Things were not going to change with another period of work, and he opted to let the defense have the day that they definitively won.
A big part of it had to do with the Jaguars' injuries up front, which have been a problem for a few days now. The Jaguars' front seven took the Jaguars' running game down with mostly ease though, with it being the first day in pads that the Jaguars did not seem to get much traction on the ground. The pass-rush was also relentless, with Travon Walker, B.J. Green, and Dennis Gardeck all record would-be sacks during team drills.
There are going to be days in training camp where one side has the edge, but this day will go down as one of the most lopsided practices of camp thus far. Coen told us exactly that with the way he concluded practice and then evaluated it afterward.
The Jaguars still have 30+ days before they kickoff against the Cleveland Browns in Week 1, but the offensive line is at a concerning point right now. Injuries have taken a toll on the line, with Patrick Mekari and Cole Van Lanen still not getting team reps, and with Walker Little missing another practice after his injury in last week's scrimmage. Add in some limited work from Ezra Cleveland and Emmanuel Pregnon and it was ... well, Liam Coen used the word "thin" several times. That sums it up.
The Jaguars' starting line for most of the day was (left from right) Anton Harrison-Jonah Monheim-Robert Hainsey-Wyatt Milum-Chuma Edoga. There is no reason to think this is going to be the Week 1 offensive line at this point, but it could create some significant challenges for the Jaguars when they share the practice field with the Saints later this week.
As things stand today, though, the Jaguars need to get healthy quickly. Anton Harrison seems secured at left tackle and we know Robert Hainsey is at center. What will the other three spots look like throughout the rest of training camp?
Even on days where the defense easily has the edge, Parker Washington is still impressing. It has become a daily occurrence during training camp this season as Washington has separated himself as Trevor Lawrence's favorite target in one of the NFL's best wide receiver rooms, and this was again the case during an otherwise lackluster offensive day on Tuesday.
Washington had the play of the day (more on that later) in team drills, but once again ultimately showed that he is a true seperator at each level of the field. It feels like the Jaguars know they can break the glass in case of emergecy and dial up a conpletion to Washington whenever they really feel like they need to. The fact it has become so easy for him even against a much-improved secondary speaks volumes about where he is at.
With the offensive line and defensive line tucked on the end of the practice field and with the receivers and defensive backs working on 3-on-3 concepts, we went to take a look at the 1-on-1s between the running backs/tight ends and linebackers/safeties, with the focus being on pass-protection and blitzing. Here are a few of the stand out reps that we saw during that period.
The best play of the day once again came from Parker Washington. Washington does not get many reps against Travis Hunter in coverage, but he was able to be one of the few receivers to beat Hunter on a downfield rep on Tuesday when he hauled in the longest completion of the day down the left sideline. It was as impressive of a win as Washington has had against any cornerback so far in camp, and it another sign of his stellar chemistry with Trevor Lawrence.

title: Surprise Camp Standout Andrew Armstrong Excited for First Game With Chiefs
full_text:
Judging by sheer numbers, the Kansas City Chiefs have boatloads of depth in the wide receiver room. The quality of that depth, however, has been questioned at every turn dating back to free agency and the 2026 NFL Draft .
Injuries and a lack of high-end overall contributions from the group have left the door wide open for someone to make a name for themselves at this summer's training camp . Multiple pieces have managed to do so, including second-year man Andrew Armstrong.
With KC's first preseason game of the year on the horizon, the former Arkansas standout believes he's settling into a groove. Speaking to the media on Tuesday, he commented on whether he's built some trust with quarterbacks Patrick Mahomes and Justin Fields.
"I mean yeah, I hope so," Armstrong said with a laugh. "I've been out there just doing the best I can be, being the best I can be. Just, like I said, learning. Going into the playbook, and I think that's one of the main goals: being trustworthy for the quarterback. I feel like I'm trying to build that with them."
Head coach Andy Reid echoed that sentiment after a recent camp practice, complimenting the 25-year-old for boasting plus traits in multiple aspects of the receiving game.
“Yeah, I like what Armstrong's doing," Reid said. "Big kid, strong. Looks like the quarterback trusts him, both of them. Top two guys, they trust him on his route running. He's got good speed for a big kid, and good transition. He's not stiff coming out of breaks, and that's important."
In two years with the Razorbacks, Armstrong hauled in 134 passes for 1,904 yards and six touchdowns. After not getting picked in last year's NFL Draft, he latched on with the Miami Dolphins and briefly spent some time with the Detroit Lions later on. Kansas City swept him up on a reserve/futures deal in January, paving the way for him to join a franchise he's long respected.
Armstrong has family in Missouri, which makes the current run he's on even sweeter. It was a no-brainer to sign with the Chiefs and have a chance to compete.
"My family's here," Armstrong said. "This has been my favorite team since I was a little kid. I'm not even worried about the city life and things like that. I'm here to play football and be around the team. Just the seriousness of it all, I really want to be around a serious environment, and this is an extremely serious environment. I love that."
Standing just under 6-foot-4 and weighing in at 202 pounds during the pre-draft process, Armstrong posted one of the best Relative Athletic Scores in his class. He's a truly impressive vertical athlete, but as Reid mentioned, there's a bit more to his game than that. He's surprised the team with a nice blend of fluidity, smarts and timing at the Missouri Western State University campus, thus making him a player to watch this weekend and beyond.
There's no denying that Armstrong has his work cut out for him to make the 53-man roster at the end of the month. Still, he feels right at home and could be a prime practice squad candidate at the very least. Now, he's looking to maximize the opportunity to put on a Chiefs uniform and show what he's made of in front of the home crowd on Saturday against the Los Angeles Rams.
"It's going to feel great," Armstrong said. "Just looking and seeing all the red. It's different playing it on a game than being in real life. I know it's going to feel amazing."

title: Chiefs Make Emmanuel Ogbah Signing Official, Part Ways With UDFA CB
full_text:
As the Kansas City Chiefs close in on their first preseason game of 2026, they're doing so with a familiar face rejoining the fold.
Early on Wednesday evening, the club announced that defensive end Emmanuel Ogbah had officially signed. Ogbah now becomes a Chief for the second time in his career, completing a move that was reported on Tuesday morning pending a physical.
The NFL's afternoon transaction wire and personnel notice originally listed Ogbah as a visit, which coincided with him attending training camp but not wearing pads or working on the field. To make room for Ogbah on the 90-man offseason roster, the Chiefs have released cornerback Bryce Phillips .
Bringing back a Super Bowl champ. Let's get to work, @EmanOgbah 🤝 pic.twitter.com/UsFSzPtHB3
Ogbah, now 32 years old, returns to the place he briefly broke out at during the 2019-20 NFL season. The former second-round pick had 5.5 sacks in 10 games with Kansas City before missing the rest of the season with a pectoral injury, but he was still regarded favorably as a member of the Super Bowl LIV-winning group.
When asked about the imminent Ogbah acquisition on Tuesday, Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo expressed plenty of optimism and said he'd kept in contact with Ogbah over the years.
“Yeah, I always had an affection for E," Spagnuolo said. "It was disappointing the one year we had him in 2019. I thought he was really coming on and then he got hurt, and then we didn't have him at the end of the year. But I've always periodically been in touch with him. We've got to get through the physical and all those other things but if he's part of our group, I'll be excited about that.”
Phillips, a former Santa Ana College player, spent his final two collegiate seasons with San Diego State. In two years for the Aztecs, he recorded 74 total tackles (five for loss), 10 passes broken up and a pair of interceptions. He joined Kansas City on an undrafted rookie free agent deal after posting an impressive 8.58 Relative Athletic Score during the pre-draft process.
The Chiefs' offseason roster is down a cornerback, but it gains someone with valuable championship-level experience as the preseason arrives.

title: Chiefs Rookie OT Kahlil Benson Embracing Whatever Role Comes His Way
full_text:
One of the best stories of the Kansas City Chiefs training camp has been offensive tackle Kahlil Benson. The undrafted rookie out of Indiana has turned enough heads at K.C.'s facility to go from a long shot for the 53-man roster to a feasible candidate to start at right tackle in Week 1.
Benson's rapid growth couldn't have been predicted by anyone but himself. The 6-foot-6, 319-pound freak still has a ways to go with his technique and footwork, but possesses exceptional raw physical tools. On Wednesday, Benson met with the media for a four-minute press conference to discuss some of the early rumblings at camp. He was asked how a player like him, who just came off an undefeated national championship season at Indiana, could have gone so under the radar among NFL scouts. Benson chalked it up to the reality of life and the challenges football players have to embrace.
"Realistically, whatever position you get put in, you got to take it on the chin," Benson said. "Being a football player, stuff happens, so just being able to move past one thing and put one foot before the other one and keep going and make sure there's nothing else on the table."
While he was primarily a tackle at the collegiate level, the Chiefs have slid him over to right guard with Trey Smith sidelined by a hip injury in camp. Given that he's a rookie whose roster spot is still up in the air, Benson is willing to do whatever he needs to get on the field and secure a long-term future in Kansas City.
He takes pride in his work as an offensive lineman, specifically his ability to be coachable and willing to learn and adapt. "Showing the humbleness, and the confidence, and the coaches being able to trust you," he said about what he values as a lineman. "Being able to move forward, and when there’s time to be corrected, being able to be corrected, and then being able to just go out to the next play and then do what you got to do the next play."
The Memphis native stressed the importance of staying ready every day and taking advice from his coaches to continue improving. His maturity is already shining through early in his NFL career.
"Being able to take those coaching points from them, as well as from your coaches, you have to be ready when your number is called. Our vets and everybody here have been making sure that all us rookies have been on point."

title: Despite Entering Year 14, Travis Kelce Is Still Focused on Improving for Chiefs
full_text:
At a certain point in the career of an eventual Hall of Fame player, they cross over the threshold of having absolutely nothing left to prove to the outside world. For Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce, that moment was likely several years ago.
Despite boasting one of the game's top statistical profiles for his position and putting out some of the best tape in tight end history, Kelce opted to return for a 14th season in KC. Even after marrying iconic singer-songwriter Taylor Swift earlier this year, he still feels the drive to continue his football career. Yet another grueling training camp has him motivated for more than just that.
Coming off a 76-catch, 851-yard, five-touchdown effort in 2025, Kelce believes he can be better for the Chiefs in 2026-27.
"I've still got a lot of love for this game," Kelce said on Wednesday. "I still think I can go out and play at a high level. I want to go out there and prove to myself that I can play at a better level than I did last year. I think that's probably the biggest thing for me, making sure that I'm accountable for the guys in this room every single play that I'm out there."
Last season was a trying one for Kelce, as he struggled with drops and also watched Kansas City limp to its worst record (6-11) since he entered the league way back in 2013. It put him to the test in a major way, and he figures to remain a critical component of the offense this coming campaign. Knowing that, he's laser-focused on leveling up and fighting off Father Time once again.
"All aspects of football, man," Kelce said of where he wants to improve. "Being more accountable when the ball's in the air. There were a few games last year that I felt like I put on myself. In the blocking world, being able to get my guys so we can spring guys for bigger gains.
"And then on top of that, just being a better leader. When we get stuck with adversity hitting, who's going to want you in that fox hole with you? That's one of those things: I want to be one of those guys that everybody counts on to be there and get us out of that fox hole."
After a down 2024, Kelce responded with a much more efficient performance a year ago. In addition to his Pro Football Focus overall grade ranking 14th out of 37 qualified tight ends, he was third overall in total EPA for tight ends (71.19, via SumerSports ) and saw his yards after catch per reception spike from 3.5 to 5.6. A tad lighter per-game workload and more short-range work did the trick.
Entering what could be the final season of his illustrious professional career, the aging curve certainly isn't working in Kelce's favor. That's been the case for a while now, however, and he's kept chugging along as one of the sport's better tight ends anyway. He takes training camp in St. Joseph, Missouri very seriously, believing it sets the tone for the team's output in the year ahead.
Kelce didn't admit whether this is his last camp at Missouri Western State University, but he did emphasize wanting to maximize the bonding time he has left.
"I mean year one, I was just trying to make the team, I guess," Kelce said. "So I think this year, not only making the team but trying to figure out how I can bring guys along with me and show them how to play championship football, I think that's a big thing. And be able to just enjoy these moments with the guys I've built this culture with — coach (Andy) Reid and guys like Pat (Patrick Mahomes), Chris Jones, George (Karlaftis) and everybody."

title: Nick Bolton and Jared Wiley Leave Chiefs Training Camp Practice Early, Ride Off in Cart
full_text:
Kansas City Chiefs linebacker Nick Bolton left training camp practice in a cart on Wednesday, but the team later confirmed that Bolton didn't suffer an injury.
Alex Gold of 96.5 The Fan shared the initial update from St. Joseph, Missouri .
"Nick Bolton in the front of the cart. Didn’t see what happened. We’ll have to see after practice."
The team later told reporters that Bolton left with an illness. That sounds unpleasant, but it's much less alarming than any kind of direct injury for the Chiefs' defensive signal-caller.
Third-year tight end Jared Wiley also left practice early on Wednesday, riding in the front of the cart, according to Nate Taylor of ESPN . Wiley was a fourth-round pick in 2024 and has been battling for a chance to be KC's No. 3 tight end throughout camp. The Chiefs announced that Wiley departed with a strained hamstring, per Taylor.
One other young Chief suffered an issue during Wednesday's practice: rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods has an ankle injury.
Woods was slow to get up after a play , but Sam McDowell of The Kansas City Star noted that Woods wouldn't be subbed off the field.
"Marcus Harris attempted to sub in for Peter Woods after this play, but Woods waved him off and insisted on staying in," McDowell shared on Twitter/X.
A great screen pass from Mahomes to Kenneth Walker for a big gain. 🔥💪🏾 Peter Woods goes down briefly at the bottom of your screen, but he worked the next few plays. 🎥 | @Farzin21 pic.twitter.com/EJuwhPVyDa
The story continues below as originally published.
Gold's detail of Bolton's positioning—sitting in the front of the cart—is a positive sign. Typically, a front-of-cart exit implies a less-serious injury (or perhaps even an equipment issue or an otherwise-planned exit).
Matt Derrick of Chiefs Digest noted that Bolton played through an injury on Tuesday .
"Bolton banged up his right knee yesterday and appeared in a lot of pain," Derrick wrote. "He did wave off the athletic trainer and stayed in the practice, however."
Bolton plays a vital role in Kansas City's defense , and his $19.25 million cap hit in 2026 is the highest of his career so far. He played 97% of the team's defensive snaps in 2025.
In addition to Wednesday's early exits, the Chiefs were already missing a usual cast of recent absences.
Right guard Trey Smith (hip), linebacker Drue Tranquill (back), cornerback L'Jarius Sneed (knee) and defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott (PUP, knee) were all sidelined again on Wednesday, according to Derrick .
It's hard to imagine any of those injured players suiting up for the Chiefs' first preseason game on Saturday . With Bolton also taking an early exit, Saturday's game could bring a major opportunity for linebackers Jeffrey Bassa, Cooper McDonald and Jack Cochrane.

title: Three Biggest Questions the Chiefs Still Face at Training Camp
full_text:
Although final roster cuts don't have to be made until the end of the month, Kansas City Chiefs training camp officially ends approximately one week from now on Aug. 20. There are still a number of lingering questions for this squad that have yet to be answered.
We'd all like to think the expected return of a future Hall of Fame quarterback will solve everything, but that's simply not the case. The Chiefs were already headed toward missing the postseason for the first time in Patrick Mahomes' tenure before he tore his ACL/LCL, and they were severely lacking in several areas that they had to address during the offseason. These three questions will heavily impact the Chiefs' early-season performance. Let's look at the first.
Head coach Andy Reid is making the right decision to sit Mahomes in the preseason this year. For the first time in his decade-long NFL career, he won't appear in a preseason game, but is expected to be ready by Week 1.
While fans should have the utmost confidence in Mahomes figuring things out with his receiving corps, it does raise questions about how much chemistry he'll have with his targets when the season gets underway. Granted, Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy have worked with him for multiple years, and Travis Kelce is still available as his security blanket, but the options start to become slim after that. Reid has assured that Mahomes is building "trust" with newcomers like Cyrus Allen and Andrew Armstrong, though the reality is that they won't see any game action together for another month.
It's tough to know how much chemistry a quarterback-receiver duo can build when they're only seeing each other in practice against their own defense.
Since the second day of training camp, the right tackle battle has begun as Kahlil Benson began stealing first-team reps from projected starter Jaylon Moore. That has since changed after Trey Smith's hip injury forced Benson to move to guard, but he's very much still in play to win the job on the outside.
The undrafted rookie out of Indiana boasts exceptional physical tools despite lacking the experience and technique of Moore. He'll need to make plenty of progress before he is seriously considered the favorite, but this competition has lasted nearly two weeks now with no clear frontrunner. This is a question that could be answered by tomorrow or persist until the day before Week 1. Either way, both players are embracing the competition and pushing each other to improve every day, which is a fantastic sign.
The offense has its fair share of injuries in the wide receiver room, not to mention making sure Mahomes' knee is steady. However, the defense is dealing with several ailments that have left the Chiefs shorthanded at certain positions.
Most of the concerns stem from the secondary, where first-round draft selection Mansoor Delane is still donning a non-contact jersey , while Kristian Fulton (hip) and L'Jarius Sneed (lower body) remain limited. Another player to pop up on the Chiefs' injury radar is Drue Tranquill, who is dealing with back spasms that have recently sidelined him.
The defensive line is also becoming a concern. Ashton Gillotte is dealing with a lengthy hamstring strain that could keep him out of the entire preseason, putting Felix Anudike-Uzomah in a starting role . Chiefs fans know it is difficult to rely on FAU, who missed the entirety of the 2025 campaign following a hamstring surgery of his own. To make matters worse, Ethan Downs tore his ACL in camp last month, while 2025 second-round pick Omarr Norman-Lott remains on the PUP list with a knee injury.
The Chiefs could be dangerously thin on defense entering the preseason. Not all of these injuries will carry over into Week 1 against the Broncos, but with so much uncertainty less than a month until the opener, it's time to sound the alarm over the defense's health.

title: Steve Spagnuolo Weighs in on Truth of Chiefs' First Unofficial Depth Chart
full_text:
There are two things about training camp that can be counted on to fuel chaos on social media. One of them is a nicely framed highlight clip, and the other is a depth chart being released. With a new week of practice in full swing, those in Kansas City Chiefs circles have been exposed to both.
The latter was posted on Monday night, ranking the club's 90-man offseason roster ahead of Saturday's 3:00 p.m. CT outing against the Los Angeles Rams. The preseason opener should feature several depth pieces jockeying for spots on the eventual 53-man group, but many fans are placing considerable stock in the depth chart as a hint at who could be held in higher regard.
Chiefs issue their first unofficial depth chart of the 2026 season. I beseech you all once again, please no wagering. pic.twitter.com/E9nXKu7MDt
There's a hangup, though. These preseason depth charts are unofficial in nature and should be viewed more as (somewhat) educated guesses by team public relations staff than a true reflection of coaching assessments. Take the cornerback position for example, where first-round pick Mansoor Delane is listed as a second-stringer but veteran L'Jarius Sneed is a starter.
Is there any validity to the rankings? Speaking to the media on Tuesday, defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo weighed in with his thoughts on Sneed, Delane and second-year man Nohl Williams.
"It's really hard," Spagnuolo said. "I mean, it's on there [that] LJ's been in the league for a while. Nohl has, too. That's probably why (vice president of football communications) Brad (Gee) did it that way. You know, neither LJ or Delane has really practiced very much, so we're way down the road on all of that. Health will be a big issue, continuity [and] how many reps they've had going in, and we'll see when we get to the first game."
Spagnuolo's comments serve as a critical reminder that some positional hierarchies have yet to be revealed. It's widely expected that Delane, for instance, will assume a starting role on the boundary once he's cleared from a lingering shoulder injury . When Sneed first reunited with the team, most assumed he was a reserve. Williams' inclusion as a starter ahead of Kristian Fulton might be the only listing worth reading into.
Between his two years with the Tennessee Titans, Sneed managed to play in just 12 of 34 possible regular-season games. Although no one has truly separated from the pack at the nickel spot, that same truth applies to him as well. It remains to be seen whether it'll be him, Kader Kohou, Chris Roland-Wallace or rookie Jadon Canady who claims that spot.
Similarly to the pre-game one depth chart, adjustments entering the following contest don't have to spell doom for one player or another. Preliminary sorting is best taken with a grain of salt on both sides of the ball.
With that said, don't confuse this with dozens of jobs being up for grabs. A majority of the Chiefs' roles and roster spots are fairly defined with Week 1 of the regular season roughly a month out. In competition-heavy rooms like cornerback, however, Spagnuolo is making it clear that there's still a long way to go.

title: Chiefs On SI Mailbag: What Are Fair Expectations for Felix Anudike-Uzomah and Cyrus Allen in 2026?
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' first preseason game is just around the corner, and there are only six training camp practices remaining in St. Joseph, Missouri . Before the team gets more information from Saturday's preseason kickoff against the Los Angeles Rams , what do you want to know about where the team stands now?
Jordan Foote and I ( Joshua Brisco ) are here for this week's edition of the Chiefs On SI mailbag, fielding your questions from the KC Sports Network Twitter/X accounts or @jbbrisco.com on BlueSky . Let's get into it.
"Does FAU become a useful rotational player? Is the contract year still undefeated?" -@jettyrat_RB
Former first-round defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah is one of the more interesting stories of the Chiefs' offseason. His first two seasons had a couple of highlights here and there, but he never approached the production you'd want from a first-round selection. Then, he missed all of 2025 due to a preseason hamstring injury. However, even after declining his fifth-year option , the Chiefs appear to expect some legitimate production out of Anudike-Uzomah in his fourth season.
Even after the Chiefs reportedly signed veteran EDGE Emmanuel Ogbah , Anudike-Uzomah still has plenty of opportunity ahead of him. I see Ogbah's signing as a larger indictment on KC's questions about their internal candidates for the No. 5 or 6 defensive end positions.
As things stand now, Anudike-Uzomah (and Chiefs fans) should forget his original draft slot and focus on what he could be as a role player in 2026. He's clearly behind George Karlaftis, Ashton Gillotte and R Mason Thomas, but if he can be an NFL-caliber rotational piece, he can certainly extend his NFL career, perhaps even by remaining in Kansas City. — Brisco
"In order, who do you currently have as players 49-58?" -@krichardson.bsky.social
Ranking end-of-roster players in order before preseason game No. 1 would keep us here for quite a while, but I do have some top bubble candidates to keep an eye on over the next couple of weeks.
On the offensive side of the ball, the perceived battle between Garrett Nussmeier and Chris Oladokun immediately jumps out. There's ample incentive for KC to keep a third quarterback this year, and why not roll with the one the club used 2026 NFL Draft capital to acquire ? At wide receiver, I'm not quite there with Jalen Royals being a cut candidate, but Andrew Armstrong delivering a quality camp thus far does have me thinking.
In the trenches, both the offense and defense are worth keeping an eye on. The Kahlil Benson hype train isn't slowing down even a bit, which might just push someone like Ethan Driskell to the practice squad. At defensive end, the Chiefs' reported pickup of Ogbah doesn't bode well for the likes of Vincent Anthony, Tyreke Smith or Anthony Dunn.
Finally, the secondary picture is quietly intriguing. Assuming health for everyone else, former first-round pick Kaiir Elam seems to be squarely on the outside looking in at cornerback. Undrafted rookie safety Xavier Nwankpa was one of the first men out in our first roster projection but continues to make a case to be included in edition 2.0.
The Chiefs have some calculus to do, but their three preseason games should provide clarity. — Foote
"Obviously Cyrus Allen is coming off an injury, but should we read anything into his days in pads having a lot less highlights?" -@EthanCo67716681 "According to Matt Verderame, Chiefs staff is high on Cyrus the Virus. Will we see more or less of him in preseason because of that?" -@Dusty_Roads_BBQ
Two questions for the price (free) of one! These are getting at different elements of the Cyrus Allen excitement, but they both help us look ahead to the preseason.
This often makes me feel like a party pooper during this time of year, but I generally try to read very little into training camp highlights in general. For what it's worth, Allen's pre-pads highlights also didn't particularly move me. However, I do take note from tweets like this one from Pete Sweeney out at camp :
"Patrick Mahomes' first two completions during the early team blitz period? Cyrus Allen."
Anything that indicates the building of trust and chemistry between Mahomes and one of his receivers matters to me, at least when it happens consistently. Either by choice or by injury-impacted necessity, it does still seem like Mahomes has given Allen lots of training camp attention; I don't really care if the highlights are spectacular until they come in an NFL stadium.
So, on that note, I do wonder how Allen will be used in the preseason. With Mahomes not expected to play in at least the first preseason game , I'd be a bit surprised to see Rashee Rice (knee) or Xavier Worthy (shoulder) take the field on Saturday while they continue their respective recoveries. I'm not sure that Tyquan Thornton needs many reps with Justin Fields, but you also probably don't want to start Fields with Royals, Armstrong, and Nikko Remigio as his starting receivers. That leads us back to Allen.
If the Chiefs are completely in love with Allen, they could sneak him through the preseason without showing the NFL what they have in mind for him when the season arrives. Still, I think Allen starts as the Chiefs' No. 4 receiver (already an accomplishment for a fifth-round rookie) and that it would be reasonable to give him a decent workload in the preseason so he can run his first NFL routes before the lights get brighter.
The last wrinkle worth noting is that Allen briefly exited practice on Tuesday and hasn't been back on the practice field for very long; perhaps he's entirely held out on Saturday, delaying this conversation by another week. — Brisco
"Which 1-on-1 would you dominate Jordan at, and vice versa?" - @bradbatchelder
This is the question we needed. After giving it some thought, I think I'm winning on both sides of the trenches. I'm betting on myself having a power advantage if I can show off some vaguely passable footwork. I'm definitely disrupting the pocket and probably dying a slow-enough death in pass protection. Heck, I think I could win my fair share of reps as a pass-catcher too. ...But I'm not covering Jordan unless the quarterback is having a terrible, terrible day. — Brisco
Even as someone who has a size advantage, I'd be a tad worried about the trenches. The individual drills up front tend to be defense-slanted, so I'm in agreement and think life as a pass rusher would be easier than as a pass protector. The bad news is I play with too high of a pad level to be consistent snap-to-snap.
I'm all over anything that puts me in coverage, whether I'm running a route to beat it or putting on a prime Darrelle Revis (Chiefs legend) performance in the defensive backfield. I'm getting physical at the line of scrimmage and setting the tone for the rep. Josh knows that, as there's video proof to back up my claim. — Foote

title: Chiefs OT Jaylon Moore Is Welcoming the Challenge From Rising Rookie Kahlil Benson
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' offensive line is almost completely set, but there is still a lingering battle between Kahlil Benson and Jaylon Moore for the starting right tackle job. The undrafted rookie out of Indiana has emerged as a starting candidate , taking first-team reps on the right side for over a week ahead of the veteran.
Moore, who is in the final season of a two-year, $30 million deal he signed last offseason, spent four years with the San Francisco 49ers as a swing tackle before signing with K.C.
He was expected to be the blindside protector of Patrick Mahomes until Josh Simmons fell to the Chiefs in the first round of last year's draft. As a result, he only started six games after beginning the year as a backup and eventually dealing with a knee injury of his own. Now that Simmons is healthy and in the best shape of his life , the only starting spot available to Moore is on the right side. Although he's predominantly played left tackle throughout his NFL career — including over 90% of his combined snaps in San Francisco — Moore is more than willing to adjust to a new spot on the offensive line.
"Honestly for me, throughout my career, I've been back and forth," Moore said. "It's good to get the reps on either side because at any point, anything can happen. And it's good to make sure that every one of our guys are able to play multiple different positions and be able to play wherever your number is called."
The last handful of days at training camp have featured Moore and Benson starting alongside each other with the first team, as projected right guard Trey Smith continues to deal with a hip injury . Moore says that working next to Benson rather than competing against him for a spot has gone a long way in building their relationship. "It's been really good for both of us," Moore continued. "Obviously, him transitioning to [guard] during this camp, he's been working in and out of both spots. So, it's been good for me as well, just being able to get camaraderie and being able to play with whoever."
Naturally, one would think there's some animosity between a six-year veteran and a bright-eyed rookie who's never even taken an NFL snap competing for a starting spot. However, Moore is a true professional who doesn't let competition get in the way of the team's goals.
Even in a contract year, Moore made it clear that while there certainly is a position battle, the two players are working in harmony and pushing each other to become the best they can be. "Honestly, we're all pushing each other to get better every single day, regardless of what the depth chart looks like," Moore promised. "It's good for him, it's good for me as well. We're all pushing each other in that room."

title: Rashee Rice Reflects on Jail Time, Goals for Contract Year With Chiefs
full_text:
For the first time since the conclusion of the 2025-26 campaign, Kansas City Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice spoke to the media and provided updates on a multitude of fronts.
The fourth-year man had one of the NFL's more unorthodox offseasons, undergoing knee surgery but spending part of that recovery time in jail after violating his probation order from a prior incident. Rice got released in time to make it to the start of Chiefs training camp , where he's been monitored closely and had his workload managed over the past few weeks.
Rice, who described his jail stint as a "learning experience" and a "reality check" on Tuesday, said he wants the world to know he's focused on being the best player and teammate possible this season.
"I'm 100% locked in on what's going on now with the team," Rice said. "I'm ready to go out there and dominate, and I've got a good group of brotherhood behind me."
The former second-round pick believes his positivity will shine through after the first half of his year was overshadowed by a dark cloud.
"I would say I'm a positive guy," Rice said. "I'm a great person to feed off as far as energy [is concerned]. A smiling guy mostly, at all times — unless it's time for work, then I'm serious. And then I'm a father, so I take the most responsibility in being a good father to my boys."
As far as the knee is concerned, Rice took a significant step last week when he participated in 11-on-11 work for the first time at camp. He's since been heavily involved in the team's practice plans, which could be a good sign for his Week 1 availability. All eyes are on him getting the green light to make impactful plays right out of the gate in the regular season.
He said he thought he merely had some nagging knee swelling earlier in the process, but the stars aligned for a clean-up procedure to occur during the offseason. Now working his way back to 100%, Rice wants to improve on plays where the ball isn't going to him in the final year of his rookie contract.
Speaking of which, a complete season may go a long way for Rice in the financial department. Being able to produce at volume for the entirety of a campaign while also staying out of trouble might just allow him to recoup some of the value he's presumably lost in the last two years.
He'd be lying if he said the opportunity to deliver in a pressure-packed environment didn't add to his drive.
"I mean, it's motivating," Rice said. "Honestly, just being able to be back on the field with my brothers is motivating. That's in the future [but] right now, I'm just focused on what's going on right now, and that's getting better for the team."
After recording career highs in targets (102), receptions (79), receiving yards (938) and touchdowns (seven) as a rookie, Rice has appeared in just 12 games across 2024 and 2025. In eight contests a year ago, his numbers would've extrapolated to roughly 113 catches, 1,213 yards and just under 11 scores over the course of 17 outings. Now, the onus is on him to string everything together and realize that potential.
Set to become a free agent next March, Rice has maintained "the right group of guys" in his circle and seeks a constant "positive attitude" moving forward. Only time will tell if he's able to put a checkered past behind him in the biggest season of his football life.

title: 6 Players to Watch During Chargers-Texans Week 1 Preseason Game
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers utilized a travel day on Wednesday and arrived in Houston, Texas, on the eve of their first preseason game. The Chargers and Texans face off at 5 p.m. on Thursday in a game that will not feature the regular starting lineup from the Chargers side.
The game will be the first true NFL action for the 2026 rookie class. There are several rookies with big questions to answer and there are several players locked in position and role battles who will have their first chance at making an impression against an opponent. Let's dive into players that require extra attention in this first matchup.
The Chargers drafted Jake Slaughter out of the University of Florida in the second round. Slaughter was a career center and the Chargers have hoped to transition him to guard and have him compete for the vacant starting left guard job.
As a prospect, Slaughter faced questions over his strength and ability to anchor against NFL-caliber defensive linemen. The Texans may not throw their starting lineup at Slaughter, but they have a deep defensive line and Slaughter will be put to the test.
Slaughter is currently in what appears to be a three-way battle for the starting job with veteran Kayode Awosika and second-year player Branson Taylor. Thursday night will provide a major test for Slaughter to see how he stacks up against the other challengers.
Genesis Smith fell to the fourth round of the draft where the Chargers selected him with their third pick of the round out of the University of Arizona. Smith has excellent instincts and great center field cover skills. He faced a massive question over his tackling in college and it was the reason he fell in the draft.
There will be no hiding from his weakness in his first NFL action. If he can prove his tackling issues were left behind in college, Smith could see a much larger role than originally anticipated for the defensive back room.
Nadame Tucker went undrafted out of Western Michigan despite leading the country in several pass-rushing categories. He is slightly undersized and an older rookie but his pass rush production, play style and connections to the coaching staff have him facing elevated expectations.
Tucker is the only undrafted rookie on the Chargers unofficial depth chart that is not listed last in their position group. He will be in a fierce battle with second-year edge rusher Kyle Kennard for potentially a final roster spot in the edge rusher room. Tucker has been destroying the Chargers backup tackles in practice with his violent and heavy-handed play style. Kennard has been playing well at practice too. Starting with the Texans, the preseason games will be a big factor for this battle and whether Tucker can perform to the expectations.
Junior Colson was once viewed as the top off-ball linebacker prospect in the 2024 draft. The Chargers selected him in the third round and unfortunately, the football gods have been cruel to Colson hitting him with injury after injury.
Colson will be facing a competition for a roster spot with the depth of the Chargers linebacker room leaving no room for error. Colson will need a dominant preseason for a shot at the roster and the physical Houston Texans will provide him the perfect showcase if he can seize the moment.
The Chargers do not have an open quarterback competition behind Justin Herbert, not yet at least. DJ Uiagalelei signed with the Chargers as an undrafted free agent following the 2025 draft in a return to his roots in Southern California.
Uiagalelei has been grinding and improving since his arrival in Los Angeles. Mike McDaniel's new offense seemed to click with him and he looked great in OTAs and has continued performing well throughout training camp. He got his first run with the second team on Tuesday and a big performance against the Texans could go a long way to inserting himself into a bigger quarterback battle.
Avery Smith was one of the most sought-after undrafted free agents and the Chargers landed him. Smith has long been favored amongst the UDFAs to have a shot to make the 53-man roster and he has lived up to the billing so far in training camp.
He will be in a battle against several other defensive backs for roster spots and his first action against the Texans can set the tone for the battle throughout the last few weeks of camp.

title: Chargers Roster Spotlights: RJ Mickens, A Sneaky Returning Key Contributor
full_text:
RJ Mickens, born on July 10, 2001, in Irving, Texas, grew up in a football family, being the son of longtime standout NFL DB Ray Mickens. With these roots, Mickens took his talents to Carroll High School in Southlake, Texas, where he played both offense and defense, notching 1,092 yards and 14 touchdowns while also producing 211 tackles with six going for a loss, two sacks, 32 pass deflections, eight interceptions, two fumble recoveries, and eight forced fumbles on defense. These elite career numbers saw Mickens ranked as a four-star prospect, according to 247Sports .
This led Mickens to commit to Clemson, where he played sparingly as a freshman. As a sophomore, he collected two interceptions, proving quickly to the team that he could be a real stalwart in the backend of a defense.
Moving on to 2022, his junior season, he added another three interceptions to his resume while adding 48 tackles, giving the team a reliable deep and box safety. 2023 had Mickens in a statistical slump, recording no interceptions on the season. He returned to school for his final year of eligibility and had his best year, recording two picks and 75 tackles (six of which were for loss).
Mickens would go into the 2025 NFL Draft, where teams viewed him as a Day 3 safety who could instantly compete for playing time, even with his limited athletic traits. His football IQ and instincts made up for his subpar testing numbers, allowing Mickens to be a real prospect in the eyes of NFL teams.
The Los Angeles Chargers were looking to get younger at the Safety position and drafted the Clemson product in the sixth round of the 2025 NFL Draft. Mickens saw action in 12 games, proving to be a key contributor down the stretch of his first NFL season.
12 Games 29 Tackles 2 Interceptions 2 Pass Deflections
"R.J. Mickens signed a 4 year, $4,374,280 contract with the Los Angeles Chargers, including $174,280 signing bonus, $174,280 guaranteed, and an average annual salary of $1,093,570. In 2026, Mickens will earn a base salary of $1,005,000, while carrying a cap hit of $1,048,570 and a dead cap value of $130,710." - Spotrac
RJ Mickens finds himself in an intriguing spot going into year two of his NFL career. The Bolts drafted Genesis Smith in the fourth round, while still having Derwin James Jr. , Elijah Molden and Tony Jefferson as veteran playmakers.
While the Chargers could keep five safeties on the final 53-man roster, Mickens will be in a tough battle to keep the same role that he had during his rookie season. If he does continue in that role, look for Mickens to once again be a solid contributor for a Bolts defense that relies heavily on its safety talent.
