title: Raiders Face Intriguing First Test in Preseason Opener
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders will be kicking off their preseason in just a couple of days, and their first opponent is the Arizona Cardinals. The NFL world already saw a glimpse of the Cardinals in the preseason as they took on the Carolina Panthers in the annual Hall of Fame game.
Personally, that was the most entertaining Hall of Fame game I've ever seen in my life. If that's a sign for the 2026 NFL season to come, I'm even more excited thinking about all of the dynamic offenses across the league. Especially for the Raiders, what is there to look forward to in their first preseason game against the Cardinals?
🚨BREAKING🚨 #RaiderNation Starters will play in the preseason opener against the Cardinals on Thursday “We do have a plan for those guys and how many snaps or series we’d like to see them go, no need for anyone else to know it. We’re going to have a lot of guys playing this… pic.twitter.com/0E2FyzviZN
Klint Kubiak has confirmed that the starters will be playing in Thursday's contest. Usually, with starters in the preseason, they'll only go in for a drive or two. Surprisingly enough, I think Raider Nation will want to see the backups more than the starters.
That's because Fernando Mendoza isn't going to be their starting quarterback, and his debut in the Silver and Black is much more exciting than Kirk Cousins '. It will be interesting to see what Kubiak prefers more with the starters: running the ball or passing it.
Carson Beck to Jalen Brooks. WOW. @ProFootballHOF Game on NBC Stream on @NFLPlus + Peacock pic.twitter.com/VjnMEP2mIQ
The biggest storyline from the Hall of Fame game was how comfortable rookie quarterback Carson Beck looked in their offense. He made a case for himself to be the Cardinals' starter in the regular season.
I think that against Rob Leonard's defensive schemes, Beck's decision-making and throw selection will be put to the test. The Raiders' defense has an opportunity to cut all the Beck hype prematurely by causing a turnover or making him look less comfortable in the pocket than he did in his preseason debut.
Carson Beck Every Completion and Rush from the Hall of Fame Game. 15/19, 188 PYDS, 1 TD, 0 INT, 125.4 RTG. pic.twitter.com/wdk3qKXxT4
A way they can do that is by using their young secondary to give Beck different looks than the Panthers' defense. It's important to remember that because this is a preseason game, I don't expect Leonard to be pulling out all of the creative defensive stops and schemes.
However, there's fierce competition right now to be the secondary option in their secondary , and I think it's only fair to give those players a chance to ball out against fellow players looking to make their names known. This is the first in-game look Raiders fans will get at this new roster and new regime. Times are changing in Las Vegas.

title: Critical Ways Raiders’ Improvements Will Lead to Better Results
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders have completed training camp and will now turn their focus to their three upcoming preseason matchups. With the regular season just weeks away, Las Vegas will soon lace up the cleats and get work in against other teams from around the league ahead of Week 1.
Losing nearly 30 games in two seasons is confirmation that more than a few things are wrong with a team. The Raiders' front office made quality moves this offseason. Those moves should help them in major ways and in subtle ways.
Las Vegas has a long way to go. Winning six games this season would be a win for a team that has won seven combined games in the past two seasons. Below are a few small but critical ways the Raiders' offseason changes will likely help them on the field in 2026.
The Raiders have been one of the worst teams in the National Football League in turnover differential over the past few seasons. Just like the stat itself, the reason Las Vegas has been at the bottom of that list is their own turnovers on offense and their inability to force turnovers on defense.
The chances of either Kirk Cousins or Fernando Mendoza leading the league in interceptions like Geno Smith did last season, and as Jimmy Garoppolo did for much of his lone season in Las Vegas, seem unlikely. That alone should help Las Vegas' turnover differential.
Time will tell whether the Raiders' defense will force more turnovers, but if the offense can stop giving the ball to the other team, there will be less pressure on Las Vegas' defense to do so.
Every defense wants to force turnovers, but when their teammates on offense turn the ball over, that want becomes a dire need. That is the last thing this rebuilding Raiders team needs.
Las Vegas has finished among the worst rushing teams in the National Football League each of the past three seasons. They finished last in the league in rushing in two of those seasons. It is literally impossible to be worse than last. Las Vegas will be better at running the ball this season.
This should help Las Vegas' defense, while improved, stay off the field much more than they did last season. It does not matter how good a defense is if it is on the field for extended periods of time, as Las Vegas' defense was last season.
There seems to be a small chance Kubiak does not improve Las Vegas' ground game at least marginally, if not more. Ashton Jeanty nearly ran for 1,000 yards last season behind arguably the worst offensive line in football and a questionable coaching staff. That will no longer be an issue.
Getting Jeanty going on the ground will shorten the game and help the defense stay fresher longer. Based on training camp, Las Vegas' coaching staff plans on doing just that. It will be up to the players to make it happen.
Two of Las Vegas' most significant problems over the past two seasons have been a lack of talent and competent coaching. Specifically, the Raiders have failed to find an offensive coordinator or play caller who can produce with the talent they have, however much or little it is.
The Raiders believe they have fixed both of those issues with Kubiak's hiring and the roster additions they made. In training camp, it was evident that the Raiders now have a coaching staff that can at least put together a logical game plan. Yet, none of that matters without execution.
The Raiders' offense has been productive in camp, racking up chunk plays against an improved defense. However, Las Vegas' offense has also left many opportunities on the board to make positive plays in practice, with false starts and plays that need cleaning up.
Under Kubiak's staff, Las Vegas will not only enter games with a clear, logical game plan, but they will also be prepared to adjust. How well they adjust on game days will be an early test for Kubiak's staff. At least now, the Raiders have a roster that allows them to actually make legitimate adjustments.

title: Why I’m Buying Early Hype Around Raiders' Tonka Hemingway
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders kick off their preseason Thursday night when they host the Arizona Cardinals at Allegiant Stadium. The Cardinals are coming off a walk-off defeat to the Carolina Panthers in the NFL Hall of Fame Game, 33-30, and the Raiders hope to continue Arizona's preseason misfortunes this week.
Training camp and the coming weeks of the preseason will open opportunities for players to find their place on the roster or force head coach Klint Kubiak , his staff, and general manager John Spytek to make difficult roster cutdown decisions.
One player who has stood out so far in camp is Raiders defensive tackle Tonka Hemingway , a former fourth-round draft selection from last spring who emerged as a quality depth player late in the season. Hemingway flashed at times in 2025, but was too inconsistent, with some discouraging moments.
However, all the former South Carolina standout has done this summer is prove he could be a key defender within the defensive front rotation. If there is one player I am buying the early hype on ahead of Thursday night, Hemingway is that player.
I spent some time watching Hemingway's game film for this piece, and one of the things that stood out most to me was his effort down to down. Everything he did last year, right or wrong, was at 100 percent effort, with his motor far from in question for anybody. I enjoyed his versatility in alignment, whether he was a 5-tech, 3-tech, or playing from the 1- or 2i-tech.
Hemingway has been showing up in camp, which is a terrific sign for the Raiders' defensive line as a whole. Thomas Booker IV, Jonah Laulu, and Adam Butler are fortified in their place in the interior odd front; Hemingway is making his presence known throughout camp and generating chaos in the process.
I don't expect Hemingway to be a starter right away. Still, his pass-rush arsenal is impressive to watch, and he knows how to make his presence known in the backfield at all times. That's valuable for a defense, and Hemingway has done enough to show Leonard and Kubiak that this is his time to be an impact defender.
There are many young and hungry defensive players ready to contribute. Hemingway is one of those young players. This gives the front seven depth and reliability this season, based on what we have seen at training camp. If this goes on, Las Vegas could have a very productive defensive front this fall.

title: Updated Raiders Depth Chart Ahead of First Preseason Game
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders have completed training camp and released their most recent depth chart. On Thursday, the Raiders will face the Arizona Cardinals at Allegiant Stadium. It will be the first time the Raiders take the field under head coach Klint Kubiak.
The Raiders took several strides in training camp. The changes implemented and the hard work put in during positional battles in camp have made an early impact on the depth chart. Las Vegas' depth chart has a few changes from what was expected entering training camp.
Las Vegas aims to turn things around after several disappointing seasons that led to the firing of multiple head coaches, most recently Pete Carroll. Kubiak knows the work to rebuild the Raiders is just beginning. He recently gave insight into how the development process has gone so far.
“Well, I think I would say, a compliment our players, is that it's not so much about listening to me; it's about what it takes to win. We want to win. Our players want to win. And the things that it takes to win is for us to be together and be connected and operate as one unit,” Kubiak said.
“So, I think it just shows the maturity of our group, knowing we're going to point things out. But at the end of the day, they decide what kind of team that they want to be, and thus far they've showed us they're a mature group that they want to go win games the right way."

title: Raiders Training Camp Report 15:  What Happened At Allegiant
full_text:
LAS VEGAS, Nev.—Today marks day 15 of the Las Vegas Raiders' full-team training camp, and tonight at here at Allegiant Stadium they just conducted their 11th practice of camp in front of their faithful fan base.
This practice was not as feisty as the others, and it shouldn’t have been.
Klint Kubiak has multiple new players, so they got to get a feel for them before their first actual game here on Thursday versus the Arizona Cardinals, but it was also a time to celebrate the historic Raider Nation.
For this fan base, it isn’t just a rooting interest; this is their life.
Raider Icon Matt Millen once described the Raider Nation to me as, “31 teams in the NFL the fans think they are part of the team, but with the Raiders, they are the only team that the team thinks the fans are part of them.”
That was the purpose of this practice.
Three things stood out most to me.  Not it wasn’t anything schematic, as opposing teams could, and probably were, in the house.  What did stand out was significant.
2. Kubiak’s desire fulfilled. Earlier today at the team headquarters, Kubiak made his expectations for tonight very clear. “Tonight's really important. Really excited about going and being in front of our fans, being on the grass that we're going to play on. Coaches communicating with the headsets; really important for the whole operation. Obviously, it's my first game in there. Played a few games on the other side of the stadium, but it'll be really important for players and coaches to get familiar with our surroundings so that we can play our best football on Thursday night."
Several of the rookies from smaller schools could be seen looking fondly at their surroundings.  Fans need to remember these are 21- 23-year-old kids who have dreamed of the NFL all of their lives.  For them, it wasn’t a practice; it was a fulfillment of a dream.
With the jitters out of the way, the new veterans learned the locker room and stadium, where to go, and this team is ready for Thursday.
3. Fernando Mendoza mania is on full display. Mendoza jerseys and signs were seen all over the stadium welcoming their new hero to the Raider Nation. The number one overall pick of the 2026 NFL Draft, who had NFL executives drooling, thrilled the crowd with whatever he did. This fan base understands the weight on the current Heisman Trophy winner and National Champion’s shoulders, and they already love him.

title: Examining Minkah's Miami Comments ... and Other Former Dolphins Updates
full_text:
Minkah Fitzpatrick got into the Dolphins record books this offseason when he tied the franchise mark in being traded away for a second time, but the circumstances were much different this time.
The four-time Pro Bowl safety and 2018 Dolphins draft pick acknowledged the well-accepted idea that he wanted out the first time around, though he specified the real reason during an appearance on The Pivot podcast with Channing Crowder, Ryan Clark and Fred Taylor.
And while previous speculation was that Fitzpatrick wanted out in 2019 because he didn't like then-head coach Brian Flores or the way he was going to be utilized, Fitzpatrick said the reason was much simpler.
"I saw what they were doing that season, and that's why I wanted out, you know what I'm saying?" Firtzpatrick said with a smirk. "Yeah, I knew what was going on. That's why I left that first time."
What the Dolphins did in 2019 was flush out most of their high-profile veterans and clear out cap space in a full rebuilding project that many analysts instead have referred to as a "tanking job."
Of course, this is where many would point out that the Dolphins are doing a lot of the same things in 2026 by jettisoning Tua Tagovailoa, Tyreek Hill, Jaylen Waddle, Bradley Chubb and, yes, Fitzpatrick, but there's one significant difference.
That difference is the Dolphins signing Malik Willis as a potential franchise quarterback, whereas in 2019 they brought in veteran Ryan Fitzpatrick at the end of his career and traded for Josh Rosen one year after he was the 10th overall selection and flopped as a rookie.
The 2026 Dolphins also have 13 rookie draft picks, to go along with an eight-player class from just a year ago, compared to only six picks in the 2019 draft.
The ironic part about Fitzpatrick's comment regarding his trade request is that Flores so vehemently rejected the notion of the Dolphins tanking in 2019 whenever the notion was brought up — and his not playing the clearly ill-equipped Rosen the whole season instead of Fitzpatrick certainly suggests he indeed was trying to win games.
This season, as in 2019, the Dolphins could use Fitzpatrick in the secondary but instead traded him away. In doing so, they made him the second player the team traded twice, along with long-ago quarterback John Stofa, traded to the Cincinnati Bengals and Denver Broncos sandwiched around signing with Miami as a free agent.
Fitzpatrick, now a member of the New York Jets, is one trade away from tying the NFL record currently held by wide receiver Brandin Cooks and Hall of Famer Eric Dickerson.
When they re-acquired him from the Pittsburgh Steelers last summer, the Dolphins adjusted his contract to lower his cap number with everyone fully aware he'd want a new contract this year.
The Dolphins weren't willing to pay him big money, which made sense considering where the organization is at this time, so they put him on the trade market and ultimately the best they could was land a seventh-round pick for him.
Keeping up with former members of the organization:
-- The Detroit Lions finally officially announced the hiring of former GM Chris Grier as a personnel advisor. Grier often was the target of fan displeasure during his tenure in Miami, which spanned from 2000 until he was fired on Halloween of last year, including nine years as general manager.
-- Former Dolphins backup QB Skylar Thompson's run of bad luck continues. The Baltimore Ravens placed him on injured reserve Wednesday, essentially ending his season or at least his time with Baltimore. This comes after Thompson spent the entire 2025 season on IR with the Pittsburgh Steelers, who he joined after leaving the Dolphins.

title: With DT Zach Sieler Set to Miss Time, Time to Step Up for Former Dolphins First-Round Pick
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins’ defense is trying to build itself from the ground up. Head coach Jeff Hafley has talked a lot this offseason about wanting players to take steps forward, and what he needs from each player as they try to identify their core players for the foreseeable future.
Unfortunately, in the NFL injuries are the rule not the exception. Now defensive tackle Zach Sieler is going to miss some time with an injury that is undisclosed as of this point.
Sieler will miss the Dolphins’ preseason opener against the Washington Commanders on Friday night. The hope is that Sieler will be ready for the season opener against the Las Vegas Raiders, but it’s not clear whether Sieler will be ready after Hafley called his status "week to week."
In the meantime, however, the popular phrase whenever a player is injured is next man up. Sieler’s shoes are not easy to fill. He’s been very productive during his career in Miami with 25.5 sacks coming in his last three seasons with the club.
With Sieler out of the lineup, there’s a big man who needs to make a big jump into a productive role.
The NFL draft is the lifeblood of almost every franchise in the NFL. Teams are often at their best when they draft guys, develop them under their rookie contracts, and sign them to extensions.
That’s the approach that GM Jon-Eric Sullivan has been used to during his time in Green Bay, and is hoping to have it carry over as he takes over as the head man in Miami. This offseason alone he’s handed out contract extensions to core players like Aaron Brewer, De’Von Achane and Jordyn Brooks.
Sullivan only has one draft class under his belt, but he and the coaching staff still have to work with what was given to them by their predecessors.
One of those picks was 2025 first-round pick Kenneth Grant. Grant was picked to be one of the anchors of Miami’s defensive line after a productive career at Michigan that saw him paired with fellow first-round pick Mason Graham.
Grant was part of a defensive line that spearheaded the Wolverines defense into a national championship-winning unit.
Grant was picked 13th overall over players like Emeka Egbuka, Tyler Warren, and Jaxson Dart.
Fair or not, that’s how any drafted player ends up being looked at. If a player does not turn into a consistent contributor, they’re going to be compared to players who are.
In fairness to Grant, he is now a second-year player, and defensive tackles typically take a year to develop as they try and get acclimated to the NFL game.
Grant’s first season saw him sack the quarterback twice with 29 pressures, which ranked 40th out of 134 defensive linemen. In addition he had 23 hurries and 20 run stops according to PFF.
That’s not a terrible rookie season by any measure, but the Dolphins are going to need more from a top-15 pick.
That was true regardless of whether Sieler was in the lineup or not. Now that he is set to miss some time, there is a big red circle around Grant. That’s true of both the Dolphins’ coaching staff and those who are set to face off against them.
To Grant’s credit, he’s done his part this season. He told Miami reporters in July that his goal for his playing weight will be 325 pounds, which is down from the 337 he played at a season ago.
The goal would be to become more explosive so he can make more plays in the passing game like Sieler did in 2023 and 2024.
When a player like Sieler is set to miss time, the onus is going to be on everyone to step up. Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips will likely need to take on bigger roles as well.
With all due respect to those guys, however, they were not drafted in the first round.
Fictional character Ben Parker once said with great power comes great responsibility. The great power, in this case, is Grant’s draft status.
Now, comes the responsibility to live up to the billing while Sieler is out of the lineup, and maintain that momentum once he returns.

title: Projecting Dolpins RB De'Von Achane's Touches in Light of Coach's Comments
full_text:
Miami Dolphins Head Coach Jeff Hafley made a joking statement about one of the team’s best players, but what does it mean for his potential workload?
In an interview Monday with Rich Eisen, Hafley laughingly said that he told star running back De’Von Achane that he could see an unheard-of workload next season.
"I just gave Achane a heads-up this morning and I told him, 'You better be in good shape... After you touch the ball 40, 45 times, I might have to pick you up, and I'll carry you back into the locker room.’”
Quite frankly, 40 touches is an absurd number. Achane’s career high in touches per game is only 29, and dating back to his college career, his personal record is still just 38, which he tallied in his final game at Texas A&M.
To find the last 40-touch game in the NFL, you have to go back to 2021, where Derrick Henry, a listed 57 pounds heavier than Achane, received 41 with the Titans.
So, knowing that 40 touches is a pipe dream, while also understanding that Achane’s workload likely will increase in the post-Tyreek Hill era after receiving a new contract extension, what’s the magic number?
De’Von Achane averaged 19.1 touches per game last season, a career high for the three-year pro. Meanwhile, the NFL’s leader, Christian McCaffrey, averaged 24.3. McCaffrey is an outlier in recent NFL history, however, as he’s the only player in the last eight seasons to record 400 or more touches in a single season (he’s done it twice in that span). Second-place Jonathan Taylor had 369 in 2025, while Achane had 305.
A more realistic target for Achane (assuming an increase) is somewhere between 20 and 22 touches per game. The league leader in yards per carry in 2025, Achane finished only 14th in total carries, with 238 — 14 more (about one more carry per game) would have gotten him into the top 10, and 32 more (two per game since he played 16 last season) would have tied him for sixth.
As for Achane’s receiving workload, it seems that a change would be in the quality of targets, rather than the quantity. He finished tied for fifth in running back targets, but had a negative air yards per target, per NFL Pro. With a young and unproven receiving group, it wouldn’t be surprising to see more opportunities out wide and farther down the field.
A projection for Achane, given this information, would be somewhere in the 320 to 340 touch range, which would have placed him between fifth and seventh among the NFL in 2025.
Achane certainly will be the focal point of the Dolphins' offense in 2026. However, a healthy workload, more than anything, will be the key to keeping the 195-pound back upright throughout his extension. Jeff Hafley will be looking to get him the ball often, but finding the sweet spot will be crucial.

title: How Tolbert Can Turn the Back the Clock In Miami ... And Earn a Big Role in the Process
full_text:
After signing with the Miami Dolphins on March 16, Jalen Tolbert finds himself in uncharted territory in his NFL career.
After spending four seasons in Dallas, Tolbert will want (and, for Miami's sake, need) to double as a leader for a young, inexperienced wide receiver corps, alongside providing production that harkens back to his 2024 season.
Where there's a new system, there's a new opportunity. Tolbert spoke about this and plenty more to media after practice on Monday, highlighting the challenges and expectations he has for the 2026 season.
Tolbert is staying positive despite the circumstances. Two seasons ago, he was the right-hand man to CeeDee Lamb, starting in 15 games while racking up 49 receptions for 610 yards and seven touchdowns, all of which were career highs.
Tolbert still believes he can reach those heights once more in Miami, with an added task of being a natural leader for the receiver corps.
"I know what I'm capable of," Tolbert said. "I know what I can do to help this team, and I know what I can do in this league. I'm earning my opportunities, some points of attack on the menu, and helping take this team to another level, being a leader for those guys in the room. Obviously, we're a young team, young room. I think that's one of my goals for this year."
It's a young room, and to Tolbert's point, he stands out age-wise. He's tied for the oldest receiver on the team at 27 years old, alongside fellow offseason acquisition Jalen Reagor. The unit features four rookies alongside multiple pass-catchers looking for their first breakout season.
Tolbert's skill set was not entirely why he had a down year in 2025. What killed his playing time was the Cowboys' acquisition of George Pickens, alongside breakout seasons for Jake Ferguson and Ryan Flournoy, which moved Tolbert down the depth chart. He started only eight games in 2025 and did not play in four of the last six games of the season.
Now, Tolbert will look to solidify himself as a day one starter for Miami. Drafted just two picks after Malik Willis in the third round of the 2022 draft (86th overall to 88th overall), Tolbert has made it a priority to build chemistry with his former teammate in the Senior Bowl.
"It's important to build that trust from your quarterback," Tolbert said. "So he trusts that you're going to be where you need to be, when you need to be there, and what he's looking for in certain routes. To talk through the tiny parts of the game means a lot, and the second part that I think is overlooked is just being able to understand each other."
Being on the same page when it comes to routes might be key for Tolbert to silence doubts about his route-running ability. Changing direction mid-play might be his biggest weakness as a receiver, as building separation from defenders has been difficult for him at times.
This con, however, has highlighted one of his best pros: contested catching. Standing at 6-1 with a 36-inch vertical jump, Tolbert can excel at making plays happen in a crowd. In addition to his speed, this made him a reliable option when running go routes or out routes, and an occasional deep threat when he can fly past the secondary.
Going back to 2024 isn't enough for Tolbert. He wants to replicate his success when he was the Sun Belt Offensive Player Of The Year in 2021 with South Alabama.
"Another goal I have, as I said a long time ago, is to get back to the version of myself I was in college,"  Tolbert said. "I want to get back to that player. I know that that player is in me. I know that it's possible. I know that it's there and I know what I can do."
In his final two seasons with the Jaguars, he recorded over 1,000 receiving yards and 16 touchdowns, breaking school records in the process. There was no CeeDee Lamb to worry about; he was the main weapon. Before discrediting his numbers due to playing in the Sun Belt, keep in mind he dropped 143 yards and a touchdown on seven receptions against the SEC's Tennessee in 2021.
He had a strong draft profile, highlighting his frame, speed, and, interestingly enough, route-running. His main weakness also happened to be catch adversity. So far in the NFL, route-running and catch adversity seem to have flipped in those regards.
Tolbert puts his time at South Alabama in high regard, even going so far as to stay with a long-standing tradition dating back to his freshman year of college.
He had surgery done on his left leg in his freshman year at USA after suffering a knee injury in preseason training camp. Since then, he has worn a sleeve on his left leg for the rest of his college career and then during practices in the NFL, since the look is outlawed during regular-season games.
"I had surgery when I was in my freshman year of college," Tolbert said. "That mental block when I first was coming back made me think that, even though this little sleeve does nothing, my leg was straight. You trick your mind; whatever it is you gotta do to make it work, you make it work. I took it and ran with it, and I've stuck with it, and so it's gonna stick with me as long as I play."

title: Examining the Under-the-Radar (But Very Significant) Dolphins Injury Concern
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins have the makings of a solid offensive line in place if Kadyn Proctor lives up to expectations and Jonah Savaiinaea can take the anticipated jump in his second season, but there is a clear problem with the group.
That problem is an alarming lack of depth, and it's a concern that's only growing with each passing day.
To help find a potential solution, the Dolphins swung the trade for New England Patriots 2024 third-round pick Caedan Wallace and an ideal world he can live up to his draft status in Miami and provide help either at guard or tackle.
But Wallace has become just one of the many unproven young players in the offensive line room, which continues to be missing the one veteran who projects as the top backup on the unit.
That would free agent acquisition Jamaree Salyer, who has not practiced since the third of training camp back on July 31.
Head coach Jeff Hafley hasn't been asked about Salyer recently, but it's not just that he hasn't practiced, he also hasn't been spotted at practice at all in August — unlike just about everybody else who is dealing with an injury, whether it be Dante Trader Jr., Kevin Coleman Jr., rookie Chris Bell or PUP cornerbacks Storm Duck and Darrell Baker Jr.
This makes it a bit concerning as to Salyer's availability at the start of the regular season. Yes, we're still a month away, but remember that Salyer was carted off the field during minicamp and missed the final week of OTAs.
And the reality is that the Dolphins really can't afford, as presently constituted, to be without Salyer for a long period of time.
Salyer joined the Dolphins as a free agent after spending four seasons with the L.A. Chargers, for whom he played both guard and tackle — and he was very durable there, played all 17 games in 2022-24 before playing 13 last year.
In light of fellow free agent pick-up Charlie Heck's well-publicized struggles in training camp — though he has practiced better the past few days — Salyer looks like he might be the one reliable backup right now at guard or at center.
Andrew Meyer is somebody who showed some promise as a rookie free agent, but the fact remains he's still an unproven commodity.
And the same applies to everybody at tackle outside of Heck.
The newest addition, Wallace, has only 10 games of NFL experience, but that's more than Marques Cox, Kevin Cline and Gottlieb Ayedze combined.
The thought coming out of the spring was that if something were to happen to Austin Jackson — and we don't need to go over his injury history — then Heck simply would fill in, but training camp has provided reason for concern.
Salyer has played right tackle before and right now he would look like a better option. He also would be the top backup at guard, even an option to start if it turned out that Savaiinaea wasn't able to take that step forward after his rough rookie season.
But Salyer has to be healthy and on the field to be able to contribute.
Right now he's not and he hasn't been for more than 10 days, with no clear picture as to when he'll be back.
So, yes, his injury is a clear concern. A major concern.

title: Dissecting the First Dolphins Depth Chart of 2026: Rookies at the Forefront
full_text:
With the Miami Dolphins set to open their preseason schedule Friday night against the Washington Commanders, we have our first depth chart of the 2026 season.
As we tell everyone every year, coaches produce a depth chart for official consumption only because it's a league requirement at this time of year and also because nothing is etched in stone.
With that in mind, here is what stood out from the Dolphins' first depth chart:
-- The first name at the top of the offensive depth is attention-grabbing because it's Caleb Douglas, and he's one of five rookies listed on the first team — including Jacob Rodriguez who listed as "or" at one of the inside linebacker spots. This isn't surprising, mind you, considering the reps Douglas has gotten in training camp.
-- Former UFL Gottlieb Ayedze is listed as the second-team left tackle and we'll honestly say here it would be a surprise if he were to take a regular season snap for Miami. But somebody has to be listed here, right?
-- Very interesting to note that new offensive lineman Caedan Wallace is listed as a backup at both right guard and right tackle, and we'd suggest that would seem to indicate he's got a pretty good chance at making the 53-man roster. Particularly noteworthy is Wallace being listed as one of top second-team right tackles along with free agent pick-up Charlie Heck. This speaks a bit to the depth concern along the offensive line.
-- Ben Sims being listed as first-team fullback/tight end tells us the Dolphins will be using a fullback in 2026, even if not in name. This matches what we've seen in camp with the usage of Sims as an H-back.
-- Jaylen Wright being listed ahead of Ollie Gordon II as the second-team running back suggests he's in the lead to be De'Von Achane's top backup, though that spot could be very fluid.
-- Rookie sixth-round pick D.J. Campbell being listed third team at right guard — and with an either/or at that — behind 2025 practice squad member Josh Priebe doesn't seem bode well for his chances of making the 53 as a rookie.
-- As with the offense, the defense lists 12 positions to account for the various personnel groupings the Dolphins will employ.
-- On the defensive line, Kenneth Grant or Jordan Philips being listed first team next to Zach Sieler makes sense because the opening defensive lineup figures to depend on whether the Dolphins are expecting a more run-happy or pass-happy opponent, Phillips being the choice to stop the run and Grant more so to rush the passer.
-- Two things that stand out at edge are rookie seventh-round pick Max Llewellyn listed ahead of veteran Cameron Goode at one spot and Robert Beal Jr. listed ahead of David Ojabo at the other. Goode flat out has outperformed Llewellyn so far in camp, while Ojabo brought better credentials to Miami than Beal when both arrived as free agents.
-- Rodriguez being listed as first-teamer alongside Tyrel Dodson with the "or" designation is eye-opening to a degree, though it's been well earned with Rodriguez really coming on in the last several days of camp.
-- Veteran Ronnie Harrison Jr. has had a very solid camp, which is why he's listed as second team along with Kyle Louis behind Jordyn Brooks when the rookie fourth-round pick otherwise normally would get the nod. It's entirely possible the Dolphins will wind up keeping Harrison along with Louis on the 53-man roster.
-- Rookie fourth-round pick Trey Moore has gotten a lot of work with the first unit in training camp, so it's not surprising to see him listed ahead of Willie Gay Jr. Gay, who left practice early with an injury Monday, remains one of the most confusing players on the roster.
-- There is nothing surprising at all in the secondary, where the only question is whether it should be taken as an automatic that starting nickel corner Chris Johnson will move outside when the Dolphins are using only four DBs. In that scenario, it likely would be Johnson and Brents as the starters.
-- On special teams, we shouldn't be surprised to see Malik Washington listed as the first-team punt and kickoff returner after the success he enjoyed last year.

title: Why the Miami Dolphins' Top Two WR Prospects Are on the Right Track
full_text:
Training camp for the Miami Dolphins has helped shine light on potential standouts at each position. As far as wide receivers go, rookie Caleb Douglas is trying to become a name to remember within the list of available offensive weapons for Miami.
Another rookie is battling hard for different reasons. Chris Bell is still recovering from a torn ACL and has ways to go before putting on the pads. Whether that happens during the preseason or after is unclear.
Despite their different directions, both players have shown potential, according to general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan. During a conversation on The Joe Rose Show, he highlighted what Douglas and Bell can provide to a wide receiver room that's desperately looking for a breakout star.
And if things work out the way the Dolphins hope, Bell and Douglas will be WR1 and WR2 before too long — and for a long time.
Douglas has shown high levels of production after 10 practices during training camp, making his case to be a major contributor off the rip.
Sullivan is excited about his set of skills, which conveniently line up with the positives of his draft profile before Miami selected him with the 75th overall pick in the third round. Combine that with a level of confidence despite being 23, and there's a lot of upside.
"Caleb has a lot of natural gifts," Sullivan said. "That was what attracted us to him in the draft process. It's the body type. He's tall, he's long, he can run. The thing that he can do for a tall, long athlete is he can bend. He can get in and out of breaks. He's got extremely quick feet."
Sullivan isn't joking about his height. Listed as 6-4, he's tied for being the tallest wide receiver on the roster alongside rookie free agent Donaven McCulley. He made the most of his slender frame at the NFL Combine, boasting a 79-inch wingspan while still running a 4.39 40-yard dash — the rare combo of speed and size that, as Sullivan noted, was a big reason the Dolphins bought into Douglas.
Douglas' athleticism was the biggest positive in his draft profile. One of the biggest negatives, however, was dropped passes in 2025 with Texas Tech. While there have been some drops by Douglas during training camp, this is par for the course when learning the ins and outs of professional football, according to Sullivan.
"He's honing his craft," Sullivan said. "He's getting better every day. He's learning that this is the National Football League, not the Big 12. Because of some of the hard lessons he's learned early on, he's starting to reap the benefits. And that's what you're seeing.”
Bell's recovery has been brutal, but it is coming along nicely, according to Sullivan. There's no clear date for when he can return to action on the field, but Miami will be patiently waiting for his return.
"He's ahead of schedule," Sullivan said. "I'm not here to put a timetable on it because I don't think it's fair to the kid. He's working extremely hard. I can't say enough good things about (head athletic trainer) Kyle Johnson, his staff, and what they've done to get him to where he is today. We're excited about him. I think that goes without saying."
In previous practices, there have been positive signs of progress that line up with Sullivan saying he's ahead of schedule. He has been seen running routes, even though offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik assured the media that he has ways to go.
Miami knew the risks of drafting Bell with the 94th overall pick in the third round. Bell had his most productive season with Louisville in 2025 with 917 yards and six touchdowns, but it was cut short due to that torn ACL in November.
The positives for Bell, when healthy, are plentiful. Being compared to A.J. Brown is no joke. At 220 pounds, he's the heaviest wide receiver on offer for the Dolphins, thanks in part to his NFL-ready frame. He's a hard receiver to bring down, but he can build up speed to break away from defenders when given open grass.
Unfortunately, there might not be a time during the preseason, or even early on in the regular season, to confirm that he'll fit into the NFL like a glove. Sullivan is fine with this, however, citing the need for a player like Bell long-term, which means giving him all the time he needs now to heal.
"I don't want to put pressure on the kid," Sullivan said. "We want him out there as soon as possible, but this is long-term big picture thinking in terms of getting him back out there. We expect him to be a really good player for this offense for years to come. So, I'd rather be a week too late than a week too early.”

title: What to Know About New Dolphins Tackle Caedan Wallace and a No-Brainer Trade
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are still looking for answers along the offensive line, and they've decided to take a shot with a discarded recent New England Patriots draft pick.
The Dolphins acquired Caedan Wallace in a trade Monday along with a 2029 seventh-round pick in exchange for a 2028 sixth-round selection, pending Wallace passing his physical.
The trade came after a report from NFL insider Jordan Schultz that the Patriots were going to waive Wallace on Monday, which would have made Wallace available to any team via the waiver wire, with the Dolphins having the 13th spot in the claiming order (until after three weeks of the 2026 regular season when the claim order will turn to the current NFL standings).
In acquiring Wallace, the Dolphins has inheriting his contract, the same as they would have by claiming him off waivers. And considering the really, really minor draft compensation (when you consider losing a sixth-round pick in two years), it made sense for the Dolphins to not want to risk a team ahead of them in the waiver order stealing Wallace.
Wallace (6-5, 314) played 10 games with two starts in his two seasons with the Patriots after arriving as a third-round pick out of Penn State in the 2024 NFL draft.
A tackle in college, Wallace played six games with two starts as a rookie before incoming head coach Mike Vrabel switched him to guard in 2025.
Wallace couldn't make much of an impact last season and an injury early in training camp pushed him down the depth chart this summer.
While Wallace played both positions with New England, the Dolphins listed him as a tackle in the press release announcing his acquisition.
At that spot, he will compete with Marques Cox, Kevin Cline, Gottlieb Ayedze and veteran Charlie Heck for roster spots behind starting tackles Patrick Paul and Austin Jackson.
The Dolphins also have a couple of guards with the flexibility to line up at tackle if necessary, including veteran Jamaree Salyer and rookie first-round pick Kadyn Proctor, but it looks like they'd prefer not moving players around the offensive line.
Considering Cox, Cline and Ayedze all are former rookie free agents, Wallace does seem to have a legitimate opportunity to earn a roster spot if he can make a quick impression on the Dolphins coaching staff.
Wallace becomes the second former New England player to join the Dolphins in the past week.
He joined tight end Jeremiah Franklin, who Miami claimed off waivers Wednesday.
This is the first trade between the Dolphins and Patriots since 2022 when Miami sent wide receiver DeVante Parker to New England. In exchange for Parker and a 2022 fifth-round pick, the Dolphins got a 2023 third-round selection that they packaged with tight end Hunter Long in the deal with the Los Angeles Rams that brought Jalen Ramsey to Miami.

title: Get Ready for More Dolphins Roster Moves (But With a Specific Profile)
full_text:
As the Miami Dolphins keep making roster moves ahead of the restart that is the 2026 season, every player released by another team will be viewed in the context of whether they should bring him in as they keep looking for hidden gems.
But the Dolphins clearly have a type, so fans shouldn't look as any new free agent as a potential addition, and that applies to those veterans still on the market.
That type, if you've been paying attention, clearly is failed former first-round picks or early-round picks or young unproven players looking to, well, prove themselves and prove they can contribute to an NFL team.
And we've now got another player to monitor now that the New England Patriots have waived 2024 third-round pick Caedan Wallace, an offensive tackle from Penn State.
While one can wonder why the Dolphins would pick up a player  New England jettisoned before even the start of the preseason despite already having paid his signing bonus and despite him having a low base salary, he most definitely would fit the mold as a young player looking to establish himself.
What's really at play here is the fact the Dolphins are looking for young, cheap talent wherever they can get it, whenever they can get.
"As we go forward and we get into the season, we will continue to churn the back end of this roster," GM Jon-Eric Sullivan said Monday morning during an interview on The Joe Rose Show. "Nobody will sit around comfortably. It's my job to go find players, whether it's practice squad or waiver wire claims or whatever. We will continue to churn and and make sure that everybody understands, you better show up every day or somebody's going to come take your job.”
The Dolphins have made about a dozen roster acquisitions since signing their undrafted rookie class in May, and that group has consisted entirely of young unproven player along with former first-round picks Clelin Ferrell and Jalen Reagor.
And the same goes for the players the Dolphins have brought in for tryouts.
Good luck finding somebody, anybody — with the exception of former Chiefs first-round pick Clyde Ewards-Helaire — with even as many as 10 games of NFL experience.
And this goes along with an offseason comment from Sullivan on the eve of Bradley Chubb's cap money coming off the books when he cautioned against expecting "splash signings."
This is why the idea of adding a veteran like Keenan Allen or Stefon Diggs before that or Trevon Diggs at cornerback or Zack Ertz at tight end just doesn't compute.
It goes against everything the Dolphins have done while putting together their 2026 roster, where every acquisition involves a one-year deal at low money, the one exception being Malik Willis.
Two of the Dolphins' most recent acquisitions involving waiver claims, first for former New England Patriots tight end Jeremiah Franklin and more recently for Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Ahmari Harvey.
They joined the earlier claim of Green Bay Packers defensive lineman James Ester, who became Dolphins offensive lineman.
Those three waiver claims already match the highest yearly total since 2021 when the Dolphins claimed five players off waivers.
But this year is more like 2019 when the Dolphins also were in reubilding mode, and that year they made an astounding 20 waiver claims.
The reality with waiver claims, though, is the percentages of hitting on real keepers always is very low.
Since that 2019 season, the Dolphins have picked up 43 players off waivers and they've hit on, let's say, five of them. The headliner, of course, is Zach Sieler, and then we have linebacker Tyrel Dodson, special teams ace Elijah Campbell, wide receiver Mack Hollins and now possibly JuJu Brents.
Make no mistake, a return to prominence for the Dolphins will have to come more than anything for the development and emergence of draft picks.
But that doesn't mean the Dolphins are going to stop looking for contributors wherever they can find them.
Just remember the kind of players they're adding this year, though, before thinking everyone is the perfect Dolphins candidate.

title: Miami Dolphins Training Camp Practice 10 Observations: More Injuries, More Interceptions, Some Chippiness
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins returned to practice at the Baptist Health Training Complex on Monday, and we saw some chippiness for the first time in training camp, perhaps a signal it's a good thing the preseason is around the corner.
More importantly, though, is the Dolphins continuing to deal with injuries, with two more players leaving practice early.
This time it was linebacker Willie Gay Jr. and edge defender Josh Uche who didn't finish practice, with Gay walking off the field accompanied by a trainer.
This was after defensive tackle Zach Sieler joined the list of sidelined players, a list that already included edge Clelin Ferrell, guard Jamaree Salyer, wide receiver Kevin Coleman Jr., safety Dante Trader Jr., safety Lonnie Johnson Jr., kicker Zane Gonzalez and tight end Ben Sims. Sieler did attend the latter part of practice but he was in sweat pants with no pads and didn't practice.
The chippiness showed up during the one-on-ones that preceded team periods, and it began when rookie seventh-round pick Max Llewellyn threw his hand on rookie sixth-round pick D.J. Campbell's face twice after being stonewalled.
There was a minor flare-up later involving Chop Robinson and Patrick Paul at the end of a second one-on-one rep. On the first rep, Robinson bull-rushed Paul and got him off balance to the point that he put him on the ground. He then visibly let Paul know about it with what we'd imagine was some trash talking. Paul won the second rep and then kept after Robinson, to the point where other defensive players walked over to make sure things didn't escalate.
Cornerback Ahmari Harvey, who the Dolphins claimed him off waivers from the Pittsburgh Steelers on Friday, practiced with the team for the first time. Safety Tanner Wall, who was signed on the same day, recorded one of the defense's two interceptions on the day, with safety Major Burns getting the other one.
The Dolphins will conduct a closed walk-through Tuesday before flying to Washington for their joint practice against the Washington Commanders on Wednesday ahead of their preseason opener Friday.
While there were no big plays by the offense, Malik Willis again was solid.
By our count, he was 7-for-12, not including a clear defensive pass interference on a day when there were no officials on hand but including an incompletion after Robert Beal Jr. got inside Jonah Savaiinaea for what probably would have been a sack in a game situation.
Maybe his best throw came off a naked bootleg when Jacob Rodriguez got immediate pressure on him, but he outran him to the outside and threw a strike on the run.
-- While Willis was solid, Quinn Ewers again didn't have a very good practice, though in fairness he wasn't helped by a couple of drops. But he wasn't good down the stretch, including the interception by Burns right into his hands and a bad underthrow when his intended receiver was wide open in the short flat.
-- Since we have criticized his work in camp, it's only fair to point out that backup tackle Charlie Heck looked much better, particularly in one-on-ones.
-- Rodriguez continues to impress at linebacker, particularly with his ability to get into the backfield on running plays.
-- On that incompletion where Willis would have been sacked, Caleb Douglas dropped a pass over the middle. He later came back to make a good contested catch despite good coverage by Ethan Bonner, showcasing the inconsistency we've seen with his hands all camp.
-- Safety Michael Taaffe had very good coverage against Greg Dulcich on a crossing route, but Willis was able to thread the pass in there for the completion. Dulcich caught passes for the first time since early last week.
-- Jordyn Brooks got to Willis quickly on a blitz for what might have been a sack.
-- A.J. Henning made a really nice catch on a pass thrown behind him by Ewers. Henning later got behind Miles Battle deep down the right sideline, but Cam Miller overthrew him.
-- Chris Johnson has had a fairly quiet camp, but he had a great pass breakup against Douglas on a third-and-goal from the 6 with Willis at quarterback. The coverage was great all along and Willis tried to thread the needle, but Johnson jumped up to knock the ball away.
-- Miller later attempted another long pass down the sideline, that one to Tahj Washington, but he was blanketed all the way down the field by Marco Wilson and it was Wilson who ended up closest to being able to catch the ball.
-- Cornerback Ethan Robinson, who has made a play seemingly every practice latey, knocked down a Ewers attempt to rookie tight end Will Kacmarek across the middle, though the ball was thrown behind him.
-- Miller, who didn't have a great day, missed a completion to Theo Wease Jr. down the left sideline when he threw the ball too much inside to allow Battle to knock it down.

title: Brian Flores Sends Clear Message About Caleb Banks' Early Role With Vikings
full_text:
When the Minnesota Vikings drafted Caleb Banks, they knew that his ramp-up to the 2026 NFL season was going to take some time. As we approach the first game of the preseason, we may have to adjust expectations for how often he is going to be on the field as a rookie.
Banks missed most of the 2025 college season at Florida due to injury and then reaggravated a foot injury at the NFL Combine. He was not able to physically participate in OTAs or minicamp. His participation in training camp has not been limited, but he has only taken a handful of full-speed reps each day.
On Wednesday, defensive coordinator Brian Flores was asked about the progress of Banks and fellow rookie defensive tackle Domonique Orange. He indicated that he is always going to take it slow with young players.
“I’m a patient guy with rookies,” Flores said. “I think we’ve got to give them time to really get their feet in the ground ... literally on the field and figuratively just as far as understanding the pro game, the routines, the habits that they’ve got to build to really reach their optimum potential. So I think [Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange] are doing a really good job, but there’s a lot of meat left on the bone.”
Flores’ track record matches his words. In 2024, first-round draft pick Dallas Turner only played 302 snaps as he developed behind Jonathan Greenard and Andrew Van Ginkel. Other players who are currently in the mix for starting jobs, like Levi Drake Rodriguez , Ty Ingram-Dawkins and Jay Ward were also not used much in their first seasons as Vikings.
Banks was talked about as a project type player coming out of college because he did not have huge production or experience at the college level. But the Vikings cut two veteran defensive tackles in the offseason, which seemed to indicate that they were going to lean on Banks’ size and raw tools right away to fill the void. That might not end up being the case from the jump.
“I know that it just takes time for most guys to get comfortable in the NFL game,” Flores said. “It’s probably 99% of players that need to develop, improve, get better, and the 1% are the guys who are All-Pro as a rookie. But oftentimes, every rookie player is putting those expectations on themselves and maybe hearing it from other people, but they’re not going to get it from me.”
If there might be a slower curve for Banks being ready to play, that wouldn’t be unusual for rookie defensive tackles. Last year, only three DTs played more than 500 snaps and one of them was fifth-overall pick Mason Graham of the Cleveland Browns.
It sounded from Flores’ comments that he will be weighing the performance of the rookie DTs in the preseason heavily into his assessment of how much they can contribute right away.
“It’s hard to play D-line in the National Football League,” Flores said. “We’ll really see more of what this is in game. But based off of what we’ve seen, they’re moving in the right direction.”
If Banks and Orange aren’t impact players from the jump, that means that defensive tackles Ty Ingram-Dawkins and Levi Drake Rodriguez will take on a heavy workload. They have been the starters on the D-line alongside underrated standout DT Jalen Redmond.
Flores said that Ingram-Dawkins and Rodriguez have improved in their confidence coming into this year’s camp.
“They’re much more comfortable,” Flores said. “They’re much more comfortable in their techniques and fundamentals. They know their strengths.”
Last year Rodriguez played a total of 461 snaps and had 11 QB pressures and 2.0 sacks while playing the majority of those reps as a run defender. Ingram-Dawkins played 250 snaps with 174 of those coming against the run.
If Banks and Orange aren’t ready to contribute with heavy workloads right away, those numbers and roles are likely to grow.
“We’re constantly talking about and then trying to put them schematically in those positions where they do the things they do well,” Flores said.

title: 3 Biggest Takeaways from Viking’s Training Camp 8/12: Offense Taking Shape After QB Announcement
full_text:
EAGAN, MN — The energy at Vikings practice has felt different the last two days. Gone is the hectic tracking of first-team rep splits and completions. Gone is the uncertainty amongst media and fans. Gone is the difficulty for wideouts trying to gain valuable experience with two different passers. Instead, we have what finally looks and feels like an NFL offense with purpose and direction. An offense that now knows who its quarterback will be and how to prepare for the Green Bay Packers on September 13.
With only one open practice remaining before the Vikings head east to face the Giants this Saturday, the offensive starters had what will likely be the heaviest workload they’ll see this week. The good news is that they continued to make the most of it.
Here are my three biggest takeaways from a humid afternoon in pads.
The Vikings enter a season with a castoff quarterback and expectations of mediocrity, only to shock the world and make a deep playoff run. Sound familiar? Those of us who have followed this team for decades know this script all too well. Now, I’m certainly not promising a soul-crushing NFC Championship performance from the 2026 Vikings, but Kyler Murray’s performance since being named the team’s starter may be cause for a healthy level of optimism.
Murray continues to operate the offense with impressive conviction, especially considering he was splitting first-team reps with J.J. McCarthy until Tuesday. He looks like a QB who’s been operating this offense for years, even though he’s brand new.
He has found a rhythm with his weapons, leading to chunk plays downfield. He connected with Tai Felton for about 25 yards and tossed a quick slant to Jordan Addison, who sprinted upfield for a big gain. The implementation of that route alone should be a sign to Vikings fans that KOC is adding new tools to his play-design arsenal to help Murray succeed.
Most importantly, he continues to build rapport with star receiver Justin Jefferson. The two connected on another big play on Wednesday as Murray hit Jefferson deep over the middle. After experiencing a career-low year for yards and touchdowns in 2025, Jefferson seems determined to get on the same page with Murray quickly.
Kyler Murray finding Justin Jefferson deep at practice. (Via Vikings IG) pic.twitter.com/9oj5qjecW3
Quarterback conversation aside, Jordan Mason has been the star of the Vikings offense this week. While he carries the label of an up-the-middle power back, Mason is showing what he’s capable of when he’s able to turn loose on the outside.
The 27-year-old back has had multiple breakaway runs in just the last two days, showcasing a level of speed we’ve rarely seen from his runs up the gut. It seems clear that Mason is a beneficiary of Frank Smith’s newly implemented outside zone scheme.
I can’t wait for the #Vikings run game in 2026. (Via Vikings IG) https://t.co/tEj7fuX2sL pic.twitter.com/AbS22M5CJt
Mason is listed as a co-starter with Aaron Jones on the Vikings' unofficial depth chart released Wednesday, but if he runs like this in season, he’ll have a strong case to hold the RB1 title entirely to himself.
If you were wondering how J.J. McCarthy has performed in practice since officially being officially made QB2, the answer is largely the same as before.
McCarthy still struggles to process the field at the speed needed from a dependable NFL starter, and, to be honest, sometimes struggles to match the processing speed of an NFL backup. McCarthy had multiple plays Wednesday where the result carried no weight, since he would have already been knocked to the turf in a real game. The question now is: where do McCarthy and the Vikings go from here?
Would he even want to be the team’s backup, or would he try to find greener pastures elsewhere?
From what McCarthy told reporters after practice, he wants to see things through in Minnesota.
"This is the place I want to be." J.J. McCarthy on his future with the Vikings. pic.twitter.com/fj4NLl7Tli
McCarthy’s preseason play will go a long way toward deciding the immediate future for the 23-year-old former national champ. A strong performance Saturday could provide renewed confidence in his potential long-term development in Minnesota. It could also open pathways to a QB-needy team if McCarthy or the Vikings decide it's best to part ways.
What’s clear, though, is a bad performance could spell continued trouble for McCarthy, who desperately needs to recapture the hope he gave Vikings fans in his 2024 preseason premiere against the Raiders.

title: 3 Burning Questions Vikings Must Answer in Preseason Opener: OL Depth Can Make or Break the Year
full_text:
Good news: the Vikings play a football game this weekend .
Sure, the results don’t matter in the standings, but the lessons learned will help to formulate what will ultimately become the 2026 Vikings roster. After two and a half weeks of training camp practices in the Minnesota humidity, players fighting to secure their spots on the 53-man roster will get their chance to prove their worth against opponents in a different jersey.
The team has put the quarterback competition to bed , allowing general manager Nolan Teasley, head coach Kevin O’Connell and their staffs to focus on the other question marks surrounding the team over their three preseason matchups.
From the trenches to the backfield to defensive utility players, here are three questions the Vikings need to answer at MetLife Stadium this weekend.
I feel confident saying this is my biggest concern for the Vikings in 2026. The Vikings experienced a rotational mess along the offensive line in 2025 as injuries impacted nearly every starter at one point or another. Ryan Kelly’s multiple concussions led to his retirement this past offseason, moving Blake Brandel into the spotlight as the projected starting center .
While O’Connell tends to avoid playing starters in preseason matchups, Brandel desperately needs the reps, especially since he had never snapped a ball in a competitive environment before last season. Backup center Michael Jurgens enters Year 3 with a significant task as well: proving the team can rely on him if and when he’s called upon.
Left tackle Christian Darrisaw seems to be back at 100%, but given his history of injuries, as well as that of right tackle Brian O’Neill, the team’s backup tackles will have a lot to prove as well. Third-round pick Caleb Tiernan and free agent addition Ryan Van Demark will be two names to keep an eye on.
Fan favorite Walter Rouse will need a great game to keep himself in consideration for the final roster
Demond Claiborne has been one of the more fascinating names to follow through Vikings camp so far. The 198th overall pick out of Wake Forest has his work cut out for him, but may have the raw physical tools to hit the ground running. At 5’10”, 188 lbs, Claiborne does not have the natural build of a traditional every-down back. What he does have is explosive, game-changing speed.
Claiborne’s camp has been inconsistent, with some early struggles with ball security and pass catching and an unspecified injury. In recent days, though, he’s come alive. Claiborne has showcased his home-run ability running (h/t VikingsFanPage) with burst around the edge and, importantly, as a pass catcher.
Demond Claiborne’s speed is something else. (Via Vikings IG) pic.twitter.com/qi7ZWSAEWW
Saturday could be the exact spotlight Claiborne needs to show what he can do in game action. I’d expect him to get more than enough opportunities to prove what he can do with the ball in his hands.
I’ll start with this disclaimer: defensive coordinator Brian Flores will not show his full defensive hand in this, or any other preseason game. The man loves surprising his opponents mid-season and won’t want to spoil the fun by putting it on tape ahead of time. But he does have some decisions to make, especially with two new additions who could make impacts in multiple spots.
Jake Golday has already surpassed expectations for many.
While it seemed that he would spend his first year largely with the MLB group, he’s already taking snaps outside with the first-team unit in camp. Maybe the early comps to Andrew Van Ginkel weren’t too far off. Flores will need to find a delicate balance this preseason of figuring out just how good Golday is as a utility player , while also making sure he gets the needed reps at the spot he sees him playing most in 2026.
Jamal Adams is another interesting rotational piece to keep an eye on. Adams changed jersey numbers shortly after joining the team to allow him to rotate in at safety and linebacker. Most of his practice snaps have been at safety over the last week, possibly due to Ivan Pace’s solid start to camp and fellow safety Jay Ward entering concussion protocol.
What will his workload and use look like on Saturday? We’ll have to see what Flores has planned for the 30-year-old former All-Pro.

title: Under-the-Radar Pass-Catcher Is Poised to Make Some Noise in Week 1 of Vikings' Preseason
full_text:
It's safe to say that Vikings tight end Gavin Bartholomew didn't have an ideal start to his NFL career. After being a sixth-round pick of the Vikings during the 2025 NFL Draft, the Pitt standout suffered a back injury that held him out of action for his entire rookie season, leaving him under the radar when the current offseason began.
Fast forward to this summer, when Bartholomew is thriving during the Vikings' training camp . The 6-foot-5, 249-pound Pennsylvania native is making a great case for earning the third tight end spot on the 53-man roster for the upcoming season.
Ben Yurosek, Bryson Nesbit, and Marshall Lang are all fighting for a tight end spot this season as well, but a solid performance during the preseason opener against the Giants could go a long way for Bartholomew.
At only 23 years old, Bartholomew has a bright future ahead of him with the Vikings. If training camp is any indication of his potential, watching him high-point passes and haul in difficult catches could help him earn a role for head coach Kevin O'Connell this season.
On Saturday, Vikings fans will want to keep an eye on Bartholomew against the Giants during the Purple and Gold's Week 1 exhibition game . He is in line to see the field as part of the offense and special teams, where he will have an opportunity to cement a role with the squad.
With his excellent training camp performance so far, Bartholomew doesn't need to have an amazing preseason performance to impress the coaching staff. He is already showing that he is ready to contribute; the only question is where he will be used and how often.
During his 50 games at Pitt, Bartholomew caught 105 passes for 1,257 yards and 11 touchdowns. That production, combined with his size and determination, should have everyone excited to watch him take the field this weekend. Still, the Giants were solid against TEs last season, allowing the 10th-fewest receiving yards and seventh-fewest yards to the position.
In his draft prospect profile on NFL.com, Bartholomew's blocking was praised for being "aggressive," and the site noted that he will likely be an in-line blocker at the NFL level despite having soft hands and a solid catch radius. It wasn't an eye-popping performance; however, the 52.7 run block grade he earned on Pro Football Focus in his final collegiate season was a career-high mark.
After not seeing Bartholomew take the field as a rookie, it is exciting to see what he will be capable of during Week 1 of the preseason. Hopefully, he can continue to build on an excellent training camp and force the Vikings to find a role for him this season.

title: Jake Golday's Outlook Could Be Limited by One Vikings Veteran's Strong Camp Performance
full_text:
The Vikings drafted linebacker Jake Golday out of Cincinnati in the second round of the 2026 NFL Draft. The intriguing prospect is a unique fit for the team because of his ability to play as an interior linebacker or play on the edge, making him one of Minnesota's rookies to watch during training camp.
Golday's versatility makes him an extremely valuable piece in defensive coordinator Brian Flores's unit. However, being able to play two positions makes it more difficult to establish him as a starter who will fill a particular role in the upcoming season.
On the edge and the inside, the Purple and Gold have several veterans—Andrew Van Ginkel, Dallas Turner and Eric Wilson—already occupying key roles, as well as another linebacker whose strong offseason performance could limit Golday's workload when the Vikings take the field against the Packers in Week 1.
Golday will eventually be a major contributor for the Vikings, but he may have to assume a backup or rotational role for the upcoming season. Taking a starting job (or even a 53-man roster spot) from one of the other linebackers is an uphill climb, and standing in his way is none other than Blake Cashman.
On the surface, Cashman should be the most threatened by the possible emergence of Golday, but a strong training camp and familiarity with the defense will make it hard for the rookie to unseat the veteran defender.
Cashman has been dealing with a finger injury that put his availability into question since the start of training camp, but that issue has been put to rest after he looked great at practice and made an astounding number of plays. He's been practicing with the first team, capitalizing on those opportunities with his interception against J.J. McCarthy on Aug. 1 being one example.
After Sunday night's practice, Bring Me The News ' Will Ragatz even lauded Cashman's success against Kyler Murray in practice.
The good news for Golday is that Cashman is in the final season of his three-year, $22.5 million contract .  Minnesota has had no problem moving on from higher-priced veterans in favor of youth and potential recently, so it might not be too long before the 23-year-old defender earns a starting role.
Until then, the Vikings will likely lean on Cashman to hold down the starting interior linebacker job next to Wilson in Flores's defense. Doing so allows Golday to move around the defense and play more situational football at multiple positions.
That versatility is a huge bonus for the team since it also allows the rookie time to develop and acclimate to the NFL level before being thrust into a starting role. And there is nothing wrong with having talent on the depth chart past the players who are named starters.

title: 3 Winners From Vikings' 8/11 Training Camp: Offense Humming With Kyler Murray at the Helm
full_text:
EAGAN, MN — There was a different energy in the air Tuesday at TCO Performance Center. Maybe it was the announcement that Kyler Murray was officially the starting QB for the Vikings, or maybe it was the fact that it was wide receiver autograph day. We may truly never know. Jokes aside, wideout day is typically the busiest non-night practice of training camp, bringing in an appropriately large crowd for the team’s first day with an established QB depth chart.
Conversations in the crowd indicated excitement from some and hesitation from others. Several J.J. McCarthy jerseys stood out in the purple-and-white crowd. Once practice kicked off, it seemed Kevin O’Connell had made the right call. The offense flowed with a consistency and purpose we had yet to see while reps were still being split. For the first time, we saw what the 2026 Vikings offense could look like, and it was promising.
Here's one player and two position groups that won the day with a more settled offense.
I mean, this one was obvious, right? Murray won the day before he even stepped on the field after O’Connell announced the team was moving forward with him as their starting QB. All he did after was put together one of his better practices of the summer.
Head Coach Kevin O'Connell on naming Kyler Murray the starting QB pic.twitter.com/YSUhnuem7J
Murray was incredibly accurate today, having only one incompletion by my count. He had several significant gains, with impressive plays to Justin Jefferson, Tai Frelton, and Jordan Addison. It was a thing of beauty.
Compared to Murray’s high-flying performance last Wednesday, this seemed more sustainable, calmer, and more like what you’d see in a real NFL game. Decisiveness and timing were key themes throughout the now-extinct QB competition, and Murray spent Tuesday proving why these assets allowed him to secure the starting gig. While the fanbase works through their feelings on the final QB decision, I hope they find the following to be an encouraging endorsement: If Murray plays like he practiced today, this season will be very fun for the purple and gold.
Kyler Murray and Jordan Addison have built a nice connection so far. Here’s another one from today. (Via Vikings IG) pic.twitter.com/RT4bvN1cNC
This one may be cheating, but a day where your QB is on fire tends to make your wideouts look pretty good. Of particular interest is Murray’s connection with Jefferson. The two connected on another big play today, and it's already ripe for debate online. Similar to their big connection last week, Murray seems to have a bit of a “frick it, Jefferson’s down there somewhere” mentality. He just seems willing to throw it up while trusting his top wideout to make a play. So far, it seems to work well.
Addison has seemingly ramped fully back into the offense after missing time last week with a thumb injury. Felton continues to stack impressive plays, this time snagging a throw from Murray for about 30 yards. Jauan Jennings had a quieter day but made his presence felt as a blocker in the run game, emphasizing the value he brings to the offense in totality. Myles Price also had a nice catch from McCarthy down the right sideline.
Dontae Fleming, Jeshaun Jones, and Dillon Bell didn’t make as much noise, but are in line for significant playing time this weekend against the Giants .
Kyler Murray calls playing with the Vikings WR group “a blessing.” “Everyone knows what we have in that room from top to bottom.” pic.twitter.com/xdRy1rWm3p
KOC has often talked about marrying the run and the pass throughout his tenure in Minnesota. Today’s practice showed what that could look like in 2026. Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason were running all over the field on Tuesday. The new-look Vikings run scheme is already showing its potential, and I think much of it is still being kept under wraps. Mason did have a fumble, but tight end Josh Oliver was able to recover it.
Rookie speedster Demond Claiborne also made his presence felt after taking a short pass for a long-distance touchdown. After having some ups and downs early in camp with ball security and drops, it's been good to see Claiborne make more impact on the offense.
Zavier Scott also had a few nice runs, lowering his shoulder and picking up multiple first downs on the ground. Both Scott and Claiborne are expected to get a significant amount of reps against the Giants on Saturday.
