title: Saints Preseason Schedule 2026: Dates, Times, TV, Opponents
full_text:
After two weeks of the players in the franchise going up against each, the New Orleans Saints will finally play another team when it begins their three-week preseason slate starting on Saturday.
New Orleans opens up the preseason slate with a game against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Saturday at the Caesars Superdome before traveking to play the Los Angeles Rams (Aug. 22). Both games are set for a 3:00 p.m. kickoff. The Saints wrap up the preseason against rival Dallas Cowboys (Aug. 28) in Arlington for a 7:00 p.m. start.
Here is some info about all three teams along with the dates, times, locations and how you can watch all three games.
The Jaguars are coming off their first playoff appearance since 2022 and the most wins in a single season in franchise history after a 13-4 season under Liam Coen , who is entering his second year on the job.
The biggest question for the Jaguars throughout training camp is the running back spot. Travis Etienne has departed for the Saints. The battle is between Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr . Those are tough shoes to fill, considering Etienne rushed for 1,000 yards or more in three of the last four seasons.
The Los Angeles Rams are coming off a 12-5 season and an appearance in the NFC Championship Game, where they lost to eventual Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks .
The Rams made the biggest offseason move of the summer when they received All-Pro defensive end Myles Garrett from the Browns in exchange for a 2027 first-round pick, a 2028 second-round pick and a 2029 third-round pick. Garrett is the reigning Defensive Player of the Year after breaking the single-season sack record with 23 sacks. It was the second time he won the award.
There’s a chance we might see first-round draft pick Ty Simpson , who was shockingly drafted by the Ram with the 13th overall pick. He’s currently battling with Stetson Bennett for the backup role and could be the heir to the keys to the offense when reigning MVP Matthew Stafford retires.
Unlike the previous two franchises mentioned, the Dallas Cowboys have been a massive disappointment. Dallas has missed the playoffs for two consecutive seasons, finishing 7-10 in both. This came after three straight 12-win seasons.
While quarterback Dak Prescott and the Cowboys lit it up offensively by finishing second in the league in total offense, they also finished 30th in yards allowed and had the league's worst passing and scoring defense.
That resulted in the Cowboys drafting five defensive players with seven picks, with their first two picks being safety Caleb Downs of Alabama and Malachi Lawrence of UCF in the first round.

title: Saints’ Kelvin Banks Jr. Reveals Key Focus After Impressive Rookie Season
full_text:
New Orleans Saints left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. is entering his second NFL season after an impressive rookie campaign.
Drafted ninth overall by the Saints, the 6-foot-5, 315-pound lineman became just the third Saints left tackle since 1978 to start every game at the position, earning consensus All-Rookie honors and a spot on the 2025 PFWA All-Rookie Team.
Banks allowed only five sacks and three accepted penalties across 681 pass-blocking snaps while ranking second among all rookie linemen in run blocking, according to Pro Football Focus.
Banks knows exactly where he wants to improve entering his second NFL season: consistency.
“Honestly, for me, it was more consistency because it'll be multitude of reps,” Banks said. "I'm looking flawless, taking the great set, doing this and that, and— and looking good. And it'll be that one or two reps where it's like, 'Oh, dang.' You know what I'm saying? Just making sure I clean the small mistakes up that I may be making throughout the game, whether it's getting fatigued or just not fully thinking throughout the play and just going out there and playing. So just small stuff like that is what I kind of took away from last year.”
Now, Banks is looking to clean up those small mistakes, build on his strong debut and help lead the Saints to an NFC South title and their first playoff berth since 2020.
Banks’ development is also tied to the growth of fellow offensive tackle Taliese Fuaga . With a full season together under their belts, the two young tackles are pushing each other to take another step, and Banks believes their shared work ethic could help them develop into one of the NFL’s top tackle duos.
“I mean, we literally just got done on the field after practice,” Banks said after the session on Aug. 6. “We were out there for an extra 30 minutes doing extra different sets and working different stuff that we may have slipped up on in practice. So I'll say that's the thing that excites me the most because I know how bad we want to be one of the best tackle duos in the league. So (it's) that eagerness to understand that we both have that same mindset.”
Fuaga, who played left tackle in 2024, started 13 games at right tackle for New Orleans in 2025.
While Banks and Fuaga give the Saints a young foundation at tackle, veteran David Edwards has brought another element to the offensive line room at guard.
Edwards, who is entering his eighth season in the league, has started 77 of the 103 games he played for the Los Angeles Rams (2019-2022) and Buffalo Bills (2022-2025), two of the league’s best teams. He was a starter for the Rams when they won Super Bowl LVI.
Banks believes Edwards’ experience, intelligence and personality have allowed him to quickly fit in with the group.
“He's brought a lot. Savviness, smarts, laughter,” Banks said. He's bringing everything to the room. I mean, he's definitely a guy who fits in well with our scheme and let alone not just our scheme, but our OLI room as a whole. So he's been a great piece to our puzzle, for sure.

title: Saints have an Intriguing New Weapon in Athletic Rookie Tight End Oscar Delp
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints drafted tight end Oscar Delp with the 73rd overall pick in the third round of the 2026 NFL Draft, and they had good reason: his athleticism and speed are stuff you cannot teach.
Delp, a 6-foot-5, 245-pound Georgia product, had an impressive pro day as he registered a 4.49-second 40-yard dash and a 38-inch vertical. In four seasons with UGA, Delp totaled 70 receptions for 854 yards and nine touchdowns in his career.
It will be interesting to see how the Saints use Delp with veterans Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant . Regardless, the Saints have been delving into multiple tight end packages and Delp’s versatility could be used there.
Delp is in a loaded tight end room led by Johnson and Fant, so he may not get the most playing time as of right now. However, his versatility could get him on the field and Delp wants to do whatever he can to get on the field and help his team win games regardless of the role.
“Right now, I'm just trying to find a way to get on the field. I know that he's been very successful with tight ends in his past, and I feel like I can bring something to the table. And we got a lot of very talented guys in our room and just different ways to get us on the field. Anything they need me to do,  I'm willing to get out there and just help us be successful.”
Delp has had a chance  to learn from the Saints’ veteran players on how to approach everything as a professional from the film room to being on the pratice field.
“It's been great. A lot of learning, a lot of growing. I’m very fortunate and blessed to be in the tight end room with some vets and some guys. I've got some games under their belt to just learn a lot from everyone, just taking everything in.”
Delp said that Georgia helped him transition to the NFL. That makes sense because the Bulldogs have been one of the NFL’s talent factories since Kirby Smart took over in 2016, especially at the tight end position. Since 2017, Georgia has produced seven tight ends that ended up being draft picks, including Pro Bowl tight end Brock Bowers .
“I think Georgia did a tremendous job preparing me and other players for the transition from college football to the NFL. I've talked to guys for years while I was in college, figuring out what's different and what happens in that transition. It's just like everyone said about Kirby — he's very big on developing players and practicing hard, and here it's a lot more mental.”
“It's not going to be as bang-bang every day as it is in college, where you're practicing six days in a row, basically scrimmaging for two hours a day. And I think they've done a really good job preparing me to be a receiving tight end, a blocking tight end, wherever they need me. I've done it in college, and I feel comfortable doing whatever they want me to do in this offense.”
A lot of Saints fans are excited about this year’s offense. That’s because they have Tyler Shough coming back after a strong rookie season, a reenergized running back room with Travis Etienne joining the franchise and a deep receiving room led by Chris Olave .
Delp has liked what he’s seen from the Saints’ offense, and he has a first-person view of what it will ultimately look like.
“I mean, I think it's just very explosive. I mean, I think it'd be a really explosive offense. You know, we got the guys to run the ball when we need to run the ball, and then we got the dudes who can go out on field and make big plays. I really think that, you know, the sky's the limit for this offense. And, you know, with the guys like Tyler and Spencer (Rattler) back there, I mean, you know, I think we have a really, really special team.”

title: Drew Brees' Hall of Fame Speech was the Ultimate Love Letter to New Orleans
full_text:
Few athletes have ever become as synonymous with a city as Drew Brees has with New Orleans
Nearly 20 years after arriving in a city that was processing the destruction that Hurricane Katrina brought to the city, Brees was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame , adding the sport’s highest individual honor to what was already a loaded resume.
After all, Brees brought the city of New Orleans a Super Bowl championship, broke many of the NFL’s passing records while active, and of course, one of the most meaningful player-city relationships that we have seen in professional sports.
During his induction speech in Canton, Ohio, Brees made sure New Orleans – the city that embraced him when a torn rotator cuff nearly derailed his career – remained the center of his story.
The circumstances that brought Brees and New Orleans together made their eventual success even more remarkable.
Hurricane Katrina devastated New Orleans and the Gulf Coast on Aug. 30, 2005, killing nearly 1,400 people, displacing hundreds of thousands and would end up being the costliest natural disaster in U.S. history. The Saints were forced to spend the 2005 season away from the Superdome and finished 3-13, leaving the franchise facing an uncertain future of its own.
Brees was at a crossroads as well.
He suffered a 360-degree labrum and rotator cuff tear in the regular season finale in 2005 while a member of the San Diego Chargers, an injury serious enough where people thought his career would bever be the same at best.
Despite those concerns, the Saints took a chance and signed him to a six-year, $60 million contract with New Orleans on March 14, 2006.
This came after the only other team to go after him, the Miami Dolphins, backed away from Brees due to concerns around his throwing shoulder , giving a chance for not only Brees to resurrect his career but to give hope to a city that desperately needed it.
Brees did not just give a city hope, he gave it 15 years of jubilation, transforming the Saints into perennial contenders and leading the franchise to its first Super Bowl championship in a 31-17 win over New Orleans native Peyton Manning and the Indianapolis Colts. He also became one of the most prolific quarterbacks in NFL history and one of the most beloved athletes New Orleans has ever known.
"New Orleans ... You trusted me with the soul of the city, and I would’ve died to protect that calling." 📺 @ProFootballHOF Enshrinement on ESPN/NFLN pic.twitter.com/S0avpW9hDS
Nearly two decades after taking a chance on New Orleans — and New Orleans taking a chance on him — Brees stood in Canton surrounded by family, friends and members of the Who Dat Nation who made the trip to witness his induction.
When it came time to explain what New Orleans meant to him, Brees made it clear that New Orleans is a special city and the bond forged in 2006 never disappeared.
“New Orleans has been through a lot to the point where in some cases the feeling was we may have lost everything,” Brees said. “It may never come back the same. Storms teach us that our greatest treasures aren’t the things we own. They’re the people we love, and the way we show up for one another. It reminds us to hold our loved ones a little closer, to love a little harder, to laugh a little louder, and to never take a single day for granted. Sometimes it takes losing what can be replaced to truly appreciate the things that can’t.
"New Orleans, you accepted me; you embraced me; you believed in me but more importantly, you trusted me with the soul of the city and I would have died to protect that calling.”
As the saying goes, “If you love New Orleans, it will love you back.”

title: Pete Werner's Starting Job Suddenly in Jeopardy as Danny Stutsman Surges
full_text:
There are always offseason position battles in the NFL, and the New Orleans Saints are no exception.
Second-year linebacker Danny Stutsman has taken first-team reps ahead of veteran Pete Werner for the second straight practice, the clearest change in Wednesday’s rotation. This move also is the most seismic of them all as Werner has been a starter for the Saints since his rookie season, racking up 408 tackles with 256 of them being solo.
However, Werner did struggle a bit last season, as he had a 46.8 tackling grade and a 15.8 missed-tackle rate, according to Pro Football Focus. Combine that with Stutsman being drafted in the Kellen Moore era and a completely different defensive playcaller in Brandon Staley when they took over last season, and Werner may be in trouble.
Nonetheless, Moore said Monday that the changes were “no big deal,” adding that the Saints were going to rotate their players throughout training camp. Even so, that competition still matters to players like Stutsman and Werner, both of whom believe they belong in starting roles.
“There’s a respect between everyone in the room, but it’s the kind of job that you want to win. Every day you’re fighting out there and putting your best thing on tape.”
Stutsman was a fourth-round pick by the Saints in 2025 as a potential successor to DeMario Davis . While that may seem far-fetched because he was drafted in the middle of the draft, his production made you believe that he was a steal.
While in college, Stutsman recorded over 100 tackles in each of his final three seasons while at Oklahoma. He posted a career-high 125 tackles as a sophomore in 2022 and finished his time as a Sooner with 376 total stops — ninth in school history — along with 36 tackles for loss, eight sacks, three interceptions, four forced fumbles, and eight pass breakups.
Now, Stutsman has a shot to live up to his “draft steal” label and claim a starting role in the linebacking corps inside the same building where Rickey Jackson, Sam Mills and Jonathan Vilma once roamed.
“That’s a dream,” Stutsman said when asked about the possibility he wants to be a starter. “That’s kind of why you wake up. That’s motivation. At the end of the day, you want to contribute as much as you can for the defense to do as much as I can.

title: Saints Have One Position Battle Everyone Should Be Watching
full_text:
There are a lot of position battles going on on Airline Drive as the New Orleans Saints are using the preseason to determine the depth chart and who will make the final 53-man roster.
There are plenty of intriguing position battles. With Tyler Shough holding down the starting quarterback role, Spencer Rattler and Zach Wilson are battling for the backup role. There’s also some interesting developments on the defensive line as John Ridgeway III has become one of the biggest standouts.
However, the biggest position battle everyone should pay attention to is in the receiving corps.
As it stands, $132 million man Chris Olave and first-round draft choice Jordan Tyson have seemingly locked up the first two spots in the receiving corps. However, one spot remains open.
Battling for the job are third-year wideout Devaughn Vele and rookies Bryce Lance and Barrion Brown .
Vele became a favorite target of Shough in the second half of the season, catching 26 passes for 238 yards and a touchdown in his final four games before missing the last three due to injury.
Lance was an All-American wideout at North Dakota State, accumulating over 2,139 yards and 25 touchdowns. The 6-3, 204-pound receiver was drafted by New Orleans on the fourth round.
Brown was drafted in the sixth round by the Saints after accumulating 2.060 yards and 12 touchdowns at both Kentucky and LSU from 2022-25. He made most of his noise as a kick returner, taking back a kick return for a touchdown at least once in all four years.
Without a doubt, Brown has been making the most noise of the three as each and every practice he is making a standout play or two,
"I knew he was an explosive player, but I didn't know he could play like that,” Saints left tackle Kelvin Banks said. “He's a dog, man. Even from the first practice, I seen him make some cuts, and run some routes and explode off the ball, and I was like 'yeah, he's going to be special.'"
Saints head coach Kellen Moore has been impressed with Brown’s mental fortitude during training camp and how well-prepared he is in practice and practice out.
“I think his just focus and his urgency to be really well-prepared,” Moore said. “I think he does an awesome job. I think that's, that's one of the parts that I'm most impressed by him, because I think that's the hardest part for these young guys: the physical part. They've played football, there's an acclimation part of that, but there's so much more of a mental wear and tear on them, um, with the preparation side, and sometimes that impacts their ability to go out there and perform. And so for Barrion, he's been really assignment-sound he's been really detailed, and so, all that credit goes to him getting ready.”

title: Giants Notebook: Beckham Set to Play, Dart's Status a Mystery, Zvada Booms a 62-Yarder
full_text:
John Harbaugh’s New York Giants will get their first taste of live action against an opponent donning another colored jersey on Saturday when the Giants host the Minnesota Vikings at MetLife Stadium in a 1 p.m. kickoff.
Harbaugh didn’t go into his plans regarding who is going to play and who won’t–the Giants still have another couple of days before needing to make that decision. But one player who will definitely be part of the action is receiver Odell Beckham Jr.
“I think he's ramped up, honestly,” Harbaugh said after Wednesday’s practice. “You saw him on the sideline over there. I mean, he almost got his feet down on that really tough catch. He's looked good. He's in shape. He's taking every rep he's supposed to take in practice.
“I feel like he's getting stronger every day. He's in a good place. He will play, and I'm looking forward to seeing him play.”
Giants fans have long awaited the chance to see Beckham back in a Big Blue uniform. While Beckham is not the same player he was the first time around with the Giants, Harbaugh apparently feels that the 33-year-old receiver is in good enough shape to give the team quality snaps.
Beckham, who last played in 2024 as a member of the Miami Dolphins, only appeared in nine games and looked far from healthy. But in 2023, when he was with Harbaugh in Baltimore, Beckham, in 14 games with six starts, gave the Ravens 35 receptions for 565 yards and three scores.
Beckham has been diligent in his training to ensure that he finishes his NFL career on his terms. When he was first signed in the spring, he seemed sluggish all around, but since camp has begun, Beckham is showing signs of having something left in the tank as far as getting open and being able to separate.
“I probably want to see him play enough, but you got to play other guys too,” Harbaugh said when asked how much time Beckham would see on Saturday.
“I think he could play the whole game and he'd be fine. He's in shape to do it, but we're not going to play anybody really the whole game just because we've got 90 guys.”
While Beckham will be among those playing on offense on Saturday, Harbaugh was a lot less forthcoming when it came to the question of who will be throwing him the ball.
“That’s a good question,” Harbaugh said when asked if quarterback Jaxson Dart would be playing in the preseason opener. “I’m gonna have to dodge. I'm going to have to bob and weave. I'll let you know later.”
Dart has been having an up-and-down camp so far as he gets acclimated to the new offense, which requires him to work under center. He did have a pair of on-target passes during Wednesday’s padded session, hitting running back Devin Singletary on a wheel route and also connecting with rookie Malachi Fields in a 7-on-7 drill.
Receiver Malik Nabers, who has been steady as far as getting some on-field work every day, worked out with a trainer for a short bit before heading inside for the rest of the practice.
But the good news is that Nabers could be ramping up further very soon, according to Harbaugh.
“Yeah, he's kind of exactly where he's been,” Harbaugh said. “And we're looking towards soon ramping him up into some group periods and perhaps some team periods. Maybe next week; we'll see.”
To date, Nabers hasn’t done anything with 7-on-7s or team drills at full speed, though he did partake in team drills during a walkthrough pace when the team was in West Virginia.
But despite that, the receiver also hasn’t had any known setbacks that have forced the team to dial back on his reps, which is a positive sign in his quest to be ready for Week 1 of the regular season.
“He's doing great. He's working hard. Spirits are high. And yeah, we'll see where we're at next week,” Harbaugh said.
The following Giants did not take part in Wednesday’s practice:
Harbaugh said that Hyatt, whose hold on a roster spot is slipping with each passing day, “should be back in a reasonable period.”
He also said that Adebo is day-to-day, but did not specify what the cornerback is dealing with.
Others who were limited included cornerbacks Greg Newsome II (knee) and Dru Phillips (knee), both of whom took part in individual drills only.
Rookie guard Francis Mauigoa (neck) took his full practice workload after being limited in Tuesday’s session.
Undrafted rookie free agent kicker Dominic Zvada ended practice with a 62-yard field goal that had plenty of distance with 11 seconds to go in a simulated end-of-game situation.
“I thought he was going to make it,” Harbaugh said of Zvada’s attempt. “(Assistant Head Coach/Special Teams Coordinator) Chris Horton told me the 42 is the line, so I had to give him a hard time after that. So, it was actually a little further back, and it was a great kick, great snap, nice to see.”
Zvada, who hit all six of his attempts (Ben Sauls went 4-of-5 on his), appears to have a slight edge in the kicking competition, but Harbaugh gave an indication that the competition with Sauls is far from being over.
“The bottom line is you got to kick it straight consistently,” he said. “So, having a big leg is a big deal. Kicking it straight consistently is a bigger deal.
“I think both those guys have done that very well, and Ben has a very good leg, too. I don't want to imply that he doesn't. Ben's a very strong leg guy, as well, but they're both having really good camps.”

title: John Harbaugh Breaks Down Giants' Risk-Reward Calculus on Terrion Arnold
full_text:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh is on a mission to hit the ground running in his first season at the team’s helm, and to accomplish that, he’s all about bringing in good players whose skill sets can help out.
That’s the reason behind the Giants’ interest in former Detroit Lions cornerback Terrion Arnold, who is currently facing felony charges that led to the Lions parting ways with their former first-round draft pick.
“We want to be aggressive in every way, whatever we can do, find everything out we can about any player that can help us be better,” Harbaugh said when asked about Arnold.
“The margins are tight in the National Football League. You try to win a game. You come up with a good play. You can find a play on the internet that somebody puts out there that one of your opponents is running in practice, man. You look for those too. So, we're looking for players that can help us all the time. And he's a player that can help us.”
The Giants hosted a visit by Arnold on Wednesday, presumably to get to know him and to gain additional clarity about Arnold’s situation. Harbaugh said that the organization has already performed a deep dive into Arnold’s circumstances and has presented the head coach with an overview.
“If there is a decision to be made on any player that you don't want to go there with a player, then this organization, they won't go there,” Harbaugh said. “And so, that decision would also have to be made.
“It's more than just what you read in the papers, though. I mean, you got to find out exactly where everything stands. And I think, I do know that our people do a great job of that.”
Arnold, who has denied any wrongdoing , could be looking at a lengthy legal process while he fights to clear his name, according to Harbaugh. And that is something the Giants have also weighed when deciding whether to make an offer.
“I think you have to decide, where does the legal process stand? What are we really talking about here? What does it look like? And you have to make a judgment along those lines,” he said, also acknowledging that the league could put the cornerback on the exempt list while he sorts out his situation," Harbaugh said.
Therein lies another consideration for the Giants. “You try to do the best you can to anticipate what that might be and see if it's worth it,” Harbaugh said.
“There's risk-reward. There are things to be gained and things to be lost. And you just got to balance it out and try to make a two-fold decision.”

title: Why the Giants Kicking Battle Isn't Nearly as Close as Fans Think
full_text:
For those who think that the New York Giants kicker battle has already been decided in favor of undrafted rookie Dominic Zvada over Ben Sauls, assistant head coach/special teams coordinator Chris Horton said no such decision has been made.
“ It's two young guys that are doing very well,” Horton said of Zvada and incumbent Ben Sauls, both of whom are listed as being dead even on the team’s newly released unofficial depth chart .
“Both guys, where they are right now from where they were during this spring, I mean, it's been tremendous growth just watching these guys go out and compete against each other. They know that they compete, and they come out every day, and they work hard.”
The Giants have had the kickers alternate during team periods, with field goal attempts from varying distances. Back in the spring, Zvada, who struggled in his final year at Michigan, was perfect during OTAs while Sauls struggled with his conversions.
So far this summer, it’s fair to say that the battle has been even as the coaches try to figure out which of the two they can trust the most.
“Trust is a big thing, right? Trust comes with a lot of responsibility,” Horton said. “It's not because they're young that you have to find a way to trust them. It's what they do when they're out there. You build trust through your work. You build trust through your preparation, and the preparation that both these guys are bringing every day—we're trusting them, right?
“We're trusting them, but we're going to have to trust them in the big moments, and we try to put them in those situations so when they go out there, we feel pretty good about it.”
The Giants obviously have enough trust in both young legs, and that was made evident when they did not bring in a veteran kicker to compete with the duo after cutting Jason Sanders earlier in the year.
But whereas past Giants staffs have preferred battle-tested kickers, this staff seems willing to take a leap of faith, realizing that even the best kickers in the game had to start somewhere.
“That's 100% correct. We think about how we all started, right?” Horton said. “When I got up to be a coordinator for the very first time, there were things that I needed to learn on the job, and so it's just like any other position, just like any other thing, that we all got to start somewhere, right?
“Somebody's just got to be willing to give you an opportunity, but that opportunity, as I said, comes with the process. Once you go through the process, you follow that process, and you believe in yourself, everything else takes care of itself because it comes with discipline and consistency.
“For the kickers, consistency is making kicks.”
And for the coaches, it’s about being patient, particularly if a kicker hits a rough spot.
“They're judged on makes and misses, right?” Horton said. “Sometimes you've got to go through a couple things to get yourself out of those things. And it's a lot easier to say, ‘Well, let's find the next guy,’ but then you're starting all over with the next guy.
“The next guy's on the street because he had the same issues that probably one of these young guys had. So, you try to go through the process. You weed out all that stuff, and you say, ‘Okay, what's the standard? What's going to be our standard?’ And as long as we uphold that standard and we're consistent in what we do, we're going to be fine.”
They’ll find out starting this weekend if Horton’s belief comes to fruition.

title: Giants Unofficial Depth Chart Takeaways: Rookies Rising, Battles Still Unsettled
full_text:
The New York Giants have released their first unofficial depth chart of the summer— unofficial because the depth chart does not come from the coaches but is instead compiled by the staff based on interpretations of where guys have taken the majority of their practice reps.
Still, the depth chart is always fun to dissect for clues as to how the team is taking shape, so let’s look at some of the key takeaways.
As anticipated, first-rounders Francis Mauigoa and Arvell Reese are listed as starters at their respective positions (right guard and inside linebacker).
Second-round pick Colton Hood is currently listed as the third cornerback behind projected starter Paulson Adebo and veteran Deonte Banks.
But with Adebo and Greg Newsome II both dealing with injuries that make them question marks for Saturday’s preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings, Hood could very well find himself with an opportunity to start.
Receiver Malachi Fields, the third-round pick, is listed as the third receiver, behind Malik Nabers and Calvin Austin III.
Defensive lineman Bobby Jamison-Travis currently is third on the chart at nose tackle, behind D.J. Reader and Leki Fotu.
Meanwhile, offensive tackle J.C. Davis, the second of the three sixth-round draft picks, is listed as the third-string left tackle, behind starter Andrew Thomas and backup Marcus Mbow.
Jack Kelly, the last of the three sixth-round picks, is listed as the backup weakside linebacker behind Reese. Kelly has been having a solid camp and projects not only to nail down a spot as the fourth inside linebacker but also a core special teams role.
No surprise here, as Darius Alexander is listed as the first-team defensive end next to Shelby Harris at defensive tackle and D.J. Reader at nose tackle.
Alexander has been pushing for a job on the first-team defense as far back as the end of last season, having continued his quest over the spring and summer.
The Giants list Aaron Stinnie OR Evan Neal as the backup right guard behind Mauigoa. There are actually several instances where two players are listed, an indication that the competition is either close or there is no clear-cut guy at that spot.
But what’s most interesting about this one is that Neal has been “glued” to the third-team offense, something that might not necessarily be the case given the depth chart listing.
What’s also interesting is that Stinnie has mainly been a career left guard and has played just 15 regular-season snaps on the right side , all coming in 2019, his rookie year.
Despite there being a rotation at cornerback on the first-team defense, Paulson Adebo is still listed among the starters.
Again, though, with Adebo nursing some injury, it remains to be seen whether he plays in Saturday's preseason opener.
Even when Adebo does return to play, it’s clear that he’s still in competition to hold onto his starting job.
In another somewhat surprising move, the unofficial depth chart lists Abdul Carter OR Kayvon Thibodeaux as the starting SAM linebacker.
Entering camp, it was thought that perhaps Carter, who finished the 2025 season in place of the injured Thibodeaux on a strong note, would lead to Thibodeaux working mostly with the second-team defense in camp.
Head coach John Harbaugh, however, didn’t see it that way when asked about Thibodeaux’s handling of being with the second-team defense.
“I don't think he's worried about it. He knows he's going to play a bunch. These guys know. We have three starters at outside linebacker. Those are all starting football players. So, slice it how you want. Do a depth chart any way you want. Those guys are all going to play a ton of football,” he said.
Finally, we get to the position group that everyone wants to know about: receivers.
The first thing that jumps out is that this depth chart doesn’t list a slot receiver. That doesn’t mean the Giants won’t have one, but it's likely a sign they will be leaning more into 12- and 13-personnel, or they could be planning to deploy tight end Isaiah Likely into more of that role.
As for how the receivers stack up, it looks like it will be a mix-and-match. As already noted, the top three receivers at one spot are Nabers, Austin, and Fields.
At the other receiver spot, Darius Slayton, Darnell Mooney, and Odell Beckham Jr. are the top three, followed by veteran JuJu Smith-Schuster, Jalin Hyatt, Dalen Cambre, and Xavier Gipson.
Nabers isn’t expected to play in any of the preseason games as he continues his ramp-up from ACL surgery.
Fields has been having a solid camp thus far, to the point where he could be in line for a bigger role on offense than maybe initially thought as his NFL career gets underway.
The Giants have the same situation at running back where they list “Cam Skattebo OR Tyrone Tracy, Jr” as the first-team running back.
New York is expected to deploy a committee approach at running back rather than name one specific guy as the bellcow, so this development really doesn’t come as a surprise, nor does it necessarily indicate which running back is going to see the bulk of the carries any given week, as the specific opponent and matchups will instead dictate that.
Braxton Berrios, who has had himself a solid camp, is listed as the main punt returner, followed by Calvin Austin III and then Xavier Gipson.
Berrios is also second on the unofficial depth chart at kickoff returner, behind cornerback Deonte Banks. Dante Miller and Eric Gray are third and fourth guys at kickoff returner.
Despite undrafted rookie Dominic Zvada having jumped out in terms of consistency this summer, he is not listed as being equal to Ben Sauls for the kicking job.

title: Matt Nagy Explains Why Giants' Offense Isn't Fully Installed With Camp Winding Down
full_text:
New York Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy didn’t mince any words when offering an opinion about how the team’s offense looked during Tuesday’s practice.
“Today was an average practice, maybe below average. It wasn't good enough,” Nagy said.
That assessment might not sit well with Giants fans, but as Nagy explained, the Giants are about “halfway through our run install and halfway through our pass install” as they try to figure out what type of plays suit quarterback Jaxson Dart and the offense the best.
Halfway through? With the season’s start just a month away?
It sounds bad, but Nagy explained that what the Giants are in fact doing is figuring out what clicks with the second-year quarterback as they look to further his and the offense’s development.
“I just go back personally to OTAs, and when we were first teaching this thing, we spent phase two just kind of trying to teach this thing from the ground up in buckets and phases, and not necessarily plays,” he said.
“We spent several weeks just teaching the concepts and teaching whether it's run or pass, circles. We called it musical chairs, not positions. Everybody had to know the concept, so we weren't running plays. So, we spent some time with them to understand, ‘Hey, if I'm in this spot or this spot, what do I do?’ That's how you understand the basis of an offense.
“And then, now we get to phase three, and you take it to training camp, and now we're running plays, and we get to see, ‘Okay, not only are we doing what we do, but now we get to see a crazy defense with (Defensive Coordinator) Dennard (Wilson) and what he does.’”
What has transpired, as Nagy said, is some subpar showings from Dart that have some people understandably concerned. But Nagy said that Dart is calling every play correctly, and that it’s just a matter of “taking it to the next level,” which is to execute against a live defense that is throwing everything it has at him.
Dart and the offense will get their first crack at putting everything together against the Minnesota Vikings on Saturday, which brings in a Brian Flores-led defense that last year totally flummoxed Dart to the tune of a career-worst 33 passing yards on seven completions.
While this weekend’s clash won’t involve game-planning, the Vikings still pose a good challenge for the young quarterback to take what he’s learned in working against his own complex-looking defense and begin tying everything together.
In the meantime, Nagy is preaching patience with Dart, a tall order for a fan base that is expecting a lot more wins this year than what the team delivered in years past.
“When I say (have patience), we have an idea of what we want to do. I'm talking play-wise – big picture we know – play-wise, you start to build a little bit of a library of what our guys do well,” Nagy said.
“We're not going to give them stuff that we just want to do because we want to do it. If we do something, it's because they like it and they do a good job at it in any phase of the game. Putting all that together and cutting it loose, it's going to be here quickly.
“Whether it's walkthrough, group install, or competitive, we have a lot of stuff on tape right now that we're able to pull and look at and decide what we want to do.”

title: With Schmitz, Patrick Banged Up, Bryan Hudson Gets His Shot at Center for the Giants
full_text:
It’s never a good thing when a starter has to miss time due to an injury, but for the New York Giants , if you have depth you believe in, it does make the situation more tolerable.
Such is the case at the center position. Starter John Michael Schmitz has been sidelined with a head injury suffered last Friday at The Greenbrier.
While his injury is not believed to be one that will keep him out for the long term, his absence, along with the ongoing knee issues that veteran backup Lucas Patrick has been dealing with, has created some questions about the depth at center.
Second-year interior offensive lineman Bryan Hudson, the ACC Jacobs Blocking Trophy winner in 2023, is trying to calm any concerns.
Hudson, who can play any spot along the interior and long snap, entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent out of Louisville with the Detroit Lions in 2024.
With Schmitz sidelined and Patrick trying to work out the issues with his knee, Hudson has a golden opportunity to become a part of head coach John Harbaugh’s first Giants team.
The 6-foot-5, 305-pound Hudson, who saw preseason action at center and guard last year for the Giants, allowed three pressures in 62 pass-blocking snaps (99.2 pass-blocking efficiency rating).
In 24 run-blocking snaps, he posted an impressive 90.7 run-blocking grade , the best run-blocking grade on the team.
Also worth noting is that per Pro Football Focus, Hudson actually got better over one year. In 114 snaps during his rookie season with the Lions (all at center), he had an overall grade of 65.6.
Last summer, he finished with a 90.1 overall grade with the Giants after receiving snaps at all three interior positions. His overall grade was the best grade out of all the Giants offensive players.
With the Giants looking to be more of a power rushing offense, Hudson’s background fits in with that objective. Hudson is often quick off the snap and precise with his hand placement, which gives him an advantage in run blocking by enabling him to climb to the second level with minimal resistance.
He also has sufficient power in his game to do battle with some of the league’s more athletic defensive linemen, and has held his own against bigger guys like Giants nose tackle D.J. Reader.
What Hudson lacks at the moment is experience, though with Schmitz unlikely to play Saturday when the Giants host the Minnesota Vikings, that will change quickly enough.
Already Hudson, working in place of Schmitz, has drawn the attention of head coach John Harbaugh.
“I think he's done really well,” Harbaugh said. “You know, it's funny because we did feel like we needed to get him in there, even with the twos, and then now with the ones, and he's risen to the occasion so far.”

title: John Harbaugh's Fingerprints Are Already All Over Giants Training Camp
full_text:
John Harbaugh's immediate impact on the New York Giants can be seen at every practice, from the way drills are being done and the attention being paid to each detail to the players' fatigue at the end of the sessions.
Of course, the club won't face its first quiz until Saturday's preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings at MetLife Stadium. But make no mistake about it: There is a different feel to the team as it goes through the third week of training camp, and its preseason record will not alter its preparation or its mission.
"We have a chance to be a good football team," Harbaugh said this week. "We're doing a lot of good things right now. Okay. Where do we go? This week, we told the guys the focus is execution, for sure, but the focus this week is technique. From now until Saturday, our individual focus is on your technique. All the little things to make you successful.
"Even at the end of practice when you're dead tired, that's a fourth quarter, win the game type drill, and you're down by 14. Okay? That's focus on your technique. Because if your technique is good, you can win the battle of fatigue. And that's what we're working on. So, I think that set us up for that. Now go forward this week and do that same idea."
The team already has gone through six fully-padded practices - sometimes in high heat, humidity and even rain. And the players aren't getting as many in-session breaks as they have under previous coaches, but they apparently understand the blueprint.
"Man, these days do stack on you, but as I said, it’s camp; it’s supposed to be hard. It isn’t really supposed to be easy," linebacker Brian Burns said.
"These days do stack on you, but it isn’t doing nothing but making us stronger. So, I'm glad to go through that with these boys, and everybody's still working hard, even though they're sore, don't feel like it, unmotivated. But that's part of camp."
Giants studio analyst and Super Bowl XLII champion center Shaun O'Hara offers his thoughts on the differences in this summer's training camp and discusses the key factors that are expected to get the team on the right track during the training camp edition of the Big Blue Breakdown podcast.

title: Giants' Offense Working Toward Cohesiveness as Defense Sets the Pace in Camp
full_text:
The best way to summarize the New York Giants training camp so far is that it’s been a tale of two units.
The defense has been ahead of the offense almost from the get-go, which is to be expected, but the hope was that by now, the offense would at least start to catch up.
That hasn’t exactly been the case. But offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said there has to be a degree of patience exercised.
“There's going to be highs and lows through this process. We talk about it as a staff, like you can’t – we have to make sure that as we go through this journey, we never get too high and we never get too low.
Today was an average practice, maybe below average. It wasn't good enough. He knows that. We know that. We'll put it on tape, but we also talk about success through struggles – there's going to be some struggles as we go through this now in training camp and during the season, but how do we react? When you can get it on tape, evaluate, and try to show them what they're doing right and what they're doing wrong, it happens quicker.
Part of the problem has been quarterback Jaxson Dart’s struggles to adapt to the new offense, which has him working more under center. Dart has had some highs and lows as he works at his own pace, and Nagy said there has been forward progress.
“Every quarterback's a little bit different based on what you're doing in the offense,” Nagy said.
“I would say, if we're evaluating Jaxson, which we are, and you sit there and you look at – I just go back personally to OTAs, and when we were first teaching this thing, we spent phase two just kind of trying to teach this thing ground up in buckets and phases, and not necessarily plays.”
Meanwhile on the defensive side of the ball, coordinator Dennard Wilson has been generally pleased with how his unit is coming together, particularly against the run.
“We're connected up front right now. We're playing with good vertical knock-back. We're setting the edge,” he said.
“I think the defensive ends and outside linebackers have been outstanding in setting the edges, and we have some linebackers that fill gaps. They come downhill with a sense of urgency. They're big players. They're aggressive, and everybody's playing with their hat in their hands.
“The biggest thing is just their eyes. They know what they're looking at, and they're fitting accordingly. And if we have something that we mess up, we correct it, we make it right, and then we come out and execute again.”
Wilson is particularly excited about the variety of talent he has at his disposal.
“It's very exciting. We built a system here. Not just the coaches but the players as well. We put in a system that's in place that the system has a lot of complex things to it, but the system is easy for them,” Wilson said.
“It looks complicated to others, but it's easy for them because it's conceptual teaching. So, the joy of being able to get guys to move in different spots, they're running the same thing over and over. You don't know where it's coming from.”
“For me, it's just exciting to see these guys grow together, exciting for them trying to be detailed and disciplined every day and coming out here and flying around and flying to the ball as fast as they can.”
WR Jalin Hyatt (leg), WR Juju Smith-Schuster (knee), C John Michael Schmitz (concussion), OL Lucas Patrick (knee), and CB Paulson Adebo (unknown) were among those not spotted at practice. This was the second straight day Adebo didn’t practice in the team drills; he did do some light work in the individual session on Monday.
Over to the side with trainers were cornerback Greg Newsome II (knee) and Dru Phillips (knee), and receiver Malik Nabers (knee), the latter of whom worked with trainers for about 90 minutes.
The cornerback depth is becoming scary with Adebo, Phillips and Newsome dealing with injuries. While it’s still early enough in the week, it’s looking more and more that the starting cornerbacks in Saturday’s preseason opener against Minnesota will be Deonte Banks and rookie Colton Hood, with Ar’Darius Washington the likely candidate for the slot.
Banks has been having a strong summer, having built off a strong spring, and is a player we’re looking forward to seeing in live game action.
Continuing the participation report, inside linebacker Abdul Carter (hand/finger) and defensive lineman Chauncey Golston (head) returned to practice. Carter sat out Monday’s session while Golston left about midway through.
Rookie right guard Francis Mauigoa, who at one point during Monday’s practice had his neck checked by a trainer before returning to finish out the session, was kept out of team drills on Tuesday, replaced by Daniel Faalele.

title: Giants Reportedly to Host CB Terrion Arnold for a Visit
full_text:
The New York Giants are starting to get banged up across the board, but no position has been as hard hit as the cornerback spot.
The Giants, who currently have slot cornerback Dru Phillips (knee), Paulson Adebo (unknown), and Greg Newsome II (knee) sidelined, are reportedly planning to host former Detroit Lions cornerback Terrion Arnold on Wednesday for a visit, according to NFL insider Jordan Schultz.
Arnold has appeared in 24 regular-season games for the Lions with 22 starts. He has one career interception, 18 pass breakups, 91 tackles (70 solos) and one fumble recovery.
Arnold’s planned visit with Big Blue has triggered questions about the long-term injury statuses of Phillips, Adebo, and Newsome and how the length of their respective absences could affect the depth at the position.
The Giants could simply be doing due diligence just in case the injury bug further hits the position group.
New York is already looking at potentially having to roll with Deonte Banks and rookie Colton Hood on the perimeter and defensive back Ar’Darius Washington in the slot when they host the Minnesota Vikings for the preseason opener this weekend.
Adding a player of Arnold’s caliber would give the team’s defensive secondary depth a big boost.
Arnold, the Lions’ first-round pick (No. 24 overall), was released by Detroit in June after he was accused of off-field indiscretions
His attorneys released a statement that “there is no credible evidence” linking the cornerback to the allegations brought against him.
Since his release by the Lions, Arnold has drawn interest from around the league , including the Colts, Jets, Seahawks, and Texans. His legal case is still pending, but he is free to engage in discussions with teams about his next stop.

title: Giants Have a Glaring Weakness at Center — And an Old Friend Could Be the Fix
full_text:
The New York Giants have invested heavily in their offensive line this offseason, bringing right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor back on a three-year, $39 million deal and using the No. 10 pick in the 2026 NFL Draft on right guard Francis Mauigoa.
Still, the unit has one significant glaring weaknesses.
Center John Michael Schmitz Jr . is entering his fourth season as a starter. He has improved since his abysmal rookie season, but still gave the Giants average center play at best in 2025. Schmitz allowed 14 pressures and one sack, posting a mediocre overall PFF grade of 60.8.
Schmitz suffered a head injur y during a training camp practice on Friday and has since missed two practices. Meanwhile, his backup, Lucas Patrick, has been dealing with a knee issue, which has raised questions about whether he can be counted on for the season.
Bryan Hudson, who came to the Giants in 2024 after a stint on the Lions practice squad and with the Patriots, has been working with the first-team offense.
Hudson has drawn positive reviews from Harbaugh, who said, “I think he's done really well. You know, it's funny because we did feel like we needed to get him in there, even with the twos, and then now with the ones, and he's risen to the occasion so far.”
That all said, the position group, which also includes newly signed Brenden Jaimes, is still painfully thin and is one more injury away from catastrophe. The Giants need to consider bringing in another, more experienced option.
The Giants decided to move on from veteran offensive lineman Greg Van Roten this past offseason. Whether that was because they wanted to upgrade or Van Roten was looking for more than what the team was willing to pay isn’t known.
But given the situation at center, it might not be a bad idea to revisit a possible third season in Blue for the Long Island native.
Van Roten recently worked out for the New England Patriots, but as of this moment, no deal has been agreed to. That means that Van Roten is still interested in playing somewhere and is thought to still be in playing shape.
While it’s understandable that the Giants want to get younger and more toward a people-mover type of offensive line, the versatile Van Roten isn’t necessarily a bad option should Hudson and Jaimes not deliver in the upcoming preseason slate.
In 2025, Van Roten, playing at right guard, finished with a 97.7 pass-blocking efficiency rating . In 2024, he saw 138 snaps at center in place of Schmitz and gave up just two pressures, none of which were sacks.
Bringing in Van Roten wouldn’t just help reinforce the center spot, but he’d also help to reinforce both guard positions, where depth is also something of a concern.
In short, it makes too much sense not to explore a reunion with Van Roten given Schmitz’s history of missing multiple games every season he’s been in the NFL, and the current state of the offensive line’s interior depth.

title: 20 Biggest NFL Draft Busts of the Last 20 Years
full_text:
NFL teams down on their luck look to the draft each offseason as a tool to help turn things around.
Although any given April can deliver a franchise-altering player, the NFL draft has also churned out its fair share of disappointments over the years. Just because a player is selected with a high pick doesn't mean that they're guaranteed to turn into a star, and several teams have learned that the hard way and will continue to do so as long as the annual event is around.
With a new season around the corner, now is the perfect time to look back at some recent draft decisions that aged poorly. Here are the rankings for the 20 biggest NFL draft busts of the last two decades, starting with...
Honorable mentions: Johnny Manziel (2014), Justin Blackmon (2012), Derrick Harvey (2008), Isaiah Wilson (2020)
It isn't unusual for first-round picks to face pressure right away, and Treylon Burks was no exception. The Titans threw him into the spotlight when they shipped off AJ Brown in a deal that brought them the  No. 18 pick used on Burks in 2022.
Since then, Burks underwhelmed, posting 53 catches for 699 receiving yards and a touchdown in 27 games over three injury-plagued years with the Titans. They eventually waived him in October, which led to his signing with the Commanders—an uneventful stint that resulted in a 10-130-1 stat line in eight games.
Considering that Brown has posted four consecutive 1,000-yard seasons, made three second-team All-Pro appearances and won a Super Bowl since then, it's safe to say that the Titans likely want this decision back .
It's also interesting to see whether a first-round quarterback lives up to the hype or not. Much to Christian Ponder's dismay, he fell into the latter category after going to the Vikings in 2011.
The former Florida State gunslinger posted a forgettable 14-21-1 record with 38 touchdowns to 36 interceptions across 38 games over four seasons with Minnesota, finishing only one year (2012) with an above-.500 record. He never amounted to anything more than a low-end starter, which he couldn't even be after leaving the Vikings. Ponder experienced quick stops with the Raiders, Broncos and 49ers before fading into the background after the 2016 season.
After ripping a 4.22-second 40-yard dash in the lead-up to the 2017 NFL Draft, the Bengals had high hopes that John Ross could become a key cog in their offense. Throw in the fact that he was coming off a career-high 1,150 receiving yards with a Pac-12-leading 17 touchdown grabs, and there was every reason to believe in his outlook.
It's safe to say that Ross never came close to living up to the hype. He was injured more often than not, only suiting up for 38 games (21 starts) between 2017 and 2024. It doesn't help that he wasn't exactly productive whenever he was available, catching only 63 balls on 145 targets (43.4%) for 963 receiving yards and 11 TDs.
While the 2017 draft wasn't great for wideouts outside of a couple of names (Chris Godwin, Cooper Kupp, etc.), that doesn't change the fact that the Bengals' drafting Ross was a colossal miss.
Cornerbacks aren't often drafted in the top three, which is why the Lions shocked a lot of people with their selection of Jeff Okudah in 2020. The risk already looked clear at the time, and it turned out that everyone's concerns proved to be true. Injuries and inconsistent performances quickly made him a headache in Detroit, prompting a trade in April 2023 that sent him to the Falcons in exchange for a fifth-round draft pick.
Given that he was a top-three pick just a few years before that, it really illustrates just how much Okudah's value plummeted. That trend continued as he failed to find a permanent home, playing games with the Texans and Vikings after leaving the Falcons as a free agent in 2024. He's still yet to play a full NFL campaign and only has two career interceptions after notching three picks in his last year at Ohio State.
He's only 27 years old and might have some juice left in him; however, it's fair to say that Okudah won't ever live up to the draft hype.
The Giants needed to find a permanent right tackle solution in 2022, leading to the drafting of Evan Neal out of Alabama. The 6-foot-7, 340-pound blocker had the perfect size to help solve that issue, but injuries and a lack of reliability on the gridiron have him among the biggest busts of the last 20 years.
Of the potential 68 regular-season games that he could've played since joining the league, Neal has only appeared in 29 contests with the Giants—an availability rate of 42.6%. When healthy, he's surrendered 98 pressures across 1,078 opportunities , according to Pro Football Focus , and has yet to finish with a pass block grade better than 49.6.
After missing all of 2025 due to injury, Neal re-signed with the Giants on a veteran-minimum contract back in March. If that doesn't show why he's more than deserving of a bust label, it's hard to say what would. There's a decent chance that his "best" days are already behind him.
A strong three-year run at Maryland resulted in Darrius Heyward-Bey being selected seventh overall by the Raiders in 2009. He was the first wide receiver selected that offseason, only adding to the sky-high expectations that the former Terrapin would never live up to.
Outside of a 975-yard performance with the Raiders in 2011, Heyward-Bey's career was nothing to write home about. Sure, he ended up making 71 starts across 144 games, which is more than a lot of players can say, but a 202-2,897-16 receiving line is pretty disappointing when taking his draft slot into account. He slowly faded away after joining the Steelers in 2014, leaving his fans forever wondering what could've been.
The Browns have made a plethora of head-scratching draft choices over the years, and selecting Brandon Weeden in 2012 is among them. The ex-Oklahoma State quarterback became the oldest first-round pick when his name was called, raising concerns about how high his ceiling might be compared to younger options.
It didn't take long for Weeden to justify those concerns, leading the Browns to a 5-15 record while throwing for 5,116 yards, 23 TDs to 26 INTs and a 71.8 passer rating in two seasons. He was released after his second year in Cleveland, bounced around three more franchises and eventually called it quits some time after the 2018 season.
Making matters worse, Russell Wilson and Kirk Cousins were eventually drafted after Weeden, leaving Browns fans even more frustrated. It's safe to say that being the oldest first-rounder is likely all Weeden will be known for whenever someone looks back at his career.
A 12-sack performance at Penn State in 2008 played a huge role in the Bills using the 2009 draft's 11th overall selection on Aaron Maybin. The All-American talent seemed primed to make an immediate NFL impact, only for his career to go the way of everyone else on this list.
The Bills ended the Maybin experiment by waiving him in August 2011, evidently disappointed by the zero sacks he amassed in 27 games over two seasons. It looked like his career was back on track with a six-sack performance with the Jets in 2011, only to fall back to zero in eight appearances the following campaign. He was cut from the Bengals ahead of the 2013 season, which he spent in the Canadian Football League, before announcing his retirement less than a year later .
Much to no one's surprise, the Browns are back on this list. This time, it's due to their decision to select Justin Gilbert out of Oklahoma State with the No. 8 pick in 2014. It was a choice that produced next to no value for Cleveland, as Gilbert only registered one interception in 23 games (three starts) before the Browns traded him to the Steelers for a 2018 sixth-round pick... in 2016.
From a top-10 pick to being worth a Day 3 dart throw in just a few years, few players have seen such a fall from grace.
Instead of rehabilitating his image with the Steelers, Gilbert's struggles continued to the tune of one tackle…

title: One Jets CB's Preseason Could Change Following Qwan’tez Stiggers's Injury
full_text:
The New York Jets’ first joint practice with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Tuesday started somewhat as expected. Competing in the heat against players who aren’t on the same team, both sides got into a pair of fights in the drills.
But then, things quickly escalated into a scary scene when Jets’ cornerback Qwan’tez Stiggers collapsed on the field. New York’s medical staff swiftly attended to the former 2024 fifth-round selection and transported him to a local hospital.
While the Jets didn’t provide details on Stiggers’ condition , the team did announce that he was released from the hospital and back home Tuesday night.
Coach Glenn provides an update on CB Qwan'tez Stiggers pic.twitter.com/oQMFzfSA0p
With Stiggers sidelined for the foreseeable future, New York’s cornerback depth will have an opportunity to make their case for a roster spot with additional reps. One Jets corner whose preseason outlook could change following Stiggers’ injury is Samuel Womack III.
Entering training camp, Womack was widely viewed as a player on the roster bubble , with New York’s cornerback room already appearing to have an established group of six. With this, Womack faced an uphill battle to carve out a spot on the 53-man roster.
But with D’Angelo Ponds and Stiggers sidelined, Womack’s preseason outlook could change dramatically. Now, the five-year veteran will have a chance to see more defensive reps in preseason play rather than trying to shine in bits and pieces.
This gives Womack a chance to build upon his strong play from the first two weeks of camp, with Jets OnSI’s Nick Faria noting that Womack has played well so far.
The former 2022 fifth-round pick has seen limited opportunities on defense since entering the league, playing only 1,034 snaps over four seasons. He did, however, show some promise in 2024 with the Indianapolis Colts, where he carved out a consistent rotational role and received meaningful reps.
In 17 games (eight starts), Womack recorded 36 total tackles, nine pass deflections, and two interceptions. While Womack fared well against the run–recording four run stops, per Pro Football Focus –he stood out in coverage.
In 440 coverage snaps, Womack allowed just 27 receptions (44 targets) for 388 yards and four touchdowns, earning a 71.3 coverage grade, which ranked 30th among 117 qualifying cornerbacks, per PFF .
Womack’s solid play in camp is particularly notable considering he joined the Jets’ practice squad in December and appeared in only one game last season. Now, with Stiggers out, the Detroit native can turn his increased reps into a stronger case to make the roster.
While all the starters are expected to play Friday night, we shouldn’t anticipate them playing more than a drive or two, with their playing time likely to remain limited throughout the rest of the preseason. This gives Womack a legitimate chance of positioning himself for a roster spot.
But a solid showing on the defensive side alone won’t guarantee him a spot. Stiggers has been the Jets’ special teams ace, and for Womack to improve his chances, he must capitalize on additional reps on special teams.
Womack has experience on special teams from his first two years with the San Francisco 49ers, where he recorded six tackles and posted special teams grades of 75 and 68.9, respectively, per PFF .
Of course, Womack isn’t the only player looking to take advantage of Stiggers’ absence. Tre Brown is also competing for a roster spot and has played well in camp, giving the Jets another option to consider.
For Womack, the time is now to showcase that he can be a meaningful contributor. But even if he does impress, it doesn’t guarantee him a roster spot. However, a string of solid performances could make New York’s roster decision much more difficult.

title: 4 Winners & 4 Losers From Jets' Final Joint Practice: Geno Smith Bounces Back While Klubnik Makes Noise
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- If the New York Jets were upset with their performance from practice on Tuesday , Wednesday's showdown with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers showed early that the team was ready to move past it.
Despite coming out to a draw by my calculations, the Jets looked far better and more competitive today than on Tuesday. Their defense made several plays and the offense won plenty of times against Tampa's difficult defense.
As always, there were clear winners and losers from the day of work. Let's get to some of the biggest ones here:
After a dismal day on Tuesday, Jets starting quarterback Geno Smith responded with a positive performance on Wednesday. Smith threw multiple touchdown passes in seven-on-seven drills, including a good throw to Adonai Mitchell in the back of the end zone.
While much of team drills were done within five yards of the line of scrimmage, it showed the team had worked well to prepare for Tampa Bay's pressure scheme this time around. Smith didn't throw any terrible passes and was on time for most decisions.
It was a good day for him.
Of note, Cade Klubnik made several eye-popping throws as well. One was a 60-yard bomb to Arian Smith, who caught it in stride over the middle of the field. It was a perfectly placed ball. Klubnik dropped another dime to Jamaal Pritchett in the red zone but the pass went off the receiver's hand. New York should be pleased with how their quarterback room looked today.
Both offenses seemed to win plenty throughout Wednesday. But it was New York's secondary that looked worse. While several deep throws saw Jets players in the right coverage, the Buccaneers offense took what they wanted throughout the day.
Baker Mayfield, specifically, had an excellent practice by threading the needle on several throws. In a two-minute situation to end the practice, the Bucs easily went right down the field and scored a touchdown.
It wasn't a good sign for New York's defense.
New York's passing offense looked good on Wednesday, but their tight end room was what stood out the most. Mason Taylor made multiple touchdown grabs throughout practice and showed why the Jets believe in him as much as they do.
Then there was Jeremy Ruckert. In the same two-minute drill that the Buccaneers drove down the field, Ruckert made an unbelievable catch over a defender on his own to corral a Smith pass. Ruckert looked more like Rob Gronkowski on the play than the former third-round pick out of Ohio State.
Making matters even better for the room, Kenyon Sadiq was seen working out on a side field as he recovers from his "setback" from hernia surgery.
The first-round rookie out of Indiana has done nothing wrong to this point. He's flashed at times, and seems to be learning the offense at his own pace. The issue for him, right now, is the fact that Isaiah Williams keeps making "wow" plays that are going to force him on the field even more.
Context is always important when it comes to position battles. In the long run, Cooper will be extremely important to the Jets offense. But as he begins his NFL journey, it appears he'll need to show his coaches more as he moves forward into the preseason.
David Bailey recorded several sacks on the day including a dominant win against Luke Goedeke in which he used Will McDonald's classic spin move to great effect.
But as practice standouts go, Bailey wasn't one. McDonald, however, was.
The Jets know what they have in the Iowa State product when it comes to rushing the passer. As a run defender, though, the team has needed to see more. The good news is that they got that in droves on Wednesday. McDonald made several key stops against the run including one in between the tackles that showed his newfound size and strength.
The more McDonald plays like he did today, the more playing time he'll get on the field moving forward.
Let's clear the air here: Membou was not bad on Wednesday. He held his own against the rookie edge rusher Rueben Bain Jr. and was solid when opening up running lanes.
But Bain did win several times throughout the day, including one in one-on-one drills and a couple in team sessions. Bain was one of the best edge rushers in college football last season and has reportedly dominated camp for the Buccaneers. It shouldn't be surprising that he stood out like Bailey has for the Jets .
But if Membou is going to take a massive jump as many expect of him in 2026, he has to win these types of showdowns. I would classify the performance as a draw today from him, which ultimately means he took a small step back.
While Membou competed with the likes of Bain, Parham not only held his own during his own one-on-one matchups, but was dominant in team drills. Several of New York's biggest runs came on the left side with Parham leading the way.
He's been overlooked at times this camp simply because he came off a solid year on a bad Raiders team, but Parham has had a good camp—the kind of camp that should excite Jets fans into believing their offensive line is ready to take the next step.
While both Jason Sanders and Cade York continue to compete, it looks like there's an early favorite in the clubhouse. Sanders missed badly on several kicks throughout the day. While York did miss from 61 yards at the end of practice, he was more consistent throughout.
If York ends up winning the kicking position battle, it may open some concern for New York as he has struggled during games. The preseason will be the deciding factor.

title: Offensive Heartbeat: How Isaiah Williams Is Changing the Jets' Attack
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — To think, there once was a time when the Jets released Isaiah Williams for a costly mistake in September of last year.
After a mishandled punt in a loss to the Dolphins, Gang Green cut ties with the former Bengals wide receiver/returner, only to bring him back shortly after . Clearly, the team saw something in Williams that fans weren't willing to see.
Now the Jets do, though. And it's not just Williams' return game that has turned New York's fans around on him.
Throughout camp, last season's top return specialist , according to Pro Football Focus, has been a central cog in New York's passing offense. While he was once considered just a special teams ace, Williams has grown into a player who will be featured prominently in Gang Green's offensive philosophy.
More than that, though, he's become something no one would have expected.
When you ask most Jets fans about the heartbeat of the team, obvious names like Garrett Wilson, Breece Hall or even Armand Membou come to mind. They are all top players on the offense with high expectations .
But if you ask certain coaches on the roster, the answer isn't any of those stars.
"(Isaiah is) a dog," Jets WRs coach Shawn Jefferson said on Tuesday. "If I was in a burning building, boop boop boop boop (dialing a phone), 'I need you to come get me.' He's on the way. Just to put it bluntly like that. He's the heartbeat on our offense."
Jefferson saying this should not be ignored. It highlights the improvement Williams has shown all throughout camp and during the offseason. His production also continued in Tuesday's joint practice against the Buccaneers.
Despite struggles from the offense, Williams remained a consistent performer during practice. He made multiple catches within traffic and even laid out a pancake block on a Buccaneer defender on a running play. The very next step, Williams caught a pass and began talking smack to the opposition.
A high profile play from a performer who continues to stand out. And demand more playing time.
The Jets—including head coach Aaron Glenn—appear more willing than ever to oblige.
To think, at this time last year, Williams was a borderline rosterable player for Cincinnati. In September, he was kicked to the curb by the Jets.
But that's the beauty of the NFL. The strongest wills tend to win out.
And for Williams, his wins keep getting added this camp.
As Williams continues to prove his worth, it is no longer a question of whether or not he'll make the roster. Instead, the bigger question is how prominent a role he will have on the offense throughout the regular season.

title: What the Jets Need From David Bailey as Historic Training Camp Tear Continues
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — History teaches NFL fans that sometimes all an organization needs to turn around its luck is an edge rusher with a mean spirit and a lightning-quick first step.
Micah Parsons had it with the Cowboys. Reggie White had it in Philadelphia. Lawrence Taylor, as New York fans know, definitely used that with the Giants.
The Jets have seen plenty of all-time great pass rushers enter their halls. None have begun their career with as big a flash as second overall pick David Bailey has. The former Texas Tech product has dominated one-on-one reps against Gang Green's own offensive tackles and has looked the part of a transcendent player.
More importantly, he's brought an edge to the Jets that is frustrating his opponents and bringing respect to Florham Park.
If there was one constant throughout Tuesday's joint practice with the Buccaneers, it was that Bailey remained the best player on the field for the Jets. What made it even more important, though, was the fact that the majority of the reps won came against veteran offensive linemen on the Buccaneers.
In one-on-one drills, Buccaneers right tackle Luke Goedeke was beaten terribly multiple times, and he was even called for a false start twice. On his last rep, when he jumped early, he "won" the matchup against Bailey and then began to smack talk.
A brawl ensued that showed the Jets, playing alongside a fiery starter like Bailey, would not compete sitting down.
Fight!!! David Bailey starts a fight with a Bucs OLinemen. Looked like he threw a punch. #Jets
Beyond the brawl, Bailey dominated practice with his pass rushing ability, recording multiple sacks in team drills including one in which Bucaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield had to bail out of the pocket to throw an incomplete pass.
For the Jets, it was just more of the same that they have seen .
"We all know that (David is) a damn good pass rusher," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said. "You expect him to win a number of his battles when it comes to that. And then you also expect things to happen to where you have to coach him, and he's going to learn some things, too. So, it really goes both ways when you look at that."
As for his teammates, Bailey's arrival has even the oldest of leaders wondering just how high his ceiling could be.
"I've been around a ton of rookies. Some that were projected high, some projected low," Jets linebacker Demario Davis said. "He looks like a No. 2 pick. He looks like everything that's been advertised."
But for as strong as Bailey looked on Tuesday, there is a nagging issue that he will need to resolve. And it has nothing to do with his run defense.
Discipline is a characteristic that the Jets organization has struggled with over the years. New York has historically been one of the most penalized teams in the league over the last few seasons, and it is a reason for the team's long-term struggles.
For Bailey, the edge on which he plays is important: it's the reason why he has been so dominant . But that edge can also get him into trouble, as seen during several incidents in college with both Texas Tech and Stanford. Bailey's fight with Goedeke during practice is just the latest example of the team needing Bailey to sometimes control that aggression.
Even if it highlights some of the best traits the team appreciates.
"It's a lot of energy that's wasted doing that," Glenn said after the fight. "Guys just have to learn, and hopefully we can come out tomorrow and just not have that, and let's have a good practice and let's finish this thing up."
New York is obviously expecting more from its top edge rusher. The second overall pick has shown his potential and future fit on a team truly devoid of star talent. The Jets and Glenn don't just want stardom from Bailey.
They want him to be the kind of transcendent player few in this league became across history.
"David will tell you, he's not looking at where he's at right now; he's looking atwhere's he's going to be two years from now," Glenn said. "And he wants to get there right now. That's how competitive he is. But that's what we're working on: how do we get him to get to that next level, and it's going to take practice after practice after practice to be able to do that."
Through it all, the Jets remain high on Bailey. Thus far, he's rewarded the team in droves.
